Price WatchLatest catch · Nov 12, 2026 — Verda rises for the fourteenth time — eight GPUs up about 1%, and the L40S holds for the first time
VerdaAll GPUs — Eight of Verda's nine tracked GPUs rose about 1% on Nov 12, read on Verda's own GPU instances page — the L40S stayed at $2.00, the first card not to rise in this run
$13.86→$14.00
GB300 — read Nov 11, 2026Read Nov 12, 2026

Verda has risen for the fourteenth time since Oct 23 — with one change in the pattern. Read on Verda's own GPU instances page on Nov 12, 2026 against the figures read there on Nov 11, eight of the nine tracked GPUs rose about 1%: GB300 $13.86 → $14.00, B300 $12.05 → $12.17, B200 $9.23 → $9.32, H200 $6.50 → $6.57, H100 SXM $5.09 → $5.14, A100 80GB $2.34 → $2.36, A100 40GB $1.67 → $1.69 and RTX PRO 6000 $2.75 → $2.78 (unrounded page figures in our research file). The L40S held at $2.00 — the first Verda card not to rise on a rise day in this run. Verda's GB300, this board's Best offer for that card, has gone from $11.82 an hour at our Oct 19 check to $14.00 today, up 18.4%. That follows Nebius's rise on Oct 1 and RunPod Secure's on Oct 14, and Lambda's announced rises of about 15% take effect Nov 16. Rising prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading of the pattern, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can also play a part). Verda holds the board's Best offers on GB300 and A100 40GB, and both rose; every other Best offer held. Everywhere else we checked today — RunPod Secure, Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute, SaladCloud, TensorDock and Hyperstack (checked first-hand by the raw-page method, all 13 rows unchanged) — prices held. Spheron's own pages disagreed with each other again today (its llms.txt snapshot prices H100 at $3.96 while its pricing-page FAQ states $5.15 the same day), so no clean both-sides change exists there and nothing was applied. Lambda's currently-effective rates are behind a login, RunPod Community was corroborated only in part today, and nafnaf.ai showed no GPUs available — those figures are carried, not checked today. This is the newest of the 35 changes reported on Price Watch. Source: Verda's own GPU instances page (verda.com/gpu-instances), read Nov 11 and Nov 12, 2026.

Nov 12, 2026Industry · NVIDIAJensen Huang resigns as NVIDIA CEO — CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim chiefNVIDIA announced on Nov 12, 2026 that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer and Board member, effective immediately, ending 33 years leading the company he co-founded. Colette Kress, NVIDIA's Chief Financial Officer since 2013, serves as Interim CEO while keeping the CFO role; Harvey C. Jones becomes the company's first-ever Chair of the Board. NVIDIA's release gives no reason for the resignation.

Lead storyNov 12, 2026Industry · NVIDIAJensen Huang resigns as NVIDIA CEO — CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim chiefNVIDIA announced on Nov 12, 2026 that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer and Board member, effective immediately, ending 33 years leading the company he co-founded. Colette Kress, NVIDIA's Chief Financial Officer since 2013, serves as Interim CEO while keeping the CFO role; Harvey C. Jones becomes the company's first-ever Chair of the Board. NVIDIA's release gives no reason for the resignation.

The tracked neocloud also raised 2026 capex to about $27bn and gave its first 2027 outlook — revenue of $12–13bn on capex of $40–45bn.

It runs out of the box on a single H100.

Nov 11, 2026Hardware · AMDAMD's 256-core EPYC ‘Venice’ is shipping — the host CPU built to feed GPU racksAMD announced general availability of its 6th Gen EPYC server processors (‘Venice’, Zen 6, SP7) on Nov 10, 2026: systems are shipping from the leading server makers now, Meta is the named lead customer, and cloud instances follow at Microsoft Azure (HDv2 in preview) and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (Compute E7). The flagship EPYC 9996 carries 256 cores and 512 threads at a $14,904 list price.

Nov 10, 2026Results · CoreWeaveCoreWeave Q3: revenue up 168% to $3.66 billion, a $132.5 billion backlog — and guidance raised againCoreWeave reported third-quarter 2026 results after the close on Nov 10, 2026: revenue of $3.661 billion, up 168% on a year earlier and more than $1 billion added in a single quarter, a revenue backlog of about $132.5 billion, and full-year guidance raised on every line. The cost of building that fast is in the same release: a $709 million net loss, with $846 million of net interest expense in the quarter alone.

Nov 10, 2026Open weights · MiniMaxMiniMax open-sources H3-Image: a 16-megapixel image model that serves on one GPUMiniMax published the weights of H3-Image on Nov 10, 2026: a 33.1-billion-parameter image generation and editing model that produces roughly 16-megapixel images — up to 4096×4096 — directly, with no upscaler, in six sampling steps, and serves from a single GPU through vLLM-Omni or SGLang. It is released under MiniMax's own community licence, not a permissive one, and the full download is bigger than the headline checkpoint suggests.
Act on this story:Compare GPU prices →All news →
Nov 10, 2026AI labs · AnthropicAnthropic sets IPO terms at up to $1 trillion — and NVIDIA, Google, AMD and TSMC are buying $26 billion of itAnthropic launched its IPO roadshow on Nov 10, 2026 and filed Amendment No. 2 to its Form S-1 with the SEC the same day: 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78, listing on Nasdaq as ANT, raising up to about $64.4 billion and valuing the company at about $1.02 trillion on shares outstanding. Alongside the offering, seven technology companies — the GPU supply chain itself — have agreed to buy $26 billion of Anthropic stock in a private placement at the IPO price.
Act on this story:Compare GPU prices →All news →
Nov 10, 2026Prices · VerdaVerda raises prices for the twelfth time — the same four GPUs up about 1% againRead on Verda's own GPU instances page today, Nov 10, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 9: the same four GPUs that rose yesterday rose again by about 1% — GB300, B300, H100 SXM and L40S. It is Verda's twelfth rise since Oct 23. The other five tracked GPUs held for a second straight day.
Act on this story:Verda in Price Watch — every change we catch →Compare GPU prices →
Nov 9, 2026Infrastructure · Deutsche TelekomDeutsche Telekom expands its sold-out Munich AI factory with Blackwell Ultra B300sDeutsche Telekom announced on Nov 9, 2026 that it will expand its Industrial AI Cloud — the “AI factory” at Munich’s Tucherpark — with additional NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra (B300) systems, after the first expansion phase sold out in seven months. The B300s join the site’s existing Blackwell B200 systems and double the number of chips in that class, taking the factory’s capacity to 20 megawatts. Telekom puts the new investment at nearly another quarter of a billion euros.
Act on this story:Compare GPU prices →All news →
Nov 9, 2026Open weights · MeituanLongCat-2.5 weights are out: Meituan's 1.6-trillion-parameter model is on Hugging Face under MITThe weights for Meituan's LongCat-2.5 are downloadable: the official Hugging Face repository (meituan-longcat/LongCat-2.5) holds 3,562 GB of files under an MIT licence for the 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, with about 48 billion parameters active per token. The model launched API-only on Nov 2, 2026 with weights marked “coming soon”; the repository was created on Nov 4 and its model card was updated again today, Nov 9. The catch for GPU renters: the card's only documented deployment route is on NPUs, not GPUs.

Nov 9, 2026Infrastructure · EdgevanaEdgevana signs $700 million-plus in Blackwell agreements — B300 and GB300 systems across two continentsEdgevana, the data-centre, energy and compute orchestration company, announced on Nov 9, 2026 that it has signed more than $700 million in fully committed, multi-year take-or-pay agreements to deploy NVIDIA Blackwell systems — B300 GPUs and GB300 systems — across North America and Europe. Every figure in the announcement is Edgevana's own, stated in its release; no customer, GPU count or contract length was disclosed.

Nov 9, 2026Hardware · GoogleGoogle adds TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max — four TPU systems in a single yearGoogle expanded its eighth-generation TPU portfolio on Nov 9, 2026 with two new systems built from its existing silicon: TPU 8tx, for confidential inference, pairing the TPU 8t chip with 5th Gen AMD EPYC hosts so data and weights stay encrypted while in use; and TPU 8i Max, which packages two TPU 8i chips together for double the compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth in the same rack footprint. Google published no price and no availability date.

Nov 9, 2026NVIDIA · Sovereign AINVIDIA AI Day Seoul opens: Rebellions' next NPU joins NVLink Fusion for SK Telecom's sovereign racksAt AI Day Seoul, which opened on Nov 9, 2026 at COEX in Seoul, NVIDIA, Rebellions and SK Telecom announced a collaboration to build sovereign AI racks in which NVIDIA GPUs handle prefill and Rebellions' next-generation Rebel R200 NPUs handle decode — connected through NVIDIA's NVLink Fusion and built on its MGX rack architecture. The R200 systems are expected to be ready for deployment in 2028.

The campus was announced in 2025 with Blackstone-backed Tallgrass as a 1.8 gigawatt project designed to scale to 10 gigawatts. Google had first approached the site as a customer; it now owns it instead. The purchase price was not disclosed.

It is not a new base model — it is a behaviour layer trained onto one, on about 52.8 million tokens, and at 27B parameters it fits on a single rented GPU.

Lambda's currently-effective rates are behind a login, RunPod Community was corroborated only in part today, and nafnaf.ai showed no GPUs available — those figures are carried, not checked today.

How Price Watch reports

Figures are read from the provider’s own published pages or live offers — never from another aggregator. A figure stated on a provider’s pages is reported as stated, attributed to that provider; it becomes a verified board price only through our full pricing check — see How we price.

All three kinds of change are reported the same way: price rises, price cuts, and disagreements — where a provider’s own pages state different prices for the same card, the disagreement itself is the change, and it is reported as caught rather than smoothed over.

For providers

The listing standard

  • Prices publicly checkable — your rates live on your own public pages, where anyone can read them.
  • Independently verified by us — we read your published pages ourselves; you never send us numbers to print.
  • Freshness maintained — fixed rates are re-verified daily; marketplace rates are stamped to the hour.
  • Listing never buys rank — Best offer goes to the lowest price, and no payment changes any order on this site.

What we check, and how often

Every price on the board is read from the provider's own published pricing pages or live offers — never from another aggregator. Fixed-rate providers are re-checked daily; marketplaces that move by the hour are labelled as live and stamped to the hour. When a provider publishes no price at all, we show no price rather than an estimate.

How to apply

Send us the public page where your prices live and the name you list under. If your prices are publicly checkable, we verify them against the standard above and you appear on the board under your own name, at full weight, beside everyone else. If they are not publicly checkable yet, that is the one thing to fix first.

/how-we-price.html:
How we price

Our sources

Providers' own published pricing pages and live offers only. No other aggregator is ever a source — if we cannot read it on the provider's own site, it does not appear here.

The cadence

Marketplaces refresh hourly and are stamped to the hour. Fixed-rate providers are re-verified daily. Every price on this site carries its checked date; no timestamp, no price.

What “verified” means

A price is verified when we have checked it against the provider's own published source. Verified and merely listed are never blurred: a GPU a provider lists without a published price appears as listed, quote-only, with no price shown. Anything we cannot verify is left out, never guessed.

The Best offer rule

Exactly one per GPU variant: the single lowest verified on-demand price, whoever offers it. Spot prices compete only for a separate Best spot price tag. The tag is arithmetic — it moves when prices move, and no one can pay to hold it.

The independence rule

GPUJournal sells nothing and rents nothing. No paid placement, no sponsored rows, no promoted listings. If referral terms are ever used, they will be disclosed — and they will never affect order.

Every change, reported

Catching and reporting every change is our business. When a check finds a price has moved, the board carries the new figure with its new date, and the change itself is reported on Price Watch — the old figure, the new figure, both observation dates and the source named. A change we cannot evidence on both sides is not reported as one.

Corrections

When we get something wrong, the correction is published here, not silently edited.

GPU Pricing · 2026-10-29 · 8 min

Six rises in seven days: what Verda's October says about GPU demand

One provider raised its GPU prices on Oct 23, Oct 24, Oct 26, Oct 27, Oct 28 and again on Oct 29 — six rises in seven days, across almost its whole range, each one small and each one in the same direction. We know the dates and the figures because we check and bank these prices every day. Here is the full record, what else moved in October, and the half of the market that still has not.

Model Deployment · 2026-10-29 · 10 min

Thinking of deploying Mistral Large 4? Here’s how — and what it actually costs

Mistral’s Large 4 — “Le Chonk” — landed on Hugging Face on Oct 29, 2026: about a trillion parameters, free to download, and far too big for any single graphics card. This page does the deployment maths in the open: how much memory each version needs, the smallest rental setups that honestly hold it, what those setups cost per hour, per day and per month — and the point where renting GPUs beats paying per token, and where it doesn’t.

GPU Pricing · 2026-10-30 · 7 min

Batch is the new spot: what RunPod’s 20% batch discount does to the maths for work that can wait

On Oct 28, 2026, RunPod made Serverless Batch Inference generally available: send requests in bulk, let them run when RunPod’s batch workers get to them, and pay 20% less than the on-demand rate on H100, H200, B200 and B300. This page does the maths on that trade — what the discount is worth in dollars, and what you give up for it.

Model Deployment · 2026-10-30 · 12 min

Thinking of deploying Kimi K3.1 Pro? Here’s how — and what it actually costs

The weights are out. Moonshot published Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face on Nov 4, 2026 — 96 safetensors shards summing to 1,561,293,160,568 bytes (about 1.56TB) in native MXFP4 — under its own Kimi K3.1-Pro License, with vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed named on the model card as the serving engines. This guide, first published Oct 30, 2026 as pre-release maths, was refreshed on Nov 6, 2026 with the real file sizes, the real licence and the official recipes: the smallest honest setup is one 8-GPU B300 node, the cheapest node-shaped setup on the current board is 16× H200 at $57.44/hr — and Moonshot’s own API, at $2.00 in / $10.00 out per 1M tokens, still beats self-hosting on price at ordinary volumes.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-05 · 11 min

MI355X vs B300: inference cost per token, priced from the board

Spheron's comparison of these two 288GB cards, published Nov 3, 2026, prices its verdicts from modelled rates — including MI355X rates no provider actually sells at. This page re-runs the same question from prices read on the providers' own pages and checked on Nov 5, 2026: TensorWave's published $2.95/GPU/hr MI355X rate and Oracle's $8.60 list price, against a B300 board that starts at $7.40/GPU/hr. The silicon is tied — same 288GB of HBM3e, same 8 TB/s of bandwidth on both makers' spec sheets. The rental market is not tied at all, and in this comparison the entry tickets matter more than the chips.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-08 · 12 min

Power is the new GPU shortage: why powered land decides your rental price

GPU rental prices have been rising for six weeks, and the usual explanation — not enough chips — no longer fits. The chips exist. What is scarce is somewhere powered to plug them in: an energised building, on a grid connection, under a signed power contract. This page walks through the verified rises, shows why they point at power rather than silicon, and tells you what to ask before you rent capacity that has not been switched on yet.

Provider Comparisons · 2026-11-12 · 13 min

H100 or B200 sold out? What to rent instead — priced

A stock alert tells you the card you wanted is gone. It does not tell you what to rent instead, or what the substitute costs. This page does: every substitute below is a real offer on our verified price board, checked Nov 12, 2026 — the card, the provider, the rate, and the terms that change the bill. One honesty note before the table: we are not reporting any provider as sold out today — our checks found prices, not stock levels. This guide is for the moment you go to book an H100 SXM or a B200 and find it gone.

Guides that cover it

GPU Selection · 2026-10-18 · 11 min

Best Single GPU for AI Inference in 2026: One Card, Decided Properly

Most inference guides assume an 8-GPU node. Most readers have one card and one job. Here is the single-card decision — by VRAM headroom and cost per finished request, using prices checked Oct 18, 2026.

GPU Selection · 2026-10-30 · 14 min

Best GPU for AI inference in 2026 — priced from a checked board

Most “best GPU for inference” pages price their verdicts from a rate card the seller itself publishes — prices stated on the seller’s own pages, with no check date a reader can test. This page works the other way round. Every price below was read on the provider’s own published page and checked on Oct 30, 2026, and every cost per token is built from a throughput assumption printed next to it, so the maths can be rerun with your own numbers. The result is not the ranking the spec sheets suggest: on a mid-size model, the cheapest tokens in our checks come off a $0.34-an-hour gaming card, and the fastest card on the board finishes mid-table.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-02 · 14 min

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: self-host it or pay for the API?

NVIDIA’s open transcription model — 40 languages, speaker labels, translation, released Oct 28, 2026 — can be rented two ways: by the minute from a hosted API, or by the hour on a GPU you run yourself. The hosted price is public and tiny. The self-host price depends on one number nobody has independently measured yet — how fast the downloadable stack really runs — so this guide costs both routes honestly: the API at its published rate, self-hosting at a clearly printed planning assumption, and NVIDIA’s own published best case shown for what it is.

GPU Selection · 2026-11-04 · 13 min

Best GPU for video generation in 2026

A video model doesn’t bill you by the token. It bills you by the second of card time — so the right question is never “which GPU is fastest?” but “which is the smallest card that runs this model well, and what does one finished clip cost on it?” This guide answers that for the six open-weight video models people actually rent cards for in 2026 — Wan 2.2 in both sizes, HunyuanVideo-1.5, LTX-2, CogVideoX-1.5 and Mochi 1 — with verified prices checked Nov 4, 2026, and a cost per 5-second clip wherever the maker publishes a generation time. Where a maker publishes none, we price the model by the hour and say so, rather than invent a number.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-08 · 12 min

Power is the new GPU shortage: why powered land decides your rental price

GPU rental prices have been rising for six weeks, and the usual explanation — not enough chips — no longer fits. The chips exist. What is scarce is somewhere powered to plug them in: an energised building, on a grid connection, under a signed power contract. This page walks through the verified rises, shows why they point at power rather than silicon, and tells you what to ask before you rent capacity that has not been switched on yet.

Provider Comparisons · 2026-11-12 · 13 min

H100 or B200 sold out? What to rent instead — priced

A stock alert tells you the card you wanted is gone. It does not tell you what to rent instead, or what the substitute costs. This page does: every substitute below is a real offer on our verified price board, checked Nov 12, 2026 — the card, the provider, the rate, and the terms that change the bill. One honesty note before the table: we are not reporting any provider as sold out today — our checks found prices, not stock levels. This guide is for the moment you go to book an H100 SXM or a B200 and find it gone.

Six rises in seven days: what Verda's October says about GPU demand

One provider raised its GPU prices on Oct 23, Oct 24, Oct 26, Oct 27, Oct 28 and again on Oct 29 — six rises in seven days, across almost its whole range, each one small and each one in the same direction. We know the dates and the figures because we check and bank these prices every day. Here is the full record, what else moved in October, and the half of the market that still has not.

Model Deployment · 2026-10-30 · 12 min

Thinking of deploying Kimi K3.1 Pro? Here’s how — and what it actually costs

The weights are out. Moonshot published Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face on Nov 4, 2026 — 96 safetensors shards summing to 1,561,293,160,568 bytes (about 1.56TB) in native MXFP4 — under its own Kimi K3.1-Pro License, with vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed named on the model card as the serving engines. This guide, first published Oct 30, 2026 as pre-release maths, was refreshed on Nov 6, 2026 with the real file sizes, the real licence and the official recipes: the smallest honest setup is one 8-GPU B300 node, the cheapest node-shaped setup on the current board is 16× H200 at $57.44/hr — and Moonshot’s own API, at $2.00 in / $10.00 out per 1M tokens, still beats self-hosting on price at ordinary volumes.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-08 · 12 min

Power is the new GPU shortage: why powered land decides your rental price

GPU rental prices have been rising for six weeks, and the usual explanation — not enough chips — no longer fits. The chips exist. What is scarce is somewhere powered to plug them in: an energised building, on a grid connection, under a signed power contract. This page walks through the verified rises, shows why they point at power rather than silicon, and tells you what to ask before you rent capacity that has not been switched on yet.

H100 or B200 sold out? What to rent instead — priced

A stock alert tells you the card you wanted is gone. It does not tell you what to rent instead, or what the substitute costs. Worth knowing

Z.ai's agentic coding flagship, released Dec 22, 2025. Its size was long carried here as unverified because Z.ai's own card never prints it; the checkpoint itself settles it — 358.3B total parameters by the weights' own safetensors count (92 layers, 160 routed experts with top-8 routing plus one shared expert, per its config), about 32B active per token, a 200K context (config maximum 202,752) and an MIT licence. Public and ungated on Hugging Face, in BF16 with an FP8 build alongside.

What it needs

Full precision (FP16)
717 GB
the weights, uncompressed
8-bit
358 GB
the weights, compressed to 8-bit
4-bit
179 GB
the weights, compressed to 4-bit

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. Real figures move with context length and software.

Worth knowing

An audio (speech) model, built for real-time use.

What it needs

Full precision (FP16)
8 GB
the weights, uncompressed
8-bit
4 GB
the weights, compressed to 8-bit
4-bit
2 GB
the weights, compressed to 4-bit

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. Real figures move with context length and software.

What it needs

Full precision (FP16)
2 GB
the weights, uncompressed
8-bit
1 GB

4-bit
1 GB
the weights, compressed to 4-bit

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. Real figures move with context length and software.

GPU rental prices are rising in 2026 — the dated evidence

If you rent GPUs at a provider's own list rates, you are probably paying more than you did a few weeks ago. This page shows the rises we have verified on providers' own pages — each one dated — and the half of the market that has not moved yet.

GPU Pricing · 2026-10-30 · 7 min

Batch is the new spot: what RunPod’s 20% batch discount does to the maths for work that can wait

On Oct 28, 2026, RunPod made Serverless Batch Inference generally available: send requests in bulk, let them run when RunPod’s batch workers get to them, and pay 20% less than the on-demand rate on H100, H200, B200 and B300. This page does the maths on that trade — what the discount is worth in dollars, and what you give up for it.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-08 · 12 min

Power is the new GPU shortage: why powered land decides your rental price

GPU rental prices have been rising for six weeks, and the usual explanation — not enough chips — no longer fits. The chips exist. What is scarce is somewhere powered to plug them in: an energised building, on a grid connection, under a signed power contract. This page walks through the verified rises, shows why they point at power rather than silicon, and tells you what to ask before you rent capacity that has not been switched on yet.

Best Single GPU for AI Inference in 2026: One Card, Decided Properly

Most inference guides assume an 8-GPU node. Most readers have one card and one job. Here is the single-card decision — by VRAM headroom and cost per finished request, using prices checked Oct 18, 2026.

The verdict

  • L40S — 7B–32B models, image generation, best all-rounder under $1/hr · $0.79/hr at RunPod Community
  • RTX PRO 6000 — 70B quantized on ONE card — the sleeper pick · $1.69/hr at RunPod Community
  • H100 — High-throughput serving, FP8, when requests per second pay the rent · $4.50/hr at Nebius
  • RTX 4090 — Tight budgets, 7B–14B models, dev and prototyping · $0.34/hr at RunPod Community

The deciding metric: cost per finished request, not $/hr

A GPU's hourly price tells you what the meter charges. It does not tell you what a request costs. Divide the hourly rate by the requests the card actually completes per hour at your batch size and context length, and the ranking flips: a $2.64/hr H100 pushing 3× the throughput of a $0.96/hr L40S is the cheaper card per request — until your traffic drops and the H100 sits idle at full price. Rule of thumb: if the card will be busy more than ~60% of the hour, buy throughput (H100 class). If it will idle between bursts, buy the cheapest card that fits the model with KV-cache headroom (L40S / RTX PRO 6000 class). Fit first, throughput second, headline price last.

Worked math: serving a 32B model for one day (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

Job: serve Qwen-class 32B, ~40 requests/min average, 24 hours. On an L40S (48GB, FP16 weights ≈ 65GB — too big; run AWQ INT4 ≈ 20GB, comfortable with KV cache): 24h × $0.96 = $23.04/day. On an H100 (FP16 fits with room to batch harder): 24h × $2.64 = $63.36/day. The H100 finishes each request faster, but at a steady 40 req/min the L40S is not saturated — you would pay $40.32/day extra for latency you may not need. Flip it: at 200 req/min the L40S queues, p95 latency blows up, and the H100's $63.36 buys the headroom that keeps the service usable. Same models, same day — the right card is decided by your request rate, not the spec sheet. Rerun this division with the current Price Board before you budget.

Steps

1. Size the weights first

Parameters × bytes per parameter: FP16 = 2 bytes, INT8 = 1, INT4 ≈ 0.5. A 32B model is ~65GB at FP16, ~20GB at INT4. If weights alone exceed the card, no flag will save you.

2. Reserve KV cache honestly

Budget at least 25–40% of VRAM on top of weights for KV cache at your real context length. A card that 'fits' the weights and OOMs at request #50 does not fit.

3. Match the card to your duty cycle

Busy >60% of the hour → throughput card (H100). Bursty or dev traffic → cheapest card that fits (L40S, RTX PRO 6000, 4090).

4. Cost the finished job

Hours the job actually runs × the dated $/hr from the Price Board. Include spin-up and idle-while-you-debug time — everyone forgets those, and they are real hours on the meter.

5. Rent for one hour and measure

Run your real prompts, record tokens/sec and p95 latency, then commit. One measured hour beats ten benchmark blog posts — including this one.

Alternatives

Two smaller cards instead of one big one

Two L40S (96GB total) can beat one H100 on price for embarrassingly parallel work — batch image generation, offline evals. For single-request latency, one fast card still wins.

An API instead of a rental

Below ~2 busy hours a day, a per-token API is usually cheaper than any rental once idle time is counted. The crossover is arithmetic, not ideology — do the division for your traffic.

Deploy Qwen 32B on a Single GPU with vLLM: The One-Card Runbook

A 32B model, one 48GB card, no cluster. VRAM math first, then the exact vLLM launch — flags explained, KV cache sized, cost per hour from the Oct 18, 2026 Price Board.

The verdict

  • Card — Smallest card that runs 32B AWQ comfortably with KV headroom
  • Weights — FP16 (≈65GB) does not fit a 48GB card — quantization is the decision
  • Context — KV cache budget ~18GB at 32k with the flags below
  • Job cost — A full working day of serving / evals

The deciding metric: VRAM after KV cache, not VRAM on the box

The spec sheet says 48GB. The model takes ~20GB in AWQ INT4. What remains — about 26GB after CUDA context and activations — is your KV cache, and KV cache is what decides how many conversations the card holds at once and how long each can run. At 32k context, one sequence's KV for a 32B-class model runs to several GB; plan for a handful of concurrent long sequences, not hundreds. If your workload is many short chats, you are fine. If it is a few very long documents, context — not the model — is your wall. Size for the workload you have, in that order: weights, KV at your context, concurrency.

RTX 4090 24GB24GB1,008 GB/sNot on the boardAWQ weights fit (~20GB) but KV headroom is ~2GB. Demo-grade only.
L40S 48GB48GB864 GB/sNot on the boardThe target card for this runbook. Balanced fit + headroom.
RTX PRO 6000 96GB96GB1,792 GB/sNot on the boardRun FP16 instead, or double concurrency. The headroom is the point.
H100 80GB80GB3,350 GB/sNot on the boardOverkill for one 32B — unless throughput per request pays.

Worked math: what a day of 32B actually costs (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

L40S on-demand at $0.96/hr: a focused 8-hour build-and-eval day = $7.68. A 24-hour always-on deployment = $23.04/day, $691.20 per 30-day month. Stepping up in VRAM from here means a bigger card class. Neither number includes storage or egress; on most providers those are small next to GPU hours, but check before a month-long commitment. Prices move — the Price Board carries the current checked date; rerun this math there.

Steps

1. Provision the card

Rent an L40S (48GB) with at least 100GB disk — model weights, cache and logs add up faster than you expect. Pick the region nearest your users; latency is geography.

2. Install vLLM

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate, then pip install vllm. Pin the version in your notes; 'latest' is a moving target when you return in a month.

3. Download the AWQ weights

Fetch the AWQ INT4 build of the 32B model from its official repo. Verify the size on disk (~20GB class) before launching — a partial download presents as a CUDA error later.

4. Launch with the flags that matter

vllm serve <model> --quantization awq --max-model-len 32768 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --enable-prefix-caching. gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 leaves breathing room; max-model-len is your KV budget made explicit — set it to the context you sized for, not the model's maximum.

5. Validate like a skeptic

Send one short prompt, one 20k-token prompt, and ten concurrent prompts. Watch VRAM and logs. The long + concurrent test is where undersized deployments confess.

6. Cost-guard the box

Set a calendar reminder or an auto-stop. The most expensive GPU is the one you forgot was running over a weekend: 60 idle hours on an L40S = $57.60 for nothing.

Alternatives

SGLang instead of vLLM

Comparable throughput, strong prefix-cache story. If your workload is many shared-prefix prompts (agents, few-shot templates), benchmark both for one hour each and keep the winner.

Step up to 70B on the RTX PRO 6000

Same runbook shape, INT4 weights ≈ 40GB, 96GB card. If 32B quality is your ceiling, the card — not the procedure — is the upgrade.

The True Cost of Renting a GPU: What the $/hr Isn't Telling You

$/hr is the beginning of the bill, not the bill. Spin-up, idle time, storage, egress and the spot-interruption tax — totalled honestly, with dated prices from Oct 18, 2026.

The verdict

  • Headline lie — $/hr ignores spin-up, idle, storage and egress — typically +15–40% on real jobs
  • H200 spot — Spot saves $1.48/hr vs on-demand — if interruptions don't eat the saving
  • Forgotten weekend — 60 idle hours nobody meant to buy
  • Rule — Budget the finished job, then add 25% the first time you run it

The deciding metric: cost per finished job

Nobody's goal is 'rent a GPU'. The goal is a trained adapter, a served model, a finished eval. So cost that. Finished-job cost = (spin-up + working + idle + teardown hours) × $/hr + storage + egress + the expected cost of interruptions. The $/hr ranking and the finished-job ranking regularly disagree: the cheapest hourly card that runs 30% longer and gets interrupted twice can cost more than the 'expensive' card that finished last night. Every worked example below uses one dated rate set — Oct 18, 2026 — so the arithmetic stays checkable. When rates move, the method doesn't.

GPUVRAMBandwidthLowest verified priceVerdict
Spin-up & setup——Not on the boardImage pulls, weight downloads, env fixes. Billed at full $/hr on most providers.
Idle time——Not on the boardThe silent budget-killer. Debugging locally while the box runs is paying rent to watch you think.
Storage——Not on the boardCheckpoints multiply. A 70B full checkpoint habit can outgrow the GPU bill on long runs.
Egress——Not on the boardDownloading a 140GB model repeatedly is a line item, not a rounding error.
Spot interruptions——Not on the boardPrice the restart: lost progress since last checkpoint + spin-up again, times how often it happens.

Worked math: spot vs on-demand on an H200 (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

On-demand H200: $4.80/hr. Spot H200: $3.32/hr — a $1.48/hr saving, 31% off. Take a 20-hour fine-tune with checkpoints every 2 hours. On-demand total: 20 × $4.80 = $96.00, done. Spot, uninterrupted: 20 × $3.32 = $66.40. Spot with two interruptions, each losing on average 1 hour of progress and 15 minutes of restart: effective hours ≈ 22.5 × $3.32 = $74.70 — still ahead by $21.30. Spot with six interruptions: ≈ 27.5 × $3.32 = $91.30, and your deadline is now fiction. Break-even sits around 7 interruptions for this job shape. Spot is a bet with knowable odds: checkpoint often, count your interruptions, and the math — not the discount — decides.

Steps

1. Write the job, not the rental

Define done: artifact produced, metric reached, service live. Estimate working hours from a one-hour pilot run, not from hope.

2. Add the invisible hours

Spin-up (measure it once), teardown, and an idle allowance: +10% if you're disciplined, +30% if you're honest.

3. Price interruptions for spot

Expected restarts × (average progress lost + spin-up) × spot rate. Compare against the on-demand total, not the on-demand hourly.

4. Cap storage before it caps you

Decide checkpoint retention before the run: keep last 2 + best 1 is a sane default. Delete on a schedule, not on a panic.

5. Set the kill switch first

Auto-stop, budget alert, calendar reminder — pick one before you start the meter. Every experienced renter has exactly one forgotten-weekend story.

Alternatives

Reserved / committed capacity

For steady, month-scale serving, committed rates can undercut on-demand by a wide margin — at the cost of flexibility. Worth it only when the workload is proven, not predicted.

Buy the card

Above roughly 55–65% sustained utilisation over the card's useful life, ownership starts to win on pure math — before power, cooling, and your time enter the ledger. Run your own numbers; the crossover is lower than most renters assume and higher than most buyers admit.

H100 vs L40S vs RTX PRO 6000: Three Answers to Three Different Questions

These three cards get compared because they overlap on price charts. They shouldn't be: bandwidth king, balanced workhorse, VRAM-per-dollar outlier — compared on the jobs each actually wins.

The verdict

  • H100 — Wins: sustained high-throughput serving, FP8, training speed · $4.50/hr at Nebius
  • L40S — Wins: balanced inference + image work under $1/hr · $0.79/hr at RunPod Community
  • RTX PRO 6000 — Wins: biggest model on one card in this line-up · $1.69/hr at RunPod Community
  • Gap — PRO 6000 gives 20% more VRAM than H100 for 45% less per hour

On-demandListed as HGX — no variant splitChecked Nov 12, 2026Launch ↗
RunPod CommunityL40S · 48GB Best offer$0.79 / GPU / hr
On-demandChecked Nov 12, 2026Launch ↗
RunPod CommunityRTX PRO 6000 · 96GB Best offer$1.69 / GPU / hr
On-demandChecked Nov 12, 2026Launch ↗

The deciding metric: what is actually scarce in your workload

Every workload is starved for exactly one thing. Throughput-bound serving is starved for memory bandwidth — the H100's 3,350 GB/s is 3.9× the L40S, and tokens/sec follows bandwidth at decode time. Capacity-bound work — a 70B model that must fit — is starved for VRAM, and there the RTX PRO 6000's 96GB beats the H100's 80GB outright — capacity and bandwidth are different currencies. Budget-bound mixed work is starved for dollars, and the L40S's sub-$1 rate with datacenter drivers wins by simply being rentable all month. Name your scarcity first. The 'best GPU' question dissolves the moment you do.

GPUVRAMBandwidthLowest verified priceVerdict
H10080GB3,350 GB/s$4.50/hr — NebiusFP8 tensor cores, NVLink pedigree. The throughput answer.
L40S48GB864 GB/s$0.79/hr — RunPod CommunityAda generation, strong image/inference mix. The budget answer.
RTX PRO 600096GB1,792 GB/s$1.69/hr — RunPod CommunityBlackwell workstation card in server clothing. The capacity answer.

Worked math: a 30-day always-on deployment (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

720 hours a month. L40S: 720 × $0.96 = $691.20. H100: 720 × $2.64 = $1,900.80. Read those as capabilities, not just costs: the $1,209.60 gap between them buys 3.9× decode bandwidth. The RTX PRO 6000 carries no monthly figure here — its rental rates are not on the board yet. If your service never saturates the L40S, the H100's extra $1,209.60 buys nothing measurable. If your model doesn't fit the L40S, its cheapness is irrelevant. Cost per month is the last step of the decision, never the first.

Steps

1. Name the scarcity

Bandwidth (tokens/sec), capacity (model must fit), or budget (hours per month). Write it down; it picks the winner in step 4.

2. Check the hard fit gate

Weights + KV at your context must fit with ≥20% headroom. Any card failing this is out, regardless of price.

3. Check the precision gate

Need FP8 for your serving plan? H100 and PRO 6000 (Blackwell/Ada-class paths differ) — verify your stack's support on the exact card before renting a month of it.

4. Let the scarcity decide

Bandwidth → H100. Capacity → PRO 6000. Budget with a fitting model → L40S. Ties are broken by the Price Board's current dated rates.

Alternatives

A100 80GB

Squeezed between all three: more VRAM than L40S, cheaper than H100, no FP8. The right answer more often than its age suggests — especially where H100 stock is thin.

Wait for B200 economics

At $9.80/hr the B200 is a different league — multi-card training and frontier serving. If your job fits this comparison, it doesn't need a B200 yet.

Fine-Tune a 70B Model on One GPU: The QLoRA Budget, Honestly Totalled

70B fine-tuning used to mean a node. With QLoRA it means one card, one Saturday, and a bill you can compute before you start — costed here on verified H200 spot rates. Here is the memory math and the money math.

The verdict

  • Card — 70B QLoRA fits easily: ~40GB base (4-bit) + adapters + activations, with room to spare
  • Run — 10k examples, 3 epochs, seq 2k on H200-class bandwidth — a Saturday, not a weekend
  • Trap — Full fine-tuning a 70B needs ~1TB+ of optimizer state. QLoRA is not optional here
  • On-demand — Same card, no interruption risk — the deadline-safe version of the same run

The deciding metric: memory that isn't the model

In fine-tuning, the weights are the small part. A full fine-tune stores gradients and two Adam optimizer states per parameter — roughly 16 bytes per parameter in mixed precision, so a 70B model wants ~1.1TB before activations. That is why 'it fits for inference' tells you nothing about training. QLoRA changes the equation: the base model stays frozen in 4-bit (~40GB for 70B), and only small LoRA adapters train, with optimizer state sized to the adapters, not the base. Memory collapses to something a single modern card holds with room for activations at seq 2048. The trade is real — adapters can't teach what full fine-tuning can — but for style, format, domain tone and task behaviour, it is the pragmatic default at this scale.

GPUVRAMBandwidthLowest verified priceVerdict
RTX PRO 6000 96GB96GB1,792 GB/sNot on the boardFits 70B QLoRA with activation headroom, and its 96GB is the value case — once its rates are on the board.
H100 80GB80GB3,350 GB/sNot on the boardTight: fits with gradient checkpointing + modest seq len. Faster per step.
H200 141GB141GB4,800 GB/sNot on the boardComfortable everything. You are buying your weekend back.
L40S 48GB48GB864 GB/sNot on the board70B QLoRA does not fit honestly. This is the 32B card — see the sibling guide.

Worked math: the weekend run, totalled (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

Plan: 10,000 examples, 3 epochs, sequence 2048, QLoRA r=64 on a 70B base. Pilot first: time 100 steps, extrapolate. Our planning figure: ~8 GPU-hours on an H200. On spot at $3.32/hr (checked Oct 18, 2026): 8 × $3.32 = $26.56. Add the honest extras from our pricing guide: ~1 hour of setup + a failed first attempt (everyone has one) ≈ +2 hours = $33.20 all-in. On-demand at $4.80/hr the same run is $38.40 before extras — you would pay ~$12 more to delete interruption risk on a run that checkpoints every 500 steps. Usually money for nothing; now you have the numbers to decide.

Steps

1. Pilot before you commit

Run 100 steps on the real card with your real data. Measure seconds/step and peak VRAM. Extrapolate the full run from measurements, never from vibes.

2. Set the memory levers

Gradient checkpointing on, per-device batch 1–2 with gradient accumulation to reach your effective batch, paged optimizer if your stack offers it. Each lever trades speed for fit — in that order.

3. Checkpoint like spot is coming

Save adapters every ~500 steps. Adapters are small (hundreds of MB) — there is no storage excuse for losing a run.

4. Validate the adapter, not the loss

Loss going down is necessary, not sufficient. Hold out 200 examples, eval before/after, read 20 raw outputs yourself. Twenty honest reads beat one benchmark number.

5. Merge and archive deliberately

Merge adapters into a copy of the base, keep the unmerged pair too, and write down the exact base revision. Future-you is a stranger; leave them notes.

Alternatives

Fine-tune the 32B instead

Half the memory, a third of the step time, fits the L40S at $0.96/hr (full weekend ≈ $13.44). For many task behaviours the 32B adapter is within noise of the 70B. Pilot both if budget allows one comparison.

Rent the H200 for the final run only

Develop and debug on the cheap card, then run the final long job on the fast one. Debugging at $4.80/hr is the most common way these budgets die.

vLLM in Production: The Six Flags That Actually Matter

vLLM exposes dozens of flags. Six of them decide whether your deployment is fast, stable, or an outage with good throughput graphs. Each one, explained with its failure mode.

The verdict

  • --gpu-memory-utilization — Above 0.95 invites OOM under fragmentation; below 0.85 wastes KV
  • --max-model-len — Default = model max context = KV budget blown on day one
  • --enable-prefix-caching — Shared prefixes (system prompts, few-shot) stop being recomputed
  • --max-num-seqs — Default 256 sequences is a latency trap for large models

The deciding metric: p95 latency at your real concurrency

Throughput graphs are how vLLM deployments look great in screenshots and bad in production. What users feel is p95 latency — the slow tail — and the tail is made by the scheduler juggling too many sequences with too little KV cache. Every flag below is really a lever on one trade: concurrency vs tail latency vs memory safety. Tune against p95 at the concurrency you actually serve, measured with your prompts — a benchmark at concurrency 1 tells you about a service nobody uses.

GPUVRAMBandwidthLowest verified priceVerdict
gpu-memory-utilization0.90 default-ish—Not on the boardSets the total VRAM budget incl. KV. 0.92 is a sane production start.
max-model-lenYou choose—Not on the boardCaps per-sequence KV. The single most-skipped setting in failed deploys.
enable-prefix-cachingflag—Not on the boardHuge for agents/RAG with shared prefixes; neutral otherwise. Almost free — turn it on and measure.
max-num-seqs32–128 typical—Not on the boardCaps concurrent sequences. Lower = better tail latency, lower peak throughput.
chunked prefillflag—Not on the boardStops one long prompt from stalling every decode in flight. Long-context workloads need it.
quantizationawq / fp8—Not on the boardHalves-to-quarters weight memory; the freed VRAM becomes KV cache = concurrency.

Worked math: what a flag is worth in dollars (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

Prefix caching on an agent workload with a 4k-token shared system prompt: if 60% of prompt tokens were being recomputed per request, enabling the cache can cut prefill work — and time-to-first-token — dramatically, which at fixed traffic means the same L40S at $0.96/hr serves the load that was about to push you to an H100 at $2.64/hr. Monthly difference at 24/7: $691.20 vs $1,900.80. One flag, $1,209.60/month of avoided upgrade — or exactly nothing, if your prompts share no prefix. Flags don't have values; flags in workloads do. Measure yours.

Steps

1. Start from a known-good minimal launch

Model, quantization, max-model-len set to your real context, gpu-memory-utilization 0.92. Nothing else. This is your baseline — write down its p95.

2. Change one flag at a time

Prefix caching on → measure. max-num-seqs halved → measure. Each change gets the same 10-minute load test with your prompts.

3. Load-test at real concurrency

Ramp to your production concurrency and hold it. Watch p95, KV utilisation, and preemption warnings in the logs — preemptions are the scheduler telling you the truth.

4. Write the final command into the runbook

The exact command, the measured numbers, and the date. Production configs that live in shell history die with the instance.

Alternatives

SGLang's RadixAttention

If prefix reuse dominates your workload, SGLang's radix-tree cache is a genuinely different design, not a flag. Benchmark both on your traffic shape.

TensorRT-LLM for the last 15%

Compiled, fussier, sometimes meaningfully faster on NVIDIA serving. Worth it at sustained scale; not worth it while your flags are still at defaults.

Run Voxtral 3 Yourself: What It Takes

Voxtral 3 is Mistral's new speech stack — transcription, text-to-speech and a voice-agent SDK, launched Oct 20, 2026. Before you rent a GPU for it, read this: the weights are not openly downloadable, and this guide says so plainly, then costs the routes that actually exist today.

The verdict

  • The download — There isn't one — yet. Checked Oct 21, 2026 against Mistral's own announcement and Hugging Face: the announcement links no weights and no weight licence, and no Voxtral 3 checkpoint exists on Hugging Face. Today Voxtral 3 is an API, plus self-deployment arranged through Mistral — not a download.
  • Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3 — Transcription in 50+ languages with diarization — API batch at $0.0035/min (Mistral-reported)
  • Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 — The accuracy pick — API at $0.0040/min (Mistral-reported); 4.0% word error rate on Mistral's own FLEURS test across 45 languages
  • Voxtral Speech 3 — Text-to-speech in 35+ languages — API at $13 per 1M characters (Mistral-reported)
  • The open alternative — The earlier Voxtral models ARE downloadable under Apache 2.0 — Voxtral Small (24B) and Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime are in the model catalogue and can be self-hosted today, on the cards in the table below

Prices for the cards in this guide

On-demandChecked Nov 12, 2026Launch ↗

The deciding question: who holds the weights?

Every deployment guide on this site starts with the same move — download the weights, size the card. Voxtral 3 breaks that move, and pretending otherwise would send you renting a GPU for a file that does not exist. Verified Oct 21, 2026: Mistral's announcement (mistral.ai/news/voxtral-3) offers Voxtral 3 through its EU-hosted API and Studio playground, and offers self-deployment on request — contact Mistral. It publishes no weights link and no licence for download. Hugging Face, checked the same day, holds no Voxtral 3 checkpoint under mistralai; the latest Voxtral checkpoints there are the February 2026 Mini 4B Realtime line, under Apache 2.0. So the honest decision tree is: use Mistral's API today; talk to Mistral if your audio legally cannot leave your infrastructure; or self-host the earlier, genuinely open Voxtral models now — and re-check this page, because the day Voxtral 3 weights are published, this guide's self-host section gets written for real.

Worked math: the API bill vs a rented card for the open Voxtral (API figures Mistral-reported; card prices checked Oct 19, 2026)

Transcription first. On Mistral's API, 10,000 minutes of batch audio on Mini Transcribe 3 costs 10,000 × $0.0035 = $35.00. The same minutes in realtime cost $80.00, and Small Transcribe 3 costs $40.00. Text-to-speech: 1M characters on Speech 3 costs $13.00. There is no idle meter on any of that — you pay per finished minute. The self-host comparison only exists for the open models: the cheapest verified card that runs the open Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime is the RTX 4090 at $0.20/hr (nafnaf.ai, checked Oct 19, 2026) — $35 buys 175 hours of that card. Whether the card beats the API depends on how many audio-minutes it transcribes per rented hour on YOUR audio, which is a one-hour pilot measurement, not a number anyone should invent for you. And for Voxtral 3 itself there is no card comparison to make: no weights, no rental — anyone who quotes you a self-host price for Voxtral 3 today is quoting fiction.

Steps

1. Verify the weights before you plan anything

Go to the source: Mistral's announcement and the mistralai organisation on Hugging Face. If no Voxtral 3 checkpoint with a licence is listed there, there is nothing to self-host — whatever a blog post or aggregator claims. We re-checked on Oct 21, 2026: nothing.

2. Start on the API — it is the product that exists

Create a Mistral API key, pick the model for the job (Mini Transcribe 3 for batch volume, Small Transcribe 3 for accuracy, the realtime model for live agents, Speech 3 for spoken replies), and run your real audio through it. Diarization and context biasing — feeding the model your names and jargon — are built in; test both on your hardest recordings, not the demo files.

3. Cost it per finished minute

Your API bill is minutes × the per-minute rate, plus characters × the TTS rate. Work your real monthly minutes through the worked math above before comparing anything else — at low and medium volumes the API usually ends the conversation.

4. If audio cannot leave your building, you have two real routes

Route one: Mistral's own self-deployment — arranged with Mistral, for their EU-hosted or your-infrastructure setups. Route two: self-host the earlier open Voxtral (Apache 2.0) on your own rented card, using the table in this guide. What you cannot do is download Voxtral 3 and run it yourself — that route does not exist today.

5. Self-host the open Voxtral like any model here

Download Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime or Voxtral Small from Hugging Face (Apache 2.0), size the card with this site's arithmetic — weights plus about 20% headroom — and serve it with vLLM, the stack Mistral's own model cards target. The model pages for both models rank every card that runs them.

6. Re-check before you commit a budget

Weight releases land without asking this page's permission. Before any build that assumes Voxtral 3 is API-only, re-run step 1 — and if the weights have appeared, with a licence you can read, the self-host maths for a 4B model is small-card maths: about 8GB of weights at full precision, about 2GB at 4-bit, before headroom.

Alternatives

Whisper, self-hosted

OpenAI's Whisper large-v3 is downloadable and self-hostable today on the same small cards. On Mistral's own published FLEURS figures it trails badly — 14.9% word error rate against Small Transcribe 3's 4.0% (Mistral-reported; test on your own audio). It wins on one axis only, but it is a real one: you hold the weights.

Wait for the weights

Mistral's earlier Voxtral launches were open from day one, which is why this one's closed start surprised the field. If your project can wait, the cheapest research you will ever do is checking Hugging Face again in a few weeks — this guide will be updated the day the position changes.

/guide/minimax-m31-flash-self-host.html:
MODEL DEPLOYMENT →  ·  2026-10-23 · 9 min read

Self-host MiniMax M3.1 Flash: The Real Multi-GPU Maths

For teams eyeing the weights that landed on Hugging Face on 23 October 2026 and asking a simple question: can we run this ourselves, and what would it actually take? MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a 428B mixture-of-experts model (~23B active per token) that handles text, images and video, with a context window of up to 1 million tokens. It is big, it is capable, and it does not fit on one card. This guide shows the memory maths plainly, the smallest node that honestly works, and what that node costs today.

The verdict

  • Can one card run it? — No. No single GPU can run it alone — the 4-bit weights alone are 214GB, about 257GB with headroom, and a B200 holds 192GB.
  • Smallest honest FP8 node — 4 x B200 = 768GB. Enough for the FP8 weights with headroom, plus real room for the context cache.
  • Cheapest honest route — RunPod Community — $23.92 per hour for the 4 x B200 node ($5.98 per GPU per hour). Price checked 23 Oct 2026.
  • Read this before you rent anything — A 3 x B200 node (576GB) looks cheaper and clears the headline number on paper. It leaves only about 60GB across the whole node for the context cache. That is too tight to recommend, so this guide does not recommend it.
  • The alternative — Use the API: $0.15 in / $0.60 out per 1M tokens, cached input $0.015. No servers to run.

The maths, plainly

Memory starts with one simple sum: parameters x bytes per parameter. M3.1 Flash has 428 billion parameters in total, and the format decides how many bytes each one takes. FP8 — the format the weights arrived in — needs about 428GB for the weights alone, about 514GB with headroom: the headline case. Squeezed further to 4-bit, the weights are about 214GB, about 257GB with headroom — smaller, with a quality trade-off to test. At full BF16 precision the weights are about 856GB, about 1,027GB with headroom, shown so the FP8 saving is clear. The headroom is our house rule: a model needs more than its weights in memory — the serving software, temporary working space and room to breathe — so we add about 20% on top of the weights before any node is called honest. A node that only just fits the weights is not a node that serves people well. And why does 'only ~23B active' not shrink the memory? This is a mixture-of-experts model: for each token, only about 23 billion of its 428 billion parameters do the work, which is what makes it fast for its size — but all 428 billion parameters still have to live in memory, ready to be called. Active parameters save compute. They do not save memory. One more warning, and it matters: every figure above is before the KV cache — the memory that holds the conversation as it grows. A full 1M-token cache for a model of this class can run to hundreds of GB and can rival the weights themselves; the exact size is not yet verified. In practice, deployments cap the serving context well below 1M. If you truly need the full 1M context, step up a node size — do not squeeze it onto the smallest node.

Nodes that honestly fit — FP8, the headline case

Needs about 514GB plus cache room. Smallest honest node: 4 x B200 = 768GB. Every price below comes from GPUJournal's daily price check dated 23 October 2026, except Hyperstack, which is carried from 22 October 2026 and labelled as such. Update — Oct 30, 2026: the official serving recipes are out

When this guide was published on Oct 23, 2026, the confirmed serving picture was vLLM, SGLang and Docker Model Runner at release. A week on, MiniMax’s official recipes have landed, AMD has published its own enablement, and the released checkpoint can be measured instead of estimated. The update, checked Oct 30, 2026:

RouteShapeWhat it is
vLLM — official recipeTensor parallelism 4 on Blackwell; TP8 on H100/H200MiniMax’s own serving recipe, linked from the model’s Hugging Face card
SGLang — official recipeRecipe linked from the Hugging Face cardThe second first-party serving route
TokenSpeed — official recipeRecipe linked from the Hugging Face cardThe third official recipe route
AMD — vLLM4× MI350XAMD’s enablement article (Oct 23, 2026), with AMD’s own measurements
AMD — ATOM4× MI355XAMD’s second serving route, from the same article
AMD — QuarkMXFP4 exportAMD’s quantisation export for the checkpoint

Two more facts from the same update. The released checkpoint is mixed low-precision — including NVFP4 experts — and the repository totals about 252 GB including the DSpark draft head. Set that real 252 GB against the roughly 214 GB the 4-bit arithmetic at the top of this guide promises: plan from the file, not the formula. And Together AI now offers a serverless endpoint for the model — the hosted route for teams that want the model without renting the node. One community report describes the model serving on 4× DGX Spark; that report is community-reported, not independently verified. None of this changes the guide’s verdicts: M3.1 Flash is still a multi-GPU model, and 4× B200 remains the smallest honest FP8 node.

Self-host, or use the API?

Self-hosting gives you control. The API gives you none of the work. The API costs $0.15 input / $0.60 output per 1M tokens, with cached input at $0.015 — prices as reported by MiniMax. You pay only for tokens you use, and there are no servers to rent or maintain; it is best for casual or bursty use. Self-hosting FP8 starts at $23.92/hr for the cheapest honest node (23 Oct 2026) — and that hourly cost runs whether you serve one token or a million. You get full control over the deployment, but you run, monitor and fix the node, and it only wins at sustained, high volume. What we will not invent: a break-even number. There is no verified throughput figure — no trustworthy tokens-per-second measurement for this model on these cards yet — and without one, any break-even claim would be a guess dressed up as maths. The honest position: break-even against the API must be measured on the node you actually rent. Rent for a day, measure your real workload, then decide. Casual or bursty use: the API wins by a wide margin.

Steps

1. Rent an honest node

Start with 4 x B200 for FP8, or 2 x B200 for the 4-bit path. Do not start smaller to save money — a node that cannot hold the model serves nobody.

2. Download the FP8 weights as released

Fetch the weights from Hugging Face (released 23 October 2026). Use the FP8 format as the headline case; treat 4-bit as a further squeeze to test, not the default.

3. Serve it with a confirmed engine

vLLM, SGLang, or Docker Model Runner — the engines confirmed at release. Spread the model across all cards on the node; no single card holds it.

4. Set a sensible context cap

Start well below 1M tokens, watch cache memory under real load, and only raise the cap when the numbers say there is room.

5. Measure before you commit

Record your real throughput and cost per million tokens on your own workload — that measurement, not a headline, tells you whether self-hosting beats the API for you.

The licence, in plain words

Licence: MiniMax Community License. Commercial use is allowed — but which rule applies depends on your revenue. Revenue under $20M: you may use it commercially; you must send a notification email to MiniMax, and show a visible 'Built with MiniMax M3.1-Flash' credit. Revenue over $20M: you need written authorisation from MiniMax first, before you deploy. Military use is prohibited — in all cases. This is a plain-words summary for planning, not legal advice. Read the full licence text before a commercial launch.

What we verified — and what we did not

Verified

  • 428B total / ~23B active, 1M context, text + image + video — from MiniMax's own launch posts and the Hugging Face card
  • FP8 weights released on Hugging Face, 23 Oct 2026
  • Serving engines: vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner
  • Official vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed recipes, AMD enablement (vLLM on 4× MI350X, ATOM on 4× MI355X, Quark MXFP4 export), the ~252 GB mixed low-precision checkpoint and Together AI’s serverless endpoint — checked Oct 30, 2026
  • Node prices from the daily check, 23 Oct 2026
  • Licence terms, disclosed 23 Oct 2026

Still unverified

  • Exact KV-cache size at full 1M context — it can run to hundreds of GB; the exact figure needs the released configuration read directly
  • Throughput (tokens/sec) — no verified figure exists yet, so no break-even number is claimed
  • Hyperstack prices are carried from 22 Oct 2026, not re-read on 23 Oct 2026

One note on the numbers: a secondary source cites 456B total / 45.9B active parameters. This guide uses the primary-source figures — 428B / ~23B — from MiniMax itself.

The bottom line

M3.1 Flash is a multi-GPU model, full stop. The smallest honest home for it is 4 x B200 at $23.92/hr (23 Oct 2026), the comfortable home is bigger, and for most teams the API at $0.15 / $0.60 per 1M tokens is the sensible place to start — until your own measured volume proves otherwise.

GPU rental prices are rising in 2026 — the dated evidence

If you rent GPUs at a provider's own list rates, you are probably paying more than you did a few weeks ago. This page shows the rises we have verified on providers' own pages — each one dated — and the half of the market that has not moved yet.

The verdict

  • Nebius — Raised rates across the board. H100 SXM now $4.50/hr.
  • RunPod Secure — Raised Secure Cloud rates. H200 $4.59 → $5.29/hr (▲ 15%); RTX 4090 $0.74 → $0.89/hr (▲ 20%).
  • Verda — Three rises in four days — all nine rose on Oct 23 and Oct 26; seven of nine rose again on Oct 24. H100 SXM $4.34 → $4.61/hr (▲ 6.2%).
  • The cheapest offers — No movement in our records. The best verified H100 offer is still $2.25/hr.

The evidence, date by date

Every rise below was read on the provider's own published pricing page on both sides of the change — the before figure and the after figure, each with its date. That is the standard our Price Watch applies to every entry. October 1 — Nebius raises across the board: Nebius lifted its on-demand rates at the start of October, and our board carries the post-rise rates (H100 $4.50/hr, H200 $5.40/hr, B200 $8.50/hr, verified Oct 19 and re-read unchanged Oct 26). October 14 — RunPod Secure goes up: RTX 4090 rose from $0.74 to $0.89/hr (▲ 20%) and H200 from $4.59 to $5.29/hr (▲ 15%) on RunPod's Secure Cloud; both rates were re-read on RunPod's own page on Oct 24 and Oct 26 — unchanged since the rise. October 23, 24 and 26 — Verda rises three times in four days: all nine Verda GPUs rose on Oct 23 and again on Oct 26, and seven of the nine rose on Oct 24 as well (A100 40GB and L40S held that day) — the full table is below. We are not the only ones seeing it: a third-party analysis published Oct 21, 2026 found H100 prices up at six of seven specialist GPU clouds during 2026. Our own records cover October in daily detail; the direction agrees.

Steps

1. Do not renew or expand at a list rate without checking the market first

A rate you agreed in September may no longer be the rate that provider's competitors charge — or even the cheapest way to buy the same GPU today.

2. Expect list rates to keep drifting up while demand grows

Three rises in four days at one provider, on top of Nebius and RunPod, is what a market short of GPUs looks like. That is our reading of the pattern — the dated rises above are the evidence; judge it yourself.

3. If you need capacity for months, price the reservation now

When on-demand rates rise repeatedly, locking a rate earlier tends to beat locking it later. Work out the real total — GPU hours plus storage and downloads — before you commit.

4. Watch the floor, not just the headlines

The day the cheapest offers start rising too, the whole market has moved. Our Price Watch reports every verified change, dated on both sides.

How we know

GPUJournal reads providers' own published pricing pages and banks the figures at every check. The checks behind this page fell on Oct 19, 22, 23, 24 and 26, 2026 — there are gaps between them, so the October rises are documented check by check rather than day by day. A price change we catch in our own checks is only reported when both the before and after figures were seen on the provider's own page, each with its date; that is how the Verda and RunPod rises above were verified. The Nebius rise of Oct 1, 2026 is different: it predates our records and was an announced rise, so we did not bank both sides of it ourselves — we verified the post-rise rates on Nebius's own page (checked Oct 19, re-read unchanged Oct 26) and report it as announced. And a price a provider merely states about itself never appears on our board as a verified price. Where a provider's pages state figures we cannot verify, Price Watch reports them labelled as stated — which is how disagreements get exposed rather than hidden: on Oct 26, Spheron's pages stated the same H100 at $2.64 on some pages and $2.98 on others, and we report the disagreement rather than pick a number.

Six rises in seven days: what Verda's October says about GPU demand

One provider raised its GPU prices on Oct 23, Oct 24, Oct 26, Oct 27, Oct 28 and again on Oct 29 — six rises in seven days, across almost its whole range, each one small and each one in the same direction. We know the dates and the figures because we check and bank these prices every day. Here is the full record, what else moved in October, and the half of the market that still has not.

The verdict

  • Verda rises — Six rises in seven days — Oct 23, 24, 26, 27, 28 and 29, across almost the whole range.
  • Biggest single card — GB300 — GB300 rose $11.82 → $12.93/hr (▲ 9.4%).
  • The workhorse — H100 SXM — H100 SXM rose $4.34 → $4.75/hr (▲ 9.4%).
  • Range-wide — Every GPU in Verda's range is up 4.6%–9.4% in seven days.
  • The cheapest offers — Mostly flat. The best verified H100 offer is still $2.25/hr; the floor has not moved.

The six rises, rise by rise

Each rise was read on Verda's own pricing page on the day it happened, against the figure banked from the previous check. Rise 1, Oct 23: all 9 GPUs up. Rise 2, Oct 24: 7 of 9 up. Rise 3, Oct 26: all 9 up. Rise 4, Oct 27: 8 of 9 up. Rise 5, Oct 28: all 9 up. Rise 6, Oct 29: 8 of 9 up. No single rise was dramatic — most were around 1% — which is exactly why the pattern is easy to miss unless prices are recorded daily. Seven days of it, in full:

The only pauses in the run: A100 40GB held on Oct 24, Oct 27 and Oct 29, and L40S held on Oct 24. What that costs in practice, on a 730-hour month (24/7 usage): one H100 rented around the clock at Verda's rate went from $4.34 to $4.75/hr in seven days — +$0.41/hr, about $299 more per month for the same card. A GB300 went from $11.82 to $12.93 — +$1.11/hr, about $810 more per month, on the same 730-hour basis. Small daily rises compound fast at 24/7 usage. And Verda was not alone in October: Nebius raised across the board on Oct 1 — an announced rise, with the post-rise rates (H100 $4.50/hr, H200 $5.40/hr, B200 $8.50/hr, B300 $9.50/hr) verified Oct 19 and re-read unchanged on Oct 26, 27 and 28 — and RunPod Secure rose on Oct 14 (RTX 4090 $0.74 → $0.89/hr, ▲ 20%; H200 $4.59 → $5.29/hr, ▲ 15%; both re-read unchanged on Oct 24, 26, 27 and 28). Three providers, three different corners of the market — a large European cloud (Nebius), a major US platform (RunPod), and a Finnish specialist (Verda) raising six times in seven days. October's rises were not one company's pricing decision.

The counterweight: the floor still has not moved

Against all of that, the cheapest verified offer for almost every GPU is exactly where it was when our records began — because the providers holding those offers did not move:

Two honest exceptions, both in the table. The 4090's best offer rose on Oct 28 — not because RunPod Community raised its price (it did not; $0.34 throughout) but because the cheaper listing underneath it moved up: nafnaf's 4090, $0.20/hr since our records began, was re-read at $0.432/hr on Oct 28. And the GB300's best offer is Verda's price, because Verda is the only provider whose GB300 rate we list — so its rises are the best offer's rises. Everywhere else, the gap between the floor and the rising list prices widened all month: on Oct 29 an H100's best verified offer ($2.25) sat at less than half of Verda's new rate ($4.75) and half of Nebius's ($4.50). Rising list prices have still not pulled the floor up — but Oct 28 showed the floor is held by individual listings, and individual listings can move.

Context, and our reading

Context — the buyers' side (Oct 28 earnings): the two biggest GPU buyers reported on Oct 28. Microsoft's capital spending was $45.2 billion in the quarter and Alphabet's was $51.4 billion — about $96.6 billion combined — with both guiding toward further GPU-led acceleration, and Microsoft's CFO noting that third-party GPU capacity deliveries were delayed. Those are the buyers' own reported figures, offered as context for the seller-side record above — not proof of anything by themselves. Our reading — interpretation, not fact: providers do not raise on-demand prices six times in seven days, across a whole range, into weak demand. The dated rises — Nebius across the board on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, Verda six times between Oct 23 and Oct 29, and the market's cheapest 4090 listing giving up its price on Oct 28 — read to us as a market where demand for GPU hours is running ahead of supply, and sellers know it. The Oct 28 earnings context points the same way: the biggest buyers are spending at record pace and still waiting on capacity. That is an interpretation of the evidence on this page, not a measured fact: we record prices, not order books. If the rises stop, or the floor starts falling, the reading changes — and our daily records will show that too, dated the same way.

Steps

1. Small rises are the expensive kind

A 1% rise is easy to wave through; six of them in seven days added about 9% to Verda's H100 and GB300 rates. If you rent there, re-price your running total against today's page — not the rate you remember from last week.

2. Do not renew or expand at a list rate without checking the market first

While Verda added about 9%, the best verified H100 offer never moved off $2.25/hr. The spread between a rising list price and the floor is now the biggest saving available to a renter.

3. If you need capacity for months, price the reservation now

When on-demand rates rise repeatedly, locking a rate earlier tends to beat locking it later. Work out the real total — GPU hours plus storage and downloads — before you commit.

4. Watch the floor, not just the headlines

The 4090's best offer changed hands on Oct 28 without any headline at all. The day the cheapest offers start rising across the board, the whole market has moved. Our Price Watch reports every verified change, dated on both sides.

How we know

GPUJournal reads providers' own published pricing pages and banks the figures on each check; a price change is only reported when both the before and after figures were seen on the provider's own page, each with its date. This guide rests on our banked daily checks of Oct 19, 22, 23, 24, 26, 27, 28 and 29, 2026 — there are no banked checks for Oct 20, 21 or 25, and we do not fill those gaps in from memory or from anyone else's data. Verda's page was re-read first-hand on each of the six rise dates. The Nebius (Oct 1) rise predates the daily series: it was an announced rise, and only the post-rise rates were verified on Nebius's own pages — we do not present before-figures for it that we did not see. One thing you will never find presented as a verified price here: a figure a marketplace states about itself on marketing pages. Where a provider's own pages disagree with each other — on Oct 28, Spheron's pages stated the same H100 at $4.20 on some pages while others still said $2.64, $2.65, $2.75 or $2.98 — we report the disagreement in Price Watch rather than pick a number. This page extends Guide 1, “GPU rental prices are rising in 2026 — the dated evidence”, which covers the first three Verda rises and the wider 2026 picture.
