Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B on a small GPU: what actually fits, and what it costs to rent

NVIDIA's Bolt E4B is an 8B-parameter agent model (about 4B working at a time) built to run small. The headlines talk in parameters; your graphics card cares about gigabytes. This page uses the real download sizes — the compressed file is 6.18 GB, the full-quality file 15.99 GB — and works out which rented cards run which version, and what that costs.

The verdict

  • Smallest sensible download — The compressed GGUF file — 6.18 GB. That, not the “4GB” in the repo name, is what your card has to hold.
  • Smallest card for it — An 8 GB card holds the weights, with little spare; 12 GB is comfortable.
  • Full-quality version — BF16 — 15.99 GB → a 24 GB card (RTX 4090 class) runs the un-compressed model with room to work.
  • Cheapest way to rent it — RTX 4090 from $0.34/hr (RunPod Community). A weekend of trying it — 24 hours — costs $8.16 on a 4090.
  • Speed claim — 272.6 tokens/sec on an RTX 5070 — NVIDIA-reported, not measured by us.
Compare prices for this model — ranked for Bolt E4B→Find a GPU→

The real file sizes

Everything below was read on the model's own Hugging Face repos on Oct 29, 2026 — the actual files you would download, not a formula. Two things stand out. First, NVIDIA's own small download lives in a repo named “4GB” — that name is the model's roughly 4-billion effective parameters, not the file. The file itself is 6.18 GB, and 6.18 GB is what your card has to hold. Second, there is no single “the model is X GB” number: you pick a compression level, and each level is a different file.

The files, as listed on Hugging Face (Oct 29, 2026)

Sizes are the files as listed on Hugging Face, Oct 29, 2026.

FileSizeWhere it livesWhat it is
Q4_K_M GGUF6.18 GBNVIDIA's own repo (…Bolt-E4B-4GB)The standard small download — the one most people run
UD-Q4_K_XL GGUF5.06 GBUnsloth GGUF repoA slightly tighter squeeze at the same rough quality tier
UD-Q5_K_XL GGUF5.83 GBUnsloth GGUF repoA step up in quality, still small
Q8_0 GGUF8.03 GBggml-org GGUF repoNear-full quality in GGUF form
BF16 (safetensors)15.99 GBNVIDIA's own BF16 repoThe full-quality weights: a 15.88 GB main file plus a 0.11 GB shared file
mmproj (vision add-on)≈0.99 GBUnsloth GGUF repoOnly needed if you want the model to read images — add it to the bill if so

Still smaller experimental compressions exist (down to about 3.5 GB); quality at that level is a trade-off we have not tested, so they are not the recommendation here.

What fits where

Memory first, speed second: a card either holds the model or it doesn't. These verdicts are the weights file plus normal working room — the context warning underneath applies to every row.

Card memoryWhat runsVerdict
8 GBQ4_K_M (6.18 GB)Runs it — weights fit with little spare, so keep contexts modest
12 GBQ4_K_M or Q8_0 (8.03 GB)Comfortable — the class of card NVIDIA's own speed figure was produced on (RTX 5070)
16 GBQ8_0 comfortably; BF16 does not fit in practiceBF16 is 15.99 GB before anything else loads — a 16 GB card has nothing left for the model to work with
24 GBBF16 (15.99 GB) with ≈8 GB spareThe full-quality route — an RTX 4090 runs the un-compressed model with room to work

Watch out — context eats memory too. Bolt E4B accepts up to 64K tokens of context. The longer the conversation or document you feed it, the more extra memory (the KV cache) it sets aside on top of the weights, and that growth is real even though the exact size depends on your settings. The fits above assume ordinary chat-length use. If you plan to fill the whole 64K window, step up a card size rather than trusting the weights figure alone.

What it costs to rent

You do not need a data-centre card for this model — the honest rental question is how cheaply a small card rents, and for how long. Cheapest verified offers, checked Oct 29, 2026, all on RunPod's Community Cloud:

CardPer hourA weekend (24 hrs)A month of evenings (90 hrs)Always on (730 hrs)
RTX 4090 (24 GB — runs BF16)$0.34$8.16$30.60$248.20
RTX 5090 (32 GB — runs BF16)$0.69$16.56$62.10$503.70
L40S (48 GB — runs BF16)$0.79$18.96$71.10$576.70

Worked lines use a 730-hour month and “a month of evenings” = 3 hours a day for 30 days (90 hours), at the Oct 29 checked rates. Community Cloud availability varies — a card at this price is not guaranteed to be free the moment you look. The same money, compared: the $30.60 that buys a month of evenings on a 4090 buys about 44 hours on a 5090 or about 39 hours on an L40S (calculated from the rates above). For this model the extra money buys newer or roomier hardware, not a bigger model — the 4090 already runs the best version of Bolt E4B there is. And a warning in the other direction: the cheapest H100 in our prices is $2.25/hr at TensorDock, but that rental carries an 8-GPU minimum — $18.00/hr in total. Renting it for a model that fits on one small card would be paying eight times for capacity you cannot use.

Compare prices for this model — ranked for Bolt E4B→Find a GPU→

Steps

1. The small-card route (GGUF)

Download the Q4_K_M file (6.18 GB) and run it with Ollama, LM Studio or llama.cpp — all three carry this model, and this is the route for 8–12 GB cards and for trying the model on a laptop-class GPU. The same GGUF files are what the rented cards above would run if you choose the compressed version there.

2. The full-quality route (BF16)

On a 24 GB card or better, serve the BF16 weights (15.99 GB) with vLLM — the standard choice when the model answers requests from other programs, not just one person chatting. NVIDIA also offers the model as a NIM for its own supported serving stack, and Unsloth publishes fine-tuning builds if you want to adapt it rather than just run it.

Alternatives

The speed figure is NVIDIA's, not ours

The 272.6 tokens/sec on an RTX 5070 is NVIDIA-reported, produced with its DFlash drafter helping generation (the drafter is itself a small extra file, about 0.40 GB in the GGUF repos). Treat it as the maker's best case until independent tests land — we have not benchmarked this model.

“4B” is the working size, not the download

Bolt E4B carries 8B parameters in total and uses about 4B at a time. That design is why it is fast for its quality — but memory is bought on the total file, 6.18 GB compressed or 15.99 GB in full, not on the 4B figure in the name.

The licence is OpenMDW-1.1 — not Apache or MIT

NVIDIA released the model under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence. It is an open release, but it is a different rulebook from the Apache 2.0 / MIT terms many open models use, so read its terms before building anything commercial on it. (Hugging Face's metadata simply tags NVIDIA's repos “other”; the licence name comes from NVIDIA's own release.) This is a pointer, not legal advice.

Compressed is a quality choice

Q4_K_M is the community's standard working compromise, not the model's full quality. If answers disappoint, the fix order is: step up a compression level (Q5, Q8), then BF16 — each step is a bigger file, which is exactly what the size table above is for.

Compare prices for this model — ranked for Bolt E4B→Find a GPU→

How we know

The model facts — 8B total / about 4B effective parameters, built from Google's Gemma 4 E4B with reinforcement-learning post-training, 64K context, OpenMDW-1.1 licence, released by NVIDIA on Oct 23, 2026 — were checked against NVIDIA's release and the model's own Hugging Face presence on Oct 24, 2026. The file sizes were re-read first-hand on Hugging Face on Oct 29, 2026: the Q4_K_M file (6.18 GB) in NVIDIA's own …Bolt-E4B-4GB repo, the BF16 safetensors (15.88 GB + 0.11 GB) in NVIDIA's BF16 repo, and the other GGUF files in the Unsloth and ggml-org repos. Rental prices are the cheapest verified offers from our daily check of Oct 29, 2026 (RunPod Community Cloud for all three cards; TensorDock's H100 rate and 8-GPU minimum as published). The 272.6 tokens/sec figure is NVIDIA's own published result with its DFlash drafter and is labelled company-reported wherever it appears; we ran no benchmark for this guide. Worked costs are arithmetic on the printed rates and hour counts — nothing else is estimated.

TensorDock pricing explained: the cheapest H100 headline, and the 8-GPU catch

TensorDock's H100 rate — $2.25 per GPU per hour — is the lowest per-GPU price in our checks. It is also a price quoted at an eight-GPU minimum, which makes the real entry ticket $18.00 an hour. Neither fact cancels the other. This page prices the same jobs both ways, so you can see exactly when the headline saves you money and when it quietly multiplies your bill.

The verdict

  • Cheapest H100 per GPU? — TensorDock, $2.25/GPU/hr — the lowest per-GPU H100 price in our Oct 28–29 checks.
  • The catch — That rate is priced at an 8-GPU minimum — TensorDock's own table labels the row “Price per GPU, 8x minimum” — so the real floor is 8 × $2.25 = $18.00/hr.
  • One H100 for 10 hours — TensorDock forces all 8 cards; RunPod Community rents a single card. $180.00 vs $26.90.
  • A full 8-card node for a week — TensorDock wins clearly when the job truly uses 8 cards at once. $3,024.00 vs $3,615.36 over 168 hours.
  • RTX 4090, single card — The headline is not a TensorDock win here: TensorDock $0.36 vs RunPod Community $0.34.
See today's H100 prices→Find a GPU→

The H100 rates, side by side

The rule this page keeps coming back to: cheapest per-GPU headline is not the same as cheapest job. Match the minimum to the size of the work. Below are the on-demand H100 SXM prices from our checks of Oct 28–29, 2026, with the minimum commitment printed next to each — the column most price lists leave off.

H100 SXM — rates, minimums and real floors

ProviderH100 SXM, per GPU/hrMinimumReal hourly floor
TensorDock$2.258 GPUs$18.00/hr

TensorDock's own H100 page adds two honest details worth knowing. First, its on-demand pricing is billed à la carte — allocating additional CPU, RAM or storage raises the cost above the GPU rate. Second, its footnote says hosts are listed at staggered pricing from $1.90 to $2.50/hr, so the rate on a given host can sit either side of the $2.25 headline. The same page also lists a monthly rate of $2.00/GPU/hr at the same 8× minimum — the headline falls further if you commit. (All read on marketplace.tensordock.com, Oct 29, 2026.) TensorDock's other rates in our checks: A100 at $1.50/GPU/hr and RTX 4090 at $0.36/GPU/hr.

The same job, priced honestly — Job 1: one H100 for 10 hours

A fine-tune, a benchmark run, a day of inference testing. Per-GPU prices only mislead when the job and the minimum don't match — three ordinary jobs, worked in full:

RouteWhat you actually rentTotal
TensorDock8 GPUs × $2.25 × 10 hrs — the minimum applies even if seven cards sit idle$180.00
RunPod Community1 GPU × $2.69 × 10 hrs$26.90

The “cheapest” H100 costs $153.10 more for this job. The per-GPU saving is real; it is simply priced in units of eight.

Job 2: a full 8× H100 node for a 168-hour week

A training run that genuinely uses every card.

RouteMathsTotal
TensorDock8 × $2.25 × 168 hrs$3,024.00
RunPod Community8 × $2.69 × 168 hrs$3,615.36

Now the headline does its job: TensorDock is $591.36 cheaper over the week — the same roughly 16% per-GPU gap, finally working in your favour because the job fills the minimum. This is the honest counterweight to Job 1: nothing about the $2.25 rate is a trick. It is a bulk price, and it rewards bulk work.

Job 3: a single RTX 4090 experiment

TensorDock lists the 4090 at $0.36/hr; RunPod Community lists it at $0.34/hr. Over 10 hours that is $3.60 against $3.40. Plainly: on the card most people rent for small experiments, TensorDock is not the cheapest option in our checks — the H100 headline does not carry across its whole range. Two things about TensorDock are stated plainly on its own pages. Billing is pre-paid: its H100 FAQ says you deposit money, then provision a server — and that once your balance nears $0, the server is automatically deleted. And its H100 capacity, per the same page, sits in Dallas. Beyond that, the steps below are questions to ask before money goes in — printed as questions because the answers are not published on a page we could verify.

Steps

1. Availability

Is the $2.25 rate actually in stock at the size and time you need, or only at the staggered host prices ($1.90–$2.50) the footnote describes? Which regions beyond Dallas hold which GPUs?

2. Billing increments

Is on-demand time billed by the second, the minute or the hour — and what exactly does the à-la-carte CPU/RAM/storage allocation add to the GPU rate on the configuration you need?

3. Storage

TensorDock's H100 page says a lower storage-only rate applies when you stop and unreserve your GPUs, but publishes no figure for it. What is the storage rate, running and stopped?

4. Egress

What does it cost to move your data and checkpoints out? No egress rate appears on the pages we read.

5. The balance rule

Pre-paid deletion at a near-zero balance is automatic — what warning do you get, and how much float should you keep so a long job is never cut mid-run?

Alternatives

It suits you if your work fills eight cards at once

Multi-GPU training runs, distributed fine-tunes, or batch jobs you can spread across a full node. At that size the $2.25 rate is the cheapest verified H100 price we have, and over a week it is worth roughly $590 against the next option. Long, steady jobs suit it too — the monthly rate on TensorDock's own page ($2.00/GPU/hr at the same 8× minimum, read Oct 29) rewards committing, and a full node run for days at a time is exactly the shape of work the pricing is built for. And you can plan around one location: TensorDock's H100 page places its H100 SXM5 capacity in a Dallas data centre — fine for most training and batch work, wherever you are.

Look elsewhere if you need one card, briefly

A single-GPU experiment at TensorDock's H100 minimum costs $18.00/hr before you have done anything; a single RunPod Community card at $2.69/hr does the same job for a seventh of the outlay. Bursty work fits badly too — minimums punish idle time: if the job runs two hours a day, you pay the floor for the hours the cards sit unused, and a no-minimum provider fits better. And if you are price-shopping a single 4090, RunPod Community's $0.34/hr beats TensorDock's $0.36/hr in our checks.

How we know

The prices on this page are from GPUJournal's own checks of Oct 28–29, 2026, read on the providers' published pages: TensorDock H100 SXM $2.25/GPU/hr, A100 $1.50/GPU/hr, RTX 4090 $0.36/GPU/hr; RunPod Community H100 SXM $2.69 and RTX 4090 $0.34, with no multi-GPU minimum; RunPod Secure H100 SXM $3.99; Hyperstack H100 SXM $3.20; Lambda H100 SXM $3.99. The terms were re-read first-hand on TensorDock's own H100 page on Oct 29, 2026: its pricing table labels the $2.25 row “Price per GPU, 8x minimum”, its footnote describes à-la-carte billing and staggered host pricing from $1.90 to $2.50/hr, its monthly column shows $2.00/GPU/hr at the same minimum, and its FAQ describes pre-paid billing and the Dallas location. Two things are deliberately missing from this guide because we could not verify them: TensorDock publishes no storage rate and no egress rate on the pages we read, so neither appears in any total here — every worked figure above is GPU time only. Billing increments are likewise unpublished on those pages, which is why they appear above as a question to ask, not a fact. All worked totals are exact arithmetic on the checked rates: 8 × $2.25 × 10 = $180.00; 1 × $2.69 × 10 = $26.90; 8 × $2.25 × 168 = $3,024.00; 8 × $2.69 × 168 = $3,615.36.

Nous Research releases Arete-27B — a 27B open fine-tune of Qwen3.8-27B that runs on one GPU

Nov 7, 2026

Released by Nous Research on Nov 6, 2026: Arete-27B, a supervised fine-tune of Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B, with weights, its evaluation dataset and its training data all published on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. It is not a new base model — it is a behaviour layer trained onto one, on about 52.8 million tokens, and at 27B parameters it fits on a single rented GPU.

Image: Nous Research via nousresearch.com

What was released, from Nous Research's announcement and the Arete-27B model card on Hugging Face, both read on Nov 7, 2026: Nous fine-tuned all of Qwen3.8-27B's language-model weights (the vision encoder was left frozen; there was no reinforcement learning, preference optimisation or architecture change) on roughly 52.8 million tokens over two epochs and 1,202 steps, using Thinking Machines' Inkling as the teacher. The weights, the Propaganda_Eval dataset and the arete-data-pairs training data are all on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 licence, per the model card.

The results are Nous's own, and are labelled as such here: on its 803-prompt evaluation across seven value categories, judged by an LLM (Grok 4.7) against Nous's own rubric and not independently reproduced, answers flagged as containing propaganda fell from 22% for the base model to 0.9% (thinking off, temperature 0), and its fact score rose from 2.32 to 2.98 out of 5. Nous reports no meaningful regression on its Hermes Bench (65.77% to 65.60%) and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 move from 67% to 70% that it explicitly does not take credit for, citing harness differences. Treat the headline numbers as the maker's measurements until someone outside Nous reproduces them.

The renter maths is the practical story. At 27 billion parameters the weights are about 54GB in BF16 and about 27GB at 8-bit, before KV cache and headroom — one 48–80GB card, not a cluster. On today's checked board (Nov 7, 2026) that means an A100 80GB at Thunder Compute, $1.09 an hour, holds it in BF16, and an L40S at RunPod Secure, $1.09 an hour, holds the 8-bit form with room to spare; a 24GB card such as an RTX 4090 takes it quantised. A behaviour change that frontier labs describe in pretraining terms was here done with about 53 million tokens of fine-tuning — an afternoon-scale job on one rented card.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Most of this autumn's open-weight drops have been trillion-parameter systems that need a node before they need a prompt. Arete-27B is the opposite shape: a single-card model whose release is really about method — proof, published with its data, that a model's behaviour layer can be retrained cheaply on rented hardware and shipped under Apache 2.0. Whether you want this particular set of values in your model is your call; that the weights, the eval and the training pairs are all public means you can check the claim yourself for about a dollar an hour.

NVIDIA widens the Nemotron 3.5 family at GTC Berlin

Oct 21, 2026

Super VL and Bolt headline an expanded open-model family — and the headline act runs on a single 24GB card.

Image: NVIDIA

NVIDIA used GTC Berlin (Oct 20–22, 2026) to widen its Nemotron 3.5 open-model family. The headliners are Nemotron 3.5 Super VL — a 120B vision-language agent model with 12B active parameters and a 1M-token context — and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B, a 74B mixture-of-experts model with 9B active. Both were announced by NVIDIA on Oct 15, 2026 and are listed in the model catalogue under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence.

The expansion around them, per NVIDIA's GTC Berlin announcement, adds new Nemotron Retriever models for embedding, reranking and document parsing, the Cosmos 3.5 world models, and Alpamayo 2 Edge for autonomous vehicles — one open family spanning language, vision, retrieval and robotics.

The renter's headline is Bolt. NVIDIA ships a native ~2-bit build of Bolt designed to fit a single 24GB card, and lists llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth and vLLM as supported runtimes. We flag that exactly as the model page does: the 24GB figure is NVIDIA's claim for its own tuned build — the plain precision arithmetic for a 74B model is far larger, and we have not checked the tuned build ourselves.

The background: Nemotron is NVIDIA's open-model family — the models NVIDIA itself releases, openly licensed under OpenMDW-1.1, to run on the hardware it sells. The 3.5 expansion is deliberately wide, one family spanning language, vision, retrieval and robotics: Super VL for vision-language agents, Bolt for large agent models squeezed onto small cards, the new Retriever models for the embedding, reranking and document-parsing work that feeds retrieval systems, Cosmos 3.5 for world models, and Alpamayo 2 Edge for autonomous vehicles. Read as a single announcement at GTC Berlin (Oct 20–22, 2026), it is NVIDIA stocking every shelf of the open-model shop in the same week.

Bolt's trick deserves the maths, stated plainly. A 74B model at ordinary precisions needs roughly 148GB of weights at full precision, about 74GB at 8-bit and about 37GB at 4-bit — the standard arithmetic the model pages show. NVIDIA's native ~2-bit build is how the single-24GB-card claim is made: at roughly two bits per weight, 74B parameters come to about 19GB before overhead. That is genuinely how such builds work, and it is also why we flag the 24GB figure exactly as the model page does — NVIDIA's claim for its own tuned build, not a figure we have checked. A ~2-bit build's quality on your own prompts is a thing to test, not a thing to take from a launch chart; the listed runtimes — llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth and vLLM — are the standard local-serving shelf, so the test costs an hour, not a procurement process.

The card in question, if the build holds up, is the RTX 4090 class: 24GB, and on our board from $0.20 an hour at nafnaf.ai, checked Oct 27, 2026, with RunPod Community at $0.34. That is already the tier most agent experiments rent — which is the point of the launch. Super VL sits at the other end of the same family: 120B parameters with 12B active and a 1M-token context, a multi-card serving job by any honest sizing, with its own catalogue page linked below. One family, both ends of the rental market.

What it means if you rent GPUs

A 74B-class agent model that genuinely fits a 24GB card changes the rental maths: the card in question is the RTX 4090 class — the cheapest useful tier on our board (from $0.20/hr, checked Oct 19, 2026) — not a datacentre flagship. If NVIDIA's tuned build holds up on your own prompts, small agent fleets stop needing H100 money. Test it for one measured hour before you believe any launch chart — including ours.

NEWS →  ·  Models · Mistral AI

Mistral's Voxtral 3 brings speech models you can run yourself

Oct 20, 2026

Speech-to-text, text-to-speech and a voice-agent SDK in one launch — with one honest catch about the download.

Image: Mistral AI

Mistral announced Voxtral 3 on Oct 20, 2026: a family of speech models covering speech-to-text (Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3, a 4B model, and the higher-accuracy Voxtral Small Transcribe 3), a realtime transcription model streaming in under 500ms, and Voxtral Speech 3 for text-to-speech in 35+ languages — plus a voice-agent SDK, built on LiveKit, that chains listening, reasoning with tool calls, and spoken replies in one pipeline. Transcription covers 50+ languages with diarization and context biasing, per Mistral's announcement.

Mistral prices the API from $0.0035 per minute for Mini Transcribe 3 in batch ($0.0040 for Small, $0.008 for realtime), and Speech 3 at $13 per million characters — all Mistral-reported figures from its announcement and docs.

The catch, verified by this desk on Oct 21, 2026: Mistral's announcement links no downloadable weights and no weight licence for Voxtral 3, and a check of Hugging Face the same day found no Voxtral 3 checkpoint — the newest Voxtral checkpoints there remain the earlier, openly licensed releases. Mistral offers Voxtral 3 through its EU-hosted API, with self-deployment arranged through Mistral. “You can run it yourself” today means their managed routes or a private arrangement — not a public download.

The background: Voxtral is Mistral's speech family, and speech is the modality where self-hosting has the clearest privacy argument — voice recordings are personal data in a way text prompts often are not, which is why an EU-hosted API and a self-deployment route both appear in Mistral's offer. The pieces do different jobs. Transcription turns speech into text: Mini Transcribe 3 (4B) and the higher-accuracy Small Transcribe 3, covering 50+ languages with diarization — labelling who spoke when — and context biasing. The realtime model does the same job as a stream, in under 500ms by Mistral's statement, fast enough to caption a live conversation. Speech 3 goes the other way, text into spoken replies in 35+ languages. The voice-agent SDK, built on LiveKit, chains them together with reasoning and tool calls in the middle: listen, think, act, reply.

The API arithmetic, from Mistral's stated prices, decides most cases on its own. Mini Transcribe 3 in batch at $0.0035 a minute is $0.21 per hour of audio, and 10,000 minutes costs $35 — no GPU, no idle meter. Realtime at $0.008 a minute is the tier for work that cannot wait for a batch; Speech 3 at $13 per million characters prices speech output by the character, not the hour. All of these are Mistral-reported figures from its announcement and docs. Self-hosting earns its keep at sustained volume, or where the audio may not leave your own infrastructure — which is exactly why the missing download matters, and why the catch in the facts above is the decision in this story.

What to watch next: Mistral's Hugging Face organisation. The earlier Voxtral checkpoints there are openly downloadable under Apache 2.0 and sit in the model catalogue today. The day a Voxtral 3 checkpoint appears beside them, the self-hosting half of this story changes from “arrange it with Mistral” to “rent a card and run it” — and the guide linked below already works through the open route, with the board's checked prices, for the day that happens. Until then, our check of Oct 21, 2026 stands: no Voxtral 3 weights, and no weight licence, were linked from the announcement or posted on Hugging Face.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters, the immediate decision is API versus waiting. At $0.0035 a minute, 10,000 batch minutes cost $35 on the API — no GPU, no idle meter. Self-hosting only enters the picture if the weights are published, or via Mistral's own deployment route. Meanwhile the earlier Voxtral models ARE openly downloadable under Apache 2.0 and sit in the model catalogue today — the Voxtral guide works through both paths, with the board's checked prices for the open route.

NEWS →  ·  On watch · MiniMax

MiniMax M3.1 Flash weights land Oct 23

Due Oct 23, 2026  Due Oct 23

A 428B MoE whose API is live but whose weights are still a promise — we are watching the date, and the licence.

Image: MiniMax

MiniMax's M3.1 Flash is a 428B mixture-of-experts model (about 23B active) with a 1M-token context, released Oct 19, 2026 with its API live. Its downloadable weights are promised for Oct 23, 2026 — until they land, nobody can self-host it, which is why its catalogue page shows the facts and the memory maths but no GPU ranking and no Select a GPU button.

The second open question is the licence: MiniMax has not disclosed M3.1 Flash's licence yet. Its predecessor M3 shipped under the MiniMax Community License (attribution required; services over $20M/year revenue need written permission) — whether Flash follows it is unconfirmed, and we will not guess.

The background, briefly: M3.1 Flash is a mixture-of-experts model — 428 billion parameters in total, but only about 23 billion active on any given token. That split is the Flash proposition in one line: a very large model's knowledge at a much smaller model's running cost per token, provided you can hold the whole 428B in memory. Holding it is the rub, and it is why the weights matter more than the API. The API has been live since Oct 19, 2026, but an API is a meter you cannot inspect; open weights turn a model into infrastructure a renter can plan around — priced from a board, sized from the real files, and pinned to a version that cannot be quietly changed underneath a running product.

The licence question is not paperwork. The predecessor M3's MiniMax Community License allows use with attribution, but services above $20 million a year in revenue need written permission — a threshold that decides whether a growing product can build on the model at all. Whether Flash inherits those terms, loosens them or tightens them is unconfirmed, and we will not guess. That is why its catalogue page carries the facts and the memory maths but no GPU ranking and no Select a GPU button until both the weights and the licence are public — the same discipline as the prices on this site: dated, sourced, or not published.

What to watch next, in order: the weights landing, the licence text that arrives with them, and the first independent serving reports on named hardware. The update on this page records what has already arrived since publication: official vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed recipes linked from the model's Hugging Face card (tensor parallelism 4 on Blackwell, 8 on H100/H200 in the vLLM recipe), AMD's enablement article of Oct 23, 2026 with its own measurements on 4× MI350X and 4× MI355X, and a released checkpoint totalling about 252GB including the DSpark draft head — mixed low-precision, with NVFP4 experts. Set that real 252GB against the roughly 214GB the 4-bit arithmetic promises, and it is the Bolt E4B lesson again: plan from the file, not the formula.

Update — Oct 24, 2026

Official serving recipes are now linked from the model's Hugging Face card: vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed. The vLLM recipe uses tensor parallelism 4 (TP4) on Blackwell and TP8 on H100/H200. Transformers, KTransformers and Unsloth support is in progress.

AMD published an enablement article on amd.com on Oct 23, 2026: vLLM measured on 4× MI350X and ATOM on 4× MI355X, plus a Quark MXFP4 export.

The released checkpoint is mixed low-precision, including NVFP4 experts, and the repository totals about 252 GB including the DSpark draft head. Together AI offers a serverless endpoint. One community report describes the model serving on 4× DGX Spark — that report is community-reported, not independently verified.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Plan nothing on an unlanded weight release. If the weights arrive on Oct 23 as promised, the memory maths is already done on the model's page: at 4-bit the weights alone need about 214GB, so this is a multi-GPU job from day one — the minimum setup by memory is on its page. The day the weights and licence are public, its GPU ranking goes live here and Price Watch discipline applies: dated, sourced, or not published.

/story/nemotron-bolt-e4b.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · NVIDIA

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B is out — NVIDIA's small model for voice agents, games and robots

Oct 24, 2026

Released Oct 23, 2026: an 8B model with 4B effective parameters, post-trained from Google's Gemma 4 E4B — plus one honest catch about the size in its name.

Image: NVIDIA

NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B on Oct 23, 2026 (source: NVIDIA AI launch post). It has 8B total parameters and 4B effective parameters, a 64K context window, and it was post-trained from Google's Gemma 4 E4B with reinforcement learning (RL) only.

It is aimed at local voice agents, game characters and robots — NVIDIA's demo runs it on a Reachy Mini robot driven by an 8GB Jetson Orin Nano. The licence is OpenMDW-1.1, which allows commercial use, and the model is available on Hugging Face, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth, Jetson AI Lab and NIM.

NVIDIA reports 272.6 tokens per second on an RTX 5070 with a DFlash drafter. That figure is company-reported — NVIDIA's number, not one we have measured.

Now the honest part, because it decides which card you need. The “4GB” in the name is a footprint goal, not the size of the file you download. The actual Q4_K_M GGUF download is 6.18 GB, and the BF16 build is 16.0 GB — so in practice this model needs a card with 6GB or more, and no 4GB card honestly runs it. The model page shows the standard memory maths (about 16GB at FP16, about 8GB at 8-bit, about 4GB at 4-bit) right alongside this real download size, so you can plan from the real number.

Some background on the shape of this model, because the name only makes sense with it. “Effective parameters” is the mixture-of-experts idea in miniature: the file holds 8B parameters in total, but only about 4B do the work on any given token, which is how a model can carry a larger model's knowledge at a smaller model's running cost. The base is Google's Gemma 4 E4B, and NVIDIA's contribution is post-training with reinforcement learning only, aimed at the jobs in the headline — voice agents that must answer without a datacentre round-trip, game characters, and robots — where the compute lives on the device, not in a cloud region.

The availability list matters for the same reason: Hugging Face, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth, Jetson AI Lab and NIM are the places small models actually get run, and a launch that lands in all of them on day one is a launch meant to be used, not admired. The Jetson detail is the tell — NVIDIA's demo runs Bolt E4B on a Reachy Mini robot driven by an 8GB Jetson Orin Nano, an edge board rather than a server card, and the 64K context window is sized for conversations and control loops, not documents. What to watch next: independent speed measurements. The 272.6 tokens per second on an RTX 5070 is NVIDIA-reported and was achieved with a DFlash drafter — a small helper model that proposes tokens for the main model to verify — so like-for-like comparisons need the same setup. And the real download sizes, 6.18GB for the Q4_K_M GGUF and 16.0GB for the BF16 build, remain the figures to plan a card around: not the 4GB in the name.

The licence completes the practical picture. OpenMDW-1.1 allows commercial use, so Bolt E4B can sit inside a sold product — a voice-agent appliance, a game, a robot — without a separate negotiation, and the NIM listing means NVIDIA's own packaged inference route is one of the supported ways to serve it. For a voice agent, the speed figure has a concrete meaning: spoken replies feel natural when generation runs well ahead of speech, and a small model producing a company-reported 272.6 tokens per second on a desktop RTX 5070 has headroom that larger models on the same card do not. The check remains the one this desk always lands on: those are NVIDIA's numbers, on NVIDIA's setup, with a drafter assisting — run your own prompts, on your own card or an hour of a rented one, before the launch chart becomes your plan.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters, a model this size lives on small cards — every card on our board has 24GB or more, so Bolt E4B is no reason to rent big iron. The lesson that travels further than this launch: a model's name is marketing; the download size is the fact. Check the real file size before you pick a card — it is the same discipline we apply on every catalogue page.

/story/spheron-price-contradiction.html:
NEWS →  ·  Prices · Spheron

Spheron GPU pricing: four different prices for the same GPU, on Spheron's own pages

Oct 24, 2026

We read Spheron's own pages across Oct 20–24, 2026. The same GPU wears different stated prices on different pages — sometimes on the same day. Every figure below is stated on Spheron's own pages and dated; none of them is a verified board price.

Start with the H100, stated on-demand on Spheron's own pages. Across different pages, all stamped Oct 20, 2026, the H100 is stated at $2.64, $2.65, $2.75 and $2.98 per hour. All stamped Oct 21, 2026, the stated figures are $2.64, $2.65 and $2.98. And on Oct 24, 2026, two Spheron pages stamped that same day state $2.64 and $2.75. One GPU, one site, one day — two different prices, every one of them stated on Spheron's own pages.

The B200's stated on-demand price, stated on Spheron's own pages, moved across the week: $9.80–$9.90 stated Oct 20, 2026, then $11.06 stated Oct 21, then $11.12 stated Oct 22 — and still $11.12 on Oct 23 and Oct 24. Its stated spot price went from $5.22 (stated Oct 21) to $5.25 (stated Oct 22 and Oct 23) — and then, on Oct 24, $5.31 on some Spheron pages and $6.12 on another Spheron page the same day. The chart below draws this chain exactly as stated.

The B300 is stated at “from $11.23” on Oct 23, 2026 and at $12.42 on Oct 24, on a different page — both stated on Spheron's own pages. And on Oct 22, on a single Spheron page, the RTX 6000 Ada's stated spot price of $0.93 sits above its stated on-demand price of $0.78. Spot is normally the cheaper, interruptible way to rent the same card, so the order itself is inverted — stated on Spheron's own pages, exactly as read that day.

Spheron's pricing FAQ also quotes its rivals — at prices dated May 2026, stated on Spheron's own pages. It quotes RunPod's B200 at $5.89; GPUJournal's verified board figure for RunPod Secure's B200 is $7.99, checked Oct 24, 2026. It quotes Lambda's B200 at $4.99–$5.29; our verified board figure is $6.69, checked Oct 24, 2026. It quotes Nebius's B200 at $5.50; our verified board figure is $8.50, checked Oct 24, 2026. The quoted figures are Spheron's, dated May 2026; the actuals are our verified board prices, dated today.

Why does one GPU wear three prices on one site in one day? Pages are written at different times, updated on different schedules, and quoted figures age at different speeds. None of that makes any single stated figure a lie — it makes an undated, unsourced figure unusable. If you cannot tell which page is current, you cannot tell which price you would actually pay.

Since this story was published, Price Watch has kept reading — and the pattern has kept not resolving. On Oct 26, 2026, Spheron's pages still stated the H100 at $2.64 on its specs and multi-node pages, while its Canada GPU availability guide and pricing comparison stated $2.98; the same Canada page stated B200 spot at $6.79, against the $5.31 the recorded series carried on Oct 24. On Oct 27, 2026, as its pages rolled to that day's stamp, Spheron's price tables stated the H200 on-demand at $7.09 while its own GB200 vs H200 vs B200 comparison, stamped the same day, stated the H200 at $5.54 — and stated B200 spot appeared as $5.25, $5.71 and $6.52 on different pages the same day. The H100, at a stated $2.64, was the one figure that agreed everywhere. Every figure in this paragraph is stated on Spheron's own pages and is carried on our Price Watch as stated — never as a verified board price. Source: Spheron's own pages, read Oct 26 and Oct 27, 2026, via Price Watch.

A word on how we treat a site like this, because it is the whole method in miniature. Spheron has no verified prices on our board — its provider page says plainly that we are still checking its rates — not because its prices are unwelcome, but because a verified price needs one figure that a provider's own current pages stand behind. Where the pages disagree with each other, the honest publishable fact is the disagreement itself, dated and sourced, which is what Price Watch carries. The same discipline runs the other way: the board figures quoted above against Spheron's FAQ — RunPod Secure's B200 at $7.99, Lambda's at $6.69, Nebius's at $8.50, all checked Oct 24, 2026 — are single figures, each read from the provider's own current pricing page. If Spheron's pages converge on single figures, they can be verified like anyone else's. Until then, the split is the story, and we will keep dating it.

For calibration, here is the verified board the stated figures land in, checked Oct 27, 2026. The H200 — the card Spheron's own pages stated at both $7.09 and $5.54 on Oct 27 — has verified on-demand prices on our board from $3.59 an hour on RunPod Community to $6.31 per GPU on CoreWeave's 8-GPU nodes, each a single figure read from the provider's own pricing page. The B200's verified range runs from $5.98 on RunPod Community to CoreWeave's $8.60 per GPU. A stated price is not automatically a wrong price — but when one site states two figures for the same card on the same day, a renter has no way to know which one a checkout would honour, and that unknowability, not any single number, is the finding.

The H100 shows why multiplicity, not level, is the problem. Spheron's stated H100 figures — $2.64 to $2.98 across the week — sit inside the range our verified board carries for the H100 SXM, checked Oct 27, 2026: from $2.25 an hour at TensorDock (an 8-GPU minimum) and $2.69 on RunPod Community, up to $3.99 on RunPod Secure and Lambda. Any one of Spheron's stated figures, on its own, would look plausible. Four of them, on one site, stamped the same day, cannot all be the price a renter would pay — and a comparison built on whichever one a search engine happened to surface would be wrong in a direction nobody chose. That is the practical harm this story exists to document: not that a number is high or low, but that it cannot be relied on.

Stated B200 prices on Spheron’s own pages, Oct 20–24, 2026 — drawn from the figures stated in this story. On Oct 24 the stated spot price is $5.31 on some pages and $6.12 on another page the same day: the two are shown side by side, with no arrow between them, because a same-day contradiction is not a move.

What it means if you rent GPUs

What GPUJournal does instead: one verified price for each GPU and provider, the provider named, the date stamped, checked daily — see Compare prices, and How we price for the full method. The takeaway for any GPU price you meet anywhere is three questions: whose page did it come from, what date was it read, and which provider actually sells at it? A price that cannot answer all three is a claim, not a price.

/story/gpu-unlock-ampere.html:
NEWS →  ·  Community · Unofficial

GPU Unlock: an unofficial module claims big Ampere gains — UNOFFICIAL

Oct 24, 2026

UNOFFICIAL: an open-source Linux kernel module says it resets Ampere instruction-issue limits for large reported gains. Every performance figure here is the project's or the community's — independently unverified.

Unofficial — read the cautions first

This brief is about unofficial, community software. It is not NVIDIA software, it is not endorsed here, and every performance figure in it is project- or community-reported and independently unverified. Warranty and stability risk sits with the user.

Image: NVIDIA

GPU Unlock is an open-source Linux kernel module, published on GitHub and reported on Oct 24, 2026 via Wccftech. It works by resetting the instruction-issue limits built into Ampere consumer cards, and it does so before the driver loads.

The project reports its headline result on an RTX 3090 Ti: BF16 GEMM rising from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS (+80%), with TF32 up 94% — project-reported figures. Community ComfyUI tests report +56–59% on image models, and one community report on a 3090 running vLLM describes +33% prompt processing with decode speed unchanged. Every one of these figures comes from the project or its community; none has been independently verified, and we have not run the module ourselves.

The project claims the module needs no VBIOS flash, and that it survives driver updates by design. Those are the project's claims, stated as it states them.

The cautions, plainly: this is unofficial software that changes how your card is allowed to run, and it is independently unverified. Any warranty and stability risk sits with you, the user — not with NVIDIA, and not with us. If the reported gains matter to you, the careful route is a spare card, a backed-up system, and your own measurements before any work you care about.

The hardware background explains why Ampere owners care. Ampere is the generation behind the RTX 30-series consumer cards and the A100 — on our board the A100 80GB is still the workhorse of the rental market, from $1.09 an hour checked Oct 27, 2026 — and the RTX 3090 Ti in this story's photo was the flagship consumer Ampere card. Consumer Ampere cards ship with instruction-issue limits set by NVIDIA: caps on how fast the card may issue work to its cores. The project's claim, in its own terms, is that resetting those limits before the driver loads lets the card run closer to what the silicon can physically do. That is the whole mechanism — no VBIOS flash, by the project's account, and designed to survive driver updates.

If even part of the reported gain held up under independent measurement, the practical effect would land on exactly the workloads the community reports name: image generation in ComfyUI, and prompt processing in local LLM serving with vLLM. The vLLM report — +33% prompt processing with decode speed unchanged — is at least the pattern you would expect if the limit being reset governs how fast work is fed to the card rather than how fast tokens come out; that is an interpretation of the community's own reports, not a measurement of ours. The cautions bear repeating in full: a kernel module runs at the deepest level of the operating system, this one is unofficial community software changing how a card is allowed to run, and stability, warranty and hardware-longevity risk all sit with the user. What to watch next: a repeatable benchmark from a source with no stake in the project — same card, same driver, same workload, before and after. When that exists, this brief will be updated with it, dated.

A short glossary for the headline figures, so the claims can be weighed properly. GEMM is the matrix-multiplication workload underneath nearly all AI computation, and TFLOPS counts trillions of arithmetic operations per second — so “BF16 GEMM rising from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS (+80%)” is the project claiming its RTX 3090 Ti does the core maths of AI work 80% faster with the module than without it, with TF32 — the other precision Ampere cards use for training maths — up 94%. Those are the project's own measurements, reported via Wccftech's coverage of the GitHub project on Oct 24, 2026. A claim that size, on hardware that common, is straightforwardly testable by any independent lab with a 3090 Ti and an afternoon — which is precisely the test this brief is waiting on.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For owners of Ampere cards — the RTX 3090 class that fills so many home and small-lab racks — even part of the reported gain would be significant, which is exactly why the figures need independent checking before anyone plans around them. We are reporting that this project exists and what it claims; we are not recommending it. When independent, repeatable measurements appear, we will update this brief.

/story/nvidia-cosmos-expansion.html:
NEWS →  ·  Robotics · NVIDIA

NVIDIA expands Cosmos: the toolkit for teaching robots gets bigger

Oct 24, 2026

Announced Oct 21–22, 2026 at GTC Berlin, with fresh coverage on Oct 24: five Data Factory blueprints, a data curator, new simulation checkpoints and a faster Cosmos 3 NIM — explained piece by piece, in plain words.

Image: NVIDIA

Cosmos is NVIDIA's platform for physical AI — the software side of teaching robots and machines about the real world. At GTC Berlin (Oct 21–22, 2026) NVIDIA expanded it with five Cosmos Data Factory blueprints, published on GitHub and available through Azure, Nebius and CoreWeave. A blueprint is a ready-made pipeline: instead of assembling your own training-data workflow piece by piece, you start from NVIDIA's working recipe and adapt it.

Cosmos Curator is the data-cleaning piece: it processes multimodal data — video, images and sensor feeds together — so it can be used to train models. Raw robot and camera data arrives messy and enormous; the Curator is the stage that sorts, filters and prepares it before training begins.

Cosmos 3 Nano simulation checkpoints are ready-made starting points for simulation — saved model states you can load and build on, rather than training a world model from zero. And the Cosmos 3 NIM, NVIDIA's packaged, ready-to-deploy inference version of the model, is stated to deliver up to 2× faster inference. That 2× figure is company-reported.

Alongside Cosmos, the Metropolis VSS Blueprint 3.3 — NVIDIA's recipe for video search and summarisation systems — is stated to handle +40% more streams per GPU. That figure is company-reported too.

The background, in plain words: “physical AI” is NVIDIA's name for models that must understand and act in the physical world — robots, vehicles, cameras — rather than in text. Those models are trained less on text and more on video, images and sensor data, and on simulation: a robot can practise in a simulated warehouse many times before it touches a real box. Cosmos is the platform layer for that work — world models that generate and understand physical scenes, plus the tooling around them — and most of this expansion is about the unglamorous half of the pipeline: getting training data cleaned, organised and generated at scale, which is what the Data Factory blueprints and Cosmos Curator are for.

Availability is the part a renter can act on. The five blueprints are published on GitHub and available through Azure, Nebius and CoreWeave — and Nebius and CoreWeave are providers on our own board, checked Oct 27, 2026: Nebius lists the H200 at $5.40 an hour and CoreWeave at $6.31 per GPU on its 8-GPU nodes. In other words, the pipeline this announcement describes can be rented today, by the hour, from two of the providers named in it. What to watch next: whether the stated gains — up to 2× faster inference for the Cosmos 3 NIM and +40% more streams per GPU for the Metropolis VSS Blueprint 3.3, both company-reported — show up in independent robotics and video-analytics work, and whether the blueprints begin appearing in providers' own solution pages. A company-reported speedup is a starting claim, not a measurement; the pattern worth trusting is the one we apply to prices: dated, sourced, and checked by someone other than the seller.

Piece by piece, the pipeline this builds looks like this. Raw material — robot camera feeds, vehicle video, sensor logs — arrives through the Data Factory blueprints, the ready-made recipes published on GitHub. Cosmos Curator cleans and organises that multimodal data into something trainable. The Cosmos 3 Nano simulation checkpoints give teams a saved, working world model to start from instead of a blank one, and the Cosmos 3 NIM is the packaged form for actually serving the model, stated to infer up to 2× faster. Alongside it, the Metropolis VSS Blueprint 3.3 does the same recipe job for video search and summarisation, stated to handle +40% more streams per GPU. Each piece is a stage of GPU work — curation, training, simulation, serving — which is why a software announcement belongs on a price journal's news desk at all.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Why a renter should care about robot software: physical-AI and robotics workloads are a growing class of GPU demand. Every team teaching a robot needs data pipelines, simulation runs and inference serving — all of it GPU hours, much of it on exactly the datacentre cards this board tracks, from providers named in this very announcement. More Cosmos adoption means more demand competing for the same B200 and H200 hours you rent. It will not move today's price — it is part of why the demand side of this market keeps growing.

NEWS →  ·  Hardware · NVIDIA

DGX Spark: the 64GB partner units are on sale — and the price is the story

Oct 24, 2026

Partner-built 64GB DGX Spark units went on sale Oct 23, 2026 from $4,999. No deep independent benchmarks of them have been found yet — and the first reaction is about the price.

Image: NVIDIA

Partner 64GB DGX Spark units went on sale on Oct 23, 2026, priced from $4,999. No deep independent benchmarks of the 64GB partner boxes have been found yet, so what these machines can really do, measured independently, is still an open question.

The price reaction has been pointed. ServeTheHome's line — “$4,999 for a 64GB machine feels quite high” — captures the mood. The arithmetic behind it: two 64GB units cost $9,998 pooled, while one 128GB unit costs $6,950. NVIDIA now supports manually configured clusters of up to 8 Sparks, pooling 1TB of memory.

The background: DGX Spark is NVIDIA's desktop AI machine, a small box built on unified memory, where the processor and GPU share one pool of memory instead of passing data back and forth. Unified memory is why capacity is the headline — a model that fits in the pool can be worked on whole — and the 128GB unit has been the reference configuration of the line. The partner-built 64GB units that went on sale on Oct 23, 2026, from $4,999, are the cheaper way into the same idea: built by NVIDIA's partners, with the pool halved to reach the price.

Set the purchase against the rental board, because that is the comparison a reader here actually faces. $4,999 buys the 64GB box outright. At the board's checked rates of Oct 27, 2026, the same money is roughly 1,860 hours of an H100 SXM on RunPod Community at $2.69 an hour — about 77 days of continuous H100 time — or close to 2,960 hours of the RTX PRO 6000's 96GB at $1.69 an hour on the same provider. The box wins when it runs for years on your desk, on your electricity, with your data never leaving the room. The rental wins when the work is bursty, or when next month's model is bigger than this month's box. Neither answer is the product's fault; it is arithmetic.

What to watch next is simple: independent benchmarks of the 64GB partner units. None had been found when this story was published — no deep third-party measurement of what these boxes sustain on real models — so until they land, every performance claim for the partner units is the manufacturer's. The pooling route also wants care: two 64GB units cost $9,998 pooled, one 128GB unit costs $6,950, and NVIDIA's support for manually configured clusters of up to 8 Sparks pooling 1TB does not change that first, deciding comparison for most desks.

What it means if you rent GPUs

A small desktop box with unified memory is a different purchase from renting datacentre hours: you buy it once and it sits on your desk. But the comparison that matters is the one above — if you need pooled memory, one 128GB unit undercuts two 64GB units by a wide margin. Until independent benchmarks of the partner boxes land, the honest position is: on sale, priced firmly, performance unproven.

/story/carbon-x-dna-model.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Hugging Face Bio

Carbon-X: an open model that reads DNA — and fits on one 80GB GPU

Oct 24, 2026

Released Oct 22, 2026 by Hugging Face Bio with Zhongguancun Academy and TIGEM / University of Naples: a 14.8B open model you paste raw DNA into, in an ordinary chat, and question in English. Apache 2.0, weights public, and sized for a single rented card.

Image: Hugging Face

Carbon-X is a 14.8B-parameter decoder-only model trained jointly on DNA and natural language, built from Qwen3-14B. You give it raw DNA inside a chat message and it answers in English: whether a mutation looks benign or pathogenic, which regions control gene activity, which organism group a sequence comes from, and what bases come next — with its reasoning. DNA and text share one token stream: a hybrid tokenizer reads DNA as 6-base chunks (6-mers) alongside ordinary text tokens. Context window is 40,960 tokens. Source: the model's own Hugging Face card, read Oct 24, 2026.

The scores are the maker's own, stated as such: across five DNA benchmarks Carbon-X averages 66.7% with thinking disabled — 27 points above the Qwen3-14B it starts from, ahead of every other open model its makers evaluated, and close to GPT-6.1 Sol's 67.5% at about 1/1,800 of the inference cost per problem, by their arithmetic. The makers estimate scoring ClinVar's 2.4 million variants of uncertain significance at about $300 with Carbon-X, against $32,000 to $4 million on the frontier models they compared. Every figure in this paragraph is maker-reported on the model card, not independently verified by this desk.

The serving facts, from the same card: the weights fit on a single 80GB GPU in bfloat16, it serves with vLLM, and it needs Transformers v5 or later plus trust_remote_code=True for its custom DNA tokenizer. The card is explicit that llama.cpp and other GGUF runtimes cannot tokenize its DNA correctly on the main checkpoint, so the usual GGUF shortcut does not apply here.

The limits, in the makers' own words on the card: Carbon-X has not been clinically validated and must not be used to make medical decisions; genetic data is highly sensitive; splice-site and histone-mark questions remain weak spots (29.8% and 34.6% on GenomeQA); and it can miscount bases or invent a sequence's identity when a prompt lacks context. Licence: Apache 2.0.

The card fills in how the trick is built. Carbon-X is a 40-layer decoder with a hidden size of 5,120 and grouped-query attention — 40 query heads sharing 8 KV heads. Its vocabulary holds 157,184 tokens: the Qwen3 BPE vocabulary for text, plus 5,515 DNA tokens made up of 4,096 tokens covering every possible 6-mer, 1,364 tail tokens for sequences whose length is not a multiple of six, and the markers that wrap a DNA span and are added automatically when a run of bases is detected in a prompt. Training ran to 302 billion tokens of mid-training on DNA, biology text, English and instruction data, then supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on DNA tasks; the makers first trained only the new DNA embeddings for about 10 billion tokens with the model body frozen, so the DNA vocabulary could bed in before full training. Source: the model's Hugging Face card.

The per-benchmark table, all maker-reported, shows where the lead is real and where it is not. Carbon-X leads the comparison on coding-variant effects (BioReason Coding: 74.9 against GPT-6.1 Sol's 71.0) and on next-base prediction (NextBase: 39.4 against 32.9), and posts 85.1 on complex variant effects — where Opus 5.5, at 94.8, still leads it — and 70.4 on single-base variant effects (FrontierVEP). Inside GenomeQA, its organism-group score is 93.2 and motifs 90.0, against the splice-site and histone-mark weak spots named above. It also remains a usable general assistant, at 79.3% prompt-level strict accuracy on IFEval. And the headline cost comparison carries a footnote worth reading: the makers computed Carbon-X's cost from measured throughput per H200-hour at $5 an hour. On our board, checked Oct 27, 2026, an H200 starts at $3.59 an hour on RunPod Community — so the rental version of their arithmetic is, if anything, kinder than the one they published. The makers also state that all training data was decontaminated against these benchmarks with three checks: whole-span DNA overlap, text n-gram overlap and sequence homology search.

Two serving details from the card are worth more than they look. First, every reported result used the model's own sampling defaults — temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, from its generation config — with thinking disabled, and the makers recommend keeping it that way; a benchmark reproduced under different settings is a different benchmark. Second, the card's prompting guidance is plain about the failure mode named in the limits above: put the sequence and the question in the same message, and include whatever context you already have — the gene, the strand, the coordinates — because without it the model may guess at a sequence's identity. For variant questions, it wants the reference and alternate sequences, or a reference with the position and the base change. None of that needs more GPU; it needs the hour you already rented, used properly.

The training detail on the card contains one finding any lab renting GPUs will recognise. In the makers' ablations, learning rate was the dominant knob at the mid-training stage: too low, and the model preserved its English but left DNA performance at chance; too high, and it learned DNA but forgot English. The published recipe — a cosine schedule from 5e-5 down to 5e-6 over 302 billion tokens, at a sequence length of 8,192 and a global batch of about 4.2 million tokens per step for 72,000 steps — is the balance point they found. It is also a quiet argument for the model's whole premise: DNA and language had to be trained into one set of weights, carefully, because the product is the conversation between the two.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Why this is a GPU story and not only a biology story: it is a specialist open model deliberately sized for one 80GB card — an H100 or A100 80GB you can rent by the hour — so a lab can keep sensitive, unpublished sequences on its own rented infrastructure instead of sending them to a closed API whose filters and data handling it does not control. That is the open-weight bargain in its clearest form, and the single-card fit is exactly the maths our model page does: 14.8B parameters at full precision is about 29.6GB of weights before headroom, comfortably inside 80GB, tight but workable at 8-bit on smaller cards.

/story/kimi-k3-1-pro-weights-nov-4.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Moonshot AI

Kimi K3.1 Pro is live — and its open weights land by Nov 4

Oct 24, 2026

Launched Oct 23, 2026 by Moonshot AI: a post-trained Kimi K3 — 2.8 trillion parameters, about 104B active, 1-million-token context — scoring within a point of Claude Opus 5.5 on Moonshot's own coding-agent test. Today it is API-only. The full weights are promised by Nov 4, and the licence that comes with them has not been stated yet.

Image: Moonshot AI

What shipped, from Moonshot's own tech blog, read Oct 24, 2026: Kimi K3.1 Pro is the first model in the K3.1 series, a post-trained version of Kimi K3 built with substantially larger post-training compute — large-scale reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains. Same 3T-class base as K3: 2.8T total parameters, about 104B active per token, a 1M-token context window, text and image input. A second version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, offers the same capabilities at 2–3× the speed, by Moonshot's statement. Both are live now on Kimi.com, the Kimi apps, Kimi Work, Kimi Code and the Kimi API.

The scores are Moonshot-reported, stated as such: Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and just behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%); BenchCAD 3D reconstruction at 92.7% with tools; OfficeQA Pro v2 at 64.4, which Moonshot calls state of the art. On its internal Kimi Hallu Bench Hard stress test, the claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3% — Moonshot itself cautions that this stress test does not represent error rates in daily use. Independently, Artificial Analysis scored K3.1 Pro 55 on its Intelligence Index, fourth overall behind only closed models, in results reported Oct 24, 2026.

The release terms are the part to watch: Moonshot states the full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026, and has not yet stated the licence they will carry. K3 shipped under Moonshot's own custom Kimi K3 License, but K3.1 Pro's terms are unknown until the drop — do not assume they match. Until then the model is hosted-only: Moonshot's API pricing page lists K3.1 Pro at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output ($0.20 cached input), a third cheaper than K3, with Highspeed at $4 / $20 — prices as listed Oct 23–24, 2026.

One unusual disclosure, in Moonshot's own words: for the open-weight release it identified and removed cyber-related data from both the mid-training and reinforcement-learning stages, so the open weights do not extend the frontier of offensive cyber capability. On its internal xdev-bench-hard test, the released model solves 81.0% at pass@3 against 90.5% for a checkpoint trained without that removal — figures Moonshot reports itself, published so users can see the trade the lab chose to make.

One piece of background unlocks the whole sizing story: K3.1 Pro is a mixture-of-experts model. Of its 2.8 trillion parameters, only about 104 billion are active for any given token; the rest must still be stored, ready for the tokens that do route to them. Compute follows the active count, which is how a model this large can be served at $2 per million input tokens at all — but memory follows the total, which is why the API price and the self-hosting price live in different worlds. Moonshot spreads the memory cost across its own fleet; a self-hoster pays all of it, up front, in cards. The Highspeed version makes the same trade from the other side: the same capabilities at 2–3× the speed, by Moonshot's statement, at double the API price — $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output.

What to watch next is a short list with dates on it. First, the weights themselves, promised by Nov 4, 2026: whether they land on the day, and in what form. Second, the licence, still unstated — K3 shipped under Moonshot's custom Kimi K3 License, and until K3.1 Pro's terms are published, no commercial self-hoster can plan around them. Third, independent measurement: the scores in this story are Moonshot-reported, Moonshot itself cautions that its hallucination stress test does not represent daily use, and Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index score of 55 is the one outside measurement so far. When the weights land, our model page does the full sizing from the real files — the same discipline this desk applies to download sizes and to prices: check the real thing, date it, name the source.

Until the weights land, the interim rental question is what the equivalent self-hosted capacity would even look like, and the board prices the shape of it. The sizing above calls for roughly 18 or more 96GB cards just for the 4-bit weights; the 96GB card on our board is the RTX PRO 6000, from $1.69 an hour on RunPod Community, checked Oct 27, 2026 — so 18 of them run to roughly $30 an hour before a single token of conversation memory, and the 1M-token context pushes the real requirement higher still. Set that against Moonshot's API at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, and the hosted route is not a placeholder for most teams; at any plausible volume this side of a dedicated serving fleet, it is the product. The weights, when they come, change who can compete to serve Kimi — they do not make serving it small.

The 1-million-token context deserves its own sentence of context, because it shapes both halves of this story. A context window that large lets an agent hold an entire codebase, or a long document set, in a single conversation — the capability behind the coding-agent and office benchmarks Moonshot leads with, BenchCAD's 3D reconstruction work and OfficeQA Pro v2 among them. It is also memory-hungry in serving: the conversation cache grows with every token held, which is part of why the self-hosting arithmetic above starts at “roughly 18 cards for the weights” and only grows from there. Artificial Analysis's independent score — 55 on its Intelligence Index, fourth overall behind only closed models, reported Oct 24, 2026 — is the figure to hold onto while the maker-reported table awaits the same outside treatment.

The hallucination figure deserves the same slow reading as the coding scores. Moonshot's Kimi Hallu Bench Hard is, by its own description, a stress test — a set of prompts chosen to provoke invented claims — and the reported fall in claim-level hallucination rate from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3% for K3.1 Pro measures behaviour on that deliberately hostile set, not error rates in daily use; Moonshot says so itself. What it does show is direction and effort: a post-training run with substantially larger compute, across hundreds of downstream domains, that measurably hardened the model against its own worst habit. For anyone planning to put an agent in front of customers, that — not a benchmark lead of a point or two — is the improvement that decides whether the thing can be left unsupervised, and it is the claim outside testers will check first when the weights land.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Update — Nov 6, 2026: the weights landed on Nov 4, 2026, on the promised date. Moonshot published moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro on Hugging Face — 96 safetensors shards summing to 1,561,293,160,568 bytes (about 1.56TB) in native MXFP4, not gated — under the Kimi K3.1-Pro License: a permissive MIT-style base whose two scale conditions (a separate agreement for model-as-a-service businesses above $20M revenue in 12 months, and prominent display of the model's name above 100M monthly users or $20M monthly revenue; internal use exempt) are set out in our Nov 4 release story and in the refreshed deployment guide. The model card confirms 2.8T total / 104B active parameters and a 1,048,576-token context, and recommends vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed; vLLM's recipe baselines one TP8 group (one B300 node, two GB300 trays, or one MI355X node). The sizing below was written on Oct 24, before any of that was public, and is kept as the launch-day record. Why this matters to anyone who rents GPUs: at 2.8 trillion parameters, the memory maths is unforgiving — about 5,600GB of weights at full precision, about 2,800GB at 8-bit and about 1,400GB at 4-bit, before headroom and conversation memory. No single card comes close, and even one full 8×H200 node (1,128GB) cannot hold the 4-bit build; by our arithmetic you are planning roughly 18 or more 96GB cards across nodes just for the compressed weights. So when the weights land on Nov 4, self-hosting K3.1 Pro is a cluster decision, not a card decision — and until then, Moonshot's API at $2 / $10 is the only way to run it. Our model page does the full sizing the day the licence and weights are public.

/story/nanbeige-4-3-33b-open-agent-model.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Nanbeige

Nanbeige4.3-33B: a 33B open agent model that out-codes Qwen3.8-27B — on its maker's own tests

Oct 25, 2026

Released on Hugging Face by Nanbeige, the AI team backed by recruitment platform BOSS Zhipin, and reported on Oct 25, 2026: a 33-billion-parameter model under Apache 2.0, built for coding agents and professional office work, with a 512K-token context window and weights that fit on a single 80GB GPU at full precision.

Image: Nanbeige

What shipped, from the model's own Hugging Face card, read Oct 25, 2026: Nanbeige4.3-33B is the flagship teacher model of the Nanbeige4.3 series — 33,118,977,024 parameters in BF16, a context window of 524,288 tokens, English and Chinese, and a companion Base checkpoint posted alongside it for anyone who wants to do their own post-training. Reasoning is on by default (set enable_thinking to False to switch it off), a preserve_thinking option keeps earlier reasoning in multi-turn tool work — the card recommends it on for coding agents, off for chat — and tool calls prefer an XML format, with JSON also supported. The point of a teacher this size, in the card's own framing, is what comes next: it anchors a distillation pipeline for smaller models, starting with a Nanbeige4.3-3B the lab names but has not dated.

The scores are the maker's own, stated as such: the card compares Nanbeige4.3-33B with Qwen3.8-27B, Muse-Glimmer-30B and Gemma4-31B, all run at their highest thinking effort on the same inference settings and harness. On agentic coding it leads clearly — Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 80.9 against Qwen3.8-27B's 73.0, DeepSWE at 65.5 against 42.5, Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 23.8 against 6.3 — and it posts 95.2 on AIME 2026. It is not a clean sweep: Qwen3.8-27B still leads on SWE-Bench Pro (61.7 to 60.3) and GDPval (86.4 to 84.8), and Gemma4-31B leads on GPQA Diamond (91.3 to 89.5). No third party had reproduced the table when coverage landed on Oct 25, 2026, so treat every figure here as Nanbeige-reported until outside runs agree.

The serving facts, from the same card: it runs with Transformers, SGLang or vLLM, and needs trust_remote_code=True. Note the card's own SGLang and vLLM examples launch it with tensor parallelism across 4 GPUs — the maker's serving examples spread it over four cards even though the weights alone fit on one large card, which tells you where the headroom goes once real agent workloads and long contexts arrive. Licence: Apache 2.0, as listed on the model card — commercial use and modification allowed, with the licence notices kept.

The cowork half of the card's table is just as pointed, and it explains the lab's parentage: Nanbeige is backed by BOSS Zhipin, a recruitment platform, so professional office work is home ground. On Automation Bench the card reports 54.2 against Qwen3.8-27B's 38.3; on JobBench, 44.8 against 34.5, with the card noting the model leads in most of the 35 occupations evaluated; and on SWE-Atlas-QnA, NL2Repo and Scicode it reports 50.8, 53.0 and 52.6, each ahead of the same comparison set, with SkillsBench at 61.1. Every figure in this paragraph is the maker's own, from the same model card, under the same caution as the coding table above: maker-reported, not yet independently reproduced.

The card is unusually specific about how it wants to be run, and renters should take the hint. For agentic and tool-use tasks it recommends temperature 1.0 with top-p 0.95 and up to 65,536 new tokens; for reasoning and chat, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95 and up to 262,144 new tokens. Those generation budgets explain the four-card serving examples better than the weights do: at output lengths like these, it is the conversation memory — the KV cache growing with every token of a 512K context — that fills the hardware. The card's SGLang and vLLM launches both use tensor parallelism across 4 GPUs with memory utilisation set to 0.8, and the benchmarks were run with preserve_thinking on, the setting the card recommends for multi-turn tool work.

How the scores were produced is on the card too, and it is the right way to read them. The card's footnotes state that Nanbeige4.3-33B was evaluated with preserve_thinking=true; that Terminal-Bench 2.1 was run with the Terminus 2 harness and Terminal-Bench 4.0 and DeepSWE with mini-swe-agent v2.4.6; that SWE-Atlas-QnA answers were judged against 1,304 task-specific rubrics by GPT-6 Sol; and that NL2Repo was run using Claude Code. In the card's own framing, the 33B is step one of a stated strategy: build a high-capacity teacher agent first, then distil its agentic capabilities into smaller models — which is why the promised Nanbeige4.3-3B, not this teacher, is the release most renters should ultimately watch for.

The cowork table's own footnotes show the same care about method — and the same limit. The card states that Automation Bench v1.0.6 covers 600 publicly released tasks; that JobBench was evaluated with the Claude Code harness equipped with a search tool, across its 35 occupations; that Claw-Eval was run on its General subset of 157 single-turn tasks; and that DeepPlanning, EnterpriseOps-Gym and Tau3-Bench were run from their official repositories. Named harnesses and named subsets are what a reader needs to reproduce a table — and reproduction by someone other than the maker remains the step that has not happened yet. Until it does, the fairest summary is the one in the headline: on its maker's own tests, this is the strongest open agent model in its size class, with the margins widest exactly where its maker's parent company does business.

For completeness, the rest of the maker's coding table, all Nanbeige-reported: Muse-Glimmer-30B posts 61.8 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 36.9 on SWE-Bench Pro, but falls to 4.4 on DeepSWE and 1.6 on Terminal-Bench 4.0; Gemma4-31B posts 47.2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 51.2 on SWE-Bench Pro, and — as noted above — beats Nanbeige on GPQA Diamond, 91.3 to 89.5. The pattern across the full table is a model built and tuned for agentic work first: its leads are largest on the terminal, repository and workplace-task benchmarks, and narrowest on the general knowledge and long-form professional tests where Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-31B still hold edges. A renter choosing between them is really choosing a workload: agent loops point one way, general chat and knowledge work the other.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Why this matters to anyone who rents GPUs: the memory maths is the friendly kind for once. At 33B parameters the weights are about 66GB in BF16, so they fit on one rented 80GB card — an H100 or A100 80GB — before conversation memory; at 8-bit, about 33GB, they fit the 48GB class; and at 4-bit, roughly 17–20GB, they fit a 24GB RTX 4090. The honest catch is the 512K context: a context window that large carries a KV cache that can dwarf the weights on long agent runs, which is why the maker's own examples reach for four cards. So the practical rental story is a strong open coding agent you can start on a single card today — and a 3B student promised from the same work, which, if the teacher's scores hold up under outside testing, is the version most renters will end up running.

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom.
