/story/coreweave-denmark-copenhagen-expa.html:
NEWS →  ·  Providers · CoreWeave

CoreWeave brings Copenhagen Blackwell capacity online and builds a global AI network

Oct 27, 2026

Announced by CoreWeave on Oct 27, 2026: the majority of its planned 22.5 MW at atNorth's DEN01 data centre in Copenhagen is now online — its first site in Denmark — alongside a petabit-scale network backbone reaching into the Middle East and Asia Pacific.

Image: atNorth

The Copenhagen facility runs NVIDIA Blackwell systems connected with NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand, and its surplus heat feeds the local district heating network under a heat reuse agreement. It takes CoreWeave's European footprint to nine data centres across five geographies, including the United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Norway. Source: CoreWeave's own announcement, Oct 27, 2026.

The network half of the announcement is a Global AI Network built for AI workloads: new points of presence in the United Arab Emirates, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Australia, Korea and Japan, beginning later in the fourth quarter of 2026 and extending to a full loop in mid-2027, with multiple 400 gigabit-per-second connections at each point of presence.

The scale CoreWeave states for itself: 51 data centres worldwide with more than 1.5 gigawatts of active power as of Jun 30, 2026, and approximately 4.2 gigawatts of contracted power as of its Aug 11, 2026 earnings call. No rental prices were published with the announcement, and none of these figures changes any price on our board.

CoreWeave's chief operating officer, Sachin Jain, set out the reasoning in the announcement: “Our customers need more than access to computing capacity. They need infrastructure that performs reliably at scale and the ability to move data and workloads wherever their business requires.” The company says it is “expanding our global infrastructure and the network connecting it together, so customers can focus on building and improving AI rather than managing the complexity underneath it.” Source: CoreWeave's announcement, Oct 27, 2026.

The host's side of the deal is part of the story. atNorth, the Icelandic operator that runs DEN01, designs the site for GPU-intensive processing and supports renewable energy development through power purchase agreements. Its chief executive, Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson, said in the same announcement: “Modern workloads demand digital infrastructure that is not only high performance, but also energy efficient and responsibly operated,” pointing to infrastructure “helping warm local homes through heat reuse, contributing to the green transition.” The heat reuse agreement is not decoration: the cluster's surplus heat feeds Copenhagen's district heating network, reducing reliance on alternative heating sources.

Some background from our own provider record: CoreWeave is the Kubernetes-native GPU cloud on our board, and it sells by the node, not the card — most of its nodes hold 8 GPUs, so its published figures are node totals, and we show the per-GPU figure beside the true node cost. On the board today, checked Oct 27, 2026, CoreWeave's B200 works out at $8.60 per GPU — $68.80 for the 8-GPU node — and its H200 at $6.31 per GPU. Copenhagen changes none of those figures; what it changes is where the capacity sits. What to watch next: whether the new European capacity shows up as new published rates or regions on CoreWeave's pricing page, and whether the network points of presence land on the schedule the announcement sets — beginning later in the fourth quarter of 2026, with the full loop extending to mid-2027.

Two phrases in the announcement are worth translating. “Petabit-scale” describes a network backbone able to move a petabit — a thousand terabits — of data; AI training and checkpoint traffic between regions is exactly the load that needs it, and the announcement specifies multiple 400 gigabit-per-second connections at each new point of presence. And the Copenhagen wording is precise: the majority of the planned 22.5 MW is online, not all of it — the remainder is still to come, which makes DEN01 a capacity story with a second instalment. The systems themselves are NVIDIA Blackwell connected with NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand, the high-bandwidth, low-latency fabric used to make many GPUs behave like one machine — the standard recipe for serious training clusters, now planted in Denmark.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters, this is capacity geography, not a price move: more Blackwell supply in northern Europe, and a provider investing in moving data between regions as seriously as in the GPUs themselves. New capacity in a new region is the kind of supply growth that can soften regional prices over time — we will be watching whether it shows up in CoreWeave's published rates, which were re-checked today and are unchanged.

/story/nvidia-meta-muse-partnership-vera.html:
NEWS →  ·  Industry · NVIDIA · Meta

NVIDIA and Meta expand their Muse partnership — and NVIDIA puts $3 billion into Meta's equity offering

Oct 27, 2026

Announced on Oct 27, 2026 in a joint NVIDIA and Meta release: deeper joint work on Meta's Muse models and agents, a broader Meta deployment of NVIDIA Vera Rubin, Vera CPUs, Spectrum-X Ethernet and BlueField-4 — and a $3 billion NVIDIA investment in Meta's equity offering.

Image: NVIDIA

The two companies will expand their partnership on Muse and the Muse family of models, working on optimisations across training and inference workflows to improve performance and total cost of ownership. They are also considering further collaboration on NVIDIA's OpenShell reference architecture for safe agent deployment and NVIDIA Sentry for monitoring agent behaviour. Source: the joint release via GlobeNewswire, Oct 27, 2026.

Meta intends to expand its deployment of NVIDIA infrastructure — Vera Rubin and Vera CPUs for its next-generation AI agents, with Spectrum-X Ethernet networking and BlueField-4 — aimed at maximum performance per watt. The release also states, in its own words, that NVIDIA will invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering.

One caution, stated plainly: Meta's own offering documents describe NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom as non-binding anchor interest of up to $5 billion combined, with no individual allocations — so the $3 billion figure is NVIDIA's statement in the joint release, not yet an allocated figure in Meta's filing.

The background a reader needs: Muse is Meta's own family of AI models and agents, and this release is about the machinery underneath it as much as the models themselves. Vera Rubin is the next NVIDIA platform generation after Blackwell — the generation that has not yet reached rental boards — alongside Vera CPUs; Spectrum-X Ethernet and BlueField-4 are the networking and data-processing pieces that tie large GPU clusters together. Meta's stated intention to expand its deployment of all of them, in the release's words for “its next-generation AI agents” and “aimed at maximum performance per watt”, is a demand signal for hardware most renters cannot yet buy an hour of.

The agent-safety half deserves a slower read. OpenShell is NVIDIA's reference architecture for safe agent deployment, and Sentry its approach to monitoring agent behaviour; the release says the two companies are also considering further collaboration on both. In plain terms: as models move from answering questions to taking actions, the guardrails and the monitoring are becoming products in their own right — and Meta and NVIDIA are signalling they intend to build those together too, alongside the training and inference optimisations for Muse itself, which the release frames as improving performance and total cost of ownership.

The money line needs its caution in full. The joint release states that NVIDIA will invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering. Meta's own offering documents, however, describe NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom together as non-binding anchor interest of up to $5 billion combined, with no individual allocations. Anchor interest is an expression of intent ahead of an offering, not a completed purchase, and “non-binding” means what it says. Until a filing names an allocation, the $3 billion is NVIDIA's statement of its own intent, and it is reported here as exactly that. What to watch next: Meta's filing, for any named allocation; any timetable the two companies give for the expanded Vera Rubin deployment; and, for renters, the first Rubin-generation listings anywhere — which is when this partnership starts to touch the prices on our board.

Why “performance per watt” is the phrase to underline: at datacentre scale, electricity is the binding constraint, not floor space. A provider's sellable capacity is set by the power it can bring to the building, so a platform generation that does more work per watt raises the ceiling on every future rental board — including, eventually, ours. That is also the honest limit of this story for renters today: nothing in the release changes a single price, a single available GPU, or a single delivery date that a renter can act on. It is a direction marker with two of the industry's largest names on it, dated Oct 27, 2026 — and direction markers are what Price Watch's demand pattern is built from, each one labelled as interpretation rather than reported as a price fact.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters this changes no price today. What it does is lock more frontier-model demand onto NVIDIA's next Rubin generation before that hardware reaches rental boards — one more dated data point in the same direction as this month's repeated price rises: demand for the newest GPUs is still growing faster than supply. Price Watch follows that pattern, labelled as interpretation.

NEWS →  ·  Providers · Oracle · NVIDIA

Vera Rubin is rentable now: NVIDIA’s next generation is generally available on Oracle Cloud

Oct 27, 2026

Announced by NVIDIA and Oracle at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on Oct 27, 2026: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and NVIDIA Vera CPUs are generally available on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure — the first cloud rental route to the post-Blackwell generation — with a multi-gigawatt expansion planned and an eight-GPU Rubin server to follow.

Image: NVIDIA

What is live now: Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs on OCI. Each NVL72 rack connects 72 Rubin GPUs through NVLink; OCI Superclusters combine the racks with Oracle Acceleron networking, NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet (Spectrum-6 switches) and BlueField-4 DPUs, on a network the release says scales across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. CPU and GPU resources scale independently, so the agent-era work between model calls — executing tools, testing code, retrieving data — is not forced into fixed GPU bundles. Source: the joint NVIDIA and Oracle release via GlobeNewswire, Oct 27, 2026.

What is planned, and stated as planned: growing those Superclusters to multi-gigawatt scale, and an HGX Rubin NVL8 — eight Rubin GPUs on NVLink in an x86 server with two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 CPUs, 4TB of DDR5 memory and 6.4 Tbps of RDMA networking — the smaller Rubin unit most teams would actually book. Neither announcement carried rental prices, so nothing changes on our price board today; we will add OCI’s Rubin rates the day Oracle publishes them.

The demand evidence inside the release is OpenAI: it says it has trained and served GPT-6 Astra on an OCI Supercluster of more than 100,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs in Abilene, that it is bringing Vera CPUs into production for its agentic sandbox workloads, and that Vera Rubin on OCI gives it the performance and scale to accelerate training and serve more demanding workloads. Those are OpenAI’s statements in the release, quoted as such — the same week our Price Watch recorded Verda’s fourth price rise in five days.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters and builders, the headline is the crossing point: Rubin has moved from roadmap to generally available cloud capacity at a hyperscaler, so ‘when can I rent it?’ has its first real answer. The honest limits: GA at NVL72 scale is aimed at frontier training and large inference, not single-card rentals; no prices were published; and the eight-GPU NVL8 is still to come. What to watch is whether neoclouds follow with published per-hour Rubin rates — that is when this starts moving the board.

Google’s TPUs are coming to Oracle’s cloud — the first time they can be rented outside Google

Oct 27, 2026

Announced by Oracle and Google at Oracle AI World on Oct 27, 2026: Google’s Tensor Processing Units will be available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure — the first hyperscale cloud outside Google to offer them — starting in calendar year 2027, built on the eighth-generation TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference.

Image: Google

The deal, from the joint release via PR Newswire, Oct 27, 2026: OCI provides the power, cooling and datacentre networking to run Google TPUs at scale inside Oracle’s infrastructure, for large-model training and post-training (dense and mixture-of-experts models) and production inference for reasoning, agentic and long-context work. Availability is calendar 2027, ramping over a multi-year period, and no prices were published — a dated commitment to track, not a product anyone can book today.

The hardware is Google’s eighth TPU generation in two purpose-built designs: TPU 8t for training — Google says nearly 3x the compute performance per pod over the previous generation — and TPU 8i for inference, built for the iterative work of many specialised agents. Google’s own TPU page, read Oct 27, 2026, puts shape on it: 8t superpods scale to 9,600 chips, and 8i claims an 80% performance-per-dollar improvement over previous generations for low-latency inference on large MoE models. Both figures are Google’s, stated as theirs.

The same event filled in the rest of Oracle’s non-NVIDIA bench: SambaNova’s own release (Oct 27, 2026) says Oracle will host its SambaRack SN50 inference systems in OCI data centres and offer the capacity to AI model builders; Reuters reported the same day that Cerebras inference systems are also joining OCI in 2027; and Oracle’s own launch post named OpenAI’s Jalapeño inference chip among the silicon coming to OCI. One cloud is assembling NVIDIA, Google, SambaNova, Cerebras and OpenAI silicon under one bill.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Until now, renting a TPU meant renting Google Cloud — the chips were a walled garden, never offered on a rival platform. From 2027, builders get a second route to TPU capacity, inside the same cloud that today made NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin generally available, which turns architecture choice into a price comparison instead of a cloud migration. The watch-outs are in the dates: nothing here is bookable until 2027, the ramp is multi-year, and neither side published rates. When OCI TPU pricing appears, it belongs on a comparison board like ours — we will check it the day it does.

/story/reflection-beam-501b-open-weights.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Reflection

Beam 1.0: a 501B open-weight agent model under Apache 2.0 — weights live on Hugging Face

Oct 27, 2026

Launched by Reflection on Oct 26, 2026, with the open weights live on Hugging Face: Beam 1.0 is a 501-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model for agentic coding and tool use — 23.4B active parameters, a 1M-token context window and an Apache 2.0 licence with no revenue gate. It is also a multi-GPU job: the BF16 weights alone are about 1,003GB.

Image: Reflection

What shipped, from the model’s own Hugging Face card and repository, read Oct 27, 2026: an instruction-tuned mixture-of-experts model (52 layers — 3 dense, 49 MoE; 256 experts, 8 active per token), 501.3B total and 23.4B active parameters, a 1M-token context window, English-first, knowledge cutoff Jun 30, 2026, a chat template and a full safety report. The release ships in three numerics — BF16 (188 files, about 1,003GB in the repository), FP8 and NVFP4 builds — public and ungated, with the Apache 2.0 licence file in the repo.

The scores are Reflection’s own, published on the card and stated as such: SWE-bench Verified 81.6, GPQA Diamond 90.6, AIME 2026 97.7, Terminal-Bench 2.1 80.1, SWE-Bench Pro 66.1 and HLE 51.1 with tools (36.0 without). The card’s efficiency claim is that Beam reaches comparable solution quality to leading open models using roughly 3x fewer reasoning tokens. No third party had reproduced the table when this story was published — treat every figure as maker-reported until outside runs agree.

The serving maths, by our published method (parameters × bytes, plus headroom): full BF16 needs about 1,003GB of weights — sixteen 80GB cards before KV cache; the 8-bit build halves that to roughly 501GB, an 8-GPU node; the NVFP4 build lands near 251GB, which fits four 80GB cards tightly. Nobody serves Beam on one card, and the 23.4B active count is what keeps its per-token cost closer to a 23B model than a 501B one. We have added Beam to the model catalogue with these figures. One honesty note: Reflection also sells a hosted API, and its card’s stated token prices disagree with launch-day reporting — so we publish no API rate for it.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For builders, a frontier-scale Apache 2.0 checkpoint with no revenue gate or custom licence changes the build-versus-buy maths for agent systems: you can download it, fine-tune it and ship it commercially today. The limits are equally plain: the benchmark table is the maker’s own, the safety report is the maker’s own, and the rental bill starts at a four-card node even in the smallest build. When independent benchmarks land, we will update this story and the catalogue entry.

AMD’s Helios rack is running at Meta — with a custom MI450 GPU and a $1 billion stake

Oct 27, 2026

Announced by AMD on Oct 27, 2026: its Helios rackscale systems are installed and being tested at Meta ahead of a broader deployment, Meta will deploy a custom Instinct GPU built on the MI450 architecture, and AMD will invest $1 billion in Meta’s equity offering — the strongest production proof yet for the non-NVIDIA rack path.

Image: AMD

What is running, from AMD’s own newsroom release, Oct 27, 2026: initial Helios rackscale systems are installed and being tested by Meta on the path to a broader deployment in the near future; Instinct GPUs are already in production at Meta for training, ranking and recommendation; and EPYC processors power the dedicated environments behind Meta’s Muse agent, with millions of EPYC chips deployed and Meta a lead customer for 6th-generation EPYC. Lisa Su’s line in the release: ‘With Helios now running at Meta, we are taking that partnership to a new scale.’

The silicon path it sets: Meta was an early definition customer for the MI450 architecture and will deploy a custom Instinct GPU optimised for its workloads; the collaboration is also informing the MI500 series and next-generation rackscale systems. On software, AMD delivered Day-0 ROCm support for Meta’s Muse Spark Open on Instinct GPUs and for Muse Glimmer on Ryzen AI PCs and Radeon GPUs — new open Meta models runnable on AMD the day they land.

The money line, stated plainly: the release says AMD will invest $1 billion in Meta’s equity offering. Read it beside today’s other Meta story — NVIDIA’s $3 billion statement in the joint Muse release, and Meta’s own filing describing the anchor interest as non-binding, with no individual allocations. The figures are the companies’ statements; allocations are still Meta’s to confirm.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters, Helios at Meta matters because rack-scale AMD only becomes bookable capacity once a hyperscaler proves it in production — that proof is what cloud hosts and neoclouds wait for before ordering racks that builders can rent. Nothing here is a rental product or a price today, and broader deployment is still ‘in the near future’ in AMD’s own words. The watch item is the first provider to publish Helios or MI450 rates; until then, the board’s AMD picture is unchanged.

Ling-3.1-flash-1019: a 560B MIT-licensed MoE drops its weights — sized for 8×H200

Oct 27, 2026

Released by Ant Group’s inclusionAI on Hugging Face on Oct 27, 2026: the weights for Ling-3.1-flash-1019, a 560-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 25B active parameters and a 1M-token context window, under the MIT licence. Until today the upgraded model was API-only; now it can be self-hosted — on a full node.

Image: inclusionAI

What shipped, from the model’s own Hugging Face card and repository, read Oct 27, 2026: a hybrid-linear mixture-of-experts model (63 KDA layers + 9 Gated MLA; 512 routed experts, 8 active per token), 560B total and 25B active parameters, a 1M-token context window, the MIT licence in the repo, public and ungated. The shipped weights total about 574GB. It is a post-training upgrade of Ling-3.1-flash, aimed at reasoning and agentic work.

The gains are as reported on the card, which cites Artificial Analysis: Intelligence Index 44, up from 41 for the predecessor; AA-Briefcase up from roughly 1,400 to 1,524 Elo; AutomationBench-AA 62% to 68%; CritPt 18% to 26%; SciCode 54% to 57%. Artificial Analysis is an independent benchmarker, but these figures are inclusionAI’s card quoting it — treat them as card-reported until checked against the underlying listing.

The serving facts are unusually concrete, from the same card: day-0 SGLang support with a published recipe for 8×H200 (tensor and expert parallelism 8) or 4×GB300, a vLLM route at tensor parallelism 8, and verified recipes also listed for H800, H100 and B200. By our published method the memory maths agree with the maker’s sizing: about 1,120GB at FP16, roughly 560GB at 8-bit — the shipped build’s class — and about 280GB at 4-bit. This is a node rental, priced like one; nobody runs it on a single card.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For builders, an MIT-licensed 560B with no revenue gate and a same-day serving recipe is the useful kind of weights drop: the licence question and the hardware question are both answered on day one. The honest limits: the benchmark figures are card-reported, the model ships with custom modelling code, and the entry ticket is an 8-GPU node. We have added it to the model catalogue with the memory maths.

/story/runpod-batch-inference-generally-.html:
NEWS →  ·  Providers · RunPod

RunPod makes Batch Inference generally available — 20% off on H100, H200, B200 and B300 for work that can wait

Oct 28, 2026

Announced by RunPod on Oct 28, 2026: Serverless Batch Inference is now generally available. Work that can wait runs on dedicated batch workers at up to 30% off on-demand pricing — 20% off on H100, H200, B200 and B300 — through the same endpoint that already serves your real-time traffic.

Image: RunPod

What launched, in RunPod's own announcement (Oct 28, 2026): batch requests go to the same queue-based Serverless endpoint as live traffic, but run on dedicated batch workers with your own model and container, so a bulk job does not take capacity from interactive requests. Limits, per RunPod: up to 3 million requests a day depending on the account, up to 5,000 requests in one batch and up to 10 active batches on an endpoint. Requests are plain JSON, sent in the console or by API call — no input file to upload and no output bucket to read afterwards.

The price angle is the headline. Batch requests are billed on compute time per request at up to 30% off on-demand pricing, depending on GPU type; on H100, H200, B200 and B300 the discount is 20%. Cancelling a batch stops the charges: queued requests are not billed, while requests already running finish and are billed. One honest gap, stated by RunPod itself: there is no cost estimate before you finalize a batch — its own advice is to run a 100-request test batch first and extrapolate. For clarity on what did NOT change: RunPod's pod prices are a separate rate card, and we re-read them today, Oct 28, 2026 — Secure Cloud is unchanged, with H100 SXM still at $3.99/hr and B200 at $7.99/hr.

The trade is time. Start times are not guaranteed, requests run in no set order, and RunPod tells users to plan for multi-hour latency — its own guidance is to keep the real-time endpoints for anything a user is waiting on. The workloads it names as fits are the classic deferrable ones: embedding a corpus, evaluation runs, dataset scoring, overnight processing and backfills over an existing image or document library, plus launch-day backlogs where the batch absorbs bulk volume while the live endpoint serves users.

Why this matters beyond one provider: batch discounts are how clouds fill idle GPUs. Off-peak capacity that would otherwise sit empty gets sold at a discount to work that is flexible about when it runs, which is why the same pattern — a cheaper tier for patient work — keeps appearing across the industry. It lands in a week when the on-demand side of the market moved the other way: Verda raised its on-demand prices today for the fifth time in six days (see Price Watch). A renter with flexible work now has a slightly wider gap between the patient price and the impatient one, and that gap, not any single rate, is the number worth watching.

What it means if you rent GPUs

If your workload can wait hours, RunPod just made it about a fifth cheaper on the four GPUs most people rent — no migration, same endpoint, same container. If it cannot wait, nothing changes for you: real-time rates are untouched, batch start times are explicitly not guaranteed, and pod prices were verified unchanged today.

A GPU spot exchange is coming: EverXCloud opens pre-launch sign-ups for hourly GPU rental by bid

Oct 28, 2026

Announced by EverXCloud Inc. on Oct 28, 2026: a US spot exchange where GPU hours are bought at the market price, or by placing a bid and waiting to be matched. Registration is open now; renting starts between mid-December 2026 and early January 2027.

Image: EverXCloud via everxcloud.ai

How it is meant to work, from the company's own launch release (Oct 28, 2026): offers from EverXCloud's own machines, partner data centres and other infrastructure providers sit in one account; EverXCloud, a Delaware corporation, is merchant of record for every rental, whichever provider sits behind it. Each offer shows its GPU, region, price and conditions, with prices per GPU-hour excluding tax. Accounts are prepaid, and rentals are managed from a web portal or a REST API. The company says it also commits its own capital to contract GPU capacity for the exchange, under the same matching and ranking rules as every other seller.

What is not live yet: the renting. The company's site, read Oct 28, 2026, says 'Offers open on launch day', and the release states plainly that prices shown during the pre-launch period are indicative. Its market page already shows a latest-rentals ticker — an H100 SXM hour at $1.68 among them — but nothing can actually be rented until launch, so no EverXCloud figure appears on our price board, and none will until the exchange is live and its prices can be checked like everyone else's. Pre-launch accounts can claim $10 of GPU credit with the code EVERXCLOUDGPU, an offer the company says runs until Jan 31, 2027.

The pitch, in director Zachary Astruc's words in the release: 'GPU compute has become one of the most important resources in the economy, yet most teams still rent it the way we bought airline tickets in the 1990s: fixed price lists, opaque availability, no real market.' The site already publishes specification pages for nearly 100 GPU models, side-by-side comparisons, rental-cost guides and a glossary in twelve languages — a content-led launch aimed at the same searching renters this journal serves, which is itself a sign of where new entrants now think demand is found.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters, this is one to watch rather than budget around: a bid-based spot exchange could undercut fixed price lists on flexible work, but only if launch-day liquidity is real — an exchange with thin supply is just another list. We have added EverXCloud to our tracked-provider census as a directory entry with no prices, the same treatment every provider gets here until its prices are public and checkable. When it launches, we will check its prices the day they open.

/story/nemotron-3-5-transcribe-open-weig.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · NVIDIA

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is open: NVIDIA’s 40-language speech model drops its weights — and runs on one GPU

Oct 28, 2026

Released by NVIDIA on Oct 28, 2026: an open-weight speech model that transcribes 40 languages, labels up to eight speakers, translates 31 languages to or from English and answers questions about a recording — 34 billion parameters in total, about 4.3 billion active, under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence, in BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 builds.

Image: NVIDIA

What shipped, from the model’s own Hugging Face card (nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B), read Oct 28, 2026: the release date is Oct 28, 2026 across Hugging Face, GitHub (NVIDIA NeMo Speech), NGC and Build.Nvidia.com. The checkpoint pairs a Nemotron-3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B hybrid Mamba-2–Transformer mixture-of-experts language backbone with a 600M-parameter speech encoder and a roughly 99M-parameter speaker encoder — 34B parameters in total including the audio encoder, about 4.3B active per token. Context is 65,536 tokens and recordings can run up to one hour. Output is steered by plain-language prompts: verbatim or cleaned-up transcripts, speaker tags, word-level timestamps, translation, or questions about the audio. NVIDIA released Granary v2 alongside it — the open data pipeline behind the model, whose public manifest covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in Granary v1.

The scores, all NVIDIA-reported on the card and its Hugging Face announcement, read Oct 28, 2026: first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard for English at 5.33% average word error rate, the lowest multilingual result in its comparison at 4.62% mean WER across seven languages, and the lowest long-form result at 10.98%. On Artificial Analysis’s speech-to-text index it ties for first among open-weight models at 2.8% AA-WER while activating about 4B parameters, against 24B for the model it ties. For speaker attribution it posts the lowest diarization error rate of the 14 systems on David AI’s 21-language track, at 18.26%. These are the maker’s published figures, not our measurements — independent reproductions are the thing to watch.

The licence is part of the news. The weights are released under OpenMDW-1.1, and the card states plainly that the model is ready for commercial or non-commercial use — no revenue gate, no separate commercial licence to negotiate. FP8 and NVFP4 builds ship alongside the BF16 reference weights, and hosted endpoints are offered by Baseten, DeepInfra and Simplismart for anyone who would rather not self-host. One honest limit, in NVIDIA’s own framing: this is an offline model for recorded audio — internal chunking does not make it a live-streaming transcription service.

The renter maths is unusually friendly for a model this capable. The card’s own deployment line is a single H100 80GB, and the arithmetic agrees: 34B parameters at BF16 is roughly 68GB of weights, which fits one 80GB card; the FP8 build is roughly 34GB, inside a 48GB card with headroom; the NVFP4 build is roughly 17GB, inside a 24GB card. NVIDIA reports that with its optimised NIM implementation, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU transcribes up to 2,238 seconds of audio per second using NVFP4 with its DFlash2 speculative-decoding draft model — while noting, on the same card, that those serving optimisations are not yet part of the open-source release, and the shipped vLLM integration is expected to run about two times slower. In its medical fine-tuning case study, adaptation cut word error rate on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt-only result.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Transcription is one of the steadiest GPU workloads there is, and it just got a strong open option that fits on a single rented card — at 4-bit, on a 24GB card. If you run speech pipelines, the build-versus-buy question now has a real open-weight candidate with a commercial-use licence and published numbers to test against. Test them: every score above is NVIDIA’s own until someone reproduces it.

/story/amazon-ecs-gpu-sharing-nvidia-mps.html:
NEWS →  ·  Providers · AWS

Amazon ECS can now share one NVIDIA GPU between several tasks — the idle half of your card is rentable again

Oct 28, 2026

Announced by AWS on Oct 28, 2026: Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS), so several ECS tasks can run at the same time on a single NVIDIA GPU — each with its own memory ceiling — instead of one task holding a whole card it only half uses.

Image: NVIDIA via developer.nvidia.com

What launched, in AWS’s own announcement (Oct 28, 2026), with the mechanics confirmed in AWS’s ECS documentation read the same day: a container now requests a GPU share instead of a whole GPU, setting a required memory amount in MiB as a hard ceiling and an optional maximum compute percentage, which works as a cap rather than a reservation — idle compute flows to neighbours on the same GPU. Placement is by memory: ECS adds up the memory requested by a task’s GPU containers and places it on a single GPU with that much free. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on EC2, and AWS says it is available in all AWS commercial and GovCloud (US) regions.

The workloads AWS names are the ones that waste cards today: small-model inference, embedding generation, multi-model serving and AV/ADAS simulation — jobs that use a fraction of a GPU and previously left the rest idle. On Managed Instances, ECS also watches the MPS daemon itself: if it stops or turns unhealthy, the instance is drained and replaced and tasks move to healthy capacity. EC2 users need ECS container agent 1.107.0 or later and the ECS AL2023 GPU-optimised AMI version 20261019 or later, per the coverage of the launch terms.

The honest limits, from the same launch material: MPS sharing is software-level, not hardware isolation — containers on one GPU share a CUDA context, so a fatal error in one can affect the others on that GPU, and AWS does not recommend sharing for large training jobs or workloads that need hardware-level isolation. Sharing is not available on Fargate, and on shared GPUs ECS stops emitting per-task GPU utilisation and memory metrics, though instance-level metrics remain. It is the same sharing technology NVIDIA has been extending on its own side: its CUDA 13.4 technical post (Oct 27, 2026) added memory-enforced GPU sharing for Kubernetes, with per-workload memory boundaries applied by its open-source GPU Fractioning Operator.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Anyone serving small models on AWS has been paying for whole GPUs and using fractions of them. ECS GPU sharing turns that idle capacity back into usable capacity on the biggest cloud there is — no code changes, at the cost of weaker isolation than a dedicated card or a MIG slice. For renters elsewhere, it is one more sign of where the market is heading: the GPU you rent is increasingly a share of a GPU, priced and packed accordingly.

RTX Spark laptops are on shelves from $2,599 — and the 64GB DGX Spark is on sale

Oct 28, 2026

In NVIDIA’s local-AI update of Oct 28, 2026: RTX Spark laptops — a Blackwell RTX GPU and a Grace CPU on one superchip, with up to 128GB of unified memory — are available now from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI, starting at $2,599, and the 64GB version of the DGX Spark desktop is now available to purchase from manufacturer partners.

Image: NVIDIA

What is on sale, in NVIDIA’s own post (Oct 28, 2026), read in full: RTX Spark laptops combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance, in designs as thin as 14mm and as light as three pounds, with 128GB configurations on shelves at the $2,599 starting price. The same post’s ICYMI section confirms the DGX Spark 64GB — the GB10 Grace Blackwell desktop with 64GB of unified memory, DGX OS and the NVIDIA AI software stack, for agent development, inference and fine-tuning — is now available to purchase from manufacturer partners; its partner rollout began Oct 23, 2026. NVIDIA states no DGX Spark price in the post, and we do not print one.

The software arriving with the hardware matters as much as the shelves: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, NVIDIA’s open-weight speech model released today (see our story), runs on RTX Spark; Liquid AI’s LFM3 open model family has day-zero support through llama.cpp and vLLM; and new resource-management controls in the NVIDIA App let a user split GPU resources between a foreground application and a background agent — the local version of the packing problem every renter knows from the cloud side.

Why the desk covers a laptop: 128GB of unified memory on a $2,599 machine changes the own-versus-rent maths at the small end. Models that fit in that pool — and a growing list of open weights do, at 4-bit — can now run locally all day for the price of a few hundred rented GPU-hours, while rented cards keep the work that needs data-centre memory, NVLink or burst scale. The DGX Spark 64GB halves the original desktop’s memory at what partners position as a lower entry point; NVIDIA has published no scaling benchmarks for the multi-unit Spark clusters it announced earlier this month, and that remains the open question on the platform.

What it means if you rent GPUs

The Spark line is NVIDIA’s attempt to own the desk the way it owns the data centre: CUDA, the same models, no cloud bill for the work that fits. For renters, every workload that moves to a $2,599 laptop is one that never reaches the board — worth watching precisely because it competes with the smallest rented cards.

Worth knowing

An open-weight speech model: transcription in 40 languages, translation between English and 31 languages, speaker labels for up to eight speakers and questions about recordings up to one hour long, all steered by plain-language prompts. 34B parameters in total including the audio encoder (a 30B-A3B hybrid Mamba-2–Transformer MoE backbone plus speech and speaker encoders), 65,536-token context, BF16/FP8/NVFP4 builds. By our method: BF16 weights are roughly 68GB — one 80GB card (the card’s own deployment line is 1× H100 80GB); FP8 roughly 34GB — a 48GB card; NVFP4 roughly 17GB — a 24GB card. NVIDIA-reported scores (not independently verified): first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR English leaderboard at 5.33% average WER, and Granary v2, its open training-data pipeline, was released alongside it. It is an offline model — not a live-streaming service.

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. Real figures move with context length and software.

Microsoft and Alphabet spent $96.6 billion in one quarter — and GPU capacity still arrived late

Oct 29, 2026

Reported on Oct 28, 2026: Microsoft's Azure grew 48% and Alphabet's Google Cloud more than doubled, both powered by demand for AI compute — and Microsoft said deliveries of third-party GPU capacity it had counted on arrived late. For anyone who rents GPUs, these two earnings calls are the demand story behind this month's rising rental prices, in the buyers' own numbers.

Image: Microsoft via news.microsoft.com

Microsoft's quarter (fiscal Q1 2027, reported Oct 28, 2026, from its earnings release and call): revenue $92.3 billion, up 19%; Azure revenue grew 48% to more than $33 billion — the first time Microsoft has sized Azure on its own; capital spending was $45.2 billion, with about 75% going to short-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs. The renter-relevant line came from CFO Amy Hood: some third-party capacity deliveries Microsoft expected in the quarter were delayed — that is GPU-as-a-service capacity Microsoft buys from outside providers, the same pool independent renters draw from. The delay is why capex landed below the more-than-$50 billion Microsoft had expected; it guides next quarter's capex above $50 billion and Azure growth of 49–50% in constant currency, and says demand still exceeds supply.

Alphabet's quarter (Q3 2026, reported Oct 28, 2026, from its earnings release and call): revenue $127.6 billion, up 25%; Google Cloud revenue $30.7 billion, up 103% year on year, with cloud operating income of $11.1 billion. Alphabet said sales of TPU systems — Google's own AI chips, sold as complete systems — were a meaningful driver of that Cloud growth, and the call disclosed new TPU partnerships with Oracle and Crux AI to put TPU systems in external data centres. Alphabet's capex was $51.4 billion in the quarter and its free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion: it is spending faster than the cash comes in to build AI capacity.

Put the two together and the quarter's AI-infrastructure spend is $96.6 billion from just two buyers — and it still was not enough to get GPU capacity delivered on time. CNBC reported that CoreWeave and Nebius shares slid about 5% in extended trading on Microsoft's delayed-deliveries line, which tells you how directly the rental market now trades on hyperscaler capacity news. Every figure in this story is from the two companies' own releases and calls of Oct 28, 2026, as reported from those documents.

What it means if you rent GPUs

This is the demand side of the price board, stated by the buyers themselves. While the largest customers cannot get GPU capacity delivered on schedule, rental prices have little room to fall — October's pattern on our own board (Nebius on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, Verda now six rises in seven days) is what that pressure looks like at retail. The second thread to watch: Alphabet selling TPU systems into other clouds — Oracle will offer TPUs from 2027 — is a new competitor surface to GPU rental, and it arrived inside an earnings release.

NEWS →  ·  Models · Mistral AI

Mistral Large 4 weights are out — the 1-trillion-parameter ‘Le Chonk’ is downloadable, and it takes eight GPUs to serve

Oct 29, 2026

Published on Hugging Face on Oct 29, 2026: Mistral has released the weights of Mistral Large 4, its 1.05-trillion-parameter multimodal flagship, for anyone to download and self-host — under a modified-MIT licence with one catch that matters directly to GPU providers. The checkpoint is FP8, a smaller NVFP4 build targets Blackwell cards, and Mistral’s own serving recipes run it across eight GPUs. Here is what it is, what the licence actually says, and what that eight-GPU node costs at today’s checked rental prices.

Image: Mistral AI

What dropped, from Mistral’s own Hugging Face model card and repository record, both read on Oct 29, 2026: the repository mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B is live and ungated (last modified Oct 29, 14:51 UTC). The card describes a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model — 1.05 trillion parameters in total, 49 billion active per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers), 128 routed experts with 4 active per token plus one shared expert, a 1-million-token context, text and image input with text output, and native fluency in 160+ languages. It was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s own European datacentres, and the final weights are stronger than the Oct 6 public preview after three more weeks of reinforcement learning: on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index it scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model GLM-5.3 while using 47% fewer tokens per task, and 26 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, the highest score among western open-weight models — all figures as reported by Mistral on the card.

The licence, in the card’s own words: Large 4 is released under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, ‘a modified version of the MIT license, for both commercial and non-commercial use — operating a Model-as-a-Service business requires a separate commercial license with Mistral.’ The trigger is what you do with the model, not how large your revenue is: use it, modify it, fine-tune it and build commercial products on it freely, but if you want to sell access to the model itself as a service, you need Mistral’s separate commercial licence first. That clause is aimed squarely at the rental and inference providers in our price board’s world. NVIDIA announced the same day that Large 4 is also available as an NVIDIA NIM microservice, with a try-out in its API catalogue — a managed route for teams that want the model without running the eight-GPU node themselves. Alongside the weights, Mistral serves the model itself as mistral-large-4 on its API at $0.70 per million input tokens, $0.07 for cached input and $2.10 per million output tokens (Mistral’s listed release pricing, Oct 29, 2026) — roughly half the $1.36 / $4.18 preview rates of Oct 6.

What it takes to run, from the same card: the main checkpoint is FP8 (the repository configuration is FP8-quantised, which is why 1.05 trillion parameters land at roughly 1,050GB of weights by our method — total parameters × 1 byte at 8-bit), and a separate NVFP4 checkpoint with a smaller footprint targets Blackwell GPUs. Mistral’s recommended vLLM recipe and its SGLang recipe both serve the model with tensor parallelism across 8 GPUs — an eight-GPU node — and the checkpoint carries an embedded DSpark speculative-decoding draft head that Mistral measures at up to 1.9× higher throughput. No single GPU can run this alone. At the board’s checked prices of Oct 29, 2026, that eight-GPU node costs $59.20/hr on B300 (8 × Hyperstack’s $7.40/hr best offer, about $43,200 a month run around the clock) or $47.84/hr on B200 (8 × RunPod Community’s $5.98/hr best offer, about $34,900 a month). The NVFP4 build roughly halves the weight memory (about 525GB by our method), which brings smaller Blackwell setups into reach — the model page below works through every fit from the same arithmetic.

What it means if you rent GPUs

This is the largest Western open-weight release of the year, and it lands directly on the rental market twice over. First as demand: a flagship that needs an eight-GPU Blackwell node to serve is exactly the high end of the board, on the same day Microsoft told investors its third-party GPU capacity had arrived late. Second as a warning label: the Model-as-a-Service clause means a provider cannot simply download Large 4 and start selling endpoints — that route runs through a separate Mistral licence, and any listing that skips it is a risk a renter is sharing. For builders choosing between the API and their own node, Mistral has priced the API keenly at $0.70 / $2.10 per million tokens, so at today’s checked prices self-hosting’s case is control, privacy, customisation and very high sustained volume — not small-scale savings. That is our reading of the dated figures above.

MODEL DEPLOYMENT →  ·  2026-10-29 · 10 min read

Thinking of deploying Mistral Large 4? Here’s how — and what it actually costs

Mistral’s Large 4 — “Le Chonk” — landed on Hugging Face on Oct 29, 2026: about a trillion parameters, free to download, and far too big for any single graphics card. This page does the deployment maths in the open: how much memory each version needs, the smallest rental setups that honestly hold it, what those setups cost per hour, per day and per month — and the point where renting GPUs beats paying per token, and where it doesn’t.

The verdict

  • Can one GPU run it? — No. About 1 trillion parameters (1.05T on Mistral’s detailed count, 49B active per token) — no single card holds it at any useful precision.
  • Smallest honest setup — 8× B200 or 8× B300, one node — the FP8 checkpoint, served tensor-parallel across 8 GPUs, the shape of Mistral’s own recipes.
  • FP8 cost — 8× B200 from $47.84/hr — $1,148.16 a day, $34,923.20 a month always-on.
  • The smaller download — NVFP4 checkpoint (610 GB) → 4× B200 from $23.92/hr or 3× B300 from $22.20/hr.
  • Self-host cost per 1M tokens — $3.32 on the 8× B200 setup — at a printed assumption of 4,000 tokens/sec (an assumption, not a benchmark).
  • Mistral’s own API — $0.70 in / $2.10 out per 1M tokens — cheaper per token than self-hosting at ordinary volumes.
  • Licence watch-out — Self-hosting is allowed. Selling access to it as a hosted service needs a separate commercial licence from Mistral.
Compare prices for this model — ranked for Mistral Large 4→Find a GPU→

The memory maths

The method is the one we print on every model page: memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter, plus about 20% headroom for the context cache and serving overhead. Mistral’s detailed count is 1.05 trillion total parameters (a 1.6B vision encoder included), with 49B active per token — 52B including embeddings and output layers. The active count decides speed; the total count decides memory. And here the arithmetic can be checked against reality, because we also summed the actual files on Hugging Face on Oct 29, 2026.

Memory by version — the method checked against the real download

VersionBy the methodThe real downloadPlan on (with headroom)Smallest honest setup
FP8 — the main checkpoint≈1,050 GB (1 byte per parameter)1,060.6 GB (54 files)≈1,260 GB8× B200 (1,536 GB) or 8× B300 (2,304 GB)
NVFP4 — the 4-bit Blackwell checkpoint≈525 GB (half a byte per parameter)610.0 GB (32 files)≈630 GB4× B200 (768 GB) or 3× B300 (864 GB)
FP16 — full precision≈2,100 GB (2 bytes per parameter)—≈2,520 GBNot a practical rental shape — nobody sane rents for this

The real NVFP4 download (610.0 GB) is bigger than the raw 4-bit arithmetic (525 GB) — the format carries scaling data alongside the weights. Plan on the real file size, not the formula, whenever the two disagree; here both point at the same setups. File sizes are the shard totals read on Hugging Face, Oct 29, 2026. Watch out — context eats memory too. Large 4 accepts up to 1M tokens of context. The longer the conversations and documents you serve, the more extra memory (the KV cache) the server sets aside on top of the weights. The 20% headroom is a planning allowance, not a promise: Mistral’s own serving notes advise lowering the maximum context length and concurrency if you run short of GPU memory. If filling the whole 1M window is your use case, the B300 setups’ extra memory per card is worth real money to you.

What the setups cost

Cheapest verified offers, checked Oct 29, 2026: B200 from $5.98/GPU/hr on RunPod’s Community Cloud, B300 from $7.40/GPU/hr at Hyperstack. Multiplied out into the whole setups the memory maths demands:

SetupPer hourPer day (24 hrs)Always-on month (730 hrs)
8× B200 — FP8 (RunPod Community, 8 × $5.98)$47.84$1,148.16$34,923.20
8× B300 — FP8 (Hyperstack, 8 × $7.40)$59.20$1,420.80$43,216.00
4× B200 — NVFP4 (RunPod Community, 4 × $5.98)$23.92$574.08$17,461.60
3× B300 — NVFP4 (Hyperstack, 3 × $7.40)$22.20$532.80$16,206.00

Every rental figure here is a whole-setup price — cards × the per-GPU rate — because that is what you actually pay. Per-GPU headlines are shown alongside, never instead. Community Cloud availability varies — a card at the best price is not guaranteed to be free the moment you look. You do not have to run a node around the clock: the same 8× B200 setup rented 8 hours a day, 30 days a month (240 hours) costs $11,481.60. Renting bills every hour the node is up, working or idle — remember that when the API comparison below looks expensive.

Compare prices for this model — ranked for Mistral Large 4→Find a GPU→

Or skip the GPUs: what the APIs charge

The honest alternative to deploying Large 4 yourself is not deploying it at all. Mistral sells the same model by the token, and the frontier closed models sell theirs. Prices below were read on each maker’s own pricing pages on Oct 29, 2026. Printed assumptions (not measurements): (1) the rented node serves an aggregate 4,000 tokens per second, input and output combined, under a realistic mixed load — we have not benchmarked Large 4; your real figure depends on your traffic shape, context lengths and settings. (2) API usage is blended at 3 input tokens to 1 output token, uncached. At half the assumed throughput, every self-host figure below doubles; at double, it halves.

RoutePriceCost per 1M tokensThe catch
Self-host — FP8 on 8× B200$47.84/hr flat$3.32 (at the printed assumption)You run it, you staff it, it bills while idle
Self-host — NVFP4 on 4× B200$23.92/hr flat$1.66 (at the printed assumption)Smaller node, same responsibilities
Mistral API — mistral-large-4$0.70 in / $2.10 out per 1M (cached input $0.07)$1.05 blended at the printed mixSame model, someone else’s GPUs — and Mistral’s batch API halves the price again for work that can wait
OpenAI API — GPT-6 Astra (frontier closed)$10.00 in / $50.00 out per 1M (cached input $1.00)$20.00 blended at the printed mixA frontier closed model: top-tier capability, zero operations, priced like it

Against Mistral’s own API, self-hosting almost never wins on price. An always-on 8× B200 node costs $34,923.20 a month. At the blended $1.05 per 1M tokens, you would need to push about 33.3 billion tokens a month through the API before it cost the same — a sustained average of roughly 12,700 tokens per second, around the clock. Almost nobody’s workload looks like that. If the model itself is what you want and per-token price is the whole question, Mistral’s API is the rational buy. Against a frontier closed API, the maths flips early. At GPT-6 Astra’s blended $20.00 per 1M tokens, the same always-on node breaks even at about 1.75 billion tokens a month — a sustained average of only about 665 tokens per second. A genuinely busy product crosses that line, and past it every additional token on your own node is effectively free until the node saturates. That is the real self-hosting bargain: not “cheaper than the model’s own API”, but “frontier-class capacity at a flat rate”.

What the money can’t settle

Control. Self-hosted weights are pinned: the model cannot be changed, deprecated or repriced underneath you, and you can fine-tune it. An API model is whatever the provider serves this month. Privacy and residency. On your own node, prompts never leave your infrastructure — for legal, medical, financial and security work (the fields Mistral says this model is aimed at) that can be the whole decision, before price enters it. Zero operations. The API side never pages you at 3am, never waits for a scarce 8-GPU node to free up, and bills nothing while you sleep. The rented node bills every hour it exists. Frontier quality. GPT-6 Astra is a frontier closed model and priced as one; Large 4’s published benchmark scores are Mistral-reported and strong among open weights, but “strongest open model” and “strongest model” are different claims, and which one your task needs is a testing question, not a pricing one.

Steps

1. The standard route is vLLM, tensor-parallel across the node

Mistral recommends vLLM for production serving of Large 4 and publishes a ready-made Docker image for it; its own example serves the FP8 checkpoint with --tensor-parallel-size 8 — the weights are sharded across all 8 GPUs of one node, which is why the smallest honest FP8 setup is an 8-GPU node and not, say, a very patient pair of cards. SGLang is the other first-class route, with its own published cookbook for this model. Feed it requests through its OpenAI-style API and it is, from your application’s side, just an endpoint.

2. Two details from the card worth knowing

The checkpoint ships with an embedded DSpark speculative-decoding draft head, which Mistral measures at up to 1.9× the throughput — that is Mistral’s own measurement, not ours. And the separate NVFP4 checkpoint targets Blackwell GPUs (B200 and B300 are both Blackwell), is served by the same vLLM/SGLang route, and Mistral states it keeps the same performance at the smaller footprint — again, the maker’s claim, printed as such. There is also an NVIDIA NIM microservice if you would rather run inside NVIDIA’s supported stack.

Alternatives

Every speed-derived figure here rests on a printed assumption

The $3.32 and $1.66 per-1M-token costs assume 4,000 tokens/sec aggregate. We ran no benchmark for this guide, and no independent Large 4 serving benchmark existed to check against at publication. If your real throughput is 2,000 tokens/sec, self-hosting costs twice what this page’s headline says — the break-even conclusions against the frontier API survive that, the ones against Mistral’s API were never close.

The maker’s speed claims are labelled, not adopted

The DSpark draft head’s “up to 1.9× throughput” and the NVFP4 checkpoint’s “same performance” are Mistral’s own statements from its model card, printed as claims. The same applies to Large 4’s benchmark scores in our news coverage — Mistral-reported.

Best-offer prices are a snapshot, and availability is real

Rental figures are the cheapest verified offers from the Oct 29, 2026 check. Community Cloud nodes at the best price come and go; an 8-GPU node in the region you need may cost more than the headline when you actually book. The live comparison carries today’s figures.

An 8-GPU node is an operations commitment

One node, one point of failure. Serious deployments budget for a second node or accept the downtime risk — either way the always-on figures above are a floor, not a ceiling.

Compare prices for this model — ranked for Mistral Large 4→Find a GPU→

The licence, in plain words

Large 4 is released under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License — a modified version of the MIT licence — read on the model’s Hugging Face card on Oct 29, 2026. Download and self-host: yes. Commercial and non-commercial use are both allowed — running it inside your own company or product is fine. Selling it as a hosted service: not on this licence. Operating a Model-as-a-Service business on these weights — charging others to query your deployment — requires a separate commercial licence from Mistral. There is no revenue threshold in the term we read; the trigger is the hosted-service activity itself. Building on Mistral’s API instead (the per-token route above) is ordinary API terms — the MaaS question only arises for the weights. This is a plain-words summary of the headline term, not legal advice. Read the licence itself before building a business on the weights.

How we know

Verified

  • Model facts — 1.05T total parameters including a 1.6B vision encoder, 49B active per token (52B including embeddings and output layers), 128 routed experts with 4 active plus 1 shared, 1M context, text and image input, trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs — read on Mistral’s own Hugging Face model card and Mistral’s documentation on Oct 29, 2026, the day the weights were released
  • File sizes are the safetensors shard totals summed from the same repos the same day: FP8, 54 files totalling 1,060.6 GB; NVFP4, 32 files totalling 610.0 GB
  • Serving route — vLLM recommended, tensor-parallel size 8, official Docker image; SGLang cookbook as the alternative; the embedded DSpark draft head — is from Mistral’s card
  • Licence summary is from the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License as linked on the card, read Oct 29, 2026
  • Rental prices are the cheapest verified offers from our daily check of Oct 29, 2026 (B200 $5.98/GPU/hr RunPod Community Cloud; B300 $7.40/GPU/hr Hyperstack), multiplied into whole setups
  • API prices read on Oct 29, 2026 on Mistral’s own model documentation (mistral-large-4: $0.70 input / $0.07 cached input / $2.10 output per 1M tokens; batch discount per Mistral’s pricing FAQ) and on OpenAI’s official API pricing page (GPT-6 Astra: $10.00 input / $1.00 cached input / $50.00 output per 1M tokens)

Still unverified

  • Throughput — the cost-per-1M-token and break-even figures are arithmetic on the checked prices and the two printed assumptions (4,000 tokens/sec aggregate throughput; a 3:1 input-to-output token mix). The throughput is an assumption for comparison, not a measured result, and we ran no benchmark for this guide
  • Mistral’s performance figures — the DSpark draft head’s up-to-1.9× figure and the NVFP4 checkpoint’s same-performance claim — are the maker’s own statements wherever they appear, labelled as claims

Nothing else on this page is estimated.

Batch is the new spot: what RunPod’s 20% batch discount does to the maths for work that can wait

On Oct 28, 2026, RunPod made Serverless Batch Inference generally available: send requests in bulk, let them run when RunPod’s batch workers get to them, and pay 20% less than the on-demand rate on H100, H200, B200 and B300. This page does the maths on that trade — what the discount is worth in dollars, and what you give up for it.

The verdict

  • H100 SXM — RunPod Secure — Real-time $3.99/hr. Batch, at the announced 20% off, works out at $3.19/hr (calculated) — save $0.80/hr, $798 per 1,000 GPU-hours.
  • H200 — RunPod Secure — Real-time $5.29/hr. Batch works out at $4.23/hr (calculated) — save $1.06/hr, $1,058 per 1,000 GPU-hours.
  • B200 — RunPod Secure — Real-time $7.99/hr. Batch works out at $6.39/hr (calculated) — save $1.60/hr, $1,598 per 1,000 GPU-hours.
  • B300 — RunPod Secure — Real-time $8.99/hr. Batch works out at $7.19/hr (calculated) — save $1.80/hr, $1,798 per 1,000 GPU-hours.
  • The price of the discount — Batch start times are not guaranteed. The trade is not “your job may be stopped” — it is “your job may be started late”. See the catch below before you move anything.
Compare prices→Find a GPU→

What batch inference actually is

Real-time inference answers one request at a time, the moment it arrives — a person is waiting on the other end. Batch inference is the opposite shape: you hand over a large set of requests at once, they are processed in bulk, and you collect the results when the set is done. Nobody is waiting on any single answer, so the work can be scheduled whenever capacity is free. RunPod’s version, per its Oct 28 announcement and its documentation: batch requests go to the same queue-based Serverless endpoint that already serves your real-time traffic, but run on dedicated batch workers with your own model and container — a bulk job does not take capacity from interactive requests. Requests are plain JSON, sent from the console or by API: create a batch, finalize it to start processing, then poll for status and progress with per-request counts. The limits, per RunPod: up to 3 million requests a day depending on the account, up to 5,000 requests in one batch and up to 10 active batches on an endpoint. Billing is on compute time per request, at up to 30% off on-demand pricing depending on GPU type — 20% off on H100, H200, B200 and B300. That last point is why the comparison on this page is drawn the way it is. Spot pricing, the older “cheap if you’re flexible” deal, discounts capacity that can be taken away. Batch discounts something different: work that can wait in a queue. Whether that trade is worth 20% depends entirely on the job, which is what the rest of this page is for.

Worked examples — what 20% is worth

Three common shapes of deferrable work, costed both ways at the verified rates above. The hours are your variable — multiply your own GPU-hours by the per-hour saving in the verdict table.

JobReal-timeBatchSaving
Overnight corpus embedding — 200 H100 GPU-hours a night$798.00 / night$638.40 / night$159.60 / night · $4,788 over 30 nights
Evaluation / dataset scoring run — 1,000 H200 GPU-hours$5,290$4,232$1,058
Synthetic data generation — 500 B200 GPU-hours$3,995$3,196$799

Arithmetic: real-time = GPU-hours × the verified Secure on-demand rate; batch = the same hours × the rate with 20% off. Your mileage varies only with your hours — the discount itself is a flat fifth on these four GPUs.

Compare prices→Find a GPU→

What did not change

Batch is a new lane, not a price cut. RunPod’s real-time and pod prices are a separate rate card, re-read on Oct 28, 2026 — the day batch launched — and again on Oct 30, 2026. Secure Cloud is unchanged, and the Community rates are unchanged in our records from Oct 19–30:

Rate cardH100 SXMH200B200B300
RunPod Secure (on-demand)$3.99/hr$5.29/hr$7.99/hr$8.99/hr
RunPod Community (pods)$2.69/hr$3.59/hr$5.98/hrNot listed

If your work cannot wait, Oct 28 changed nothing about what you pay. It is also worth noting the week batch landed in: on-demand list prices elsewhere rose again the same day (Verda’s fifth rise in six days at that point — and Verda has risen twice more since, seven rises in eight days to Oct 30; see Price Watch). The patient lane is getting cheaper relative to the impatient one; that gap is the number to watch.

The catch, stated plainly

Start times are not guaranteed. RunPod says so itself: requests run in no set order, and its own guidance is to plan for multi-hour latency and keep real-time endpoints for anything a user is waiting on. There is no cost estimate before you commit — RunPod states this openly: you cannot see the bill before you finalize a batch, and its own advice is to run a 100-request test batch first and extrapolate from what that costs. Cancelling is fair, but not free: cancel a batch and the charges stop — queued requests are not billed — but requests already running finish, and are billed. And the discount is against on-demand rates. One honest check: RunPod’s Community Cloud pod rates are lower than Secure on these cards (H100 $2.69/hr, H200 $3.59/hr, B200 $5.98/hr, checked Oct 30, 2026) — a batch H100 at $3.19/hr does not beat a Community pod you manage yourself. Batch wins against the on-demand rate card, on the endpoint you already run, with no pod to babysit. If your alternative was already a self-managed Community pod, run that comparison before switching.

Steps

1. Split your workload by deadline, not by habit

Most inference estates are a mix: some requests a user is waiting on, and a long tail of bulk work that drifted onto real-time endpoints because that was the default. The bulk tail is where the 20% lives.

2. Run RunPod’s own test first

A 100-request test batch tells you your real per-request compute time. Extrapolate from that, never from a guess — there is no estimate screen coming to save you.

3. Cost the switch honestly

Batch hours × your per-hour saving (the verdict table) is the gross win. Set it against the cost of results arriving hours later. If the second number is zero — genuinely zero — the switch is free money.

4. Keep the real-time endpoint for the front door

RunPod’s own guidance, and ours: batch behind it, for the work that can queue.

Alternatives

Switch: work with a deadline measured in hours or days

Embedding a corpus or re-embedding it after a model change; evaluation runs and benchmark sweeps; dataset scoring, labelling and filtering; overnight processing and backfills over an image or document library; launch-day backlogs — the overflow a real-time endpoint cannot absorb; synthetic data generation. These are also the workloads RunPod itself names as fits. The common thread: the result is wanted by morning, not by the second.

Do not switch: anything someone is waiting on

Interactive chat and API traffic with a person on the other end; endpoints with a latency promise to your own users; jobs with a hard deadline inside the multi-hour window — a start time you cannot control is the wrong tool; and small one-off jobs: two GPU-hours of batch saves you roughly $1.60–$3.60 at these rates, so if waiting costs you anything at all, it costs more than that.

Compare prices→Find a GPU→

How we know

Batch terms (20% off on H100/H200/B200/B300, up to 30% off on other GPU types, up to 3M requests/day, 5,000 requests per batch, 10 active batches per endpoint, start times not guaranteed, cancellation billing, no upfront cost estimate, the 100-request test advice) are from RunPod’s own announcement of Oct 28, 2026, read in full the day it published; the create–finalize–poll mechanics are from RunPod’s documentation (docs.runpod.io, Batch Jobs), checked Oct 28, 2026. Real-time rates are RunPod Secure Cloud on-demand prices read on runpod.io/pricing in our full verification sweep of Oct 19, 2026, re-read unchanged on Oct 28 and Oct 30, 2026, and banked in our daily price records (Oct 19–30). RunPod publishes the batch discount as a percentage, not a per-GPU batch price list — every batch figure on this page is the verified real-time rate with that announced discount applied (exact: $3.192, $4.232, $6.392, $7.192 per hour), and is labelled “calculated” for that reason. Pod prices are a separate RunPod rate card and are quoted here only for the comparison in the catch section.

/guide/h200-vs-mi325x-rental.html:
GPU SELECTION →  ·  2026-10-30 · 8 min read

H200 vs MI325X for inference — the honest rental maths

On paper, AMD’s MI325X beats NVIDIA’s H200 where inference hurts most: 256GB of memory against 141GB, and 6 TB/s of bandwidth against 4.8. But there is a catch nobody puts in the headline — you can barely rent an MI325X at all: no verified price list we checked carries one. This page does the comparison honestly: the H200 prices you can actually pay today, the AMD prices that actually exist (MI300X and MI355X, verified on Oracle’s own list), and the one comparison the spec sheet can’t settle for you.

The verdict

  • NVIDIA H200 — Rentable today — cheapest verified rental $3.59/hr on RunPod Community.
  • AMD MI300X — Rentable today — $6.00/hr at Oracle OCI’s list price.
  • AMD MI355X — Rentable today — $8.60/hr at Oracle OCI’s list price.
  • AMD MI325X — The one you searched for — no published price on any list we verified (checked Oct 27–28, 2026). See the honest section below.
Compare prices→Find a GPU→

The specs that matter for inference

Inference is a memory game. Two numbers decide most of it: how much model and KV cache a card can hold (capacity), and how fast it can stream weights while generating tokens (bandwidth). Everything in the table below is from the makers’ own product pages, checked Oct 28, 2026. The short version of the whole guide: the H200 is cheaper per GPU-hour everywhere we can verify a price. The AMD cards win on memory per card — and memory, not the hourly rate, is what decides the bill when your model doesn’t fit on one H200. The maths for both cases is below.

The spec sheet

Sources: NVIDIA’s H200 product page (nvidia.com); AMD’s Instinct product pages (amd.com) for MI300X, MI325X and MI355X. Bandwidth figures are the makers’ published peak figures — spec-sheet numbers, not measured throughput on any provider’s machines.

GPUMemoryMemory typePeak bandwidthArchitecture
NVIDIA H200141GBHBM3e4.8 TB/sHopper
AMD MI300X192GBHBM35.3 TB/sCDNA 3
AMD MI325X256GBHBM3e6.0 TB/sCDNA 3
AMD MI355X288GBHBM3e8.0 TB/sCDNA 4

Read the table the way an inference engineer does. Every AMD card here holds more than an H200 — the MI300X by about a third, the MI325X by over 80%, the MI355X by more than double. AMD makes the same point itself: its MI325X platform material claims 1.8× the memory capacity and 1.3× the memory bandwidth of the competing platform — that is AMD’s own comparison, attributed to AMD, and on the raw spec numbers it is fair. NVIDIA’s counter is not in this table: it is the CUDA software ecosystem and the sheer number of places you can rent the card, which is where the rental maths starts.

The H200 rental market, verified

The H200 is one of the most widely rented GPUs in the world, and it shows in the spread of prices. These are the verified on-demand rates from our checks — the specialist-cloud rows from our daily board check of Oct 30, 2026, the hyperscaler rows from Oracle’s and Microsoft’s official lists as dated in the method box (monthly figures at 730 hours, the standard month we use across the site):

ProviderPer GPU/hrPer month (730h)Terms to know
RunPod Community$3.59$2,621Community cloud — availability varies by host
Hyperstack$3.99$2,913Single-GPU VMs
RunPod Secure$5.29$3,862Secure Cloud tier
Nebius$5.40$3,942Excl. VAT
