Same GPU, a near-3× spread between the cheapest community offer and hyperscaler list. That spread — not the chip — is the first thing to get right when you rent an H200.

Compare prices→Find a GPU→

The AMD side: the prices that actually exist

AMD silicon rents through far fewer doors. The cleanest verified public prices we found are on Oracle’s own cloud price list, read Oct 27, 2026 — Oracle publishes AMD Instinct per GPU per hour, globally, in USD:

GPU (Oracle OCI)Per GPU/hrPer month (730h)The shape you actually buy
MI300X — 192GB HBM3, 5.3 TB/s$6.00$4,3808-GPU bare-metal shape, $48.00/hr ($35,040/mo)
MI355X — 288GB HBM3e, 8.0 TB/s$8.60$6,2788-GPU bare-metal shape, $68.80/hr ($50,224/mo)
H200 on the same list — for a like-for-like read$10.00$7,3008-GPU bare-metal shape, $80.00/hr ($58,400/mo)

Two honest observations. First, like-for-like on one provider’s list, AMD is cheaper: on OCI, an MI300X GPU-hour costs 40% less than an H200 GPU-hour, and the MI355X — with double the H200’s memory and two-thirds more bandwidth — still costs less per GPU-hour than Oracle’s H200. Second, the buying shape is different: OCI sells these as 8-GPU bare-metal machines, so the real entry ticket is the shape total, not the single-GPU rate. Specialist clouds rent the H200 one card at a time from $3.59/hr; that door does not exist for AMD silicon on any price list we verified this week.

What the maths actually says

If your model fits on one H200, rent the H200. A 70B model at 8-bit needs roughly 70GB of weights — comfortably inside 141GB with room for KV cache. At the cheapest verified rates you pay $3.59/hr for the H200 against $6.00/hr for the cheapest verified AMD card. Per GPU-hour, per month, and per GB of memory ($0.025/GB/hr for the best H200 offer vs $0.031/GB/hr for OCI’s MI300X), the H200 wins every simple comparison. There is no honest way to make AMD cheaper for a workload a single H200 already holds. If your model does not fit on one H200, the comparison flips. Take a workload needing about 180GB — say a 70B model at full FP16 precision (≈140GB of weights) with a long-context KV cache on top. On NVIDIA you rent two H200s: 2 × $3.59 = $7.18/hr at the best verified rate. One MI300X holds it on a single card at $6.00/hr — about 16% less per hour, one card instead of two, and no tensor-parallel split to manage. At 288GB, one MI355X ($8.60/hr) replaces two H200s for anything up to that size and still undercuts two mid-priced H200s (2 × $5.29 Secure = $10.58/hr). Capacity is the AMD argument, and when capacity is the binding constraint, it is a real one. Bandwidth per dollar is closer than the headlines suggest. Dividing published peak bandwidth by the cheapest verified hourly rate: H200 ≈ 1.34 TB/s per $/hr, MI355X ≈ 0.93, MI300X ≈ 0.88. That is spec-sheet arithmetic, not a benchmark — real token throughput depends on the serving stack — but it shows why “AMD has more bandwidth” does not automatically mean “AMD is cheaper to run”: the H200’s low rental floor buys a lot of bandwidth per dollar.

Steps

1. Pick the H200 if your model fits in 141GB

Most 70B-class serving at 8-bit or 4-bit does. You also start today at the lowest verified rate, on the CUDA stack your team probably already uses, with no porting project. Cheapest verified start: RunPod Community at $3.59/hr; the steadier tiers run $5.29–$6.31/hr.

2. Pick the MI300X if your workload sits in the 141–192GB band

Too big for one H200, wasteful on two — and your serving stack runs on ROCm (vLLM and SGLang both support it). One card at $6.00/hr on OCI beats two H200s at any verified rate above $3.00/hr each.

3. Pick the MI355X if you need the biggest single-card memory on the rental market

288GB — very large models, very long contexts, big KV caches — and you are buying at node scale anyway. At $8.60/hr per GPU on OCI it is the strongest memory-per-card offer we can verify.

4. Don’t plan a rental around the MI325X

As of Oct 28, 2026 there is no published self-serve price for it on the lists we verified. If your heart is set on that exact card, you are in talk-to-a-sales-team territory, and any quote you get is a negotiation, not a market price.

Alternatives

The honest part: you can barely rent an MI325X

This guide is titled H200 vs MI325X because that is the comparison people search for. Here is what we found when we went looking for an MI325X rental price, checked Oct 27–28, 2026. No provider on our verified board publishes a self-serve MI325X rental price — not one. Every AMD figure in this guide therefore runs on the MI300X and MI355X, the AMD cards with real, checkable prices, and is labelled as such. The hyperscaler lists we verified don’t carry it either: Oracle’s official price list — the most complete public AMD list we found — prices the MI300X and MI355X and skips the MI325X entirely. And the card itself is a generation behind AMD’s flagship: the MI325X is a CDNA 3 part; AMD launched its CDNA 4 successor line, the MI350 series, on June 12, 2025, and the MI355X is the card hyperscalers are building new capacity around. The MI325X mostly lives in enterprise clusters bought outright, not in hourly rental catalogues. So if a page quotes you a precise “MI325X rental price” to two decimal places, ask where it was read and on what date. We couldn’t find one on any provider’s own published pages — and rather than invent one, we have compared the H200 against the AMD cards you can genuinely rent today. If a verifiable MI325X rate appears, this page will carry it, dated, like every other price we publish.

The software question underneath all of this

It is a real cost either way: the H200 runs the CUDA ecosystem your team probably already uses; the AMD cards run ROCm, which is open-source and much improved, but still the path more likely to need tuning time from your engineers. Price that time honestly — a cheaper GPU-hour that costs a week of porting is not cheaper.

Compare prices→Find a GPU→

How we know

H200 rental prices are GPUJournal’s own board figures: read on each provider’s published pricing pages and banked daily (records Oct 19–30, 2026; the Oct 30 check carries RunPod Community $3.59, Hyperstack $3.99, RunPod Secure $5.29, Nebius $5.40, Verda $6.25 and CoreWeave $6.31, the last normalised from its published 8-GPU node rate of $50.44/hr). AMD and OCI H200 prices come from Oracle’s official Cloud Price List, read Oct 27, 2026, which publishes per-GPU hourly USD prices (MI300X $6.00, MI355X $8.60, H200 $10.00); Oracle sells these as 8-GPU bare-metal shapes, and the shape totals in this guide are Oracle’s per-GPU price × 8. Azure’s H200 figure ($84.80 per 8-GPU VM/hr, East US 2, = $10.60/GPU) comes from Microsoft’s official Retail Prices API, read Oct 28, 2026. Hardware specs are from NVIDIA’s H200 product page and AMD’s Instinct MI300X, MI325X and MI355X product pages (amd.com, nvidia.com), checked Oct 28, 2026; AMD’s “1.8× capacity, 1.3× bandwidth” platform claim is AMD’s own and is attributed to AMD where used. Monthly figures use 730 hours. The worked examples use the site’s standard weight arithmetic (parameters × bytes per parameter: FP16 = 2, 8-bit = 1) before KV cache and overheads — they are fit estimates, not benchmarks, and no throughput figure in this guide is presented as measured. The MI325X availability finding is dated Oct 28, 2026 and covers the providers and official lists named above; it will be re-checked as new lists are verified.

/guide/inference-metrics-gpu-cost.html:
INFERENCE OPTIMIZATION →  ·  2026-10-30 · 8 min read

TTFT, TPOT, throughput, goodput — the inference metrics that decide your GPU bill

Every explainer defines these four metrics and stops there. Definitions don’t pay rent. This page puts a price on each one: what a slow first token, a slow stream, and a flattering throughput average actually cost you at real, dated rental prices.

The verdict

  • TTFT — How long before the first token appears. It decides whether users wait — and how much you pay for prompt processing.
  • TPOT — How long each following token takes. It decides how fast one user’s answer streams.
  • Throughput — Total tokens per second, all users together. It decides your cost per token — the number your bill is made of.
  • Goodput — Throughput counting only requests fast enough to count. It decides your real cost per token, after the flattery is removed. The bill itself is one line: cost per million tokens = hourly price ÷ tokens per hour — everything below is about which metric sets the tokens per hour you actually get.
Compare prices→Find a GPU→

The four metrics, in plain words

When a model answers, two different kinds of work happen. First the GPU reads your whole prompt and works out what to say — that’s prefill. Then it writes the answer one token at a time — that’s decode. Each metric watches a different part of that process. TTFT (time to first token) is the time from sending your request to the first token coming back; it covers queueing plus prefill, so long prompts — big documents, agent histories — make it grow, and users feel it as “is this thing working?”. TPOT (time per output token) is how long each token after the first takes to arrive — one user’s reading speed: 20 ms per token = 50 tokens a second for that user; 120 ms per token = about 8 a second, which feels like a slow typewriter. NVIDIA reported 272.6 tokens/sec single-stream for its Nemotron Bolt E4B on an RTX 5070 (NVIDIA, Oct 23, 2026, company-reported) — that’s a TPOT of about 3.7 ms, the fast end of what one stream can feel like. Throughput is every token produced for every user at once — the number in vendor headlines, and the one that sets your cost per token, because you rent the GPU by the hour, so tokens per hour is what your money buys. Goodput is the honest version of throughput: throughput counting only the requests that met your latency targets — say, first token under half a second and TPOT under 50 ms. Tokens delivered too slowly to use are not output you can sell, serve, or ship; goodput counts them as what they are — waste you paid for. You don’t buy tokens; you buy GPU hours, and the metrics decide how many tokens each hour contains. Three formulas cover almost every inference bill: cost per 1M output tokens = hourly price ÷ (throughput in tokens/sec × 3,600) × 1,000,000; cost per request = hourly price ÷ (requests/sec × 3,600); one user’s stream speed = 1,000 ÷ TPOT in ms, in tokens/sec.

Worked example 1 — the same work, priced two ways

Stated assumptions (a worked example, not a benchmark): a 70B-class model served on one H100 SXM, producing 2,000 output tokens/sec in total. Hold the serving speed exactly the same and rent the card from two real offers on our board:

Offer (checked Oct 30, 2026)Hourly priceTokens per hourCost per 1M tokens
TensorDock — H100 SXM (8-GPU minimum at this rate)$2.25/GPU/hr7.2M$0.31
RunPod Secure — H100 SXM$3.99/GPU/hr7.2M$0.55

Same GPU, same model, same speed — the hourly gap flows straight through. RunPod Secure’s rate is 77% higher, so its cost per million tokens is 77% higher: $0.55 vs $0.31. When throughput is equal, the cheapest hour wins, full stop. Throughput is rarely equal, which is the next example.

Worked example 2 — when the pricier card is the cheaper token

Stated assumptions (a worked example, not a benchmark): the same model, now served on a B200 that delivers 4,000 output tokens/sec — twice the H100’s throughput above. Rent it at RunPod Community’s verified B200 rate:

SetupHourly priceAssumed throughputCost per 1M tokens
H100 SXM — RunPod Secure$3.99/hr2,000 tok/s$0.55
B200 — RunPod Community$5.98/hr4,000 tok/s$0.42

The B200 hour costs 50% more and produces tokens about 25% cheaper — if it really doubles throughput on your model. That “if” is the whole game, and it is checkable before you rent: the B200 breaks even at roughly 3,000 tok/s (1.5× the H100 figure), because $5.98 ÷ $3.99 ≈ 1.5. Below that, the cheaper hour wins; above it, the faster card wins. Never argue about which GPU is “faster” — argue about tokens per second per dollar on your own workload, and measure it in the first rented hour. Requests work the same way: at 2,000 tok/s with an average 500-token reply, one H100 handles 4 requests/sec — 14,400 an hour. At RunPod Secure’s $3.99/hr that is about $0.28 per 1,000 requests. Long replies cost more per request at the same throughput; the formula above is the honest way to see it.

Compare prices→Find a GPU→

Which metric matters for your workload

WorkloadMetric that decides the billWhy
Chat / live productTTFT and TPOT, judged as goodputUsers feel the wait and the stream speed. A cheap hour that answers slowly is churn, not savings — price your tokens at the goodput rate, not the headline rate.
Batch / offline jobsRaw throughput, nothing elseNobody watches a batch job run. Latency targets vanish, so cost per token is pure throughput per dollar — and providers know it: RunPod’s Batch Inference, made generally available Oct 28, 2026, sells exactly this at up to 30% off on-demand (20% off on H100/H200/B200/B300), with start times not guaranteed.
AgentsTTFT, paid again at every stepAn agent waits for the model dozens of times per task, often with a long history to re-read — prefill and TTFT dominate, and the honest unit is cost per completed task, not per token. A slow first token, multiplied by every step, is where agent bills quietly grow.

Worked example 3 — the goodput trap, with numbers

Stated assumptions (a worked example, not a benchmark): the same H100 SXM at RunPod Secure’s $3.99/hr, your latency target is TPOT under 50 ms, and you tune the same server two ways:

TuningHeadline throughputRequests meeting the targetGoodputReal cost per 1M tokens
A — big batch3,000 tok/s60%1,800 tok/s$0.62
B — moderate batch2,200 tok/s98%2,156 tok/s$0.51

Tuning A wins every headline and loses the only comparison that matters. Its average is fast; its goodput — tokens delivered at a speed users accept — is lower, so each usable million tokens costs about 20% more. This is the goodput trap: averages hide the tail, and the tail is where your users live. Whenever a benchmark, a provider, or your own dashboard gives you a tokens-per-second figure, ask the follow-up: at what latency, and what share of requests met it?

Batching: the trade you are always making

Serving one request at a time wastes most of a GPU — decode reads the model’s weights from memory for every token, so the card spends its time fetching, not computing. Serving many requests together (a bigger batch, more concurrency) lets one weight-read feed many tokens at once. Total throughput climbs steeply. That is real, and it is why throughput headlines are quoted at batch sizes you would never serve to a live user. The bill for that throughput arrives in the other two metrics. Every added stream shares the same GPU, so each stream slows: TPOT rises. And when requests queue behind a full batch, TTFT rises with them. A 200-token reply at a TPOT of 20 ms takes 4 seconds to stream; at 120 ms it takes 24. The provider’s dashboard calls both configurations “3,000 tokens a second”. Your users call one of them broken. So: raise concurrency until goodput peaks, not until throughput peaks — throughput keeps rising long after your latency targets start failing, and the setting that maximises throughput is almost never the setting that maximises saleable output. Quote your own numbers at your own batch size: any throughput figure without a batch size and a latency figure beside it is marketing, whoever publishes it. And split the workloads if you can — live traffic on a latency-tuned instance, bulk work on a throughput-tuned (or batch-priced) one. The two optima are different machines on purpose.

Steps

1. Decide your latency targets before you rent

A TTFT and TPOT your users accept, written down. Without targets there is no goodput, and without goodput there is no honest cost per token.

2. Price GPUs in tokens per dollar, not dollars per hour

The hourly rate is half the equation. Our comparison board carries the verified half; the throughput half is yours to measure, in the first hour, on your model.

3. Re-run the maths when prices move

The break-even between two cards moves with their prices — and prices have been moving: in October 2026 alone we verified rises at Nebius, RunPod Secure and Verda (seven rises in eight days, Oct 23–30). A GPU choice that won in September can lose in November on price alone.

4. Send batch work to batch pricing

If the work can wait, it should not pay live-serving rates. That discount exists precisely because throughput-only work is cheaper to serve.

How we know

The rental prices are GPUJournal’s own verified board prices, read on the providers’ own published pages and banked daily: TensorDock H100 SXM $2.25/GPU/hr (8-GPU minimum), RunPod Secure H100 SXM $3.99/hr and RunPod Community B200 $5.98/hr, all checked Oct 30, 2026 (full sweep Oct 19, 2026; daily snapshots since). Every throughput figure in the worked examples is an assumption chosen to make the arithmetic visible — 2,000 tok/s, 4,000 tok/s, the batch tunings — stated at the top of each example and never presented as a measured result; run the same formulas with your measured figures. The one measured figure quoted is NVIDIA’s own: 272.6 tokens/sec single-stream for Nemotron Bolt E4B on an RTX 5070, reported by NVIDIA on Oct 23, 2026 and labelled company-reported wherever we use it. RunPod’s Batch Inference discount (up to 30% off on-demand; 20% on H100/H200/B200/B300) is from RunPod’s own launch announcement, Oct 28, 2026. Definitions follow the standard serving vocabulary (TTFT, TPOT/inter-token latency, throughput, goodput as SLO-meeting throughput); the money arithmetic is ours.

AWS Trainium vs Inferentia vs just renting NVIDIA by the hour

AWS sells two chips of its own — Trainium for training, Inferentia for inference — and says they beat renting NVIDIA GPUs. Sometimes that’s true. It depends on whether you can commit, whether your models survive the move to AWS’s Neuron SDK, and whether you were going to stay inside AWS anyway. Here is the honest maths, profile by profile.

The verdict

  • A training run — Pick Trainium2 (Trn2), if your stack ports to Neuron — the cheapest big-node training hour inside AWS, level with the best open-market H100 rate before any throughput argument. 16 chips for $35.76/hr — $2.235/chip/hr.
  • A steady inference service — Pick Inferentia2 (Inf2) on a 1–3 year commitment — rental NVIDIA if you can’t commit. On-demand Inf2 is level with the cheapest rented L40S; the committed rates are where it pulls away: $0.76/hr on-demand → $0.30/hr on a 3-year term.
  • Bursty / experimental — Rent NVIDIA by the hour — no reservation, no SDK port, no commitment; you pay only for the hours you actually run. H100 from $2.25/GPU/hr, only when running.
  • One warning — A Trainium or Inferentia chip-hour is not the same amount of finished work as an NVIDIA GPU-hour. AWS’s own claim is that Trn2 delivers 30–40% better price-performance than its GPU-based P5e/P5en instances — that is AWS’s claim about its own instances, not something we have measured, and it says nothing directly about the open rental market. We compare prices and fit; we do not pretend chip-hours are interchangeable units of work.
Compare prices→Find a GPU→

What each chip actually is

AWS Trainium is the training chip. Trainium (in EC2 Trn1 instances) and Trainium2 (Trn2) are AWS-designed accelerators built for training large models. A Trn1 node carries 16 Trainium chips with 512 GB of shared HBM and up to 3 petaflops of FP16/BF16 compute. A Trn2 node carries 16 Trainium2 chips with 1.5 TB of HBM3 (96 GB per chip), up to 20.8 FP8 petaflops, linked by NeuronLink and 3.2 Tbps of EFA networking; four Trn2 nodes combine into a 64-chip UltraServer. Both are built to scale out in EC2 UltraClusters — tens of thousands of chips. The catch, in one sentence: your training stack has to run on the AWS Neuron SDK, not CUDA. There is also an access catch: Trn1 can be rented plain on-demand, but Trn2, on AWS’s own pages, is sold through EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML — capacity you reserve in advance and pay for up front. There is no walk-up, pay-as-you-go Trn2 rate on AWS’s pricing pages; the single-chip trn2.3xlarge appears in AWS’s Capacity Block table only in Hyderabad, Melbourne and São Paulo. AWS Inferentia is the inference chip. Inferentia2 (EC2 Inf2 instances) is built only for serving models, not training them. Each chip carries 32 GB of HBM; the largest Inf2 instance packs 12 chips (384 GB) with NeuronLink between them for models that don’t fit on one chip, and the family reaches up to 2.3 petaflops per instance. AWS claims up to 40% better price performance than comparable EC2 instances — again, AWS’s claim, about EC2. Inf2 is sold on-demand and on 1-year and 3-year Reserved terms, and it too runs on the Neuron SDK: your model must compile for Neuron before it serves a single request. The NVIDIA route comes two ways. Inside AWS, NVIDIA arrives as EC2 GPU instances: P5 (H100), P5e/P5en (H200), P6 (B200/B300) for training-scale work, G5/G6/G6e (A10G, L4, L40S) for smaller inference. Outside AWS, the same NVIDIA GPUs rent by the hour from specialist providers — the market our price board tracks daily. Either way you get CUDA: the ecosystem almost every open-weight model, serving stack (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang) and tutorial assumes by default. No port, no special SDK — in exchange, AWS’s own GPU instances are the most expensive way to rent an H100 we can price, as the ladder below shows.

The price ladder — per accelerator, per hour

AWS prices instances, not chips. Where AWS itself prints a per-accelerator figure on its Capacity Blocks pricing page, we use it; every other per-chip number below is an exact division, shown as such. Rental figures are the best verified on-demand offers on our board, checked Oct 30, 2026; AWS figures were read on AWS’s own pages on Oct 28, 2026.

Capacity Block rates are reservation rates — charged up front when you book, at the rate prevailing at purchase; AWS’s page says the current rates are scheduled to be updated next in January 2027. They are not walk-up on-demand prices, and we have not presented them as such anywhere in this guide. Read the ladder carefully and it tells the whole story in one view: inside AWS, AWS’s silicon is dramatically cheaper per accelerator-hour than AWS’s own NVIDIA instances — a Trainium2 chip-hour costs about 37% of an H100 chip-hour on the same AWS pricing page. But against the open rental market, AWS’s NVIDIA prices are the expensive option — the same H100 rents from $2.25/hr — and AWS’s silicon lands roughly level with the rental market’s best rates, not below them. Which side of that comparison decides your bill depends on your profile.

Profile 1 — the training run

One 16-accelerator node, running flat out for a two-week run (336 node-hours). Assume the job genuinely fits each platform — the porting question is dealt with below, and it is a real one.

OptionRate336 hours
Trn1 — AWS Capacity Blocks$9.532/node/hr$3,202.75

The honest reading: a Trn2 node-hour costs almost exactly the same as the cheapest rented H100 capacity ($35.76 vs $36.00) and far less than AWS’s own H100 nodes. But a two-week run only costs the same as the same two weeks of wall-clock if the job takes the same time on both — and that is precisely what we cannot promise from price pages. AWS claims Trn2 trains with 30–40% better price-performance than its P5e/P5en GPU instances; if that held against the rental H100s too, Trn2 would win this profile clearly. If your model hits a Neuron operator gap and trains 30% slower, the rental wins. The price pages can’t settle that — a one-day benchmark of your own model can, and at these run sizes it is worth doing before you book two weeks of anything. Note also that Trn1’s Capacity Block rate is the cheapest serious training capacity on this page by a wide margin — for jobs that fit the older chip, it is not close.

Profile 2 — the steady inference service

One accelerator, serving around the clock for a month (730 hours), month after month. This is where commitment changes everything.

OptionRatePer month (730 hrs)
Inf2 — 3-year Reserved$0.30/hr$219.00

On-demand, Inf2 and the cheapest rented L40S are level — $0.76 against $0.79 an hour buys you nothing by itself, and the L40S runs your existing CUDA serving stack today while the Inferentia chip needs the Neuron port first. The Inf2 case is the commitment: at the 3-year Reserved rate the same serving hour costs $0.30, well under half the rental floor — if the model still needs serving, on the same architecture, three years from now, and if it compiles and performs well on Neuron. Scale the model up and the picture tightens: AWS’s 12-chip inf2.48xlarge is $12.98/hr on-demand, against $9.48/hr for twelve L40S at the best rental rate — per raw accelerator-hour, big Inf2 on-demand is the more expensive option, and only its Reserved rates ($7.79/hr at 1 year, $5.19/hr at 3 years, from AWS’s Inf2 page) bring it back in front. Throughput per chip differs between all of these and is not measured here; treat these as capacity prices, not cost-per-request figures.

Profile 3 — bursty and experimental

Forty accelerator-hours a month, in irregular bursts: a fine-tune here, an evaluation there, a weekend prototype.

OptionRate40 hours

H100 SXM — RunPod Community rental$2.69/hr$107.60
H100 — AWS P5 (p5.4xlarge, Capacity Block rate)$5.970/hr$238.80

Bursty work is where the AWS silicon story mostly falls down — not on price, but on shape. Trn2 and the big Trn1 nodes are sold as advance reservations: you book the window, you pay up front, and an experiment you haven’t thought of yet can’t use them. Capacity Blocks are a planning tool, not a tap you turn on. The rental market is the opposite: an H100 in a few minutes, billed by the hour, gone when you stop it, running the CUDA stack your experiment already uses. The two honourable exceptions are in the table — Inf2 on-demand and the single-chip Trn1 are genuinely walk-up AWS silicon — but both still demand the Neuron port before the first experiment runs, which is a strange price to pay for work whose whole point is trying things quickly.

The hidden costs

The Neuron port is real work. Trainium and Inferentia do not run CUDA. Models move through the AWS Neuron SDK — compilation, operator coverage checks, and re-validation for every new model architecture you adopt. AWS says Neuron integrates natively with PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX, and for mainstream models that path is well trodden. But every custom kernel, exotic quantisation scheme or day-one open-weight release is a question mark until you’ve compiled it. Budget engineering days, not minutes, and budget them again each time your model changes. Commitment is the discount — and the risk. The prices that make AWS silicon win are commitment prices: Capacity Blocks paid up front for a reserved window, Reserved Instances over one to three years. If the workload shrinks, changes architecture, or moves, the commitment doesn’t. Rental NVIDIA by the hour has no equivalent trap: the worst case is this month’s bill. Lock-in compounds. A model tuned for Neuron, training scripts built on Trainium, serving compiled for Inferentia — each one makes the next move away from AWS more expensive. That may be a price worth paying; pay it knowingly. The CUDA route runs, unchanged, at dozens of providers and on your own hardware. Data transfer is a quieter line item: AWS charges per gigabyte for data transferred out to the internet, on a tiered schedule published on its EC2 on-demand pricing page — a cost that grows exactly when an inference service succeeds. Against that, the big names on our rental board include data downloads in the price: RunPod, Lambda, CoreWeave and Hyperstack all showed free egress in our Oct 19, 2026 verification. Moving training data and checkpoints in and out of AWS is a line item; at most rental providers it isn’t. And availability has a geography: on AWS’s own Capacity Block table, Trn2 capacity lists in US East (Ohio) and Hyderabad, and the single-chip Trn2 only in Hyderabad, Melbourne and São Paulo. If your data has to live somewhere else, the silicon may simply not be there. The rental market’s constraint is the opposite one — the cheapest offers move, and availability at the floor price is never guaranteed.

Steps

1. Pick Trainium

If you train repeatedly at node scale or beyond, you already live on AWS, your models are mainstream enough to compile cleanly on Neuron, and you can plan capacity ahead. Trn1’s Capacity Block rate is the cheapest training capacity in this guide; Trn2 is the current-generation pick, priced level with the best rented H100s before any throughput claim.

2. Pick Inferentia

If you serve the same models, at steady volume, for a year or more — and verify the Neuron port on your actual model before signing anything. The win lives in the 1-year and 3-year rates, not the on-demand one.

3. Rent NVIDIA by the hour

If your work is bursty, experimental, model-of-the-week, or simply not on AWS. You give up the commitment discounts and get back total flexibility: any model, the standard CUDA stack, any provider, stop any time. For a first training run or a new serving idea, that flexibility is usually worth more than the discount.

4. Use AWS’s own NVIDIA instances

Mainly when something other than price decides it — data already in AWS, compliance, an enterprise agreement. On price alone, they were the most expensive option in every profile above.

How we know

Every AWS price in this guide was read on AWS’s own pages on Oct 28, 2026: the Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing page (per-instance and per-accelerator effective hourly rates for Trn1, Trn2, P4d, P5, P5e, P5en, P6-B200), the Amazon EC2 Trn1 instance page (on-demand $1.34 / $21.50 / $24.78 and Reserved effective rates), the Amazon EC2 Trn2 instance page (chip and instance specifications; the page carries no on-demand price, consistent with Trn2’s Capacity Blocks availability), and the Amazon EC2 Inf2 instance page (on-demand $0.76 / $1.97 / $6.49 / $12.98 and Reserved rates). Where AWS prices per instance, we present the instance price; per-accelerator figures are AWS’s own printed per-accelerator rates, or exact divisions shown in the table — the multi-chip Inf2 instance prices are presented per instance only, because they do not divide exactly. Rental prices are GPUJournal’s verified board offers, checked Oct 30, 2026 and banked in our daily price-history snapshots; egress terms are from our Oct 19, 2026 storage-and-egress verification of the providers’ own pages. Performance claims (“up to 50% cost-to-train savings”, “30–40% better price performance”, “up to 40% better price performance”) are AWS’s own published claims about its own instances, labelled as such wherever they appear — we have not benchmarked these chips and this guide makes no throughput claims of its own. Not used, and why: AWS’s G5/G6/G6e on-demand prices (A10G, L4, L40S inside EC2) could not be read cleanly on an official AWS pricing page in this pass, so they are excluded from the maths rather than copied from third-party listings; the same applies to first-generation Inferentia (Inf1) pricing, which this guide does not quote. If we can verify those on AWS’s own pages, a future revision will add the EC2 G-series to Profile 2, where it belongs.

Thinking of deploying Kimi K3.1 Pro? Here’s how — and what it actually costs

The weights are out. Moonshot published Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face on Nov 4, 2026 — 96 safetensors shards summing to 1,561,293,160,568 bytes (about 1.56TB) in native MXFP4 — under its own Kimi K3.1-Pro License, with vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed named on the model card as the serving engines. This guide, first published Oct 30, 2026 as pre-release maths, was refreshed on Nov 6, 2026 with the real file sizes, the real licence and the official recipes: the smallest honest setup is one 8-GPU B300 node, the cheapest node-shaped setup on the current board is 16× H200 at $57.44/hr — and Moonshot’s own API, at $2.00 in / $10.00 out per 1M tokens, still beats self-hosting on price at ordinary volumes.

The verdict

  • Can you download it today? — Yes. moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro is public on Hugging Face, not gated: 96 safetensors shards, 1,561,293,160,568 bytes summed from the repository file list on Nov 6, 2026 — about 1.56TB in native MXFP4.
  • Can one GPU run it? — No. 2.8 trillion total parameters (104B active per token, per the model card) — the real MXFP4 checkpoint alone is 1,561 GB. This is a multi-GPU node job, at minimum.
  • Smallest honest setup — 8× B300 in one tensor-parallel group — the baseline shape in vLLM’s official recipe (read Nov 6, 2026): 2,304 GB of card memory against a 1,874 GB planning figure (the real 1,561 GB checkpoint plus 20% headroom). The recipe’s other baseline shapes are two GB300 trays or one 8× MI355X node, also TP8.
  • Cheapest node-shaped setup — 16× H200 (two 8-GPU nodes, the SGLang Hopper shape) from $57.44/hr — $41,931.20 a month always-on — at RunPod Community’s $3.59/GPU/hr. Two flags: that Community rate is carried, not re-read, in the Nov 6 check, and Hopper is the slower dequantised path, not the recipe baseline.
  • Recipe-baseline cost — 8× B300 from $59.20/hr at Hyperstack’s $7.40/GPU/hr — carried, not re-read for nine straight checks — or $71.92/hr at RunPod Secure’s $8.99/GPU/hr, the cheapest B300 offer from a provider checked on Nov 6, 2026 ($52,501.60 a month).
  • Self-host cost per 1M tokens — $7.98 on the cheapest node-shaped setup — at a printed assumption of 2,000 tokens/sec aggregate (an assumption, not a benchmark; vLLM reports far higher GB300 figures under its own AgentX tests, attributed in the tables and not used in this maths).
  • Moonshot’s own API — $2.00 in / $10.00 out per 1M tokens — $4.00 blended at our printed mix, still cheaper per token than self-hosting at ordinary volumes.
  • Licence — Published with the weights and read in full: free to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell, derivatives included. Two scale conditions: a model-as-a-service business above $20M aggregate revenue in any 12 months must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before commercial use, and a commercial product above 100M monthly users or $20M monthly revenue must display “Kimi K3.1-Pro” prominently. Internal use is exempt from both.

The memory maths — now with the real checkpoint

The method is the one we print on every model page: memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter, plus about 20% headroom for the context cache and serving overhead. The model card (read Nov 6, 2026) confirms the shape: 2.8 trillion total parameters, 104B activated per token, a 1,048,576-token context, 93 layers (69 Kimi Delta Attention + 24 Gated DSA), 896 experts with 16 selected per token and 2 shared, and a 401M-parameter MoonViT-V2 vision encoder; Hugging Face’s safetensors metadata counts 2,780,110,363,392 parameters in the checkpoint itself. The active count decides speed; the total count decides memory. And now the formula can be checked against the real thing: the native MXFP4 checkpoint’s 96 files sum to 1,561,293,160,568 bytes — about 161 GB more than the 1,400 GB the raw 4-bit arithmetic predicted, because MXFP4 routed-expert weights sit alongside BF16 for everything else, plus scales and metadata. That gap is exactly the failure mode the Oct 30 version of this page warned about. The planning figure that governs the card counts below is therefore built on the real download: 1,561 GB × 1.2 ≈ 1,874 GB. No FP16 or 8-bit checkpoint is published — those rows stay in the table as conversion maths, clearly labelled, because readers still ask what an upconverted copy would take.

Update — Nov 6, 2026: the weights are out, the licence is published, the maths is now real

This guide was published on Oct 30, 2026, before the weights existed, with honest labels: weights not yet released, licence not yet stated, no official serving recipe. All three gaps closed on Nov 4, 2026. What changed, verified first-hand on Nov 6, 2026 from Moonshot’s own Hugging Face repository, its LICENSE file, its model card and the vLLM recipe the card links to:

Why 8× B300 and not the arithmetic minimum of 7: serving shapes are not arbitrary card counts. vLLM’s official recipe — the one Moonshot’s model card links to — baselines this model as a single tensor-parallel group of 8 GPUs, and nodes rent as 8-GPU units. Seven cards (2,016 GB) clear the 1,874 GB planning figure on paper and buy you a shape no recipe publishes. On Hopper the shape is two nodes: 16× H200 (2,256 GB) under SGLang, whose cookbook carries Hopper profiles — with the dequantisation tax that path paid on Kimi K3, it is the cheaper-but-slower route, not the baseline. Watch out — context eats memory too. The 1,048,576-token window is the joint-largest we catalogue; vLLM’s recipe notes its decode-context-parallel layout holds about 7× the KV tokens of plain TP8 (about 18.5M vs 2.6M tokens with FP8 KV on 8× B300) — pick the layout for your context load, not just for the weights. The 20% headroom is an allowance, not a promise.

Or skip the GPUs: what the APIs charge

The alternative to deploying K3.1 Pro yourself is Moonshot’s own API — no longer the only route, but still the benchmark the self-host maths has to beat. Moonshot’s prices below are as listed on its API pricing page on Oct 23–25, 2026 (its batch terms were re-read on that page on Oct 30, 2026, and its $2/$10 rates were reported again on its pricing page in our Nov 4 weights story); the frontier closed comparator was read on OpenAI’s pricing page on Oct 29, 2026. Printed assumptions (not measurements): (1) the rented setup serves an aggregate 2,000 tokens per second, input and output combined, under a realistic mixed load — a deliberately moderate, conservative figure kept from the Oct 30 edition for comparability. vLLM’s own day-0 post reports far higher throughput on GB300 under the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark (up to 37.8K total tokens/sec per GPU at the throughput end, its figures, on NVL72 test hardware with speculative decoding in the mix) — attributed here, not used: no independent serving benchmark on a rental B300 or H200 shape exists yet. At half of the printed assumption, every self-host figure below doubles; at double, it halves. (2) API usage is blended at 3 input tokens to 1 output token, uncached.

Against Moonshot’s own API, self-hosting still does not win on price at any plausible volume. An always-on 16× H200 setup costs $41,931.20 a month. At the blended $4.00 per 1M tokens you would need to push about 10.48 billion tokens a month through the API before it cost the same — a sustained average of roughly 3,989 tokens per second, around the clock, which is more than the setup itself is assumed to serve. Against Moonshot’s batch rate ($2.40 blended) the break-even is about 17.47 billion tokens a month. If per-token price is the whole question, Moonshot’s API is the rational buy — full stop. Against a frontier closed API, the maths flips early. At GPT-6 Astra’s blended $20.00 per 1M tokens, the same always-on setup breaks even at about 2.10 billion tokens a month — a sustained average of only about 798 tokens per second. Moonshot positions K3.1 Pro directly against that class of model (its own Terminal-Bench 4.0 table puts K3.1 Pro at 65.7%, ahead of Astra’s 58.2% and just behind Claude Opus 5.5’s 66.4% — Moonshot-reported figures, printed as such; Artificial Analysis independently scored K3.1 Pro 55, fourth overall, in results reported Oct 24, 2026). A genuinely busy product crosses 798 sustained tokens a second, and past that line every additional token on your own node is effectively free until it saturates. That — not beating Moonshot’s own per-token price — is the real self-hosting bargain, and the licence (below) allows it for most readers: the scale conditions bite only above $20M of model-as-a-service revenue.

What the money can’t settle

Control. Self-hosted weights are pinned: the model cannot be changed, deprecated or repriced underneath you, and you can fine-tune it — the licence expressly includes fine-tuning and derivative works. Note that Moonshot has already announced its K2 series retires by the end of December 2026 — API line-ups move on the provider’s schedule, not yours. Privacy and residency. On your own node, prompts never leave your infrastructure. For legal, medical and financial work — the fields Moonshot’s own material showcases for this model — that can be the whole decision, before price enters it. Zero operations. The API side never pages you at 3am, never waits for a scarce 8-GPU node to free up, and bills nothing while you sleep. The rented node bills every hour it exists. Availability. Both routes are live now — the API since Oct 23, 2026, the weights since Nov 4, 2026. The choice is no longer about waiting; it is about whether the licence’s two scale conditions and the operations bill fit your product.

Steps

1. The official recipe: one TP8 group on Blackwell or MI355X

Moonshot’s model card names three recommended inference engines — vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed — and links to their recipes. vLLM’s recipe (published Nov 2, 2026, updated Nov 5, 2026, read Nov 6, 2026) baselines the simplest working NVIDIA setup as one tensor-parallel group of 8 GPUs: either one B300 node or two GB300 trays, in its kimi-k31 container images, with throughput explicitly not tuned. On AMD, one MI355X node takes the same TP8 layout. The recipe’s refinements are named, not hidden: tensor + expert parallelism for the lowest long-prompt time to first token (a single 340K-token prompt prefills in about 10 seconds against about 15 at plain TP8, on a pre-release checkpoint, by vLLM’s account), decode context parallelism (DCP8) when KV capacity is the limit, and an NVFP4 KV cache option that holds about 1.5× the FP8 cache tokens, with long-context accuracy not yet measured. Start from the baseline; adopt the refinements when your workload matches them.

2. The other engines: SGLang’s cookbook and TokenSpeed

SGLang serves K3.1 Pro from its day-0 branch with a cookbook of generated launch commands by hardware and strategy — TP8 low-latency, DCP8 high-concurrency, and prefill/decode disaggregation — across NVIDIA Blackwell and Hopper, AMD MI350X/MI355X and other platforms; its Hopper profiles are the route behind the 16× H200 row in our cost table. TokenSpeed is the third engine the model card names, with its own recipes. All three are young: the SGLang support had not shipped in a stock release at day 0, by its own account, so pin your engine version and test on your own traffic before committing a fleet.

3. What the API still gives you

K3.1 Pro remains live on the Kimi API (with a Highspeed variant Moonshot rates at 2–3× the speed, by its own statement), and the model card’s usage notes carry two operational facts a self-hoster should know before migrating: thinking effort is set with the top-level reasoning_effort field (low / high / max, default max), and multi-turn and tool-call conversations must pass the complete assistant message back — reasoning_content and tool_calls included — or the model loses its own thread. Self-hosting removes the per-token bill; it does not remove those behaviours.

Alternatives

The real checkpoint beat the formula — by 161 GB

The Oct 30 edition of this page warned that the real download might not match the 4-bit arithmetic, citing Mistral Large 4, whose real 4-bit download was bigger than the raw figure. K3.1 Pro did the same: 1,561 GB real against 1,400 GB by the method, because only the routed experts are MXFP4 — the rest of the checkpoint is BF16, with scales and metadata on top. Every planning figure on this page is therefore built on the summed files, and the method rows are kept only as the comparison.

Every speed-derived figure rests on a printed assumption

The $7.98, $8.22 and $9.99 per-1M-token costs assume 2,000 tokens/sec aggregate — kept from the Oct 30 edition so the two editions compare honestly. vLLM reports much higher GB300 throughput under its own AgentX testing, and SGLang reports up to 449 tokens/sec per user at concurrency 1 on GB300 NVL72 — makers’ figures, on rack hardware, not a rental node. If the real figure on your shape is 1,000 tokens/sec, self-hosting costs twice what this page’s headline says. The break-even against the frontier API survives that; the one against Moonshot’s API was never close.

The benchmark scores are Moonshot-reported, labelled as such

Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 65.7%, GPQA-Diamond at 94.2%, BrowseComp at 92.1% — the model card’s own table, Moonshot’s numbers. The one independent score we can cite is Artificial Analysis’s 55 on its Intelligence Index (reported Oct 24, 2026), measured on the API model. The weights have been public since Nov 4, 2026, so independent reproductions on self-hosted hardware are now possible — none is cited here yet, because none we have verified exists yet.

Best-offer prices are a snapshot, and two are carried

Rental figures are from the board checked Nov 6, 2026. Hyperstack’s $7.40 B300 rate could not be re-read that day — the ninth straight check it has been unreadable — and RunPod Community’s $3.59 H200 rate could not be separated from its Secure tier in that day’s read; both are carried from earlier verified checks and flagged wherever they are used. The checked-today alternatives are priced alongside them. An 8-GPU node in the region you need, free at the moment you book, may cost more than the headline; the live comparison carries today’s figures.

A full node is an operations commitment

At this scale there is no single box to lean on: an 8-GPU node is one failure domain, the H200 route is two nodes and their interconnect, and serious deployments budget redundancy — either way the always-on figures above are a floor, not a ceiling.

The licence, in plain words

The weights ship under the Kimi K3.1-Pro License (Moonshot AI, copyright 2026) — the full text sits in the repository’s LICENSE file, read in full on Nov 6, 2026. In plain words: The base is permissive, MIT-style. Permission is granted free of charge to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software — expressly including the model weights — and to run, deploy, fine-tune and create derivative works, provided the copyright and permission notices are kept in copies and use complies with applicable laws. Condition one — model-as-a-service at scale. “Model as a Service” is defined as giving a third party access to inference or fine-tuning in a way that lets them meaningfully control inputs, parameters or training data; end-user products with the model embedded in specific features, and mere relaying of requests to models hosted by others, are expressly not MaaS. If you or your affiliates run a MaaS business and your aggregate revenue exceeds $20 million over any consecutive 12 months, you must enter a separate agreement with Moonshot AI before using the weights or derivatives commercially. Condition two — attribution at very large scale. If the weights or a derivative power a commercial product or service with more than 100 million monthly active users, or more than $20 million in monthly revenue, “Kimi K3.1-Pro” must be prominently displayed on its user interface. The exemptions matter as much as the conditions: neither condition applies to internal use — anything that does not make the software, its outputs or its capabilities available to third parties — nor to use through Moonshot’s official products or certified inference partners. The software is provided “as is”, without warranty. Two honest cautions: this is a custom licence, not MIT itself, whatever its family resemblance — the two thresholds are the difference, and a hosted business anywhere near them should read the 3,077-byte text itself (licence questions go to Moonshot at the address in the file); and nothing here is legal advice.

Best GPU for AI inference in 2026 — priced from a checked board

Most “best GPU for inference” pages price their verdicts from a rate card the seller itself publishes — prices stated on the seller’s own pages, with no check date a reader can test. This page works the other way round. Every price below was read on the provider’s own published page and checked on Oct 30, 2026, and every cost per token is built from a throughput assumption printed next to it, so the maths can be rerun with your own numbers. The result is not the ranking the spec sheets suggest: on a mid-size model, the cheapest tokens in our checks come off a $0.34-an-hour gaming card, and the fastest card on the board finishes mid-table.

The workload behind the numbers — read this before quoting any figure

Cost per token is an hourly price divided by a speed. The prices on this page are verified; the speeds are assumptions, chosen once, printed everywhere, and applied identically to every card so the comparison is fair. They are not benchmark results, and no figure on this page should be quoted as one. The workload: a 32B-class open model, 4-bit weights (~18GB), continuous batching at roughly 32 concurrent sequences, output tokens only. Cost per 1M output tokens = hourly price ÷ (assumed tokens/sec × 3,600) × 1,000,000. Worked check: RTX 4090 — $0.34 ÷ (600 × 3,600) × 1,000,000 = $0.157 → $0.16. The assumed speeds are set roughly in line with each card’s memory bandwidth — the thing that limits batched decode — anchored on the two figures our inference-metrics guide uses (H100 SXM 2,000 tok/s, B200 4,000 tok/s) so the two pages agree. The sensitivity is simple and worth stating plainly: if your stack delivers half the assumed speed on every card, every cost on this page doubles and the order of the table does not change. What changes the order is one card beating its assumption while another misses its own — which is why the first rented hour on any card should be a measurement, not a commitment. One scope note: these are output token costs. Reading the prompt (prefill) costs compute too, and long-prompt workloads — document question-answering, agent histories — shift the balance toward cards with more raw compute. The ranking above is a serving-decode ranking, stated as such. And the ranking’s one footnote: the H100 SXM’s lowest per-GPU price in our checks is TensorDock’s $2.25/GPU/hr, quoted at an 8-GPU minimum — an $18.00/hr floor; at fleet scale that rate gives $0.31 per 1M tokens on the same assumed speed. The table ranks the best single-card price, because that is what most inference renters actually buy.

The ten cards, in three tiers

The budget tier — cheap hours, real tokens. Four of the five cheapest token costs on this page come from cards under $0.80 an hour; their limits are memory and manners, not speed. The memory tier — where the model has to fit before it can be cheap. Past 32B, the question stops being “cheapest token” and becomes “smallest card that holds the model at the precision you need” — two cards own that territory below Hopper prices. The speed tier — Hopper and Blackwell, priced honestly. The flagship cards are not the cheapest tokens on a mid-size model; what they sell is throughput ceiling, memory, and the precision formats (FP8, FP4) that the cheaper generations don’t have.

Steps

1. RTX 4090 · 24GB · $0.34/hr at RunPod Community → $0.16 per 1M tokens

Assumed 600 tok/s; always-on month $248.20. Offers run $0.34–$0.89 across four providers. Good for: prototyping and small-model serving for almost nothing. Models up to ~13B at full precision, or a 32B at 4-bit held tightly, on the cheapest useful card on the board — and it doubles as the budget image-generation card. Not good for: anything that must hold more than 24GB — the memory wall arrives fast — and there is no NVLink, so two cards cannot pool memory into one bigger card. It is a consumer card: no ECC memory, and production serving stacks treat it as a guest, not a resident.

2. RTX 5090 · 32GB · $0.69/hr at RunPod Community → $0.18 per 1M tokens

Assumed 1,050 tok/s; always-on month $503.70. Offers run $0.69–$1.19. Good for: 32B-class serving on a budget. Its GDDR7 bandwidth (1,792 GB/s) is close to double the 4090’s, which is why its assumed speed — and its token cost — sit so close to the 4090’s despite double the rent. A 32B at 4-bit fits with room for a working KV cache. Not good for: models past 32GB, pooled multi-card serving (no NVLink), and anyone who needs datacenter driver and ECC behaviour for a production service — the same consumer-card caveat as its sibling.

3. RTX A6000 · 48GB · $0.35/hr at Thunder Compute → $0.22 per 1M tokens

Assumed 450 tok/s; always-on month $255.50. Thunder Compute is the only offer on our board. Good for: 48GB of ECC memory at the lowest hourly rent we verify anywhere — cheaper per hour than every card on this page except the 4090, with twice the 4090’s memory. Two can be bridged with NVLink, a trick almost nothing else at this price offers. On older, proven CUDA stacks it is a known quantity. Not good for: modern serving speed tricks — it is an Ampere card, so there is no FP8 — and its assumed speed is the lowest on this page: its tokens are cheap because its rent is, not because it is fast. One provider on our board also means one point of supply: if that listing is gone, so is this price.

4. L40S · 48GB · $0.79/hr at RunPod Community → $0.44 per 1M tokens

Assumed 500 tok/s; always-on month $576.70. Offers run $0.79–$2.25 across five providers. Good for: everyday 7B–32B serving with datacenter manners — ECC memory, proper drivers, five providers deep on our board so the price is contestable. This is the card our board calls its all-rounder, and for a first production deployment it is the lowest-drama pick on the page. Not good for: 70B at FP16 — it does not fit, and no setting fixes that — and there is no NVLink for pooling. On this page’s single workload its tokens cost more than the A6000’s and the consumer cards’; what the extra rent buys is memory behaviour and provider choice, not speed.

5. L40 · 48GB · $0.79/hr at Thunder Compute → $0.44 per 1M tokens

Assumed 500 tok/s; always-on month $576.70. Offers run $0.79–$1.00. Good for: the same 48GB and the same memory bandwidth as the L40S at the same best price in today’s checks — light serving and image work from a card with datacenter manners. When an L40S listing is sold out or repriced, this is the honest substitute. Not good for: being anyone’s first choice while the L40S sits at the same price — the L40S is the slightly stronger card (more compute headroom for prefill-heavy work), and the L40 also has no NVLink. Watch the pair of them together: whichever dips first is the one to rent.

6. A100 80GB · 80GB · $1.09/hr at Thunder Compute → $0.26 per 1M tokens

Assumed 1,150 tok/s; always-on month $795.70. Ten listings run $1.09–$2.79 across eight providers. Good for: 70B-class serving without Hopper money — a 70B at 8-bit fits with headroom, at 4-bit with room to spare, on the most battle-tested serving stack in the field. It also slices: MIG lets one card present as several small instances, so a single A100 can serve several small models side by side. Third-cheapest tokens on this page, with real memory — the honest workhorse earns the name here. Not good for: FP8 serving — an Ampere card doesn’t have it, so the newer speed tricks don’t apply — and check the variant on the cheapest listings before you rent: PCIe A100s carry less memory bandwidth (1,555 GB/s) than SXM cards (1,935 GB/s), and the assumed speed above follows the faster card.

7. RTX PRO 6000 · 96GB · $1.69/hr at RunPod Community → $0.45 per 1M tokens

Assumed 1,050 tok/s; always-on month $1,233.70. Offers run $1.69–$2.65 across five providers. Good for: its real job — a 70B on ONE card. At 8-bit a 70B needs roughly 71GB before any KV cache; this card’s 96GB holds it with about 25GB to breathe, at $1.69/hr, the cheapest single-card home for that model size we verify. That is why it ranks last in the verdict table above and still belongs on this page: the table prices a 32B workload, and on a 32B workload you are paying for memory you aren’t using. Not good for: scale-out (no NVLink) and raw token speed per dollar on mid-size models — its GDDR7 bandwidth (1,792 GB/s) is well under half the H200’s, so on models that fit everywhere, the datacenter cards outrun it. The Max-Q version of this card is listed separately on our board and runs slower; the figures here are the full card. A live footnote: on Oct 30 a small marketplace (nafnaf.ai, Zug) listed the Max-Q version at $0.80/hr — the cheapest 96GB-class hour we have seen — after showing $0.42 two days earlier. A single two-GPU listing that moves that fast is an opportunistic rent, not a fleet price, so it is reported here rather than ranked in the table.

8. H100 SXM · 80GB · $2.69/hr single-card at RunPod Community → $0.37 per 1M tokens

Assumed 2,000 tok/s; always-on month $1,963.70. Offers run $2.25–$4.79 across seven providers. Good for: busy FP8 serving fleets — high-throughput serving is what this card is for, and at TensorDock’s $2.25/GPU/hr 8-GPU-minimum rate the same assumed speed gives $0.31 per 1M tokens, the fleet figure in the verdict table’s footnote. Seven providers deep, its price is the most contested on the board. Not good for: bursty work. It pays off only when the card stays busy; on spiky traffic you pay H100 rent for idle silicon, and a cheaper card with the same memory would have served the same peaks. Note also the spread: the same card, same day, runs from $2.69 to $3.99 at single-card providers — at RunPod Secure’s $3.99 the token cost is $0.55, not $0.37. Provider choice is worth more than most card choices.

9. H200 · 141GB · $3.59/hr at RunPod Community → $0.35 per 1M tokens

Assumed 2,850 tok/s; always-on month $2,620.70. Offers run $3.59–$6.31 across six providers. Good for: 70B+ and long-context serving — the cheapest big-memory tokens on this page. Its HBM3e bandwidth (4,800 GB/s) is 43% above the H100 SXM’s, which is why its tokens come out cheaper than the H100’s despite a third more rent (the full comparison is in the “When the pricier card wins” section). The 141GB also holds the KV cache that long contexts eat. Not good for: small work — it is more card than most jobs need, and the trap is paying for it to serve a 13B. If your model and your context fit an 80GB card comfortably, this is memory you are renting for decoration.

10. B200 · 192GB · $5.98/hr at RunPod Community → $0.42 per 1M tokens

Assumed 4,000 tok/s; always-on month $4,365.40. Offers run $5.98–$8.87 across seven providers. Good for: the largest single-card jobs — a 70B at full FP16 (~140GB of weights) fits on this one card with cache room, which no cheaper card on the page can claim, and its FP4 support is the newest serving lever there is. When the model is frontier-size, this is the entry ticket, not a luxury. Not good for: mid-size serving economics. On this page’s 32B workload its tokens cost more than the H200’s, the H100’s and every budget card’s — double the H100’s assumed speed does not cover 2.2× the rent. Frontier money should follow frontier-size work; anything smaller is budget burned for a spec sheet.

Alternatives

When the pricier card wins — 1. The model doesn’t fit

A card that can’t load your model has an infinite cost per token. Memory ceilings are binary. A 70B at 8-bit needs roughly 71GB before KV cache: every 48GB card on this page is out at that precision, whatever its token cost says, and the cheapest card that holds it — the RTX PRO 6000 at $1.69/hr — wins by default. At full FP16 the same model is ~140GB of weights, and the only single card here with honest room for it is the B200. The honest caveat runs the other way too: if 4-bit quality is acceptable for your model (~36GB for a 70B), the cheap 48GB cards are back in play and win easily. The pricier card wins when you need the size and the precision — check both before paying for either.

When the pricier card wins — 2. Bandwidth converts

A third more rent, cheaper tokens. Same workload, same assumptions, two verified prices: an H100 SXM at RunPod Community’s $2.69/hr, assumed 2,000 tok/s, gives $0.37 per 1M tokens; an H200 at RunPod Community’s $3.59/hr, assumed 2,850 tok/s, gives $0.35. The H200’s hour costs 33% more and its tokens cost about 6% less, because its memory bandwidth is 43% higher and batched decode is a bandwidth business. The same effect, wearing a provider’s clothes: an H100 SXM at RunPod Secure’s $3.99/hr gives $0.55 per 1M tokens on the same assumed speed, while a B200 at RunPod Community’s $5.98/hr — an hour that costs 50% more — gives $0.42. Card, provider and price are one decision, not three.

When the pricier card wins — 3. The tokens have to arrive on time

Every figure on this page is a cost per token produced. Tokens produced too slowly for your users — a stream that reads like a typewriter, a first token that arrives after a second of silence — are output you paid for and cannot sell. A faster card running at the same batch size holds per-user speed targets that a cheaper card misses at that batch, and holds them again at batch sizes where the cheaper card’s users start queueing. If your workload has a latency target, price the cards at the speed each one delivers inside that target, not at its headline throughput. For chat and agent products, that correction — not the hourly rate — is usually where the real ranking hides.

The short version

Rent the cheapest card that fits your model at the precision you need, from the cheapest provider you trust, and measure its real speed in the first hour. Every price behind that sentence is on the live board, checked daily.

How we know

The prices are GPUJournal’s own verified board prices, read on the providers’ own published pages and banked daily (full sweep Oct 19, 2026; daily checks since). Best offers checked Oct 30, 2026: RTX 4090 $0.34 and RTX 5090 $0.69, H200 $3.59, B200 $5.98, RTX PRO 6000 $1.69, L40S $0.79 (all RunPod Community); RTX A6000 $0.35 and L40 $0.79 (Thunder Compute); A100 80GB $1.09 (Thunder Compute); H100 SXM $2.69 single-card (RunPod Community) and $2.25/GPU/hr at TensorDock’s published 8-GPU minimum. “Best verified price” throughout means the lowest verified on-demand price at which one card can actually be rented, with any minimum printed next to it; monthly figures are the hourly price × 730 hours. The contrast behind this page: the best-known competing roundup, Spheron’s “Best GPU for AI Inference in 2026” (refreshed this week), prices its verdicts from rates stated on Spheron’s own pages — Spheron sells the capacity it ranks. Those stated rates carry no independent check we can test: its own Mamba-3 guide, read Oct 30, 2026, states the L40S at $1.80, and $0.96 elsewhere on its pages, while the cheapest L40S price we could verify on Oct 30 was $0.79 at RunPod Community. Stated prices are reported on our Price Watch labelled as stated; they never appear in this guide as verified prices. Every throughput figure here is an assumption, set roughly in line with memory bandwidth and anchored on the worked examples in our inference-metrics guide (H100 SXM 2,000 tok/s; B200 4,000 tok/s): 4090 600, 5090 1,050, A6000 450, L40S 500, L40 500, A100 80GB 1,150, PRO 6000 1,050, H200 2,850 tok/s — aggregate output tokens for a 32B-class model at 4-bit weights under continuous batching at ~32 concurrent sequences. No throughput figure on this page is a measured benchmark, and none is presented as one; the one formula used throughout is cost per 1M tokens = hourly price ÷ (tokens/sec × 3,600) × 1,000,000, and every figure in the tables is exact arithmetic on the printed price and the printed assumption (e.g. $3.59 ÷ (2,850 × 3,600) × 1,000,000 = $0.35). Hardware facts (memory sizes, bandwidths, NVLink and FP8/FP4 support, MIG on the A100) are the makers’ published specifications. Prices move — Verda alone rose seven times in the eight days to Oct 30 — so the board, not this page, is the live source.

Oct 30, 2026

Released by DiffuSpace on Oct 30, 2026: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, a 35-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that writes by diffusion instead of one token at a time — open source under Apache, with the weights on Hugging Face and a serving build in SGLang. It is aimed squarely at agentic coding, and at BF16 it fits on a single 80GB rental card.

Image: DiffuSpace

What shipped, from DiffuSpace’s Hugging Face launch blog and the model card for Diffuspace/Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, both read on Oct 30, 2026: DiffuSpace is the team behind the University of Hong Kong NLP group’s Dream 7B, the 2025 diffusion language model with more than 2.7 million Hugging Face downloads, and Clover is its scaled-up successor — a text-only mixture-of-experts diffusion model with 35 billion total parameters and about 3 billion active per token, a 128K context window and a thinking mode. The card adds the architecture detail: derived from Alibaba’s Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 40 layers, 256 routed experts with top-8 routing plus one shared expert per layer, on a hybrid Gated DeltaNet / full-attention backbone redesigned for block diffusion — the model generates a block of masked tokens in parallel, then commits the confident positions and moves on. The licence is Apache: the blog calls it open source under an Apache license, and the card preserves the upstream Qwen Apache-2.0 licence and copyright. Weights and code are on Hugging Face, GitHub and ModelScope, with the maker’s own SGLang implementation recommended for serving and evaluation, a llama.cpp route, and a Transformers path (which the card notes can differ slightly in output from the SGLang kernels).

The scores, all DiffuSpace-reported in the launch blog and not independently verified: across all six agent benchmarks in its comparison Clover posts the highest scores of the models evaluated — 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified, 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 65.3 on τ³ Overall — ahead of the autoregressive Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it derives from and of the diffusion models LLaDA2.2 flash and Mercury 2.5. On general benchmarks it reports 83.8 on GPQA Diamond, 84.8 on MMLU-Pro and 95.8 on ZebraLogic. Treat every one of these as the maker’s own numbers until a third party reproduces them — the honest caveat that applies to every launch-week model, this one included.

The speed claim is the architecture’s reason to exist, again in the maker’s own tests: 680 tokens per second on a single NVIDIA GB300 at BF16 with a batch size of 1, measured on its internal agent workloads, and 515 tokens per second on a single H200 against 365 for a DFlash-accelerated build of the similar-sized Qwen model. At the other end of the market, DiffuSpace says an INT4 build ran on an NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti with 16GB of memory at 101.8 tokens per second on MATH-500, against 48.5 for the comparison models it tested. Diffusion generates whole blocks in parallel rather than one token per step, which is why the maker expects the advantage to grow on exactly the multi-step agent loops where generation delay compounds.

The renter maths is what makes this a launch renters can actually try today. The card’s own quick-start line is a GPU with enough memory for the BF16 weights — approximately 69GB, matching our method (35B parameters at 2 bytes is about 70GB) — so the full-precision model is a one-card job on any 80GB card: on our board, checked Oct 30, 2026, the cheapest single-card home is an A100 80GB from $1.09 an hour at Thunder Compute, an H100 SXM is $2.25 an hour at TensorDock, and the H200 the maker measured its 515 tokens/s on rents from $3.59 an hour at RunPod Community. An 8-bit quant would be about 35GB by the same arithmetic — 48GB-card territory — and the INT4 class is about 17.5GB, inside a 24GB RTX 4090 from $0.34 an hour. Two preview-grade cautions from the card itself, stated plainly: this is a Preview release, and the maker warns that very long generations can sometimes become repetitive — the shipped defaults already carry repetition controls tuned to counter it.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Diffusion language models stop being a 7B research curiosity with this release: a 35B, Apache-licensed agent model that fits on one rented card, with a serving stack from day one, is something any builder can test this weekend for the price of a few GPU-hours. What would settle it is independent reproduction — of the agent scores and of the speed advantage on hardware that is not the maker’s own test bench. Until then, every figure above is DiffuSpace’s, labelled as such.

A Google TPU just answered a prompt from orbit: Project Suncatcher’s first AI response

Oct 30, 2026

Published by Google on Oct 30, 2026: its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite has returned the first-ever AI response from a data-centre-class TPU in orbit — a haiku about being in space, generated on board by the open Gemma 4 model. A brief, because there is nothing here to rent yet — and it is still a genuine first.

Image: Google via blog.google

What happened, from Google’s own post, published Oct 30, 2026 (17:00 UTC) and read the same day: the Suncatcher prototype satellite, launched on Oct 1, 2026, finished its commissioning checklist — powering up the host and the TPU trays and running early machine-learning tests — and this week reached what Google calls its ‘Hello World’ milestone. During a ground-station pass, the team uplinked a prompt to the onboard Gemma 4 open model asking for a haiku about being in space; as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, the downlinked poem confirmed the round trip worked. Google says it has since tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the payload’s technical status.

What comes next, in the same post: a series of tests on how the TPUs hold up under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit, ahead of the programme’s next milestone — twin interconnected satellites in 2027. Suncatcher is described by Google as a long-term research moonshot into powering AI compute in space, not a product in development.

The honest limits, plainly: there is no capacity to rent, no service to sign up for and no date for anything a GPU or TPU renter can book — possibly for years. We run this as a brief because the milestone itself is real and first-of-its-kind, and because the model that answered from orbit is an open one — Gemma 4, which sits in our catalogue as a model builders can download and run on ordinary rented cards today.

What it means if you rent GPUs

File this under signals, not shopping: a data-centre-class AI chip has now run a real inference workload in orbit and phoned the answer home. Nothing about renting GPUs changes this week — but the list of places AI hardware is being proven to work just got stranger, and Google is spending real programme money on finding out how far that goes.

Verda raises prices again — all nine GPUs up about 1%, the eighth rise since Oct 23

Nov 2, 2026

Read on Verda's own pricing page today, Nov 2, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 1: every GPU in Verda's range rose by about 1% — GB300, B300, B200, H200, H100, both A100s, the RTX PRO 6000 and the L40S. After two flat checks, the October rise run has resumed.

Image: Verda via verda.com

What changed, read on verda.com/pricing on Nov 2, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.05 → $13.18 [$13.18], B300 $11.35 → $11.46 [$11.46], B200 $8.87 → $8.96 [$8.958], H200 $6.25 → $6.31 [$6.313], H100 SXM $4.79 → $4.84 [$4.841], A100 80GB $2.25 → $2.27 [$2.270], A100 40GB $1.61 → $1.63 [$1.625], RTX PRO 6000 $2.65 → $2.67 [$2.671] and L40S $1.90 → $1.92 [$1.920]. Each move is within a cent of +1.0% — a uniform list adjustment, not one card repricing.

The pattern: Verda rose on Oct 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30, then held on Oct 31 and Nov 1 — and has now risen an eighth time. Its GB300, the only GB300 rate we list, has gone from $11.82 an hour at our Oct 19 check to $13.18 today, up 11.5% in two weeks. Verda is not alone in the pattern: Nebius raised across the board on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, and SaladCloud's 21-class Priority rise took effect on Nov 1, with SaladCloud saying demand had outpaced supply. Rising list prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can produce the same shape).

What it costs: Verda holds the board's Best offer on only two cards — the GB300 and the A100 40GB — and both rose today, so those two best offers rose with it. Everywhere else the cheapest verified offers are other providers' and none moved: the board's H100 SXM best is still TensorDock at $2.25 an hour (at an 8-GPU minimum) and its B200 best is still RunPod Community at $5.98. If you rent at Verda around the clock, today's rise adds about $95 a month per GB300, $65 per B200 and $35 per H100 on a 730-hour month — small per hour, real per fleet.

Checked today and unchanged: RunPod Secure, Lambda, Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute and TensorDock all held at the rates read on Nov 1, and SaladCloud's new Priority rates (RTX 5090 High $0.60, RTX 4090 High $0.44) are still the live ones. Not checked today, and named rather than covered by the stamp: RunPod Community (its tier could not be separated in today's read), Hyperstack (its pricing table could not be read) and nafnaf.ai (its homepage showed no GPUs available today, so there was no live listing to verify).

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters, the lesson of the Verda run is the spread, not the rise: list prices at the rising providers keep stepping up about 1% at a time while the market's best verified offers have not moved since mid-October. A workload priced off one provider's list page in October can be 10% adrift by November. Check the board before renewing or expanding at a list rate — and if you are on Verda's GB300 or A100 40GB, your best-offer price moved today.

SaladCloud raises prices on 21 GPU classes — RTX 4090 High Priority up 33%

Nov 1, 2026

Announced on SaladCloud's own blog and in effect from 00:00 UTC on Nov 1, 2026: High, Medium and Low Priority prices rose on 21 consumer GPU classes, because — in SaladCloud's words — demand has outpaced supply. The interruptible Lowest Priority tier did not move.

Image: Salad via blog.salad.com

What changed, from SaladCloud's announcement (read Nov 1, 2026) and confirmed live on salad.com/pricing the same day: at High Priority the RTX 5090 rose $0.50 to $0.60 an hour (+20%), the RTX 4090 rose $0.33 to $0.44 (+33%), the RTX 5080 rose $0.26 to $0.32 (+23%), the RTX 5070 Ti rose $0.225 to $0.27, the RTX 4080 rose $0.23 to $0.27, the RTX 3090 rose $0.17 to $0.20 and the RTX 2060 rose $0.05 to $0.062 (+24%). Medium and Low Priority rose by smaller amounts on the same 21 classes. Every price is per GPU per hour, and SaladCloud's table shows both sides — previous and new — for all three tiers.

What did not change matters as much: Lowest Priority — the tier that can be preempted by higher-priority work — is unchanged on every class, so a batch RTX 4090 still starts at $0.16 an hour and a batch RTX 5090 at $0.25. SaladCloud says the rises are weighted toward High Priority on purpose: when nearly everything runs at High, priority stops meaning much, and widening the gap is meant to keep High available for work that needs it while making the lower tiers easier to get.

The reason, in SaladCloud's own words: over the past several weeks demand has outpaced supply on many of its most popular GPUs, several classes have been running almost entirely at High Priority, and people have waited for capacity or not gotten it at all. Because SaladCloud's machines belong to individuals who share their GPUs with the network, it is also raising provider payouts alongside the prices to keep the machines it has and bring new ones online.

The renter context: SaladCloud is a different product from the datacentre clouds on our price board — containers on shared consumer cards in people's homes, in 190+ countries, with preemption risk that rises as priority falls. It is not on the board, and these rates are not board offers. For a like-for-like anchor, the board's cheapest verified RTX 4090 today is $0.34 an hour at RunPod Community and its cheapest verified RTX 5090 is $0.69 an hour, both checked Nov 1, 2026 — dedicated machines, at prices SaladCloud's new High Priority now sits much closer to than it did yesterday.

What it means if you rent GPUs

This is the fourth provider-side rise in the run this journal has tracked since October — Nebius on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, Verda seven times between Oct 23 and 30, and now a consumer-GPU marketplace raising 21 classes at once while openly saying demand outpaced supply. One rise is a pricing decision; a month of them, across datacentre clouds and a home-GPU marketplace alike, is a pattern — consistent with growing demand for GPU hours (our reading of it, labelled as interpretation). If you rent consumer cards for batch work, your cheapest tier just held; if you buy priority, budget the new rates from today.
