/story/nvidia-rubin-shipping-specs-revis.html:
NEWS →  ·  Hardware · NVIDIA

Rubin's shipping specs are lower than the preview: HBM4 bandwidth cut to 19.2 TB/s, NVLink to 3.0 TB/s

Nov 1, 2026

Reported by ServeTheHome on Nov 1, 2026 from NVIDIA's own updated product pages and architecture datasheet: the Rubin GPU that is now shipping carries 19.2 TB/s of HBM4 bandwidth per GPU, not the 22 TB/s of the preview figures — and NVLink scale-up bandwidth is 3.0 TB/s, not 3.6. Memory capacity and compute are unchanged, and scale-out networking actually went up.

Image: NVIDIA

What changed, per GPU, from NVIDIA's preliminary figures to the shipping specifications tabulated by ServeTheHome (read Nov 1, 2026): HBM4 bandwidth 22 TB/s → 19.2 TB/s (the HBM4 stacks run at 9.375 Gbps per pin instead of the targeted 10.75 — about 11% down); NVLink scale-up bandwidth 3.6 TB/s → 3.0 TB/s (17% down); scale-out networking bandwidth 0.4 TB/s → 0.45 TB/s (up). Unchanged: 288GB of HBM4 per GPU, and compute at 50 PFLOPS NVFP4 inference and 35 PFLOPS NVFP4 training. NVIDIA posted the updated figures on its webpages and in its architecture datasheet in September; they were first spotted by IT Home and are now the specs of the production systems reaching customers.

The rack follows the chip. A Vera Rubin NVL72's aggregate GPU memory bandwidth goes from 1,580 TB/s to 1,400 TB/s and its NVLink bandwidth from 260 TB/s to 216 TB/s, while its scale-out networking rises from 28.8 TB/s to 32.4 TB/s; the rack's 20.7TB of HBM4 is unchanged. The hardest hit lands on the smaller systems: an HGX Rubin NVL8's total GPU memory drops from 2.3TB to 2.0TB — which works out at roughly 250GB usable per GPU, seven of the eight HBM4 stacks — its memory bandwidth falls 26% to 130 TB/s (about 16.8 TB/s per GPU), and its training figures ease to 270 PFLOPS NVFP4 and 130 PFLOPS FP8. Both NVL8 variants and the DGX systems built on them carry the same changes.

NVIDIA's position, given to Wccftech and reported Oct 29, 2026: the earlier numbers were preliminary architectural targets, and the revised figures are the specifications for systems in qualified volume production — Vera Rubin NVL72 is in full production and shipping. NVIDIA has not said why the bandwidth targets came down, and ServeTheHome is clear that the reason is not stated: memory controller speeds, stack speeds or yields are the candidates it names, labelled as assumption. One point of context in Rubin's favour even after the cut: at 9.375 Gbps per pin its HBM4 still runs well above the roughly 7.6 Gbps per pin ServeTheHome cites for AMD's MI455X.

Why this reaches a price journal's news desk: Vera Rubin capacity is already rentable — NVL72 went generally available on Oracle Cloud on Oct 27, 2026 — and the first per-GPU Rubin offers will be priced against these numbers. Any comparison, guide or listing still quoting 22 TB/s of HBM4 bandwidth, 3.6 TB/s of NVLink or a full 288GB per GPU in an NVL8 node is working from the preview sheet, not the shipping one. Memory-bandwidth-bound work — large-model inference and training — has about a ninth less headroom per GPU than the preview promised; multi-GPU scale-up jobs have about a sixth less NVLink; scale-out-heavy clusters gain a little. Nothing here is benchmarked yet: these are the shipping specifications, not measured performance.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Spec sheets set expectations — and prices. Rubin still lands as a large step up in capacity per rack, but the honest baseline for judging any Rubin offer from today is 19.2 TB/s, 3.0 TB/s and, on NVL8 nodes, about 250GB per GPU. We have updated nothing on the price board for this — Rubin is not a board GPU yet — but when the first verified Rubin offers appear, they will be checked against the shipping specs, and any provider marketing the preview numbers will be called out on the listing.

One GPU, five “current” prices: how to tell which rental price is real

Search for an H100 rental price and you will meet several different numbers, every one of them presented as current. In late October 2026 we counted five different on-demand prices for the same H100 on a single provider’s own pages — on the same day. This guide puts the stated figures next to the verified ones, names the five mechanisms that pile prices up around one GPU, and ends with the three-step check that separates a price from a claim.

The verdict

  • H100 SXM — Stated on Spheron’s own pages: $2.64, $2.65, $2.75 and $2.98/hr on-demand across pages stamped Oct 20–28, 2026 — and $4.20/hr on pages refreshed Oct 28; spot stated $2.21/hr (Oct 28), then $2.79/hr (Oct 29). Verified best offer: TensorDock $2.25/GPU/hr at an 8-GPU minimum — an $18.00/hr floor; cheapest single card, RunPod Community $2.69/hr. Five stated on-demand figures live at once on Oct 28 — a $1.56 spread; the highest stated figure sits 56% above the cheapest verified single-card price. · $2.25/hr at TensorDock
  • B200 — Stated on Spheron’s own pages: $9.80–$9.90/hr on-demand (Oct 20), $11.06 (Oct 21), $11.12 (Oct 22, still stated Oct 30) — and on Oct 31 its own pages disagreed again: $11.06 on most pages, $11.12 in its refresh post; spot stated at $5.31 and $6.12 on the same day (Oct 24). Verified best offer: RunPod Community $5.98/hr. The stated on-demand price runs $5.14/hr above the verified best offer — 86% more for the same card. · $5.98/hr at RunPod Community
  • H200 — Stated on Spheron’s own pages: $7.09 and $5.54/hr on the same day (Oct 27); $4.80 and $5.51/hr inside a single refresh post (Oct 31). Verified best offer: RunPod Community $3.59/hr. Same-day stated figures $1.55 apart; the highest stated figure is nearly double the verified best offer. · $3.59/hr at RunPod Community
  • RTX 4090 — No split in our record. The two prices you will meet most are both verified, and both sit on RunPod’s own pricing page — Community $0.34/hr (Best offer) and Secure $0.89/hr are different service tiers, not a disagreement. No gap to explain: two real prices, each labelled with what it buys. Multiplicity only becomes a problem when the labels and the dates go missing. · $0.34/hr at RunPod Community

Why one GPU has five prices

Two words on this page carry exact meanings. Stated means a figure a site publishes, reported here exactly as stated, with its source and date — never as a verified price. Verified means read by us on the provider’s own current pricing page and re-checked on Oct 31, 2026. Five mechanisms produce the pile-up. None of them requires anyone to invent a number — pages are written at different times, updated on different schedules, and quoted figures age at different speeds. Each mechanism below is illustrated with figures we read first-hand, on the dates printed.

1 · Pages refreshed at different times — the H100 on Spheron’s own pages

A site with hundreds of pages does not update them all at once, so yesterday’s price survives on the pages nobody has touched yet. The H100 on Spheron’s own pages, read across eleven days:

Date readStated on-demand (Spheron’s pages)Stated spot
Oct 20, 2026$2.64, $2.65, $2.75 and $2.98/hr — four figures, different pages, the same day’s stamp—
Through Oct 27$2.64/hr$1.84/hr
Oct 28, 2026$4.20/hr on refreshed pages (its specs, slow-inference and multi-node guides and its pricing FAQ) — while the four older figures were still live on other pages: five stated on-demand prices at once$2.21/hr
Oct 29, 2026$4.20/hr on the refreshed pages, $2.64/hr still standing elsewhere$2.79/hr

No single row of that table can honestly be quoted as “the” Spheron H100 price — and that is the point. A renter landing on any one page meets exactly one figure, presented as current, with no way to tell whether it is the newest or the oldest on the site.

2 · Spot and on-demand get mixed together

Spot is the interruptible way to rent a card, and it normally prices below on-demand — so the two figures for one GPU can legitimately sit far apart. On Spheron’s own pages:

GPUStated on-demandStated spotRead
B200$11.12/hr$5.31/hr — and $6.12/hr on another page the same dayOct 24, 2026
RTX 6000 Ada$0.78/hr$0.93/hr — spot stated above on-demand, on a single pageOct 22, 2026

Any summary that lifts one of those numbers without its label misprices the card by a factor of two. And sometimes the labels themselves invert — the RTX 6000 Ada row is the proof: on a single page, the interruptible price sits above the guaranteed one.

3 · A per-GPU price can hide a per-node minimum

TensorDock’s H100 rate — $2.25 per GPU per hour — is the lowest verified per-GPU H100 price in our checks, and it is quoted at an eight-GPU minimum, which makes the real entry ticket $18.00 an hour:

RoutePer-GPU priceWhat you must takeReal hourly floor
TensorDock — H100 SXM$2.25/GPU/hr8 GPUs minimum$18.00/hr
RunPod Community — H100 SXM$2.69/hrA single card$2.69/hr

The figure is real; the shape is the story. We priced that shape in full in our TensorDock pricing guide, so this page only borrows its headline: a per-GPU number means nothing until you know how many GPUs you must take with it.

4 · Commitment prices get advertised as “starting at”

Together AI’s Google ad, seen on Oct 31, 2026, offers “B200s starting at $6.79”. Read on Together’s own pricing page the same day, the B200 carries five labelled tiers:

Together AI B200 tierPer GPU/hr
Preemptible$4.09/hr
Reserved — 3–30 days$7.99/hr
Reserved — 31–90 days$7.79/hr
Reserved — 91–180 days$6.79/hr
On-demand$8.19/hr

The advertised figure is real — it is the three-to-six-month commitment tier. The table on Together’s page labels every tier honestly; the ad keeps the number and drops the basis. (Together AI is not on our price board yet — we read its pricing page first-hand for this guide, and its figures are reported as read there, not as board offers.)

5 · Rivals get quoted from old snapshots

A comparison is only as current as its stalest figure. Spheron’s pricing FAQ, stated on Spheron’s own pages, quotes its rivals at figures dated May 2026. The verified figures, read on each provider’s own pricing page (checked Oct 24, 2026, and unchanged at our Oct 31 check):

Provider — B200Quoted in Spheron’s FAQ (May 2026)Verified on the provider’s own page
RunPod$5.89/hr$7.99/hr
Lambda$4.99–$5.29/hr$6.69/hr
Nebius$5.50/hr$8.50/hr

The quotes understate the real prices by $2.10, $1.40–$1.70 and $3.00 an hour. Whether the effect is intended is not something a price page can prove; the arithmetic is what a renter budgets on, and the arithmetic is five months old.

Compare prices→Find a GPU→

When five prices are all honest

Multiplicity itself is not the offence, and this page would mislead if it pretended otherwise. RunPod sells the same RTX 4090 at two verified prices — $0.34/hr on Community and $0.89/hr on Secure — because they are different service tiers with different guarantees, both current, both on the provider’s own pricing page. Together AI’s pricing page labels all five of its B200 tiers correctly; the failure there happened in the advertisement, not the table. Our reading, labelled as interpretation: a price becomes unreliable at the moment it travels — into a search result, a comparison table or an AI answer — without its basis and its date. Strip those away, and even a figure that was true somewhere misleads everywhere else.

Steps

1. Go to the provider’s own pricing page

Not the comparison site, not the advertisement, not the blog post: the page the provider itself sells from. If the figure you were quoted does not appear there, it is not a price anyone has to honour.

2. Find the basis before the number

On-demand or spot? Per GPU or per node? A minimum of one card, or eight? Pay-as-you-go, or a reserved term of months? The basis is part of the price — a figure quoted without it is half a fact.

3. Look for the date

When was the figure read, stamped or updated? A dated figure can be checked again tomorrow and corrected in the open. A figure with no date is asking to be trusted forever. No date, no trust. Applied to the title of this guide, the check takes under a minute: of the five H100 prices in the verdict, not one of the stated figures survives all three steps — they come from a comparison site’s pages (step 1), with their refresh dates scattered across eleven days (step 3). The verified figures do survive it, because each one names its provider, its basis and its check date.

Alternatives

Providers’ own pages only

Board prices are read on each provider’s own current pricing page — never on its marketing or comparison pages, and never copied from another aggregator.

Both-sides dated evidence before anything changes

A board figure moves only when we hold the old figure and the new one, each read on the provider’s own page, each with its date.

Stated figures are published as stated

Where a provider’s own pages disagree with each other, the honest publishable fact is the disagreement itself, dated and sourced — which is why Spheron’s prices appear on GPUJournal only in stated form, and why Spheron has no verified prices on our board.

Every check is stamped, and corrections are published

The board carries the date it was last checked, and when we get a figure wrong the correction goes on the record — never a quiet edit. Check today’s prices in the live comparison: it carries one verified figure per GPU and provider — the provider named first, the minimum printed next to the price, the check date stamped on the page.

Compare prices→Find a GPU→

How we know

Every stated Spheron figure in this guide was read on Spheron’s own pages (spheron.network) between Oct 20 and Oct 31, 2026, and is carried in our Price Watch with its read date: the H100 on-demand set ($2.64, $2.65, $2.75, $2.98, all stamped Oct 20, 2026; $4.20 on pages refreshed Oct 28); H100 spot ($1.84 through Oct 27; $2.21 read Oct 28; $2.79 read Oct 29); B200 on-demand ($9.80–$9.90 stated Oct 20; $11.06 stated Oct 21; $11.12 stated Oct 22 and still stated Oct 30; $11.06 on most pages vs $11.12 in its refresh post, read Oct 31); B200 spot ($5.31 and $6.12, both stated Oct 24); H200 ($7.09 and $5.54, both stated Oct 27; $4.80 and $5.51 in one refresh post, read Oct 31); RTX 6000 Ada spot $0.93 above on-demand $0.78 on one page stamped Oct 22; and the pricing FAQ’s rival quotes, dated May 2026 on Spheron’s pages. Together AI’s tiers were read on together.ai/pricing on Oct 31, 2026, and its “starting at $6.79” advertisement was seen the same day. The verified column is our board check of Oct 31, 2026: TensorDock H100 SXM $2.25/GPU/hr at an 8-GPU minimum (terms read on TensorDock’s own H100 page, Oct 29, 2026); RunPod Community H100 SXM $2.69, B200 $5.98, H200 $3.59, RTX 4090 $0.34; RunPod Secure RTX 4090 $0.89, B200 $7.99; Lambda B200 $6.69; Nebius B200 $8.50. The gap arithmetic: $4.20 vs $2.69 is 56% above; $11.12 vs $5.98 is $5.14/hr, or 86%, above; $7.09 is 1.97× $3.59 (“nearly double”); $7.09 − $5.54 = $1.55; the FAQ gaps are $7.99 − $5.89 = $2.10, $6.69 − $5.29/$4.99 = $1.40–$1.70, and $8.50 − $5.50 = $3.00. Two things this guide deliberately does not claim: that any stated figure is what a checkout on Spheron’s own platform would charge — we cannot verify that, and the inability is the finding — and that any provider intends to mislead. Pages age at different speeds; the dated record is what we publish.

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: self-host it or pay for the API?

NVIDIA’s open transcription model — 40 languages, speaker labels, translation, released Oct 28, 2026 — can be rented two ways: by the minute from a hosted API, or by the hour on a GPU you run yourself. The hosted price is public and tiny. The self-host price depends on one number nobody has independently measured yet — how fast the downloadable stack really runs — so this guide costs both routes honestly: the API at its published rate, self-hosting at a clearly printed planning assumption, and NVIDIA’s own published best case shown for what it is.

The verdict

  • Hosted API — DeepInfra — $0.00200 per minute of audio, read on DeepInfra’s own model page on Nov 1, 2026 — $120 per 1,000 hours of audio. Low or spiky volume, no setup, results in minutes. But speaker labels are not in the API yet — DeepInfra lists them as coming soon.
  • Self-host — RTX 5090 — RunPod Community $0.69/hr. The cheapest card on NVIDIA’s own supported list. At the planning assumption below, an hour of audio costs about 17× less than the API. Steady batch work: call archives, meeting libraries, media back-catalogues.
  • Self-host — L40S — RunPod Community $0.79/hr. A 48GB data-centre card on NVIDIA’s supported list, at near-5090 money, at the same planning assumption.
  • Self-host — A100 80GB — Thunder Compute $1.09/hr. The full-precision reference build on the 80GB shape NVIDIA’s own quick start uses, at the same planning assumption.
  • Self-host — RTX PRO 6000 — RunPod Community $1.69/hr. $0.0169/hr of audio at the planning assumption — and $0.0008–$0.0015 at NVIDIA’s own published throughput figures (below). The only card NVIDIA publishes serving numbers for: the pick if you want the maker’s measured stack, not an assumption.

What it needs: one card, and not the cheapest one on the board

Two numbers on this page carry exact meanings, and both are printed wherever they are used. The planning assumption: the open-source serving stack processes audio at 100× real-time — 100 seconds of audio per second of card time. NVIDIA’s published peak for its optimized build is 2,238× on one RTX PRO 6000, and NVIDIA itself says the downloadable open-source stack is expected to run roughly two times slower than that build; we plan at 100× to leave room for long files, speaker labels and unbatched work. Sensitivities at 50× and 200× are in the cost table. An assumption is not a benchmark — nobody has published an independent throughput measurement for this model yet. Memory sizing follows our standard method — total parameters × bytes per parameter, plus about 20% headroom — and matches the sizing on this model’s catalogue page. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is one open-weight checkpoint (nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B) that takes a recording of up to one hour plus a plain-language instruction and returns a transcript shaped by that instruction: verbatim or cleaned-up text, speaker tags for up to eight speakers, word-level timestamps, translation between English and 31 languages, or answers to questions about the recording, across 40 languages. The checkpoint holds 34 billion parameters in total, including its audio and speaker encoders, but only about 4.3 billion are active per token — which is why one GPU can carry it. It is an offline model: finished recordings, not live streams. The accuracy headline is NVIDIA’s own and is labelled that way throughout: NVIDIA reports a 5.33% average word error rate on the Hugging Face Open ASR English leaderboard — first among open-weight models — and its card’s results table (captured Oct 12, 2026) shows a 4.71% mean across the nine English sets, 4.62% multilingual and 10.98% on long-form. No independent reproduction of those figures had been published when we checked.

Memory alone is not the whole test, because NVIDIA publishes a hardware compatibility table on the model card — the list of GPUs its runtimes are actually built and tested for. That table, read Nov 1, 2026, is the next one.

Its 32GB holds the ~17GB NVFP4 build with room to spare, it is on NVIDIA’s supported list (vLLM, Transformers and GGML runtimes), and at $0.69/hr it is the cheapest supported route on the board. The honest catch sits one row below it in price: the RTX 4090, at $0.34/hr on RunPod Community, is the cheapest card we list and its 24GB would hold the NVFP4 build by memory — but the 4090 is NOT in NVIDIA’s compatibility table, and its Ada-generation hardware has no native FP4 path in the official runtimes. Community builds may close that gap in time; today, planning a deployment on the 4090 means planning on unsupported ground. We do not recommend it as the plan.

What an hour of audio costs

The API side is a single published number: DeepInfra — one of the hosts NVIDIA’s launch names, serving the model through an OpenAI-compatible speech-to-text endpoint — lists $0.00200 per minute of audio on its own model page (read Nov 1, 2026): $0.12 per hour of audio, $120 per 1,000 hours, $1,200 per 10,000 hours. Requests can run to 60 minutes; transcription, word and segment timestamps, contextual prompts and translation into English are live today. If the real stack runs at half that speed on your audio, the 50× column is your cost; at double, the 200× column. Even the slowest column beats the API rate on every card — the gap is wide enough that the assumption would have to be wrong by more than an order of magnitude before the ranking flipped.

The break-even: it’s about the card’s month, not the minute

Rent by the hour and shut the card down between batches, and self-hosting is cheaper per hour of audio from the first batch — the only real minimum order is your own setup time (downloading a 17–68GB checkpoint and standing up vLLM with the NeMo Speech plugin). The break-even that matters is the other rental shape: a card kept for a full month (730 hours) whether or not audio is flowing. Against the API’s $0.12 per hour of audio, a month of card has to process this much audio before it has paid for itself:

Card kept for a monthMonth cost (730 hrs)Break-even vs the API

Below those volumes, the API wins on money alone — and wins outright on everything operational: no setup, no idle card, no stack to patch. Above them, self-hosting wins on money and on three things the API cannot sell you at any price today: speaker labels (in the open model now; DeepInfra lists them as coming soon in its API), your audio never leaving your own machine (DeepInfra states zero data retention, which is a policy promise rather than an architecture), and fine-tuning — the NeMo Speech toolkit adapts the model to your vocabulary and accents, which no hosted endpoint offers. One more honest line in the API’s favour: a 10,000-hour archive costs $1,200 there, against $69 of card time on a 5090 at the planning assumption — but the $69 route also costs the days of engineering to build and babysit the pipeline. Price your own time before you call it cheaper.

The serving reality: a published recipe, and a faster build you can’t download yet

The open serving path is real and documented on the model card. NVIDIA’s quick start serves the checkpoint on one H100 80GB with vLLM 0.32.0 plus the NeMo Speech plugin (VLLM_PLUGINS=nemo_speechlm), exposing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint — code written against OpenAI-style chat and audio APIs ports over with small changes. SGLang-Omni 0.2.0 is listed for H100 and the RTX PRO 6000, Hugging Face Transformers runs it in-process, and GGML covers the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000, including native Windows. The card’s own configuration turns on native multi-token prediction for speed, with an optional DFlash2 draft model for speculative decoding. Then the caveat, in NVIDIA’s own words on the same card: its fastest published serving numbers come from the Nemotron Transcribe NIM, NVIDIA’s optimized container build — and “these serving optimizations are not yet part of the open-source release”. NVIDIA says the open-source vLLM integration that shipped on release day “is intended for model development and is expected to be roughly two times slower”. So the stack you can download today is the development-grade one, by the maker’s own description; the optimized build sits behind NVIDIA’s NIM route and its own terms. Budget on the open stack; treat anything faster as a bonus. NVIDIA’s own published figures, for the one card it measured: on the model card’s Efficiency section, NVIDIA reports that its optimized NIM build on one RTX PRO 6000 transcribes up to 2,238 seconds of audio per second (NVFP4 with DFlash2 speculative decoding), and returns a 30-second transcript in 0.13 seconds. Priced at the verified $1.69/hr, that peak works out to about $0.0008 per hour of audio — $0.76 per 1,000 hours. At the roughly-two-times-slower speed NVIDIA states for the open-source stack (~1,119×), it is about $0.0015 per hour of audio, $1.51 per 1,000 hours. Both figures are the maker’s, the first is an “up to” peak, and the NIM build behind it is not the downloadable one. We show them because they are published and checkable — not as the basis for a budget.

Steps

1. Count your monthly audio hours first

Under roughly 4,000 hours of audio a month — or any volume you can’t be bothered to operate — pay DeepInfra’s $0.12 an hour and spend your time elsewhere. The break-even table above gives the exact line for each card kept for a full month; rent-by-the-hour with the card shut down between batches has no break-even to cross at all.

2. Check the feature list, not just the price

If who-said-what is the whole point of your project, the route is already settled: speaker labels are in the open model today and listed as coming soon in DeepInfra’s API. The same goes for keeping audio on your own machine, or fine-tuning on your vocabulary and accents — no hosted endpoint sells those today.

3. Self-host on the smallest supported card

Rent an RTX 5090 at $0.69/hr and run the NVFP4 build yourself — not the cheaper RTX 4090, which fits by memory but is not on NVIDIA’s supported list. Download the checkpoint, stand up vLLM 0.32.0 with the NeMo Speech plugin per NVIDIA’s quick start, and test the maker’s accuracy figures on your own recordings before you budget around them.

Alternatives

Watch out — the cheapest card is not a supported card

The RTX 4090 ($0.34/hr) fits the NVFP4 build by memory but is absent from NVIDIA’s compatibility table. The cheapest supported route is the RTX 5090 at $0.69/hr.

Watch out — every accuracy figure is the maker’s

The 5.33% leaderboard average and the card’s results table are NVIDIA-reported and labelled that way wherever we use them. No independent throughput or accuracy benchmark for this model had been published when we checked — including for the 2,238× serving peak.

Watch out — the fast stack is not the free stack

NVIDIA’s published serving peak comes from its NIM build, whose optimizations are “not yet part of the open-source release” (NVIDIA’s words). The downloadable vLLM path is described by NVIDIA as a development integration, expected to run roughly two times slower.

Watch out — it is not a live-captioning model

Offline only, recordings up to one hour per request. Speaker labels cover 13 of the 40 languages; translation covers 31 languages to or from English; question-answering about a recording was evaluated in English only. Check the card’s language matrix against your audio before committing.

Good to know — the API’s feature list is shorter than the model’s

On DeepInfra today: transcription, timestamps, contextual prompts and translation into English — speaker attribution is listed as coming soon. NVIDIA itself publishes no per-minute price for a hosted version of this model — its build.nvidia.com route is a free trial, not a priced production API — and Baseten and Simplismart, the other hosts NVIDIA’s launch names, publish no per-minute price either. DeepInfra’s is the only public per-minute figure to budget against.

The licence: OpenMDW-1.1 — commercial use allowed, conditions attached

The model is released under the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1 (OpenMDW-1.1), and the model card states plainly: “This model is ready for commercial or non-commercial use.” The licence text itself (read in full, Nov 1, 2026) grants permission “to deal in the Model Materials without restriction” across copyright, patent, database and trade-secret rights; imposes no restrictions on outputs — transcripts you produce are yours to use; and requires that if you distribute the model materials, you keep a copy of the licence and the copyright notices with them. Two clauses deserve a careful read before a commercial launch: your rights terminate if you sue someone claiming the model materials infringe a patent or copyright (unless you were sued first), and the materials come “as is” with no warranty — clearing any third-party rights in what you feed it is expressly your responsibility. This is a plain-words summary, not legal advice; the licence is short and linked from the model card.

NVIDIA and Cisco unveil USFP — 400Gb/s-per-lane pluggable optics for AI factories

Nov 3, 2026

Announced on Nov 3, 2026: NVIDIA and Cisco plan USFP, an Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable optical module running 400Gb/s per lane — four times the bandwidth and front-panel density of today's 200Gb/s-per-lane modules at about 1.3 times the power efficiency, in a module comparable in size to OSFP.

Image: Cisco via newsroom.cisco.com

What was announced, from the joint NVIDIA and Cisco release of Nov 3, 2026: USFP is designed to let AI-factory builders scale from 200Gb/s-per-lane to 400Gb/s-per-lane Ethernet fabrics without overhauling their data-centre infrastructure. Against 200Gb/s-per-lane pluggables it claims 4× the bandwidth and front-panel bandwidth density and roughly 1.3× the power efficiency, which lowers networking's share of a factory's overall power budget as clusters grow.

The ecosystem: NVIDIA and Cisco are working with TE Connectivity and Amphenol on USFP cages, connectors and modules, with more partners expected to join, and the two companies plan to create an open industry specification for USFP through a community-led multi-source project. The work builds on the existing effort to make NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet and Cisco Silicon One-based Ethernet networks run together — the two main Ethernet paths a large GPU cluster can be wired with.

What the companies said: Gilad Shainer, senior vice president at NVIDIA — “Building the world's largest AI factories starts with rethinking the smallest of connections.” Bill Gartner, Cisco's senior vice president for optical systems and optics, said scaling pluggable optics to 400Gb/s per lane “required more than another incremental extension of today's module designs” and that USFP is meant to keep the serviceability and deployment flexibility of pluggable optics at the new density.

Why it reaches a price journal: optics and switching are a real and growing share of what a GPU cluster costs to build and to power, and every watt the network takes is a watt the GPUs do not get. Denser, more efficient pluggables do not change any rental price today — there is no USFP product to rent yet, and no pricing was announced — but they are the kind of supply-side step that decides what the next generation of B300- and Rubin-class capacity costs to run, and therefore what it rents for.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Nothing on the price board moves on this story. File it as a forward cost signal: the interconnect layer of AI factories is being rebuilt for 400Gb/s per lane, as an open specification rather than one vendor's proprietary link — and open, multi-source optics are what keep that layer's prices honest when the clusters built on it start appearing on rental boards.

Marvell to acquire Lumentum in a $115 billion AI-connectivity deal

Nov 2, 2026

Announced on Nov 2, 2026 in Marvell's own investor release: a definitive all-stock agreement to combine Marvell with Lumentum, the laser and photonics maker — about $115 billion of enterprise value, aimed squarely at the interconnect layer that AI factories run on.

Image: Lumentum via lumentum.com

The deal, from Marvell's investor press release of Nov 2, 2026: Lumentum shareholders receive 4.500 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share — about $1,132 a share, a 23.9% premium to Lumentum's Oct 28 close — valuing the combination at roughly $115 billion of enterprise value and about $80 billion of equity value. Marvell holders will own about 67% of the combined company and Lumentum holders about 33%. The close is expected in the first half of 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approval — this is an agreement, not a completed merger.

Why these two: Marvell builds custom silicon and networking chips for AI data centres; Lumentum makes the lasers and photonic components that move data between GPUs over fibre. Together they cover the connection layer of an AI factory — the part that has become a bottleneck and a major cost as clusters scale from racks to buildings. Coverage of the deal notes that NVIDIA has about $2 billion invested in each of the two companies, which underlines how central both already are to the GPU supply chain.

The market's first verdict was sceptical: both stocks fell on Nov 2 (Marvell about 12.7% in market reports), and the deal was cited among the drivers of a wider AI-infrastructure selloff on Nov 3. A close two years out, at a premium, in a market this volatile will be argued over for a while; the terms above are the ones in the release, and the reaction figures are market reporting, labelled as such.

What it does not do: change any GPU rental price today. No provider's rates, capacity or regions move because of this announcement, and nothing on our price board is affected. Its significance for renters and buyers is slower and structural — consolidation among the handful of suppliers every large cluster depends on for optics and interconnect is worth watching long before it shows up in an hourly rate.

What it means if you rent GPUs

A $115 billion bet that the scarce layer of the AI build-out is not the GPU but the connection between GPUs. For renters there is no action today; for anyone planning capacity into 2027–28, the ownership of the optics supply chain just became a question worth tracking alongside GPU supply itself.

/story/runpod-serverless-price-rise-nov-.html:
NEWS →  ·  Prices · RunPod

RunPod Serverless GPU prices are up — B200 up about 25%, every tier higher

Nov 2, 2026

RunPod's Serverless GPU rates have risen on every tier, recorded between the Oct 26 and Nov 2, 2026 captures of its own pricing page: B200 $8.64 → $10.79 an hour is the largest move, up about 25%. RunPod announced nothing — the new figures are simply the ones live on runpod.io/pricing today, which we read first-hand on Nov 2.

Image: RunPod via runpod.io

What changed — the new figures read on RunPod's own pricing page (runpod.io/pricing) on Nov 2, 2026, against the figures captured from the same page on Oct 26, 2026: B300 $10.65 → $11.99 (up about 13%), B200 $8.64 → $10.79 (up about 25%), H200 $5.93 → $6.99 (up about 18%), H100 $4.79 → $5.39 (up about 13%), RTX 5090 $1.58 → $1.79 (up about 13%), RTX 4090 $1.10 → $1.34 (up about 22%), and the grouped L4 / A5000 / 3090 rate $0.69 → $0.75 (up about 9%). Every Serverless tier rose; none fell. On sourcing, plainly: the after-figures are RunPod's own page as we read it today; the before-figures are PricingSaaS Pulse's dated Oct 26 capture of that same page, because our own archive does not hold the October Serverless buckets — the comparison is recorded at pricingsaas.com/companies/runpod/diffs/2026W45. There is no RunPod announcement and no stated effective date; the honest date for the change is the window between the two captures.

Also recorded between the same two captures: the Serverless line “Save 25% over other Serverless cloud providers on flex workers” was removed from the page, and the section now points to contract pricing instead of the long-term-commitment savings copy that sat there before.

What did not change: RunPod's Pods. Re-read on Nov 2, 2026, Pods Secure prices are exactly where they were — B300 $8.99, B200 $7.99, H200 $5.29, H100 SXM $3.99, A100 $1.79, L40S $1.09, RTX 5090 $1.19, RTX 4090 $0.89 and RTX PRO 6000 $2.49 an hour. Serverless is billed per second of worker time for inference endpoints, and its rates are not price-board rates, so the board does not move on this story — but anyone serving inference on RunPod Serverless is paying the new figures now.

What it costs: a Serverless worker that runs around the clock on a B200 now bills about $7,877 a month at $10.79 an hour, against about $6,307 at the old $8.64 — roughly $1,570 more per always-on GPU. An H100 worker running 24/7 goes from about $3,497 to about $3,935 a month. Serverless is normally bought for spiky traffic, where the per-second billing still beats an idle pod; the rises narrow that advantage at exactly the high end — B200 and H200 workers — where always-on endpoints are most common. This is RunPod's second rise in the recent record (Secure Cloud rose on Oct 14) and it extends the autumn pattern — Nebius on Oct 1, Verda eight times from Oct 23 to Nov 2, SaladCloud on Nov 1: rising prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can also play a part).

What it means if you rent GPUs

If you serve models on RunPod Serverless, re-price your endpoint today: every tier costs more than it did in late October, the B200 tier about a quarter more, and nothing on the page still promises a saving over other serverless providers. The cross-check that matters is your per-request cost at the new per-second rates against a Pods Secure instance at its unchanged prices — for steady traffic, the pod side of RunPod just got relatively cheaper, because it did not move at all.

/story/nebius-spot-ceiling-removed-nov-2.html:
NEWS →  ·  Prices · Nebius

Nebius removes its spot-price ceiling — preemptible GPUs can now cost more than on-demand

Nov 2, 2026

In an update note dated Nov 2, 2026 on its own blog, Nebius says the cap that kept its dynamic spot price one cent below the on-demand rate is gone. Spot still has a floor — it just no longer has a top, and setting your own max price is now the only brake.

Image: Nebius via nebius.com

What changed, from Nebius's own post “Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs” (published Sep 22, 2026; read Nov 2, 2026): its update note, dated Nov 2, 2026, reads — “this section previously stated that the spot price always stays between a floor and a ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate. We have removed the ceiling. Customers can cap what they pay by setting a max price.” The post's how-it-works section now states plainly: “There is no upper limit, so during periods of high demand the spot price can rise above the on-demand GPU-hour rate.”

How the mechanism works, in the same post: the spot price for a GPU type in a region is set from available capacity and real-time demand, recalculated up to every 15 minutes, and it still cannot fall below a set floor — only the ceiling has gone. A renter who sets a max price keeps the old protection by hand: when spot rises above the cap, the instance stops, data is retained, and it can restart when the price falls back — automatically for Kubernetes clusters, manually (or via Terraform, SDK, API or CLI) for standalone VMs. A renter who instead chose to follow the spot price has no cap at all after today's change.

What did not change: Nebius's on-demand list. Re-read on Nebius's own prices page on Nov 2, 2026, B300 is $9.50 an hour, B200 $8.50, H200 $5.40, H100 $4.50, RTX PRO 6000 $1.80 and L40S from $1.55 — every figure the same as our Nov 1 read. This is not a price rise in the list; it is the removal of the guarantee that the interruptible lane is always the cheaper one.

Why it matters in this market: spot and preemptible capacity is where budget inference, batch jobs and short fine-tunes live, and its whole pitch was a discount in exchange for interruption risk. A spot price that can pass the on-demand rate in a busy hour inverts that pitch exactly when capacity is tightest — which, in the autumn pattern this journal has been tracking (Nebius's own across-the-board rise on Oct 1, Verda's eight rises since Oct 23, SaladCloud's demand-cited rise on Nov 1), is more and more of the time. Rising prices and now an uncapped spot market are consistent with growing demand for GPUs (our reading of the pattern, labelled as interpretation).

What it means if you rent GPUs

If you rent preemptible VMs on Nebius, do one thing today: set a max price. The ceiling that used to do that job for you was removed on Nov 2, and a workload set to follow the spot price can now be billed above the on-demand rate in a high-demand hour — paying a premium for capacity that can still be reclaimed. The discount lane still exists, but from today the discount is something you enforce yourself.

/story/verda-ninth-rise-nov-4.html:
NEWS →  ·  Prices · Verda

Verda raises prices for the ninth time — all nine GPUs up about 1% again

Nov 4, 2026

Read on Verda's own pricing page today, Nov 4, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 3: every GPU in Verda's range rose by about 1% — GB300, B300, B200, H200, H100, both A100s, the RTX PRO 6000 and the L40S. One flat day, then the rise run resumed.

Image: Verda via verda.com

What changed, read on verda.com/pricing on Nov 4, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.18 → $13.31 [$13.31], B300 $11.46 → $11.57 [$11.57], B200 $8.96 → $9.05 [$9.048], H200 $6.31 → $6.38 [$6.376], H100 SXM $4.84 → $4.89 [$4.889], A100 80GB $2.27 → $2.29 [$2.293], A100 40GB $1.63 → $1.64 [$1.641], RTX PRO 6000 $2.67 → $2.70 [$2.698] and L40S $1.92 → $1.94 [$1.939]. Each move is within a whisker of +1.0% — a uniform list adjustment, not one card repricing.

The pattern: Verda rose on Oct 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30, held on Oct 31 and Nov 1, rose an eighth time on Nov 2, held on Nov 3 — and has now risen a ninth time. Its GB300, the only GB300 rate we list, has gone from $11.82 an hour at our Oct 19 check to $13.31 today, up 12.6% in just over two weeks. Verda is not alone in the pattern: Nebius raised across the board on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, SaladCloud's Priority rise took effect Nov 1 and RunPod Serverless rose by Nov 2. Rising list prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can produce the same shape).

What it costs: Verda holds the board's Best offer on only two cards — the GB300 and the A100 40GB — and both rose today, so those two best offers rose with it. Everywhere else the cheapest verified offers are other providers' and none moved: the board's H100 SXM best is still TensorDock at $2.25 an hour (at an 8-GPU minimum) and its B200 best is still RunPod Community at $5.98. If you rent at Verda around the clock, today's rise adds about $95 a month per GB300, $66 per B200 and $37 per H100 on a 730-hour month — small per hour, real per fleet.

Checked today and unchanged: RunPod Secure and RunPod Serverless, Lambda, Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute and TensorDock all held at the rates read on Nov 3, and SaladCloud's Priority rates (RTX 5090 High $0.60, RTX 4090 High $0.44) are still the live ones. Not checked today, and named rather than covered by the stamp: RunPod Community (its tier could not be separated in today's read), Hyperstack (its pricing table could not be read, for the seventh straight day) and nafnaf.ai (its homepage showed no GPUs available today, so there was no live listing to verify).

What it means if you rent GPUs

Nine rises in thirteen days is no longer noise — it is one provider repricing steadily upward while the market's best verified offers stay put. The spread is the story for renters: a workload priced off Verda's list page in mid-October is about 13% adrift on the GB300 today, while the cheapest way to rent most cards has not moved at all. Check the board before renewing or expanding at a list rate — and if you are on Verda's GB300 or A100 40GB, your best-offer price moved today.

/story/tencent-hy4-launch-nov-4.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Tencent

Tencent launches Hy4 — a 770B flagship with vision and computer use; open weights promised in the coming days

Nov 4, 2026

Announced by Tencent on Nov 4, 2026: Hy4, the new flagship in its Hunyuan line, is live today across Tencent's own products and cloud — the first in the line that can see images and operate a computer. The open weights are not out yet: Tencent says they arrive, with a system card, in the coming days.

Image: Tencent via tencent.com

What launched, from Tencent's own release of Nov 4, 2026: Hy4 adds visual understanding to the Hunyuan line for the first time — fine-grained image processing, complex chart analysis and mathematical visual reasoning — and computer-use capabilities, driving both command-line and graphical interfaces, with specialised training on professional software such as Blender and CAD. It is available now on Tencent Cloud TokenHub, in WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, ima and WeCom's Dayuan assistant, and its API is being made available via OpenRouter, Hermes and OpenCode.

The scale, in Tencent's launch figures: 770 billion total parameters in a mixture-of-experts design, about 49 billion active per token — the full version of the model previewed in August. Tencent ranks it among the world's leading open-source models on its own blind financial evaluation (213 professionals scoring real tasks: Hy4 3.04, ahead of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 at 2.97 and Kimi K3.1 Pro at 2.68). That is Tencent's internal evaluation, reported as such — independent benchmarks will take time.

The catch, stated plainly: there is nothing to download today. Tencent says the model weights and system card will be released in the coming days, and no licence has been published yet — so despite the open-source framing, Hy4 cannot be self-hosted, fine-tuned or inspected until the files actually appear. A cheaper Hy4 Flash is also scheduled, with no date given. We have added Hy4 to the model catalogue with its status marked exactly that way.

The price of using it hosted, from Tencent's release: about $0.90 per million input tokens, $2.70 per million output and $0.045 per million cached input — the same pricing as the Preview — with TokenHub at 50% off through Dec 31, 2026 and WorkBuddy/CodeBuddy free from Nov 4 to 15. For GPU renters the number that matters comes later: at 770B parameters, the plain arithmetic says even a 4-bit build of the weights is about 385GB, roughly 462GB with working headroom — at least five 96GB cards or six 80GB cards when the weights land. Until then, Tencent's API is the only way in.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Another frontier-scale model joins the open-weight queue — and, as with Kimi K3.1 Pro, the honest headline is the gap between the announcement and the download. When the Hy4 weights do appear, the deployment maths is cluster maths, not single-card maths, and the licence that ships with them will decide who can actually use them commercially. Both are worth checking here before planning around them.

/story/amd-helios-live-data-center-doubl.html:
NEWS →  ·  Market · AMD + Supermicro

AMD’s data-centre revenue nearly doubles as Helios racks go live at five AI giants — and Supermicro’s sales quadruple

Nov 3, 2026

Reported by both companies after the close on Nov 3, 2026: AMD’s Data Center revenue hit a record $8.5 billion, up 97% year over year, and its release names Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle Cloud as already running models and workloads on the first Helios rackscale systems. The same evening, Supermicro — the server builder that turns GPUs into shippable systems — reported quarterly sales of $19.9 billion, nearly four times a year ago. Two supplier scorecards, one message for renters: AI hardware demand is still accelerating.

Image: AMD via newsroom.amd.com

AMD’s quarter, from its own Q3 2026 results release (Nov 3, 2026): revenue was a record $13.4 billion, up 45% year over year; Data Center segment revenue was a record $8.5 billion, up 97%, “driven by strong demand for AMD EPYC processors and the launch of AMD Instinct MI450 Series GPUs”; non-GAAP earnings were $2.09 a share. CEO Lisa Su: “Demand for our Instinct and EPYC products continued to strengthen, and we expect growth to accelerate further in the fourth quarter as we scale Helios and ‘Venice’ production.” The fourth-quarter guide is about $17 billion of revenue, plus or minus 3% — roughly 66% above a year ago.

The step that matters most to this market: the same release says Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure “are running models and workloads on the first AMD Helios rackscale solutions, powered by AMD Instinct MI450 Series GPUs and 6th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs” — and that HPE has announced Vultr will deploy the first AMD Helios by HPE systems. A week ago (Oct 27) the verified position was narrower: initial Helios systems installed and being tested at Meta. ‘Installed and testing’ has become ‘running workloads’ at five of the largest AI buyers, and the first named rental-cloud deployment (Vultr, via HPE) is now on the record. Trade coverage of the earnings call (Earnings Whispers’ account, Nov 3) reports management adding that MI450 Helios racks began revenue shipments in the quarter and that 2027 revenue is now expected to grow more than 80% — call remarks as reported, not release text.

Supermicro’s quarter, from its own release (Nov 3, 2026): net sales of $19.9 billion for its fiscal Q1 2027 (quarter ended Sep 30, 2026), against $11.1 billion the prior quarter and $5.0 billion a year ago — a near-quadrupling — with net income of $1.59 billion and non-GAAP earnings of $1.81 a share. It guides next quarter to $19.5–$21.5 billion and the full fiscal year to $72–$82 billion, a range trade coverage notes is raised from the $65–$72 billion given in August. Two honest cautions from the release itself: the figures are preliminary and unaudited, and operations still used $434 million of cash in the quarter — growth this fast eats working capital.

Why a price journal is reporting earnings at all: these are the supply lines behind every row on our board. Helios is the first rack-scale alternative to NVIDIA’s NVL72 line to reach production workloads at the biggest buyers, which is how non-NVIDIA capacity eventually reaches rental boards — Vultr’s Helios order is the first thread of that. And Supermicro’s near-quadrupling is the server-assembly end of the same demand that has pushed rental lists up all autumn (Nebius on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, Verda’s eight rises to Nov 2, SaladCloud on Nov 1, RunPod Serverless by Nov 2). Read as a pattern it is consistent with still-growing GPU demand — our interpretation, labelled as such; supplier revenue is not rental pricing, and neither company announced a rental price today.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Nothing on the price board moves on this story — no provider changed a rental price this evening (Verda was re-read first-hand tonight: all nine tracked GPUs identical to this morning). What changes is the map: the AMD rack path is no longer a promise being tested at one customer, it is production hardware at five, with a rental-cloud name attached. Watch for the follow-through that would touch this board — the first bookable Helios or MI450-series offer from Vultr or any tracked provider — and expect the demand side of the autumn price-rise pattern to stay firm while the two biggest non-NVIDIA suppliers are printing numbers like these.

Best GPU for video generation in 2026

A video model doesn’t bill you by the token. It bills you by the second of card time — so the right question is never “which GPU is fastest?” but “which is the smallest card that runs this model well, and what does one finished clip cost on it?” This guide answers that for the six open-weight video models people actually rent cards for in 2026 — Wan 2.2 in both sizes, HunyuanVideo-1.5, LTX-2, CogVideoX-1.5 and Mochi 1 — with verified prices checked Nov 4, 2026, and a cost per 5-second clip wherever the maker publishes a generation time. Where a maker publishes none, we price the model by the hour and say so, rather than invent a number.

The verdict

  • HunyuanVideo-1.5 (step-distilled build, 480p) — RTX 4090 (24GB), RunPod Community $0.34/hr. Tencent reports the distilled build makes a ~5-second clip in 75 seconds on a single 4090 — about $0.007 a clip. The full 50-step base model runs on the same card at the same price, slower per clip; Tencent publishes no base timing.
  • Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B (720p) — RTX 4090 (24GB), RunPod Community $0.34/hr. Wan’s own table measures 534.7 seconds and 22.9GB peak for a 5-second 720p clip on one 4090 — about $0.05 a clip. The default starting point for rented video work.
  • Wan 2.2 T2V-A14B (720p) — A100 80GB, Thunder Compute $1.09/hr. Wan’s single-GPU run needs an 80GB-class card; its measured peak at 720p is 59.8GB. 2,735.7 seconds a clip on the A100 — about $0.83; on an H100 SXM at $2.69/hr, 1,041.5 seconds — about $0.78.
  • CogVideoX-1.5-5B (1360×768) — A100 80GB, Thunder Compute $1.09/hr. The maker publishes ~1,000 seconds per 5-second video on one A100 at 50 steps — about $0.30 a clip; ~550 seconds on an H100 works out to ~$0.41.
  • Mochi 1 (480p) — A100 80GB, Thunder Compute $1.09/hr. The official route needs ~60GB of VRAM on one card. Genmo publishes no generation time, so there is no honest cost per clip — priced per hour only.
  • LTX-2 (video with sound) — A100 80GB, Thunder Compute $1.09/hr. Lightricks publishes neither a VRAM floor nor a generation time; the 80GB pick is our sizing from its checkpoint files (the bf16 transformer alone is a 43.3GB file), explained in the guide. Priced per hour only.

Why video is different: you rent seconds, not tokens

Our language-model guides price work per token, because a language model’s cost really does scale with tokens in and out. A video model has no tokens to count. Its cost is set by two numbers: whether it fits — the VRAM it needs at the resolution and length you actually render — and how long a clip takes — the seconds of card time between pressing run and holding a finished file. Multiply the second number by the card’s hourly price and you have the only figure that matters: cost per finished clip. That is also why video guides are so easy to get wrong. Makers publish memory figures measured with different switches on — offloading to system RAM, tiling, reduced precision — and most publish no generation time at all. A “fits in 14GB” claim and a “runs well” claim can both be true of the same model while describing experiences an hour apart. So this guide holds a hard line: every timing below is published by the model’s own maker and labelled maker-reported; every price is from our board check of Nov 4, 2026; and where a maker publishes no timing — Mochi 1 and LTX-2 — the model is priced per hour, with the reason stated, instead of a clip cost built on air. One boundary before the tables: the newest Wan you can download is Wan 2.2. Wan-AI’s Hugging Face organisation, checked Nov 4, 2026, lists no Wan 2.5 or later weights — those versions are API-only, so if you want them you are buying API credits, not renting a card. Wan 2.1’s 14B is covered by its successor — Wan 2.2’s A14B is the same job, newer weights, same Apache 2.0 licence. (Wan’s own card notes the small Wan 2.1 1.3B makes a 5-second 480p clip on an RTX 4090 in about 4 minutes — fine for a first experiment, not a production pick.)

“Runs it well” in this guide means the full model at the resolution people actually use, on one card, without shrinking the job to fit — not the maker’s absolute minimum with every memory-saving switch on. The minimums are real, and they are in this table, next to the cards we would actually rent:

The pattern to notice: the honest dividing line in video is not 24GB versus 48GB — it is 24GB versus 80GB. The two small models (Wan’s 5B and HunyuanVideo-1.5) are built to live on a 4090-class card, and their makers prove it with timings measured on that card. Everything bigger either states an 80GB-class requirement outright (Wan’s A14B, CogVideoX’s full-precision route, Mochi’s official route) or, like LTX-2, ships checkpoint files so large that an 80GB card is the sensible planning unit. The 48GB cards (L40S, RTX A6000) earn their place in exactly one way: the offload routes — Mochi’s 42GB diffusers example fits there, and LTX-2’s FP8 checkpoint is the lighter way into that model. On LTX-2’s sizing, plainly: Lightricks publishes no minimum VRAM and no speed on the LTX-2 card, and its own example pipeline offloads parts of the model to the CPU. What can be checked is the weight of the download — the bf16 transformer checkpoint is a 43.3GB file, the FP8 build 27.1GB, the NVFP4 build 20.0GB — and the text encoder those files pair with is heavy in its own right. We would not plan a production run on less than an 80GB card for the bf16 build, and we label that as our sizing from the published files, not a maker specification. Lightricks has also since shipped LTX-2.3 (the card flags it as the newer version); every figure here is for the LTX-2 checkpoints listed.

What a finished clip costs — maker-reported times only

Every row is arithmetic on a timing the model’s maker publishes, at a card price from our board check of Nov 4, 2026: clip cost = seconds per clip ÷ 3,600 × $/hr. The clips are the makers’ own reference jobs — a 5-second clip at each model’s standard settings — so the rows compare fairly with each other, and none of them is a benchmark we ran:

Three things this table teaches. First, the cheap card wins more often than you’d expect: CogVideoX is faster on an H100 but cheaper per clip on an A100, because the A100’s hourly price falls further than its speed does. Second, for Wan’s big model the two 80GB cards tie at 480p ($0.24 either way) and nearly tie at 720p — so the H100’s real product is not cheaper clips, it is time: about 3.5 clips an hour against the A100’s 1.3. Third, the distilled small models are in a different economy altogether — at 75 seconds a clip, a 4090 turns out roughly 48 HunyuanVideo clips an hour for $0.34. And one honest multiplier applies to every row: these are costs per generation. Nobody ships the first roll of a video model, so budget two to three generations per clip you keep — the ranking doesn’t change, the budget does. The models, one by one: Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B is the default starting point — Alibaba’s 5B does text- and image-to-video at 720p and 24fps under Apache 2.0, and Wan calls its 4090 result “under 9 minutes” unoptimized on a consumer card. HunyuanVideo-1.5 generates at 480p and 720p with super-resolution to 1080p, and its 75-second figure belongs to the step-distilled build, not the full 50-step base model. Wan 2.2 T2V-A14B is the quality pick — and its measured 59.8GB peak is why claims that it needs a 96GB card are wrong on the maker’s own numbers; a matched image-to-video twin (I2V-A14B) sits under the same licence. CogVideoX-1.5-5B, out since November 2024, renders 1360×768 at 5 or 10 seconds and publishes the most complete speed table of any model here. Mochi 1 is a 480p preview (848×480) whose maker recommends an H100 and publishes no timing at all. LTX-2 is the only model here that makes sound with its picture — a 19B two-stage pipeline with bf16, FP8 and NVFP4 checkpoints plus a distilled build that runs in 8 steps — and the least documented: treat your first rented hour as its benchmark.

The counterweight: when renting is the wrong answer

For a handful of clips, a hosted video API beats every row in this guide: no download, no stack, a finished clip in minutes, and somebody else’s queue to wait in. Renting wins when the volume is steady, when the footage can’t leave your own machine, or when you need the model itself — fine-tunes, LoRAs, a fixed-seed pipeline an API won’t expose. And a note on the other big guide to this question: Spheron’s “Best GPU for Video Generation” coverage, read Nov 4, 2026, puts Wan 2.2 at 720p in a 65–80GB bracket with an H100 as the floor, and builds its clip costs on Spheron’s own stated rates. Wan’s published table measures 59.8GB peak on one GPU, and at a verified $1.09/hr the A100 run in the table above costs $0.83 a clip. Dated, checkable prices change the answer — which is rather the point of this page.

Steps

1. Pick the model by the clip, not the headline

Need 720p cheaply and in volume: Wan’s 5B or distilled HunyuanVideo-1.5 on a 4090. Need the best open quality at 720p: Wan’s A14B on an 80GB card. Need sound with the picture: LTX-2, priced by the hour. Need it under Apache 2.0 for a commercial pipeline: Wan or Mochi — and read the licence box below before choosing the others.

2. Rent the smallest card that runs it well — for one hour first

The makers’ timings are their settings: their prompts, their step counts, their reference clips. Your first rented hour is for timing your prompts at your settings. Your seconds-per-clip × the card’s $/hr ÷ 3,600 is the only cost figure worth budgeting from after that.

3. Scale by the arithmetic, not by feel

Clips per hour is 3,600 ÷ your seconds per clip. If the queue outgrows one A100, check the makers’ tables before adding a second card: on Wan’s own numbers the H100 is roughly 2.6× faster at 720p for roughly 2.5× the single-card price — a wash on cost per clip, a clear win on turnaround.

Alternatives

Watch out — the $2.25 H100 is a fleet price

TensorDock’s $2.25/GPU/hr for an H100 SXM — the cheapest H100 figure on our board — carries an 8-GPU minimum: $18.00/hr before you have made a single frame. Every single-card H100 figure in this guide uses RunPod Community’s $2.69/hr, the cheapest H100 you can actually rent one of.

Watch out — minimum-VRAM figures are offload figures

HunyuanVideo-1.5’s 14GB and CogVideoX’s “from 10GB” both need model offloading switched on, and the makers’ headline timings were not measured at those minimums. Renting the smallest card a model can technically start on, and expecting the headline speed, is how an hour’s budget becomes an afternoon.

Watch out — three of these licences are not Apache

HunyuanVideo-1.5 is under the Tencent Hunyuan Community licence (its repository is flagged EU-disallowed on Hugging Face), LTX-2 under the LTX-2 Community License Agreement, and CogVideoX-1.5-5B’s weights under the CogVideoX licence. Wan 2.2 and Mochi 1 are Apache 2.0. Read the licence that covers your model before commercial work.

Watch out — per-clip cost is per generation, not per keeper

Every figure in the cost table buys one roll of the model. At the two to three generations a usable clip usually takes, multiply accordingly — on the 4090 rows that is still cents; on the A14B at 720p it is the difference between $0.83 and about $2.50 per kept clip.

Good to know — you do not need a 96GB card for 720p Wan

Wan’s own table peaks at 59.8GB for a 5-second 720p A14B clip on one GPU, so an 80GB card runs it with headroom to spare. Bigger cards buy speed and batch room on this model, not permission to run it.

The licences, in plain words

Wan 2.2 (both the A14B and the 5B) and Mochi 1 are Apache 2.0 — the permissive licence most commercial pipelines are built on. HunyuanVideo-1.5 is under the Tencent Hunyuan Community licence; Hugging Face’s metadata names that licence and flags the repository as disallowed in the EU. LTX-2 is under the LTX-2 Community License Agreement. CogVideoX-1.5-5B: its code is Apache 2.0, its weights are under the separate CogVideoX licence. This is a plain-words summary, not legal advice — each licence is linked from its model’s repository, and the three community licences deserve a full read before you sell anything made with them.

GPU PRICING →  ·  2026-11-05 · 11 min read

MI355X vs B300: inference cost per token, priced from the board

Spheron's comparison of these two 288GB cards, published Nov 3, 2026, prices its verdicts from modelled rates — including MI355X rates no provider actually sells at. This page re-runs the same question from prices read on the providers' own pages and checked on Nov 5, 2026: TensorWave's published $2.95/GPU/hr MI355X rate and Oracle's $8.60 list price, against a B300 board that starts at $7.40/GPU/hr. The silicon is tied — same 288GB of HBM3e, same 8 TB/s of bandwidth on both makers' spec sheets. The rental market is not tied at all, and in this comparison the entry tickets matter more than the chips.

The verdict

  • MI355X — The cheapest frontier tokens we can price — with two catches printed in the open. TensorWave publishes $2.95/GPU/hr, but only on an 8-GPU bare-metal node, so the real entry ticket is $23.60/hr, and the buying route is contact sales; Oracle's list price is $8.60/GPU/hr, a $68.80/hr 8-GPU shape. At the printed assumed speed of 4,000 tok/s (see below) that is $0.20 per 1M tokens at TensorWave's rate and $0.60 at Oracle's. Rent it if you take whole nodes and your stack runs on ROCm.
  • B300 — The card you can actually book today. The board's best verified rate is a single self-serve card; RunPod Secure, re-read on Nov 5, 2026, is $8.99/hr, and Together AI's on-demand cluster rate, also re-read Nov 5, is $9.99/hr. At the same assumed 4,000 tok/s that is $0.51 per 1M tokens at the best rate and $0.62 at RunPod Secure. Rent it if you need capacity this week, one card at a time, on the CUDA stack your team already runs. · $7.40/hr at Hyperstack

The assumption set — read this before quoting any cost per token

Cost per token is an hourly price divided by a speed. The prices on this page are verified; the speeds are assumptions, chosen once, printed here, and applied identically to both cards so the comparison is fair. They are not benchmark results, and no cost figure on this page should be quoted as one. The workload: a 70B-class open model at FP8 (about 70GB of weights), continuous batching at roughly 32 concurrent sequences, output tokens only — a job both 288GB cards hold easily, with most of their memory left for KV cache. The formula, the same one used across this site: cost per 1M output tokens = hourly price ÷ (assumed tokens/sec × 3,600) × 1,000,000. The assumed speed is set the way our other inference guides set it — roughly in line with memory bandwidth, the thing that limits batched decode. Both makers publish 8 TB/s of peak bandwidth for these cards, the same figure as NVIDIA's B200, which our inference guides anchor at 4,000 tok/s; so both cards are assumed at 4,000 tok/s here. Worked check: $2.95 ÷ (4,000 × 3,600) × 1,000,000 = $0.205, printed as $0.20. Real published benchmarks do exist, and they are reported in this guide attributed to their sources — MLPerf Inference v6.0 (MLCommons, published Apr 1, 2026) put an 8-GPU MI355X node at 100,282 tok/s against 115,730 tok/s for an 8-GPU B300 node on the Llama 2 70B Server scenario, as reported in Spheron's Nov 3, 2026 post from AMD's MLPerf submission — but they were measured on the submitters' own stacks, not on rented machines, so they are context, not inputs to the price maths. The sensitivity is the same as everywhere on this site: if your stack delivers half the assumed speed on both cards, every cost on this page doubles and the order does not change. What changes the order is one card beating its assumption while the other misses — which is why the first rented hour on either card should be a measurement, not a commitment.

The spec sheet — a tie at the top

Sources: AMD's Instinct MI355X product page (amd.com) and NVIDIA's Blackwell Ultra material (nvidia.com and NVIDIA's developer blog), checked Nov 5, 2026. Peak figures are the makers' published spec-sheet numbers, not measured throughput on any provider's machines.

GPUMemoryPeak bandwidthArchitecturePeak FP4 (maker figures)Max power
AMD MI355X288GB HBM3e8 TB/sCDNA 4 — ROCm10.1 PFLOPS (MXFP4)1,400W
NVIDIA B300288GB HBM3e8 TB/sBlackwell Ultra — CUDA15 PFLOPS (NVFP4, dense)Up to 1,400W

On the two numbers that decide most inference bills — how much a card holds and how fast it streams weights — these chips are identical on paper. The differences sit one layer down: NVIDIA publishes the higher peak FP4 figure (in its own NVFP4 format; AMD's is MXFP4, and cross-vendor FLOPS in different 4-bit formats are not a like-for-like speed test), AMD's card is direct-liquid-cooled only at 1,400W, and the two run entirely different software ecosystems, ROCm against CUDA. None of that is in the hourly rate — which is where this comparison is actually decided.

The B300 rental market, verified

The B300 is rented the way mainstream NVIDIA cards are rented: per card, self-serve, from a spread of providers. Board rows are from our daily check of Nov 5, 2026 (banked snapshot 2026-11-05); Together AI's row was re-read on its own pricing page on Nov 5, 2026. Cost per 1M tokens uses the printed assumed speed of 4,000 tok/s throughout (hourly price ÷ 14.4). Monthly figures elsewhere in this guide use 730 hours.

Same GPU, a 2× spread between the cheapest verified self-serve offer and hyperscaler list — the first thing to get right when you rent a B300. One stated figure for contrast, labelled as stated and never used in our maths: Spheron's own post of Nov 3, 2026 lists B300 on Spheron at $11.52/hr as of Nov 5, 2026 — a rate stated on the seller's own pages, which we report the way we report all Spheron prices: as their claim, not as a verified board price.

The MI355X side: the prices that actually exist

AMD's flagship rents through far fewer doors, and both verified doors sell the same shape: a whole 8-GPU node. Both pages were re-read first-hand on Nov 5, 2026. Cost per 1M tokens uses the same printed assumed speed of 4,000 tok/s (hourly price ÷ 14.4).

ProviderPer GPU/hrCost per 1M tokens (assumed speed)The shape you actually buy
TensorWave$2.95$0.208-GPU bare-metal node — $23.60/hr the node ($17,228/mo). Published rate on TensorWave's MI355X product page; the page does not label it on-demand and states no term; the site's buying route is contact sales
Oracle OCI$8.60$0.608-GPU bare-metal shape BM.GPU.MI355X.8 — $68.80/hr the shape ($50,224/mo). Oracle's global list price, per GPU per hour

Two honest observations. First, there is no single-card MI355X rental on any price list we have verified — if you want this chip, you are buying nodes, and the honest comparison is node against node. Second, the roughly $2.50/GPU/hr MI355X rate behind the year's biggest AMD cost-per-token claims is not a rate any provider publishes: the closest real published figure is TensorWave's $2.95, and it comes with the node and the sales call attached. Spheron, for its part, does not carry the MI355X at all — its Nov 3 post says so — so its comparison is priced from other people's listings and modelled rates, a point it is open about and we simply underline.

The worked maths — and what survives of the 45% claim

Start with the claim this guide answers. The widely shared MI355X cost-per-token advantages — up to about 40–45% better tokens per dollar — are built on modelled hourly rates: SemiAnalysis's InferenceX, the benchmark behind most of them, turns its measured throughput into dollars using its own TCO model rates (about $1.50/hr for MI355X against $2.26/hr for B300, per its chip pages), not rates anyone rents at. Priced instead at verified rental rates, with both cards at the same bandwidth-anchored assumed speed, the picture splits by which door you walk through. At TensorWave's published rate, MI355X tokens cost $0.20 per 1M against $0.51 at the B300's best verified rate — about 60% cheaper per token, a bigger edge than the headlines, but one you can only collect at node scale, through a sales process, on ROCm. Like-for-like on one provider's own list, Oracle prices the MI355X at $8.60 against its own B300 at $15.00 — $0.60 against $1.04 per 1M tokens, about 42% cheaper per GPU-hour for the same 288GB and the same published bandwidth. And where real throughput measurements are paired with real rates, the edge narrows hard: Spheron's Nov 3 post, re-running Kimi K3 at verified on-demand rates, found 13.8 tokens/sec per dollar for MI355X against 13.1 for B300 — a 6% AMD edge, not 45% — because on that workload the B300's measured per-chip throughput is higher. All three statements are true at once; they answer different questions. The node maths changes nothing per token and everything per invoice: an 8-GPU node at the assumed speed produces 32,000 tok/s on either chip, so the per-token figures hold — what changes is the smallest cheque, $23.60/hr at TensorWave against $7.40/hr for one B300 card at Hyperstack. If your workload is one card's worth of serving, the B300 is the only side of this comparison you can buy in that size at all.

Steps

1. Pick the MI355X at TensorWave if you serve at node scale and already run on ROCm

Published $2.95/GPU/hr on 8-GPU bare-metal nodes ($23.60/hr, $17,228/mo) — the cheapest frontier-class tokens we can price, at $0.20 per 1M tokens under the printed assumptions. Budget the sales conversation into your timeline: the rate is published, but the page labels no on-demand term and the route in is 'get in touch with our team', so treat the timeline as days, not minutes.

2. Pick the MI355X at Oracle if you want AMD inside a hyperscaler contract

Oracle's list is the one true published on-demand MI355X rate we can verify: $8.60/GPU/hr as the BM.GPU.MI355X.8 shape, $68.80/hr ($50,224/mo). On the same list Oracle's B300 is $15.00/GPU/hr, so if your organisation already buys from Oracle, the AMD shape is the cheaper 288GB door by about 42% per GPU-hour.

3. Pick the B300 if you need to start today, scale by the card, or stay on CUDA

Self-serve from $7.40/hr at Hyperstack and $8.99/hr at RunPod Secure, re-read Nov 5, 2026 — live in minutes, one card at a time ($0.51–$0.62 per 1M tokens at the assumed speed). You pay more per token than the TensorWave node rate and you buy immediacy, elasticity and the TensorRT-LLM/vLLM ecosystem with it. For bursty or interruptible work, Together AI's preemptible B300 at $4.99/hr ($0.35 per 1M, re-read Nov 5, 2026) undercuts every on-demand figure in this guide.

4. Don't build a plan on a $2.50 MI355X rate — or on any single benchmark

No provider publishes $2.50/GPU/hr for this card; the verified floor is TensorWave's $2.95 with its node and sales caveats, and the only list on-demand rate is Oracle's $8.60. And the measured record cuts both ways by model and interactivity target — MLPerf v6.0 has the B300 node ahead on Llama 2 70B Server throughput, InferenceX has model families on each side — so rent one hour of each stack you are seriously considering and measure your own model before committing a node-month to either.

Alternatives

Watch out: the 8-GPU minimum is the real MI355X price

Every verified MI355X figure in this guide is a per-GPU rate on an 8-GPU bare-metal node. The smallest MI355X bill that exists is $23.60/hr at TensorWave or $68.80/hr at Oracle — there is no $2.95 hour of MI355X to buy. Comparing $2.95 against a single-card B300 price without the node totals is exactly how this comparison gets mis-sold, including in some of the coverage this guide answers.

Watch out: a published rate is not always a self-serve rate

TensorWave publishes its $2.95/GPU/hr openly, which puts it ahead of quote-only sellers — but its product page does not call the rate on-demand, states no minimum term, and the buying route is contact sales. Whether it is true pay-as-you-go, and at what commitment, is a question for that conversation, and we label it a published rate rather than a verified on-demand rate for exactly that reason. Oracle's $8.60, by contrast, is a list price anyone can read — at nearly three times the per-GPU figure.

The software reality: ROCm vs CUDA, stated plainly

The B300 runs the CUDA ecosystem — TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, SGLang and two decades of kernels and profiling tools. The MI355X runs AMD's open-source ROCm stack: vLLM and SGLang both serve on it, AMD's AITER kernels posted the MLPerf v6.0 results cited in this guide, and standard LLM serving is genuinely competitive. What ROCm does not give you is TensorRT-LLM, and custom CUDA kernels do not port themselves. Price your engineers' time honestly on both sides: a cheaper GPU-hour that costs a week of porting is not cheaper, and a CUDA team that never tests ROCm is paying the NVIDIA premium by habit rather than by measurement.

The counterweight: why the B300 still wins most rentals

Strip the price floor away and the B300 leads this comparison on almost everything else a renter feels: it is bookable today from at least five verified providers against the MI355X's two node-only doors; MLPerf v6.0's Llama 2 70B Server scenario measured the B300 node about 15% ahead on throughput (115,730 vs 100,282 tok/s, both 8-GPU nodes, as reported from the official submissions); NVIDIA publishes the higher peak FP4 figure; and the CUDA ecosystem removes the porting question entirely. The MI355X case is narrower and real: at the published rates that actually exist, its tokens can cost far less — if your work fits the way AMD capacity is sold.
