How we know

B300 board prices are GPUJournal's own: read on each provider's published pricing pages and banked daily (snapshot 2026-11-05, checked Nov 5, 2026 — RunPod Secure $8.99, Nebius $9.50 and Verda $11.57 re-read first-hand that day; Verda's figure is the after-side of its ninth rise, on Nov 4, 2026). Hyperstack's $7.40 is the board's carried figure: Hyperstack's pricing table has been unreadable in our fetches for over a week of daily checks, so it is carried from the last readable check and flagged here and on the board, not presented as re-verified on Nov 5. Together AI's B300 rates (on-demand $9.99, preemptible $4.99) were re-read on together.ai/pricing on Nov 5, 2026. TensorWave's MI355X rate ($2.95/GPU/hr, 8-GPU bare-metal standard node, $23.60/hr derived) was re-read on TensorWave's own MI355X product page on Nov 5, 2026 — the figure stands unchanged from our Oct 31, 2026 verification; the page states no on-demand label or term and shows a contact-sales route. Oracle's prices come from Oracle's official Cloud Price List: the USD figures (MI355X $8.60, B300 $15.00, per GPU per hour) were read on Oct 27, 2026, and corroborated unchanged on Nov 5, 2026 on Oracle's own Swedish price-list edition, which publishes the same list at Oracle's fixed conversion (MI355X 82.96334 kr, B300.8 144.7035 kr, against H100/H200 at 96.469 kr = $10.00); shape totals are Oracle's per-GPU price × 8, by Oracle's own rule. Hardware facts are the makers' published specifications, checked Nov 5, 2026: AMD's MI355X product page (288GB HBM3e, 8 TB/s, CDNA 4, 10.1 PFLOPS MXFP4, 1,400W, launched Jun 12, 2025) and NVIDIA's Blackwell Ultra material (B300 288GB HBM3e, up to 8 TB/s, up to 1,400W). Spheron's post 'MI355X vs B300: AMD vs NVIDIA Inference Cost Per Token' (spheron.network, Nov 3, 2026) was read on Nov 5, 2026; every figure taken from it — including its stated Spheron B300 rate of $11.52/hr, its InferenceX and MLPerf reporting, and its Kimi K3 re-run at verified rates (13.8 vs 13.1 tok/s per dollar, via Beri.net's survey) — is labelled stated or attributed wherever used, and none of its figures is presented as verified by us. InferenceX's modelled rates (about $1.50/hr MI355X, $2.26/hr B300) are SemiAnalysis's TCO model figures from its chip pages, cited as the basis of the claims this guide examines. Every throughput figure in our own maths is the printed assumption of 4,000 tok/s per card, set out in full above; monthly figures use 730 hours.

What we verified — and what we could not

Verified

  • Every rental price in the tables, read on the provider's own published pages and dated above — TensorWave and Together AI re-read Nov 5, 2026; Oracle corroborated on Oracle's own list Nov 5, 2026; the B300 board rows banked in the Nov 5, 2026 daily check
  • Both cards' headline hardware facts (288GB HBM3e, 8 TB/s) on AMD's and NVIDIA's own pages, checked Nov 5, 2026
  • That no single-card MI355X rental appears on any provider price list we have verified — both verified routes sell 8-GPU nodes only

Still unverified

  • A measured head-to-head of the two cards on identical rented stacks — none exists that we could find. The published measurements (MLPerf v6.0, InferenceX) come from the submitters' and benchmarkers' own setups and are reported attributed, never folded into our price maths
  • Whether TensorWave's published $2.95/GPU/hr is true pay-as-you-go on-demand, and on what minimum term — its page states neither
  • Hyperstack's B300 price re-read on Nov 5, 2026 — its pricing table was unreadable in the day's fetch, as it has been for over a week of daily checks; the $7.40 board figure is carried and flagged, not re-verified
  • The 4,000 tok/s figure is an assumption chosen by us, anchored on published memory bandwidth the same way across this site — it is not a measurement, ours or anyone's

Nothing else on this page is estimated.

/guide/why-gpu-rental-prices-are-rising.html:
GPU PRICING →  ·  2026-11-08 · 12 min read

Power is the new GPU shortage: why powered land decides your rental price

GPU rental prices have been rising for six weeks, and the usual explanation — not enough chips — no longer fits. The chips exist. What is scarce is somewhere powered to plug them in: an energised building, on a grid connection, under a signed power contract. This page walks through the verified rises, shows why they point at power rather than silicon, and tells you what to ask before you rent capacity that has not been switched on yet.

The verdict

  • Nebius — Raised rates across the board — post-rise H100 $4.50/hr. A fleet-scale repricing of capacity Nebius already runs — not a response to any new chip.
  • RunPod Secure — RTX 4090 $0.74 → $0.89/hr (▲ 20%), H200 $4.59 → $5.29/hr (▲ 15%). Existing cards, existing buildings, higher price — the cost being repriced sits behind the GPU, not inside it.
  • Verda — Ten rises in fifteen days — H100 SXM $4.34 → $4.94/hr (▲ ~14%), GB300 $11.82 → $13.44/hr. Small, repeated ~1% steps — the signature of a provider passing through rising capacity costs, not launching anything.
  • SaladCloud — Priority tiers rose — RTX 4090 High $0.33 → $0.44/hr (▲ 33%), RTX 5090 High $0.50 → $0.60/hr. Even a network of home machines repriced its priority tier — demand for available capacity outran supply at every level.
  • RunPod Serverless — B200 $8.64 → $10.79/hr (▲ ~25%) between our Oct 26 and Nov 2 reads; the same day, Nebius removed the ceiling on its spot prices. A provider lifting its own price cap is a provider expecting the market to clear higher.
  • Lambda — B200 $6.69 → $7.69/hr, H100 $3.99 → $4.59/hr, A100 80GB $2.79 → $3.19/hr (about ▲ 15%); A100 40GB stays $1.99. Announced ten days ahead, across the range at once — a cost-base change, not a product launch. Not yet in effect.
  • The cheapest verified offers — Did not move — the best verified H100 SXM offer is still $2.25/hr. The rises are hitting big-provider list prices first; the floor of the market is a different story — see the counterweight below.
Compare prices→See Price Watch→

The evidence, briefly

A note on the verdict above: the dated rises and the figures in it are our verified record — every rise was read on the provider’s own published pricing page on both sides of the change. What the pattern points at is our reading; the argument fills the rest of this page, and you can judge it against the dated facts. Our companion guide, “GPU rental prices are rising in 2026 — the dated evidence”, carries every rise in full and is linked at the foot of this page. This page needs only the shape of it. Between Oct 1 and Nov 6, 2026, five providers raised prices we could verify: Nebius across the board on Oct 1; RunPod’s Secure Cloud on Oct 14; Verda ten times between Oct 23 and Nov 6, roughly 1% at a time, pausing only on Nov 5 and flat since; SaladCloud’s priority tiers on Nov 1; and RunPod’s Serverless B200 rate, up about 25% between our Oct 26 and Nov 2 reads. Lambda’s rise of about 15% is announced for Nov 16 and has not happened yet — we list it because a dated announcement from the provider itself is a fact, but no Lambda price on our board changes until the new rates are in effect and re-read. One thing stands out about who moved. The rises came first and most often from providers selling capacity out of large, power-hungry facilities — the operators closest to the cost of energised space. Nobody in that list launched a new GPU in those weeks, and no chip shortage was announced. The prices moved anyway. That is the observation the rest of this guide explains.

How a rental price is really set — the chain

A rented GPU hour looks like a chip product. It is actually the end of a chain, and the price is set at the chain’s slowest link:

The linkWhat has to happen
The chipA GPU has to exist and be bought. This was the binding constraint in the shortage years — and it is the link that has eased. Cards ship, launches land on schedule, and the rises above happened with no silicon news attached.
The buildingThe chip earns nothing on a loading dock. It has to sit in a rack, in a hall, with cooling that can carry it — modern AI halls draw power at a density ordinary data centres were never built for.
The powerThe hall has to be energised: a grid connection approved and built, substations and transformers installed — equipment with lead times measured in years — and a power purchase agreement that fixes what the electricity costs.
The queueBehind each step is a line of other buyers waiting for the same connection, the same transformers, the same contracted megawatts.

When the slow link was the chip, rental prices tracked chip supply. When the slow link is the energised building, rental prices track powered land — and powered land cannot be manufactured faster by anyone, at any price.

The worked example: a customer that bought the campus

The clearest single example landed this month. On Nov 6, 2026, Crusoe confirmed — in its own announcement, carried by GlobeNewswire — that it has sold its unfinished Wyoming campus to Google. Google had first come to that campus as a customer. It ended up buying the site itself: the land, the build-out and, above all, the power position that comes with it. One caution our news desk applied to this story, and this guide repeats: the sale price was not disclosed, and Google’s separate $17bn Wyoming commitment, announced on blog.google on Nov 5, is not the purchase price — the two figures sit side by side in coverage of this deal, and only one of them is a price for anything. What the sale does show, without any number attached, is where the value in the chain now sits: a hyperscaler that can buy chips in any quantity chose to buy an unfinished campus, because the campus is the part it could not simply order. The quarter’s spending, from the same companies’ own results, shows the scale of the chase for capacity:

CompanySeptember-quarter capex (reported Oct 28, 2026)
Microsoft$45.2B — including finance leases
Alphabet$51.4B
The two together≈ $96.6B in one quarter

The spending figures point the same way. Microsoft and Alphabet reported their September-quarter results on Oct 28, 2026: capital spending of $45.2B and $51.4B — about $96.6B between two companies in one quarter, much of it aimed at AI capacity. And in the same results, Microsoft’s chief financial officer pointed to delayed third-party GPU capacity deliveries while guiding the next quarter’s capex above $50B. Read that slowly: the constraint named by one of the biggest buyers on earth was not chips it could not buy, but capacity — other people’s powered buildings — arriving late. Two further reports belong in this picture, labelled for what they are. IREN’s Nov 5, 2026 results reported H100s being recontracted at double their original price — that is IREN’s own reporting of its own contracts, not a figure we can verify from a pricing page. And Bloomberg has reported that renewed capacity on older GPUs is reselling at a premium of roughly 20%, with Microsoft reportedly walking away from some of it; Bloomberg’s account rests on anonymous sources, so treat it as a lead, not a fact. Both reports are consistent with the same mechanism — when a contract on energised capacity comes up for renewal, the new price is set by the scarcity of powered space, not by the age of the cards inside it — but consistency is not proof, and we print them as reported, not verified.

Compare prices→See Price Watch→

The honest counterweight — the cheapest offers did not move

Everything above would mislead if it left you thinking every GPU costs more than it did in October. It does not. The cheapest verified offers on our board did not move between Oct 19 and Nov 8, 2026:

GPUBest verified offerProviderOct 19 → Nov 8
H100 SXM$2.25/hrTensorDock (8-GPU minimum)— unchanged
H100 SXM, single card$2.69/hrRunPod Community— unchanged
H200$3.59/hrRunPod Community— unchanged
B200$5.98/hrRunPod Community— unchanged

So the two halves of the market are genuinely telling different stories, and both are true. List prices at the big providers — the prices attached to contracted, energised, large-scale capacity — have risen steadily for six weeks. The floor of the open market, where a renter who compares can still buy a single card by the hour, has not moved. If you rent at spot or community rates today, today’s checkout is not where this shortage reaches you. It reaches you at renewal, when a contract reprices against a tighter market for powered space — and it reaches you at scale, when the quantity you need only exists inside the big facilities whose prices are the ones rising. Knowing which situation you are in is worth more than any single rate.

What to ask a provider promising future capacity

Scarcity of powered space creates a specific sales pattern: capacity sold today against a building that will be energised later. Some of those promises will be kept. Before you build plans on one, five questions separate a phase that exists from one that is hoped for. 1 — Is this capacity energised today, or is it a future phase? Ask which it is, in those words. “Available Q3” can mean racks live in Q3 or a grid connection applied for in Q3, and the difference is your launch date. 2 — Whose power contract stands behind it? A provider with a signed power purchase agreement and an approved connection has something to sell. A provider “in discussions” with a utility has a plan. Ask which document exists. 3 — What happens to my price at renewal? The rises in this guide landed on list prices and renewals, not on contracts mid-term. If the powered-space market is tighter when your term ends, your renewal is where the rise will find you. Ask what, if anything, caps it. 4 — What do I get if the phase slips? Microsoft, with all its leverage, publicly absorbed delayed third-party capacity in its Oct 28 results. A smaller renter should know in advance whether a slipped phase means a refund, a credit, substitute capacity somewhere else — or nothing. 5 — Can I see the same GPU, live, somewhere today? A provider already running the card you want, in a building already energised, has proven the part of the chain that matters. Future capacity from one with no live equivalent is a different risk class.

How we know

GPUJournal reads providers’ own published pricing pages and banks the figures daily; a price change is reported only when the before and after figures were each seen on the provider’s own page, with their dates. The rises used here: Nebius’s across-the-board rise of Oct 1, 2026 (post-rise H100 $4.50/hr, carried on our board since our records began Oct 19); RunPod Secure Cloud, Oct 14, 2026 (RTX 4090 $0.74 → $0.89, H200 $4.59 → $5.29); Verda, ten rises between Oct 23 and Nov 6, 2026 (H100 SXM $4.34 read Oct 22 → $4.94 read Nov 6; GB300 $11.82 → $13.44 over the same span; flat Nov 5, 7 and 8); SaladCloud priority tiers in effect Nov 1, 2026 (RTX 4090 High $0.33 → $0.44, RTX 5090 High $0.50 → $0.60, from SaladCloud’s own announcement and pricing page); RunPod Serverless B200 ($8.64 read Oct 26 → $10.79 read Nov 2); Nebius’s removal of its spot-price ceiling, Nov 2, 2026. Lambda’s figures (B200 $6.69 → $7.69, H100 $3.99 → $4.59, A100 80GB $2.79 → $3.19, A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99) are Lambda’s own announcement of Nov 6, 2026, effective Nov 16 — announced, not yet in effect, and not applied to our board. Best offers are from our board check of Nov 8, 2026, unchanged since Oct 19: TensorDock H100 SXM $2.25/GPU/hr at an 8-GPU minimum; RunPod Community H100 SXM $2.69, H200 $3.59, B200 $5.98. The Crusoe sale is Crusoe’s announcement of Nov 6, 2026 (GlobeNewswire); the price was not disclosed, and Google’s $17bn Wyoming commitment (blog.google, Nov 5, 2026) is a separate commitment, not the sale price. Microsoft and Alphabet figures are the companies’ reported September-quarter results of Oct 28, 2026 (capex $45.2B including finance leases, and $51.4B), including Microsoft’s guidance of following-quarter capex above $50B and its reference to delayed third-party GPU capacity deliveries. Two items are reported, not verified, and are labelled as such wherever they appear: IREN’s Nov 5, 2026 results describing H100s recontracted at double their original price (IREN’s own reporting), and Bloomberg’s report of renewed older-GPU capacity reselling at roughly a 20% premium, with Microsoft reportedly walking away from some of it (Bloomberg, anonymous sources). Our records began Oct 19, 2026; nothing in this guide claims a price from before that date except where a provider’s own dated announcement is the source.

What this means for 2027 prices

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. Everything in this box is GPUJournal’s judgement on the verified record above it; the record itself is in the tables and the method note. If the binding constraint is powered land, list prices will keep drifting up for as long as energised capacity is scarcer than the demand for it — because a grid connection, a substation and a power contract cannot be sped up the way a chip production line can. Expect the pattern of the last six weeks to repeat: rises landing first at the providers closest to the constraint, renewals repricing harder than new spot offers, and the cheapest end of the market moving last, if it moves. The things that would change our reading are concrete and checkable: a run of verified list-price cuts at the big providers, hyperscalers reporting capacity arriving ahead of schedule rather than delayed, or contract renewals reported at flat rates. Until one of those shows up in the record, plan as if capacity you will need in 2027 costs more than the same capacity costs today — and lock the price of anything you cannot afford to reprice.

/story/kimi-k3-1-pro-weights-released-no.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Moonshot AI

Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights are out — 2.8 trillion parameters, a 1.56TB download, licence included

Nov 4, 2026

Promised by Nov 4, delivered on Nov 4: Moonshot AI has published the full weights of Kimi K3.1 Pro — its 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight flagship — on Hugging Face, with the model card, deployment recipes and the licence that was missing at launch. This morning the repository still was not public; by this afternoon it was, all 96 shards of it.

Image: Moonshot AI via kimi.ai

What is out, verified on Moonshot's own Hugging Face repository (moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro, read Nov 4, 2026): the complete checkpoint in 96 safetensors shards whose files sum to 1,561,293,160,568 bytes — about 1.56TB (the checkpoint index's own tensor total is 1,561,217,377,280 bytes; the file sum, re-verified Nov 6, 2026, is the download size) — stored as MXFP4 weights with MXFP8 activations from quantization-aware training, plus the configuration, tokenizer and vision-processing code. The model card describes an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model: 2.8 trillion total parameters, 104 billion active per token, 93 layers, 896 experts with 16 selected per token, a 1,048,576-token context window and a 401M-parameter MoonViT-V2 vision encoder. Against Kimi K3, 24 of the 93 attention layers swap full Gated MLA for sparse Gated DSA, Moonshot's change for cheaper long-context work. The card recommends vLLM, SGLang or TokenSpeed to serve it, and the hosted API (kimi-k3.1-pro, $2 in / $10 out per million tokens on Moonshot's pricing page) remains the alternative.

The licence, published with the weights and read in full: the Kimi K3.1 Pro License is MIT-style — free to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell, derivatives included. Two conditions bite only at scale: a model-as-a-service business whose aggregate revenue exceeds $20 million over any 12 months must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before commercial use, and a commercial product with more than 100 million monthly users or more than $20 million in monthly revenue must display “Kimi K3.1-Pro” prominently in its interface. Internal use is exempt from both. That answers the question that was open at the Oct 23 launch — and it is a custom licence, not MIT itself, so the two thresholds are worth reading before building a hosted business on it.

The scores on the card are Moonshot's own, reported as such: Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 65.7, a point behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4) and ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2); GPQA-Diamond 94.2; BrowseComp 92.1; OSWorld V2.1 79.6; and a first place on SWE Marathon v1.1 at 51.7. No independent reproduction exists yet — the checkpoint has been public for hours, not days — so treat the table as the maker's claims awaiting outside testing, exactly as we treated its launch numbers on Oct 24.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Why this matters to anyone who rents GPUs: the largest open-weight model in the catalogue is now actually downloadable — but the rental maths is fleet maths. The 1.56TB checkpoint needs roughly that much GPU memory before a single token of its 1-million-token context is cached: six 288GB GB300s just to hold the weights, and realistically an 8-GPU node of B300/GB300-class cards to serve it. On this morning's checked board that is Verda's GB300 at $13.31 an hour per card — about $106 an hour for an 8-card node, around the clock — against $2/$10 per million tokens on Moonshot's own API. Self-hosting this model is a control and privacy decision, not a saving, until serving stacks squeeze it onto fewer cards. We updated the model's catalogue entry with the published licence and the real checkpoint size on Nov 4, and on Nov 6, 2026 the costed deployment guide — published Oct 30 as pre-release maths — was refreshed in place with the summed checkpoint, the licence's actual terms, the official vLLM/SGLang recipes and the Nov 6 board: the smallest honest setup is one 8-GPU B300 node, and the cheapest node-shaped setup is 16× H200 at $57.44/hr.

/story/ripple-65b-preview-open-weights-n.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Ricursive Intelligence

Ripple-65B Preview is out — a 65B Apache 2.0 coding model that runs on one GPU

Nov 5, 2026

Released on Nov 4, 2026 by Ricursive Intelligence — the lab founded by the researchers behind Google's AlphaChip — Ripple-65B Preview is a dense 65-billion-parameter model under a plain Apache 2.0 licence, with a self-reported agentic-coding score ahead of open models eight to fifteen times its size, and an NVFP4 checkpoint built to fit on a single GPU.

Image: Ricursive Intelligence via ricursive.com

What was released, from Ricursive's launch blog and the model's Hugging Face card, both read on Nov 5, 2026: a 65B-parameter dense Transformer (80 layers, all 65B active on every token — no mixture-of-experts shortcut), pretrained from scratch on 12 trillion tokens, with context up to 1 million tokens. Three checkpoints are public: the instruction-tuned model in BF16 (16 shards, about 130GB), an NVFP4 build, and a BF16 base model — all under Apache 2.0, which allows commercial use, modification and redistribution with no separate agreement and no revenue threshold. That licence is the cleanest we have seen on a frontier-class release this autumn.

The headline claim, reported as Ricursive's own and not independently reproduced: 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, the terminal-agent benchmark, ahead of Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8) and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4) in Ricursive's comparison table. The caveats are in the card itself: the figures mix official model-card scores with Ricursive's in-house runs, scores moved when re-run under the official Terminus 2 harness, and the Preview has had, in Ricursive's words, relatively light post-training. Treat the ranking as a claim to test on your own tasks, not a settled result.

Why renters should care — the size: this is frontier-claimed capability in a 65B envelope, not a cluster job. The BF16 weights are about 130GB, so two 80GB cards or one 141GB H200 hold them; the NVFP4 checkpoint is the single-card route — Ricursive says the model fits on consumer hardware such as the NVIDIA DGX Spark, and its own serving note reports 250 tokens per second on 2×B200 at batch 8 before quantization or custom kernels. At the RunPod Secure rates we read on Nov 5, 2026, that is one H200 at $5.29 an hour for the full BF16 model, or one 96GB RTX PRO 6000 at $2.49 an hour for the NVFP4 build — against the 8-GPU Blackwell nodes this week's 2.8-trillion-parameter release points at.

The backstory, from Ricursive's launch blog: a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers the company's AI chip-design platform, built by a team that grew from one to five people, at a stated full R&D cost of $32 million — which Ricursive calls one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight agentic-coding leader. The hosted routes at launch are Together AI, GMI Cloud and OpenRouter, with Fireworks announced as following; the weights themselves are a free, ungated download on Hugging Face.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Most of this autumn's open-weight headlines have been trillion-parameter releases that only the scarcest rental tier can serve. Ripple-65B Preview runs the other way: a dense 65B model, a licence with no strings, and a checkpoint sized for one GPU. If its coding scores hold up under independent testing, the cheapest verified cards on our board just became a credible way to run a frontier-class coding agent — and if they do not, the licence and the size still make it the easiest big release of the season to test for yourself.

/story/ernie-5-5-flash-base-open-weights.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Baidu

Baidu opens ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base — a 280B open-weight base model with a licence that stops at three borders

Nov 5, 2026

Baidu has published the weights of ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base on Hugging Face: a 280-billion-parameter sparse mixture-of-experts model, released deliberately at the end of pre-training — before any instruction tuning — as a starting point for other people's fine-tunes. It is Baidu's first open-weight release at this scale in about 16 months, and its custom licence is the part to read before the download finishes.

Image: Baidu via huggingface.co

What is out, verified on Baidu's own Hugging Face repositories (baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base and its BF16 twin, read Nov 5, 2026): a text-only MoE base model with 280 billion total parameters and 14 billion active per token, pre-trained from scratch on 33.5 trillion tokens with the Muon optimizer. The architecture is 43 layers — 37 of heavily compressed attention (one cache entry per 128 tokens) and 6 of latent attention with sparse attention — with 512 routed experts per MoE layer, 10 selected per token. Training context reached 128K tokens; fine-tuning and inference support 1 million. Two checkpoints are public: the FP8 build (128 shards, 304,360,870,583 bytes of storage on Hugging Face) and a BF16 build (572,984,599,112 bytes). The card documents serving with SGLang and vLLM, and Baidu says a post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash will follow — what is out today is a base model with no chat tuning, no refusal behaviour and no tool format built in.

The scores are Baidu's own, run — the card states — under one unified pipeline against DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base, Hy3-preview-Base and MiMo-V2.5-Base, and reported here as the maker's claims, not independently reproduced: MMLU 93.3, MMLU-Pro 78.4, GPQA 60.2, HumanEval+ 82.3, LiveCodeBench 40.1 and LongBench-v2 48.7, leading most of the 30-benchmark table. It is not a clean sweep on Baidu's own numbers — Hy3-preview-Base leads FullStackBench and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base leads InfiniteBench — and the comparison set is each rival's publicly released base checkpoint rather than its newest model, a caveat trade coverage of the release also flagged.

The licence, read in full (ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0, dated Nov 5, 2026): this is a custom licence, not Apache 2.0 as ERNIE 4.5 used. Its Territory is the whole world except the European Union, the United Kingdom and South Korea — use, modification and distribution outside that territory are not authorised at all. Non-commercial use is free of licence charges. Commercial use at or below $50 million in annual revenue from related products or services needs a one-time notice to Baidu and a prominent “Powered by ERNIE” display; above $50 million it needs Baidu's separate written authorisation before use. And the materials, derivatives or outputs may not be used to improve an unrelated AI model. Any team in London, Berlin or Seoul, and any hosted service built on top, has to stop at those clauses before the hardware question even starts.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Why this matters to anyone who rents GPUs: the week's open-weight story has been size — a 1.56TB frontier checkpoint on Monday's board maths, a one-GPU 65B model yesterday. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base sits between them and points at a different job: not serving a finished assistant, but renting GPUs to train one. The FP8 checkpoint is about 280GB of weights, so the card's own four-way serving recipes fit on four large cards — at the rates we checked this morning, four H200s on RunPod Secure at $5.29 an hour per card is about $21 an hour to hold and serve it, and the BF16 build (about 573GB) doubles the memory before fine-tuning state is counted. Fine-tuning a 280B base is the real rental event here, and it is exactly the workload the licence's revenue threshold and territory limits will shape: a well-funded lab outside the excluded regions gets a strong, fixed pre-training baseline for the cost of its own post-training run; a lab inside them gets nothing, however cheap the GPUs are. We have added the model to the catalogue with its licence terms stated plainly.

Licence: ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0 — Baidu’s custom licence: use is authorised only outside the EU, UK and South Korea; non-commercial use is free; commercial use at or below $50M annual revenue from related products/services needs a one-time notice to Baidu plus a “Powered by ERNIE” display, and above $50M needs separate written authorisation; outputs may not be used to improve an unrelated AI model. Read it before commercial self-hosting.

Worth knowing

Baidu’s open-weight base model, released Nov 5, 2026: a sparse MoE checkpoint at the end of pre-training (no mid- or post-training) — 280B total parameters, 14B active per token, 43 layers, 512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared, pre-trained on 33.5T tokens; 128K training context, 1M for fine-tuning and inference. Checkpoints on Hugging Face: FP8 (128 shards, about 304GB) and BF16 (about 573GB). Baidu-reported benchmarks under a unified pipeline (MMLU 93.3, HumanEval+ 82.3) are the maker’s figures, not independently reproduced. At FP8 the weights alone are about 280GB — the card’s serving recipes use four-way parallelism on large cards; BF16 doubles the memory before any training state.

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. /story/verda-tenth-rise-nov-6.html:
NEWS →  ·  Prices · Verda

Verda raises prices for the tenth time — eight GPUs up about 1%, the L40S holds

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Verda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 5: eight of Verda's nine tracked GPUs rose by about 1% — the tenth rise since Oct 23. The L40S held, the first card Verda has left flat on a rise day in this run. The same morning, Lambda announced rises of about 15% for Nov 16.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on verda.com/pricing

What changed, read on verda.com/pricing on Nov 6, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.31 → $13.44 [$13.44], B300 $11.57 → $11.69 [$11.69], B200 $9.05 → $9.14 [$9.138], H200 $6.38 → $6.44 [$6.440], H100 SXM $4.89 → $4.94 [$4.938], A100 80GB $2.29 → $2.32 [$2.316], A100 40GB $1.64 → $1.66 [$1.657] and RTX PRO 6000 $2.70 → $2.73 [$2.725]. The L40S held at $1.94 [$1.939]. Each rise is within a whisker of +1.0% — the same uniform list adjustment as the nine before it.

The pattern: Verda rose on Oct 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30, held Oct 31 and Nov 1, rose an eighth time on Nov 2, held Nov 3, rose a ninth time on Nov 4, held Nov 5 — and has now risen a tenth time. Its GB300, the only GB300 rate we list, has gone from $11.82 an hour at our Oct 19 check to $13.44 today, up 13.7% in eighteen days. And Verda is no longer the pattern's only mover: Nebius raised across the board on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, SaladCloud's Priority rise took effect Nov 1, RunPod Serverless rose by Nov 2, and Lambda today announced rises of about 15% effective Nov 16. Rising list prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can produce the same shape).

What it costs: Verda holds the board's Best offer on only two cards — the GB300 and the A100 40GB — and both rose today, so those two best offers rose with it. Everywhere else the cheapest verified offers are other providers' and none moved: the board's H100 SXM best is still TensorDock at $2.25 an hour (at an 8-GPU minimum) and its B200 best is still RunPod Community at $5.98. If you rent at Verda around the clock, today's rise adds about $95 a month per GB300, $66 per B200 and $36 per H100 on a 730-hour month.

Checked today and unchanged: RunPod Secure, Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute, TensorDock and SaladCloud all held at the rates read on Nov 5. Not checked today, and named rather than covered by the stamp: Hyperstack (its pricing table could not be read, for the ninth straight day), Lambda's currently-effective rates (now visible only after logging in; its announced Nov 16 rates are reported separately today), RunPod Community (its tier could not be separated in today's read) and nafnaf.ai (its homepage showed no GPUs available today).

What it means if you rent GPUs

Ten rises in fifteen days, and now a second provider announcing a rise five times larger in a single step: the autumn pattern has widened from one provider's steady repricing into something broader. The renter's spread is still the story — a workload priced off Verda's list page in mid-October is nearly 14% adrift on the GB300 today, while the cheapest verified way to rent most cards has not moved at all. Check the board before renewing at a list rate — and if you are on Verda's GB300 or A100 40GB, your best-offer price moved today.

NEWS →  ·  Prices · Lambda

Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

What it does to the board when it lands: Lambda's B200 at $6.69 is currently the cheapest verified HGX B200 instance rate we list from a self-serve cloud; at $7.69 it would sit above RunPod Community's $5.98 marketplace rate and just below RunPod Secure's $7.99. Its H100 at $4.59 would remain above the board's best H100 SXM offer (TensorDock, from $2.25 at an 8-GPU minimum) but move Lambda from the middle of the H100 pack toward its top. Around-the-clock, the announced rises add about $730 a month per B200, $438 per H100 and $292 per A100 80GB on a 730-hour month.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Until today, this autumn's rises were either quiet list adjustments caught after the fact (Verda's ten) or rises read on the day they landed. Lambda has done the renter-friendly thing — announced, dated and quantified, ten days ahead — and the size is the story: about 15% at once, on the three cards that anchor most training budgets. Anyone renewing or reserving Lambda capacity this month now has a hard date to plan around, and Nov 16 becomes a date this desk will verify first thing.

/story/cosmos3-nano-open-weights-nov-5.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · NVIDIA

NVIDIA opens four Cosmos 3 Nano checkpoints — 16B world models for driving and robot simulation

Nov 6, 2026

Published by NVIDIA on Hugging Face on Nov 5, 2026: four post-trained Cosmos 3 Nano checkpoints, 16 billion parameters each, under the OpenMDW 1.1 licence that permits commercial use — world models that generate synchronized camera video and LiDAR for driving, and video from robot actions, sized to run on a single rented GPU.

Image: NVIDIA via huggingface.co

What was released, from NVIDIA's Hugging Face announcement of Nov 5, 2026 and the Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto model card, both read on Nov 6, 2026: four checkpoints, each a post-trained example of Cosmos 3 Nano with 16B trainable parameters. Transfer-Auto generates synchronized multi-view driving video (up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes) with joint LiDAR output, varying weather, lighting and time of day. Sim-Auto is its streaming variant, generating camera and LiDAR observations in small chunks as driving controls change. Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator's controls and a text prompt into photorealistic video. Sim-Bimanual predicts video from a two-arm robot's actions, for YAM and AgiBot embodiments.

The licence and the size are the renter story. All four use OpenMDW 1.1, which NVIDIA states permits commercial and non-commercial use under its terms — read the terms before production use, as with any open licence. At 16B parameters the weights are about 32GB in BF16 and about 16GB at 8-bit; NVIDIA's own technical material puts Cosmos3-Nano generation at 58 GiB of GPU memory in BF16, 44 GiB in FP8 and 31 GiB with FP8 plus offloading (NVIDIA-reported figures, from its Nov 2 technical blog). That is one ordinary rented card — an L40S or an A100 — not a cluster: world-model teams can now test NVIDIA's driving and robotics stack on the cheapest tier of our board.

The honest limits, from the announcement itself: these are post-trained examples meant as starting points for adaptation to your own sensor rig and domain, not finished products; the published serving setup was tested on one GB200, which is a test rig, not a minimum specification; and no one outside NVIDIA has yet published independent quality measurements for the checkpoints. The post-training recipes for all four stages — bidirectional adaptation, teacher forcing, consistency distillation and self-forcing — are published alongside the weights, so the adaptation path is part of the release.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Cosmos is NVIDIA's platform for teaching machines about the physical world, and until now its newest checkpoints were the part you read about rather than downloaded. Four 16B open checkpoints change who can experiment: a driving-data or robotics team with one rented GPU can generate synchronized camera-and-LiDAR scenes this week, at single-card prices, under a licence that allows commercial work. The frontier open-weight race this autumn has mostly been trillion-parameter language models; this is the same opening-up, at the opposite end of the size scale.

NEWS →  ·  Providers · Infrastructure

Crusoe sells its unfinished Wyoming campus to Google — the customer becomes the owner

Nov 8, 2026

Crusoe confirmed on Nov 6, 2026 that it has sold its unfinished south-east Wyoming data-centre campus to Google. The campus was announced in 2025 with Blackstone-backed Tallgrass as a 1.8 gigawatt project designed to scale to 10 gigawatts. Google had first approached the site as a customer; it now owns it instead. The purchase price was not disclosed.

Image: Google via blog.google

What happened, from the primary sources read on Nov 8, 2026: Crusoe's announcement (GlobeNewswire, Nov 6, 2026) confirms the sale of the unfinished campus to Google. TechCrunch's reporting (Nov 7, 2026) adds that Google had tried to land at the campus as a customer and raised cost and timeline concerns while Crusoe was building it. Separately, Google's own announcement (blog.google, Nov 5, 2026) describes its first Wyoming data centre in Laramie County as a $17 billion long-term investment — that figure is Google's wider Wyoming commitment, not the price it paid Crusoe, which was not disclosed. The Google plan names partners Tallgrass, Black Hills Energy, AEP and Related Digital, a 702 MW Bloom Energy fuel-cell development with carbon capture at the Tallgrass Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub, air cooling, and Google paying 100% of the power it uses. Crusoe is still developing a separate Google campus near Amarillo, Texas.

Why a sale like this happens: a gigawatt-class campus has to be carried — powered land, generation, cooling and construction — long before the first GPU earns anything. Crusoe, one of the best-funded independent AI infrastructure developers, chose to hand that carrying cost to a hyperscaler rather than finish the campus itself. Google, for its part, gets a powered site with its partners already attached instead of starting from raw land.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For anyone renting GPUs, the lesson is that power, not cards, is now the binding constraint on supply. The next year of rental capacity will be decided less by who orders the most accelerators than by who controls powered gigawatts — and this sale shows even a major independent developer can decide a campus is a hyperscaler's job to finish. When a smaller provider promises you future capacity, the question worth asking is the one this deal answers in reverse: who is carrying the power bill until it opens?

Google adds TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max — four TPU systems in a single year

Nov 9, 2026

Google expanded its eighth-generation TPU portfolio on Nov 9, 2026 with two new systems built from its existing silicon: TPU 8tx, for confidential inference, pairing the TPU 8t chip with 5th Gen AMD EPYC hosts so data and weights stay encrypted while in use; and TPU 8i Max, which packages two TPU 8i chips together for double the compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth in the same rack footprint. Google published no price and no availability date.

Image: Google via blog.google

What Google announced, in its own post (blog.google, Nov 9, 2026) read the same day: TPU 8tx is built for regulated enterprises and governments running proprietary models and agents on sensitive data — hardware-enforced confidential computing, using the same low-latency Boardfly network as TPU 8i, with up to 2× lower latency than TPU 8t claimed by Google. AMD's own newsroom release the same day confirms the 5th Gen EPYC host half of the design from AMD's side. TPU 8i Max targets massive context windows: two 8i chips in one package, doubling compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth per package at the same rack footprint. The same post made Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing generally available and open-sourced TPU Sync.

What Google did not announce matters as much: no price, no region and no availability date appear in its post. Google Cloud's Amin Vahdat told Bloomberg the two systems are due next year, 2027 — so neither belongs in any 2026 or early-2027 capacity plan, whatever the headlines imply.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and buyers this is the strongest non-NVIDIA accelerator signal of the month, on a delay. Confidential inference is a hard buying requirement for finance and health workloads that today pushes people onto specific GPU clouds; TPU 8tx is a direct alternative to price against once it can actually be rented. And 8i Max aims at exactly the long-context agentic serving that is driving H200 and B200 rental demand — doubling HBM bandwidth per package attacks the same memory wall renters pay Blackwell premiums for. Until Google prices them, the honest use of this news is as context and leverage, not as capacity.

NEWS →  ·  NVIDIA · Sovereign AI

NVIDIA AI Day Seoul opens: Rebellions' next NPU joins NVLink Fusion for SK Telecom's sovereign racks

Nov 9, 2026

At AI Day Seoul, which opened on Nov 9, 2026 at COEX in Seoul, NVIDIA, Rebellions and SK Telecom announced a collaboration to build sovereign AI racks in which NVIDIA GPUs handle prefill and Rebellions' next-generation Rebel R200 NPUs handle decode — connected through NVIDIA's NVLink Fusion and built on its MGX rack architecture. The R200 systems are expected to be ready for deployment in 2028.

Image: NVIDIA via blogs.nvidia.com

What was announced, from the primary sources read on Nov 9, 2026: the three companies' release (GlobeNewswire, Nov 9, 2026) describes a memorandum of understanding, backed by Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT, under which Rebellions connects its R200 to NVIDIA's platform via NVLink Fusion and SK Telecom deploys the racks in its AI data centres for its sovereign AI services. No R200 specifications, volumes or prices were disclosed, and the 2028 readiness date makes this a roadmap, not a product, an order or a contract. NVIDIA's own live blog from the event (blogs.nvidia.com, Nov 8–9, 2026) carries the wider Seoul package: a deeper sovereign-AI collaboration with the ministry, physical-AI work with Samsung, SK hynix, Hyundai and LG, and planned investments in Korean startups.

The part renters can use now: NVIDIA is publishing Dynamo-optimised deployment recipes for four Korean open models — SK Telecom's A.X K2, LG AI Research's K-EXAONE 2.0, Upstage's Solar Open 2 and Motif Technologies' Motif-3 — optimised for B200, with NVIDIA claiming up to 2× out-of-the-box performance (NVIDIA's claim; the post publishes no workload or GPU count to check it against). Also at the event, LG AI Research opened its K-EXAONE 2.5 API free of charge: a 750-billion-parameter model with 31 billion active, text-only, with a 512K context — API access only, no weights, and no end date or quota published for the free tier.

What it means if you rent GPUs

NVLink Fusion opening to a third-party NPU inside MGX racks is the clearest sign yet that future rental fleets may be heterogeneous — GPU prefill plus cheaper NPU decode — which would change inference price-per-token maths. With readiness set for 2028 it changes nothing bookable today. What it does tell a renter in 2026 is where Korean sovereign demand is heading, and that NVIDIA is willing to let other silicon into its rack standard to keep that demand inside its ecosystem.

Verda raises prices for the eleventh time — four GPUs up about 1%, five hold

Nov 9, 2026

Read on Verda's own GPU instances page today, Nov 9, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 8: four of Verda's nine tracked GPUs rose by about 1% — the eleventh rise since Oct 23, and the first selective one. The other five held, after two flat days.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on verda.com/gpu-instances

What changed, read on verda.com/gpu-instances on Nov 9, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.44 → $13.58 [$13.580], B300 $11.69 → $11.81 [$11.810], H100 SXM $4.94 → $4.99 [$4.987] and L40S $1.94 → $1.96 [$1.958] — each within a whisker of +1.0%. Held: B200 $9.14 [$9.138], H200 $6.44 [$6.440], A100 80GB $2.32 [$2.316], A100 40GB $1.66 [$1.657] and RTX PRO 6000 $2.73 [$2.725]. Verda's confidential-computing B300 rose the same ~1% ($11.93 → $12.05), which we do not list on the board.

The pattern: Verda rose on Oct 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30, Nov 2, Nov 4 and Nov 6, held on Nov 7 and Nov 8 — and has now risen an eleventh time, but narrowly: the October and early-November rises lifted almost the whole card at once, while this one touches only the GB300, B300, H100 SXM and L40S. Its GB300, the cheapest GB300 rate we list, has gone from $11.82 an hour at our Oct 19 check to $13.58 today, up 14.9% in three weeks. Rising list prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can produce the same shape).

Everywhere else we checked today held: RunPod Secure (all 11 tracked offers), Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute, SaladCloud and TensorDock were re-read on their own pages, and Hyperstack was checked by a first-hand read of its raw pricing page — all 13 of its on-demand rows unchanged. Lambda's page still prints only the rates it has announced for Nov 16; its current rates sit behind a login, and nafnaf.ai again showed no GPUs available.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters, the practical point is narrow: Verda's GB300 is this board's Best offer for that card, so the cheapest verified GB300 in our index just rose to $13.58 an hour. The other three rises sit above their cards' Best offers and change no recommendation. The wider signal is the shape — after ten broad rises, a selective one suggests Verda is now adjusting card by card rather than lifting the whole list, and the next checks will show whether the held five follow.

/story/longcat-2-5-weights-nov-9.html:
NEWS →  ·  Open weights · Meituan

LongCat-2.5 weights are out: Meituan's 1.6-trillion-parameter model is on Hugging Face under MIT

Nov 9, 2026

The weights for Meituan's LongCat-2.5 are downloadable: the official Hugging Face repository (meituan-longcat/LongCat-2.5) holds 3,562 GB of files under an MIT licence for the 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, with about 48 billion parameters active per token. The model launched API-only on Nov 2, 2026 with weights marked “coming soon”; the repository was created on Nov 4 and its model card was updated again today, Nov 9. The catch for GPU renters: the card's only documented deployment route is on NPUs, not GPUs.

Image: Meituan LongCat via huggingface.co

What is in the repository, read first-hand on Hugging Face on Nov 9, 2026: a native multimodal MoE — text and image input — built for long-horizon agentic work, at the same 1.6T total / ~48B active scale as LongCat-2.0, with a 1M-token context on Meituan's API. The licence is MIT, the most permissive of the widely used ones. Meituan's own scores on the card (in-house, labelled indicative by Meituan itself) put it at 88.4 on Terminal-Bench v2.1, up from 70.8 for LongCat-2.0. Its API price, from Meituan's own platform docs checked Nov 3, is a limited-time $0.30 per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output — the hosted route exists today; the self-host route is the hard part.

The deployment watch-out, from the same card: under “Deployment” the card documents NPU platforms only, pointing to an SGLang-FluentLLM build, and its efficiency story is a W4A4 quantisation scheme built for domestic AI accelerators. No GPU serving recipe is published on the card. By our standard memory maths the BF16 weights alone are about 3,200 GB — the shipped files total 3,562 GB — so even a 4-bit build at roughly 800 GB is a multi-node job, never a single card. Treat any “runs on my GPUs” claim for this model as unverified until a GPU serving path is published and reproduced.

What it means if you rent GPUs

This is one of the largest open-weight drops of the year, and the licence is genuinely clean — MIT, no Model-as-a-Service clause of the kind Mistral attached to Large 4. But a weights drop is only useful to GPU renters when the weights run on GPUs, and today Meituan documents only an NPU path. For now the practical routes are Meituan's own API at its stated limited-time prices, or waiting for the community GPU ports that usually follow a release this size. We have added LongCat-2.5 to the model catalogue with the memory maths shown, and we will update its page when a verified GPU serving route exists.

Edgevana signs $700 million-plus in Blackwell agreements — B300 and GB300 systems across two continents

Nov 9, 2026

Edgevana, the data-centre, energy and compute orchestration company, announced on Nov 9, 2026 that it has signed more than $700 million in fully committed, multi-year take-or-pay agreements to deploy NVIDIA Blackwell systems — B300 GPUs and GB300 systems — across North America and Europe. Every figure in the announcement is Edgevana's own, stated in its release; no customer, GPU count or contract length was disclosed.

Image: Edgevana via edgevana.com

What Edgevana announced, in its own release (PR Newswire, Nov 9, 2026, 15:00 UTC): the agreements are take-or-pay, meaning the customers pay for the contracted capacity whether or not they use it. Edgevana says it will orchestrate and deploy the systems across its network of 17 operational data-centre locations, with another 10 in active development, unifying pre-energised land, facilities and high-speed networks so customers can bring tens of megawatts of high-density AI compute online in 90 to 120 days. Alongside the signed $700 million, the company states $7 billion in contracted customer demand and an active pipeline exceeding $20 billion — its own figures, reported here as stated, not verified by us.

The company's framing is an inference pivot: co-CEO Ryan Fay argues training rewarded centralised mega-campuses while live inference traffic rewards capacity closer to users, which is the edge model Edgevana says it built for hyperscalers and trading firms before AI. That is the company's pitch, not a measured result — the release publishes no deployment that has yet gone live under these agreements, no per-GPU price and no named end customer.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters this is a demand signal, not a price. Another $700 million of take-or-pay money has been committed to Blackwell capacity that does not exist yet, on top of a stated $7 billion demand book — the same pattern as this autumn's list-price rises: buyers are paying to lock future B300 and GB300 supply rather than waiting for spot capacity. Nothing here can be booked by a reader today, and Edgevana sells orchestrated enterprise capacity, not hourly rentals. What it tells a renter planning 2027 capacity is that the queue for Blackwell systems is still lengthening, which is why the rental prices on our board keep facing upward pressure.

Licence: Apache 2.0 — free for any use, including commercial. Just keep the licence notice.

Worth knowing

SenseTime's looped-transformer multimodal model: 9B of stored weights that loop internally, so each pass computes like a model of about 14.6B parameters (the maker's framing) — the memory maths here prices the 9B you actually download. 262K training context, Apache 2.0, and single-GPU deployment examples on its card. It is a Preview: SenseTime's scores are vendor-reported only and no technical report has been published.

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. Real figures move with context length and software.

/story/telekom-munich-b300-expansion-nov.html:
NEWS →  ·  Infrastructure · Deutsche Telekom

Deutsche Telekom expands its sold-out Munich AI factory with Blackwell Ultra B300s

Nov 9, 2026

Deutsche Telekom announced on Nov 9, 2026 that it will expand its Industrial AI Cloud — the “AI factory” at Munich’s Tucherpark — with additional NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra (B300) systems, after the first expansion phase sold out in seven months. The B300s join the site’s existing Blackwell B200 systems and double the number of chips in that class, taking the factory’s capacity to 20 megawatts. Telekom puts the new investment at nearly another quarter of a billion euros.

Image: Deutsche Telekom via telekom.com

What Telekom announced, in its own release (Deutsche Telekom media information, Nov 9, 2026): the Munich factory only went live in February 2026, and its initial expansion — which Telekom says alone increased Germany’s available AI computing capacity by 50 percent — was fully booked just seven months later; planning for further stages began as early as May. The site will keep using NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs alongside the new B300s. A federal minister quoted in the release, Katherina Reiche, put the result as “doubling its capacity to 20,000 graphics processing units”. Trade coverage of the same Munich press conference (TelecomTV and Light Reading, Nov 9) put the expansion cost at about €250 million and current capacity at 12 MW, rising to the 20 MW Telekom states. Telekom says the factory runs at a PUE of 1.2 and its waste heat will supply the Tucherpark district.

Who is using it, per the same release: industrial companies and institutes including Siemens, Daimler Truck, Currenta, Synopsys, Agile Robots, Wandelbots, PhysicsX, Noxtua and EDAG, for simulations, digital twins, robotics and language models — including Soofi, a German language model trained on the infrastructure. Telekom is also exploring a further, larger expansion of its Bavarian commitment with partners, but states plainly that no final investment decision has been made on that stage — it is an exploration, not a commitment, and we report it as such.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and builders this is the European version of the same story this autumn keeps telling: sovereign, in-region Blackwell capacity sells out. A factory that opened in February was fully booked by September, and its owner is now spending roughly another quarter-billion euros to double its Blackwell-class fleet with B300s — the third demand data point today alone, after Edgevana’s $700 million-plus in take-or-pay Blackwell agreements and Verda’s eleventh list-price rise holding through our evening check. The honest limits: this is enterprise Industrial AI Cloud capacity sold to industry, research and the public sector under European data rules, not self-serve hourly rental — Telekom publishes no per-GPU price, and nothing in this announcement can be booked from our price board today. What it tells a renter planning European capacity for 2027 is that the queue for B300s in Europe is lengthening, not shortening.

/story/anthropic-ipo-terms-nov-10.html:
NEWS →  ·  AI labs · Anthropic

Anthropic sets IPO terms at up to $1 trillion — and NVIDIA, Google, AMD and TSMC are buying $26 billion of it

Nov 10, 2026

Anthropic launched its IPO roadshow on Nov 10, 2026 and filed Amendment No. 2 to its Form S-1 with the SEC the same day: 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78, listing on Nasdaq as ANT, raising up to about $64.4 billion and valuing the company at about $1.02 trillion on shares outstanding. Alongside the offering, seven technology companies — the GPU supply chain itself — have agreed to buy $26 billion of Anthropic stock in a private placement at the IPO price.

Image: Anthropic via anthropic.com

The terms, from Amendment No. 2 to Anthropic's Form S-1 filed with the SEC on Nov 10, 2026, as reported the same day by Reuters, CNBC and Axios from the filing: Anthropic itself sells 801,351,354 of the 825 million shares and existing stockholders sell 23,648,646; underwriters hold a 30-day option on a further 123,750,000 shares, which at $78 would take the total raise to about $74 billion. A draft circulated to banks late on Nov 9 showed about 867 million shares at $70 to $80; Anthropic told the banks those details were inaccurate, and the Nov 10 amended filing — $70 to $78 — is the version of record. CNBC reports pricing on Nov 18 and trading from Nov 19; the filing itself gives no dates, so we report that timing as reported, not filed.

The placement is the part this desk cares about: Google and NVIDIA have each agreed to buy about $10 billion of non-voting Class N shares at the IPO price, AMD $2.5 billion, and Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC $1 billion, $1 billion, $1 billion and $500 million respectively — $26 billion in all, per the filing summaries. The filing's use-of-proceeds language covers general corporate purposes including compute and infrastructure. One widely flashed sub-claim — up to $120.5 billion of NVIDIA GPU compute agreements with SpaceX — appears in none of the detailed filing summaries we read, so we do not print it as fact.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and buyers, this is the largest single demand signal of the autumn. The companies buying the placement are the companies that make and sell the chips, the memory and the foundry capacity — and the buyer is one of the largest GPU consumers in the world, now capitalised at a trillion-dollar scale with compute named in its use of proceeds. A newly funded Anthropic is a multi-year buyer of exactly the capacity renters are competing for, which is the same direction as everything else in this week's record: Verda's twelfth rise today, Lambda's announced rises landing Nov 16, and CoreWeave reporting tonight with a backlog its last quarterly filing put at $103.7 billion. None of that makes any single rental cheaper.

/story/verda-twelfth-rise-nov-10.html:
NEWS →  ·  Prices · Verda

Verda raises prices for the twelfth time — the same four GPUs up about 1% again

Nov 10, 2026

Read on Verda's own GPU instances page today, Nov 10, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 9: the same four GPUs that rose yesterday rose again by about 1% — GB300, B300, H100 SXM and L40S. It is Verda's twelfth rise since Oct 23. The other five tracked GPUs held for a second straight day.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on verda.com/gpu-instances

What changed, read on verda.com/gpu-instances on Nov 10, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.58 → $13.72 [$13.720], B300 $11.81 → $11.93 [$11.930], H100 SXM $4.99 → $5.04 [$5.037] and L40S $1.96 → $1.98 [$1.978] — each about +1.0%, exactly the pattern of Nov 9. Held: B200 $9.14 [$9.138], H200 $6.44 [$6.440], A100 80GB $2.32 [$2.316], A100 40GB $1.66 [$1.657] and RTX PRO 6000 $2.73 [$2.725]. Verda's confidential-computing B300 rose the same ~1% ($12.05 → $12.17), which we do not list on the board. Across two days the four movers are up about 2.1% in all; Verda's GB300, this board's Best offer for that card, has gone from $11.82 an hour at our Oct 19 check to $13.72 today, up 16.1% in three weeks.

Everywhere else we checked today held: RunPod Secure (all 11 tracked offers), Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute, SaladCloud and TensorDock were re-read on their own pages, and Hyperstack was checked by a first-hand read of its raw pricing page — all 13 of its on-demand rows unchanged. Lambda's page still prints only the rates it has announced for Nov 16 (about +15% on B200 and H100); its current rates sit behind a login, and nafnaf.ai again showed no GPUs available. Rising list prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can produce the same shape).

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters the practical point is again narrow: Verda's GB300 is this board's Best offer for that card, so the cheapest verified GB300 in our index just rose to $13.72 an hour. The other three rises sit above their cards' Best offers and change no recommendation. Two identical selective rises in two days look less like a one-off adjustment and more like a daily step on those four cards — the next checks will show whether the step continues, and whether the held five ever join it.
