Monetize idle GPUs, honestly: marketplace, colocation — or sell the card

Every guide to renting out your GPU starts at the signup button. This one starts at the arithmetic. What an idle card earns is decided by three numbers nobody can promise you — how many hours it rents, what the platform keeps, and what your power costs — so this page works all three openly, at rates verified on Nov 10, 2026, and then gives the option the funnel guides leave out: sometimes the best way to monetize an idle GPU is to sell it.

The verdict

  • One consumer card at home — List it on a host marketplace — and run the sell comparison below first. About $84–$146 a month after power at 40–70% utilisation, worked in full below. Selling the same card today brings roughly $2,400–$2,800 once — renting takes well over a year to match it.
  • A few gaming cards — Marketplace, all of them — colocation maths does not work at this size. The same per-card maths, times the cards: roughly $84–$146 per 4090-class card per month after power. Your real cost is babysitting uptime across several machines.
  • 8+ datacenter cards — Colocation, or a host programme — the facility contract comes first, the listing second. An 8× H100 node grosses $13,140 a month at the best verified node rate if rented every hour — and about $5,060 after power alone at 40%, before the fixed facility bill. The bill is owed whether the node rents or not.
  • An enterprise fleet — Contract / colocation at negotiated rates — you are running a small cloud, price it like one. No honest per-card net exists here: it is your negotiated facility cost against your booked utilisation. For scale, Spheron’s own cost model puts colocation plus networking at roughly $73 per GPU per month on a 1,024-GPU cluster (their figure, stated Oct 2026) — a small fleet pays more.
Compare prices→For providers→

The three routes, without the funnel

Every “net” figure here is worked step by step below — gross at three utilisation levels, minus power — where a platform takes a host-side cut, that depends on the model and is handled in the fee section. Nothing here is an earnings promise; utilisation is the renter’s decision, not yours. Route 1 — list on a marketplace that takes hosts. You install the platform’s software, pass its verification, set or accept a price, and renters find you. The platform handles the customer, the billing and the metering, and takes its side of the money — how much, and taken from whom, differs by platform and gets its own section below. Your costs are power, wear, and keeping the machine online. This is the only route that makes sense below a rack of hardware. Route 2 — colocation. You rent rack space, power, cooling and bandwidth in a data centre, put your machines in it, and list them yourself (or through a marketplace on top). The facility bill is fixed and monthly: it arrives at 100% whether your machines rent at 100% or at zero. Colocation buys the density and uptime a home connection cannot offer — an 8-GPU node wants kilowatts, not a wall socket — and only pays once the fleet is big enough that the fixed bill is a small slice of the gross. Route 3 — sell the hardware. No funnel will suggest this, because nobody earns a commission when you sell your own card. It belongs in the comparison anyway: a used RTX 4090 sells today for roughly what 16–34 months of realistic renting nets (worked below), and the card at the end of two years of renting is worth less than the card today. Renting wins when you want the card kept, or genuinely believe utilisation will run high for years. Selling wins more often than the hosting guides admit.

The marketplace maths: one RTX 4090

Worked at the cheapest verified renter price for a 4090 hour on our board — $0.34/hr (RunPod Community, checked Nov 10, 2026). That is what a renter actually pays for this card today, so it is the honest rate for a host listing to compete at. A month is 730 hours. Power is the card alone at its rated 450W TDP, at an assumed $0.12/kWh — home rates vary widely, and the rest of the PC draws more, so treat the power line as a floor.

One RTX 4090, listed at $0.34/hrRented every hour (100%)70% of hours40% of hours
Rented hours in a 730-hour month730511292
Gross$248.20$173.74$99.28
Power while rented (450W × hours × $0.12/kWh)−$39.42−$27.59−$15.77
Net before any host-side platform cut$208.78$146.15$83.51

Two honest footnotes. First, the platform’s cut: on nafnaf’s model the 5% fee is added on the renter’s side, so a host asking $0.34 receives $0.34 and the renter pays $0.357 — the table stands as written there. On a platform that deducts from the host’s side, take that percentage off the gross line before power; the section below says which models we could verify. Second, a PC left on around the clock draws idle power too — at an assumed 50–100W (labelled assumption), roughly $4–$9 a month, owed whether or not a job ever lands.

The same maths at node scale: 8× H100

Datacenter cards rent as nodes. The best verified 8-GPU H100 rate on our board is TensorDock’s $2.25 per GPU per hour at an 8-GPU minimum — $18.00 per node-hour (checked Nov 10, 2026). Power is the eight cards alone at the H100 SXM’s rated 700W TDP each — 5.6 kW, before CPUs, networking and cooling, so again a floor.

One 8× H100 node at $18.00/hr100%70%40%
Gross$13,140$9,198$5,256
Power while rented (5.6 kW × hours × $0.12/kWh)−$491−$343−$196
Net before facility bill and any platform cut$12,649$8,855$5,060

The node’s gross is just over fifty times the single 4090’s — and unlike the home card, the node has a landlord. The line missing from this table is the facility bill, and it is missing on purpose: there is no honest universal figure for it. It gets its own section, as a formula, below.

Compare prices→For providers→

What the platforms take — verified, and what is not published

PlatformWhat it takes — and what it does not publish
nafnaf5%, charged to the renter, not deducted from you. nafnaf’s own provider pages (read Nov 10, 2026) state a 5% consumer fee on your rate: “Ask $1.00, receive $1.00; the renter pays $1.05.” You set the rate for compute, storage and transfer; operating costs and taxes remain yours.
Vast.aiNo host-side hosting fee since June 2024; the renter-side surcharge is not published. Vast’s own 2024 round-up says it “eliminated hosting fees entirely” in June 2024 and moved to “a more flexible internal surcharge model” — the price a host sets is the price the host earns, and Vast’s margin sits inside the price the renter sees. What that surcharge is, Vast does not publish; third-party write-ups quote everything from the mid-teens to 25%, which tells you they are guessing. Treat any exact Vast percentage on a blog as unverified — including, if we ever printed one, ours.
SaladCloudYou are paid in Salad Balance, not cash. Salad’s own documentation (read Nov 10, 2026) says owners earn rewards in Salad Balance, redeemed through its storefront for PayPal, gift cards, games and subscriptions; the rate on a job is set by the priority the customer chose, and Salad’s own FAQ states many providers earn $100–$200 a month — Salad’s figure, not ours, and its terms guarantee no earnings. Balance is worth less than the same number in cash: you can only spend it where Salad lets you.
Everyone elseCheck the current split before you list. Host programmes revise their terms, and a percentage from last year’s blog post is how hosts get surprised. The split, the payout currency, the minimum payout and the payout schedule are four separate lines in every host agreement; read all four.

One structural point matters more than any percentage: whether the fee comes off your side or is added to the renter’s. A fee added on top (nafnaf’s model, and Vast’s since 2024) leaves your rate intact but makes your listing look pricier to a comparing renter. What decides your month is never the fee alone — it is the fee model multiplied by the utilisation that platform actually delivers to a card like yours.

Colocation: the fixed bill, as a formula

Colocation is priced per kilowatt or per rack per month, negotiated per facility, per region, per power contract — Spheron’s own colocation guide concedes the same point, in its words that a colocation quote “is closer to a real estate lease than a cloud price list.” So this guide will not quote you a colo price. It gives you the only number that matters, computable the moment a facility quotes you:

The break-even formula
Break-even utilisation = your fixed monthly facility bill ÷ (your hourly rate × 730)

That is the share of the month your machines must rent just to cover the facility, before power and before any platform cut. Worked example with a clearly illustrative bill: at a facility bill of $1,500 a month (illustrative — get quotes; your market will differ) and the node’s $18.00/hr, break-even is $1,500 ÷ $13,140 ≈ 11% of hours to cover the facility alone, and roughly 12% once the node’s power margin is counted. Double the bill to $3,000 and break-even doubles with it, to about 23%. The formula is the deliverable: a quote you cannot run through it is a quote you do not understand yet. Two anchors, both labelled. Spheron’s own cost model for a 1,024-GPU H100 cluster (their post, figures stated as of early Oct 2026) itemises colocation and networking at roughly $75,000 a month — about $73 per GPU per month — with power billed separately. That is a thousand-GPU buyer’s number; a single-rack tenant has none of that leverage and should expect a far higher per-GPU cost, which is why route 2 starts at “8+ datacenter cards” above and not at two. And density is the gate before price: Spheron states GPU colocation runs 10–15 kW per rack as the 2026 baseline against 3–5 kW for standard server colocation — so a standard enterprise colo contract may not be able to power your rack at any price.

The 70% question, tested

Hosting content routinely models 70% utilisation or better, because the numbers look good there. Nothing about a marketplace promises it: utilisation is set by how many renters want your exact card, in your location, at your price, against every other identical listing — for a consumer card, thousands of them. Look at the same 4090 across the range, from the table above: $208.78 a month rented every hour, $146.15 at 70%, $83.51 at 40%. The card did not change; the assumption did, and it moved the answer two and a half times. Any earnings figure quoted without its utilisation assumption printed next to it is marketing, not maths.

Renting one RTX 4090What it takes — or what it pays
Match $2,400 in one yearNet about $200 a month — the card would need to rent about 96% of all hours for a year straight, against a ceiling of $208.78 a month if it rents literally every hour.
Match $2,800 in one yearAbout $233 a month — no utilisation level gets there at all at the worked rates.
24 months at 70% utilisationAbout $3,500 net before any host-side cut, against $2,400–$2,800 today — while the rented card ends those two years older, more worn, and worth less.

Now the comparison the funnel leaves out — renting against selling. A used RTX 4090 sold for roughly $2,400–$2,800 in recent completed eBay sales (sold-listing trackers read Nov 10, 2026; condition and model move the figure, and trackers disagree with each other — the method works with whatever your card would actually fetch). At the worked rates above, matching even the low end within a year means netting about $200 a month, against a ceiling of $208.78 if the card rents literally every hour: the card would need to rent about 96% of all hours for a year straight. Against the top of the range ($2,800, or $233 a month), no utilisation level gets there at all. Over two years the picture flips, but only just, and only at sustained high utilisation: 24 months at 70% nets about $3,500 before any host-side cut, against $2,400–$2,800 today — while the rented card ends those two years older, more worn, and worth less, and the $0.34 rate has to survive a market that has repriced everything else. The honest summary: renting a single 4090 is a reasonable way to keep a card you want anyway and offset its cost. As a pure investment against selling, it needs years and luck.

The demand is real — and it still is not a promise

The renter side of this market is genuinely tight, and our own record shows it. Providers do not raise prices twelve times into weak demand:

ProviderWhat our Price Watch record shows
VerdaA mid-size provider on our board — has raised its prices twelve times since Oct 23, 2026; its GB300 rate is up ▲ 16.1% since Oct 19 ($11.82 → $13.72/hr, both read on Verda’s own pricing pages on those dates).
RunPod ServerlessIts B200 rate rose about 25% between our Oct 26 and Nov 2 reads.
LambdaHas announced rises of about 15% taking effect Nov 16, 2026.

Hold the counterweight in the same hand. A rising list price at a datacenter provider is evidence renters pay more for capacity in facilities — it is not evidence that your specific card, in your specific postcode, beside thousands of identical marketplace listings, rents one hour more. Datacenter demand concentrates on datacenter cards in datacenter buildings; the consumer-card end clears at $0.34 an hour precisely because supply there is deep. Both facts are in our record. Quote either one alone and you are selling something.

When not to bother

SituationWhy it does not pay
One old or low-memory cardThe maths scales with the hourly rate; a card renting for a few cents an hour cannot outrun its own power bill, let alone your time.
Expensive home electricityEvery figure here moves with your power price. At double the assumed $0.12/kWh, the 4090’s 40% month nets about $68 instead of $84 — run your own rate through the table before listing, not after.
You cannot keep the machine onlineMarketplaces verify hosts, rank on reliability, and delist or bury listings that drop offline or fail jobs. A gaming PC that sleeps, updates and reboots on its own schedule is not inventory; it is a future delisting.
You need the money soon, or certainlyRental income is variable and starts at zero; a sale is one amount, once, now. If the point is a known sum by a known date, route 3 is the only honest answer.
The payout is not moneyBalance, credits and tokens are worth what the platform lets you redeem them for, when it lets you. Price that in before counting the earnings.
Compare prices→For providers→

How we know

Rental rates are from GPUJournal’s verified price board, checked Nov 10, 2026 on providers’ own published pages and banked daily since Oct 19, 2026: RTX 4090 best verified offer RunPod Community $0.34/GPU/hr (RunPod Secure lists the same card at $0.89); 8× H100 node rate TensorDock $2.25/GPU/hr at an 8-GPU minimum, $18.00/node/hr. Platform terms were read on the platforms’ own pages on Nov 10, 2026: nafnaf’s provider pages state a 5% consumer fee added to the host’s rate (“Ask $1.00, receive $1.00; the renter pays $1.05”); Vast.ai’s 2024 round-up on vast.ai states hosting fees were eliminated in June 2024 in favour of an internal surcharge model whose percentage Vast does not publish — third-party percentages for Vast (mid-teens to 25% across the write-ups we found) conflict and are treated as unverified; Salad’s documentation states hosts earn Salad Balance redeemable via its storefront (PayPal, gift cards, games), that job rates depend on customer-set priority, and that many providers earn $100–$200/month (Salad’s own figure; its terms guarantee no earnings). Power figures are labelled planning assumptions: card draws are the manufacturers’ rated TDP (RTX 4090 450W, H100 SXM 700W), GPU only — whole-system draw is higher; electricity is an assumed $0.12/kWh; a month is 730 hours; idle draw of 50–100W is an assumption, not a measurement. The colocation worked example uses an explicitly illustrative facility bill of $1,500/month — no colocation price is quoted in this guide because none is published in a form we could verify; the $73/GPU/month colocation-and-networking figure and the 10–15 kW/rack density baseline are Spheron’s stated figures from its colocation post (stated as of early Oct 2026, read Nov 10, 2026), as are its supplier programme terms. Resale: two completed-eBay-sale trackers read Nov 10, 2026 (GetPCParts average ≈$2,387, sales through Nov 7, 2026; pcprice.watch median $2,780) — this guide uses the rounded range $2,400–$2,800, and the rent-vs-sell method works with any figure you substitute. Demand evidence is our own Price Watch record: Verda’s twelve rises, Oct 23 – Nov 10, 2026 (GB300 $11.82 read Oct 19 → $13.72 read Nov 10); RunPod Serverless B200 ($8.64 read Oct 26 → $10.79 read Nov 2); Lambda’s announced rises of Nov 6, 2026, effective Nov 16 — announced, not yet in effect, and not applied to our board.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. Everything in this box is GPUJournal’s judgement on the verified record above it; the record itself is in the tables and the method note. We sell nothing, list nothing and take no commission from any route on this page — which is more than the author of the guide this one answers can say. Spheron’s posts on this question (read Nov 10, 2026) walk a rack owner through GPU colocation and land where you would expect: colocate the facility, then let a demand marketplace — theirs — fill it. For a datacenter fleet that framing is mostly fair, and their supplier programme’s stated terms (you set prices, you sign your own contracts, they handle billing and settle monthly) are reasonable ones to compare against. But the funnel starts at rack owners because that is who it can sell to. It does not run a home card’s net after power, does not test the utilisation its route implies for a card like yours, its programme covers H100-class datacenter SKUs only, and “sell” does not appear as a route. Start from your situation instead: one card — marketplace, with the sell comparison run first; a rack or more — get colo quotes, run the break-even formula on each, and only then argue about which marketplace’s demand is worth its cut.

MiniMax open-sources H3-Image: a 16-megapixel image model that serves on one GPU

Nov 10, 2026

MiniMax published the weights of H3-Image on Nov 10, 2026: a 33.1-billion-parameter image generation and editing model that produces roughly 16-megapixel images — up to 4096×4096 — directly, with no upscaler, in six sampling steps, and serves from a single GPU through vLLM-Omni or SGLang. It is released under MiniMax's own community licence, not a permissive one, and the full download is bigger than the headline checkpoint suggests.

Image: MiniMax via huggingface.co

What shipped, from MiniMax's blog (Nov 10, 2026) and the official Hugging Face card (MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image), both read first-hand: one checkpoint unifies text-to-image and image editing, accepts up to 16 reference images, and is distilled to six sampling steps with no classifier-free guidance. MiniMax claims 4K images in under 10 seconds — the maker's own figure, not measured by us — and says 4K-and-above API requests are 50% off for launch week. An optional prompt-expander model, MiniMax-H3-Image-PE (17.9 GB, NVFP4), shipped quietly alongside it.

The hardware maths, from the same card: the image checkpoint itself is 68.65 GB (66.28 GB transformer + 2.34 GB VAE), but its text encoder is NOT in the repository — it loads from the separate MiniMax-H3 release and adds 66.7 GB, so budget about 135 GB of downloads and memory for the full BF16 stack. The card lists NVIDIA H200, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and AMD Instinct MI350X as supported, gives a one-GPU start command for both vLLM-Omni and SGLang, and the serving recipes carry per-hardware configurations — on a 96 GB card the full BF16 stack plainly does not fit at once, so check the recipe for your card before renting. The licence is the MiniMax-H3-Image Community License Agreement, with a separate written-authorisation route described in the licence itself: read it before planning a commercial service.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For image workloads this changes the rental question. A flagship-class open image model that generates 16 megapixels natively and serves on one GPU means the default rental is a single high-memory card, not a node — and AMD's MI350X is a named day-one target alongside NVIDIA, which is still rare for a launch this size. The honest watch-outs are the two in the facts above: the real footprint is about twice the headline checkpoint once the text encoder is counted, and the community licence is MiniMax's own terms, not MIT or Apache. Teams that clear both can price this against per-image API bills from a single card's hourly rate on our board.

NEWS →  ·  Results · CoreWeave

CoreWeave Q3: revenue up 168% to $3.66 billion, a $132.5 billion backlog — and guidance raised again

Nov 10, 2026

CoreWeave reported third-quarter 2026 results after the close on Nov 10, 2026: revenue of $3.661 billion, up 168% on a year earlier and more than $1 billion added in a single quarter, a revenue backlog of about $132.5 billion, and full-year guidance raised on every line. The cost of building that fast is in the same release: a $709 million net loss, with $846 million of net interest expense in the quarter alone.

Image: CoreWeave via coreweave.com

The reported numbers, from CoreWeave's own results release (Nov 10, 2026, quarter ended Sep 30, 2026), read first-hand: revenue $3,661 million against $1,365 million a year earlier; operating income $207 million (6% margin); adjusted operating income $379 million (10% margin), which the company says reached double digits a quarter ahead of plan; net loss $709 million, or $1.27 a share, against $110 million a year earlier, with net interest expense of $846 million against $310 million. Backlog — committed contracts not yet recognised as revenue, subject to delivery and availability requirements, in the release's own definition — was about $132.5 billion at Sep 30, up from about $104 billion at Jun 30 per the company's second-quarter reporting.

The build-out and the outlook, from the same release: CoreWeave added more than 200 MW of active power in the quarter to pass 1.7 GW, double its live footprint since the start of the year, and grew contracted power by more than 900 MW to over 4.6 GW. It says multi-rack NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 deployments are online, with first production workloads for Cognition at 4.8 times the token throughput of GB200 NVL72 (CoreWeave's own figure). Full-year 2026 guidance is raised: revenue to $13.0–$13.3 billion, adjusted operating income to $1.275–$1.375 billion, capital expenditure to $37–$39 billion, exit run-rate revenue to $20–$21 billion, with more than 1.85 GW of active power expected at year-end and fourth-quarter interest expense guided at $1.05–$1.15 billion. The chief executive says about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits is expected in the next three months alone.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For anyone renting GPUs, this is the demand side of the price board reporting itself. The largest listed neocloud grew revenue 168%, carries $132.5 billion of contracted backlog and is still raising guidance and capex — while paying $846 million a quarter in interest to do it. That combination is exactly the backdrop to the pattern our Price Watch has tracked all autumn: providers raising list prices in small, repeated steps because contracted demand keeps absorbing capacity. It does not make any single provider's hourly rate fair or unfair — our board still judges that card by card — but it explains why the rises keep coming, and why CoreWeave's own capacity is sold against contracts first and a public price list second. Next demand tests: Nebius reports Nov 12, Lambda's announced rises take effect Nov 16, and NVIDIA reports Nov 17.

AMD's 256-core EPYC ‘Venice’ is shipping — the host CPU built to feed GPU racks

Nov 11, 2026

AMD announced general availability of its 6th Gen EPYC server processors (‘Venice’, Zen 6, SP7) on Nov 10, 2026: systems are shipping from the leading server makers now, Meta is the named lead customer, and cloud instances follow at Microsoft Azure (HDv2 in preview) and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (Compute E7). The flagship EPYC 9996 carries 256 cores and 512 threads at a $14,904 list price.

Image: AMD via newsroom.amd.com

The launch, from AMD's own newsroom release dated Nov 10, 2026: 6th Gen EPYC SP7 platforms are shipping from leading OEMs and ODMs; the portfolio is workload-split across general-purpose, high-frequency host-node and high-density parts. The high-frequency host-node chips boost to 5.3 GHz, and AMD claims (vendor figures, from its release footnotes) up to 1.8× the LLM output throughput of the previous EPYC generation for host-node parts and up to 3.7× the SPECrate2017 performance of an NVIDIA Vera CPU-based system for the 9996. The same release folds in AMD's Helion agentic-AI rack blueprint (up to 73,728 threads per rack) and names Azure's forthcoming ND MI455X v7 — built on AMD's Helios rackscale design — for production AI inference.

Why a CPU launch belongs on a GPU desk: every GPU node a renter pays for is paired with host CPUs that feed the accelerators, run the agent sandboxes and orchestration around the models, and increasingly carry whole agent workloads themselves. Venice is the x86 host platform the next wave of GPU racks — AMD Instinct and multi-vendor alike — will ship with into 2027, and Azure HDv2 and OCI E7 are the first cloud doors renters will meet it through. It is also AMD's direct counter to NVIDIA's Vera CPU, whose first full independent reviews landed the same week.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters the practical read is about the whole node, not the card alone: when Venice-based instances reach Azure and OCI, the CPU side of those GPU-adjacent instances gets faster host feeding and far denser agent capacity per rack — worth checking in the spec sheet before comparing two otherwise identical GPU offers. No rental price changes follow from this launch today; it is the platform the 2027 capacity will stand on.

/story/runway-praxis-1-open-weights-nov-.html:
NEWS →  ·  Open weights · Runway

Runway open-sources Praxis-1: a 27B robot model that runs on one H100, under Apache 2.0

Nov 11, 2026

Runway released the weights of Praxis-1 on Nov 11, 2026: a 27-billion-parameter world action model that predicts video and robot actions together, tops NVIDIA's RoboLab-120 leaderboard on Runway's own figures, and is released — weights, inference code and fine-tuning code — under Apache 2.0, including for commercial use. It runs out of the box on a single H100.

Image: Runway via runway.com

What shipped, from Runway's own announcement (Nov 11, 2026), read first-hand: Praxis-1 is a 27B-parameter mixture-of-experts diffusion transformer, first introduced in September as Runway's first world action model, now open to every developer. Runway reports 46.2% success across 1,200 episodes on NVIDIA's RoboLab-120 benchmark, ahead of FLUX 3 Action at 42.9%, Cosmos3 Nano at 36.8% and π0.5 at 28.0% — Runway's figures, data as of November 2026, not measured by us. The release is on GitHub, on Hugging Face with native LeRobot support, and in vLLM-Omni, with hosted inference on Reactor; launch partners Noble Machines, Standard Bots and Ultra have been running it on their own hardware, and fine-tuned on Google's RT-1 robot — which never appeared in its training data — it reaches 80.0% on SimplerEnv against the original RT-1 policy's 52.4% (Runway's figure).

The hardware maths, from Runway's research page: 27.2 billion parameters in total, 54.4 GB in BF16 — so the full model fits one 80 GB GPU — and packing the routed experts in NVFP4 shrinks the policy weights to 17.5 GB. Runway lists H100 and B200 data-centre GPUs, RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000 workstation cards, and Jetson Thor on the robot itself as running it out of the box. Three checkpoints are in the Hugging Face collection: the base model and DROID and bimanual YAM fine-tunes.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Most open-weight drops on this desk are language or image models; Praxis-1 is a frontier-class robot brain that a single rented H100 can run and fine-tune, under the most permissive licence there is — the exact opposite of this week's territorial community licences. For GPU renters it is a new, concrete workload to price: one 80 GB card for the BF16 model, a workstation card for the NVFP4 build, and LoRA fine-tuning without retraining the full model. Physical-AI teams no longer need a cluster, or a closed API, to work with the current RoboLab-120 leader.

/story/nvidia-ceo-transition-nov-12.html:
NEWS →  ·  Industry · NVIDIA

Jensen Huang resigns as NVIDIA CEO — CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim chief

Nov 12, 2026

NVIDIA announced on Nov 12, 2026 that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer and Board member, effective immediately, ending 33 years leading the company he co-founded. Colette Kress, NVIDIA's Chief Financial Officer since 2013, serves as Interim CEO while keeping the CFO role; Harvey C. Jones becomes the company's first-ever Chair of the Board. NVIDIA's release gives no reason for the resignation.

Image: NVIDIA via nvidianews.nvidia.com

The announcement is NVIDIA's own, published via GlobeNewswire at 13:48 UTC on Nov 12, 2026, following press reports on Nov 11 that the Board was weighing Huang's future — reports this desk held as unverified until NVIDIA itself spoke. From the release: the Board is searching for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates; Kress joined NVIDIA in September 2013 after nearly 25 years in finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft; Jones, Chair of the Board, is a former Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys. Jones, in the release: the Board expects “the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” Kress: “I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.” NVIDIA's third-quarter fiscal 2027 results stay on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, with the earnings call at 2 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled. Reuters reported NVIDIA shares fell more than 10% in premarket trading.

Why this belongs on a GPU desk: NVIDIA supplies effectively every card on this board, and its roadmap — Blackwell today, Vera Rubin next — sets the capacity and pricing weather for every provider a renter buys from. A leadership change at the top of that supplier, five days before earnings, is the single largest company event in the GPU market this year.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and buyers, the dated facts today are narrow and worth stating plainly: no product, pricing or roadmap change has been announced, and continuity of operations, customer commitments and the roadmap is NVIDIA's stated position in its own release. The first real test is the Nov 17 earnings call, now led by Interim CEO Kress. Anything beyond the release — including reporting about the circumstances around the resignation — is not something NVIDIA has confirmed, and this desk is not presenting it as fact.

/story/nebius-q3-nov-12.html:
NEWS →  ·  Providers · Nebius

Nebius Q3: revenue up 571% to $980.8m — and 2027 capex guided at $40–45bn

Nov 12, 2026

Nebius reported third-quarter results before the open on Nov 12, 2026: revenue of $980.8m, up 571% year on year and ahead of the roughly $907.5m consensus, with adjusted EBITDA of $465.8m. The tracked neocloud also raised 2026 capex to about $27bn and gave its first 2027 outlook — revenue of $12–13bn on capex of $40–45bn.

Image: Nebius via nebius.com

From Nebius's own release (BusinessWire, Nov 12, 2026): AI Cloud revenue was $973.8m, up 643%; adjusted net income was +$90.9m against a GAAP net loss from continuing operations of $37.5m. Annualised recurring revenue reached $6.4bn at the end of September, and the $7bn ARR milestone now lands in February rather than December. Full-year 2026 revenue is guided to the low end of the $3.0–3.4bn range, 2026 capex rises to about $27bn (from $20–25bn), cash stood at $7.4bn, and the company signed more than $12bn of new contract value since the quarter began. Shares fell roughly 10–15% in premarket trading on the guidance and capex mix, despite the revenue beat.

Nebius is a priced provider on this board, and its numbers are the demand story in financial form: a neocloud spending $40–45bn on capacity in 2027 is building for contracted demand, not speculation — the same pattern as CoreWeave's $132.5bn backlog reported on Nov 10. The other side of the coin for renters: revenue recognition slipping a quarter (December into February) says new capacity is landing slightly later than planned, which is one more reason near-term GPU supply stays tight.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters the read is capacity, not the share price: Nebius is quadrupling down on build-out, which points to more Nebius inventory through 2027, while the slipped ARR milestone is a small, dated signal that supply arrives a little slower than promised. No Nebius board prices changed today — its rates were re-read unchanged in today's check.

/guide/h100-b200-sold-out.html:
PROVIDER COMPARISONS →  ·  2026-11-12 · 13 min read

H100 or B200 sold out? What to rent instead — priced

A stock alert tells you the card you wanted is gone. It does not tell you what to rent instead, or what the substitute costs. This page does: every substitute below is a real offer on our verified price board, checked Nov 12, 2026 — the card, the provider, the rate, and the terms that change the bill. One honesty note before the table: we are not reporting any provider as sold out today — our checks found prices, not stock levels. This guide is for the moment you go to book an H100 SXM or a B200 and find it gone.

The verdict

  • H100 SXM — one card — H200 at RunPod Community — same Hopper generation, 141GB of memory instead of 80GB, rented by the single card. On-demand, no minimum.
  • H100 SXM — an 8-GPU training job — The H100 SXM itself, at TensorDock — “gone” is usually one provider's shelf, not the market's; this is the cheapest verified H100 SXM rate on our board. On-demand, 8-GPU minimum — $18.00/hr for the node.
  • H100 SXM — single card, budget first — H100 PCIe at RunPod Community — same chip family, same 80GB; no NVLink and lower power, so a single-card substitute, not a training-node one. On-demand, no minimum.
  • B200 — B300 at Hyperstack — Blackwell Ultra, a step up not down: 288GB instead of 192GB. On-demand (RunPod Secure lists the same card at $8.99). · $5.98/hr at RunPod Community
  • B200 — budget first — H200 at RunPod Community — a generation down, 141GB instead of 192GB, and 40% below the cheapest B200 on the board. On-demand, no minimum.
  • Either card — and your work fits in 80GB without FP8 — A100 80GB at Thunder Compute — the previous generation, the honest workhorse; no FP8, so the newest serving speed-ups do not apply. On-demand, no minimum.
  • B200 — you actually need more card, not less — GB300 at Verda — rack-scale Blackwell Ultra, listed per GPU-hour on Verda's own page. On-demand.

First move: check the same card somewhere else

Every rate in the verdict above is the lowest verified on-demand price for that card on our board on Nov 12, 2026 — one best offer per card, the same rule the board itself uses. Terms that change the bill (minimums, whole-node rental, VAT) are printed with the price wherever they apply. “Sold out” is almost always a sentence about one provider's shelf. The H100 SXM is listed by eight providers on our board, and the spread between them is wider than the gap between most substitutes: on Nov 12, 2026 the same card, on-demand, runs from $2.25 to $5.14 a GPU-hour before you reach the hyperscalers — TensorDock $2.25 (8-GPU minimum), RunPod Community $2.69, Thunder Compute and Hyperstack $3.20 each, RunPod Secure and Lambda $3.99 each, Verda $5.14. Microsoft Azure lists it at $12.29 per GPU — but that is an 8-GPU VM at $98.32 an hour, a whole machine, not a card you can rent one of (see “What not to do”). Before you substitute anything, price the card itself across the board — the substitute decision only starts when the card is gone everywhere you would actually rent it. The B200 tells the same story. And one specialist: CoreWeave's GH200 ($6.50, 1-GPU instance, 96GB) pairs its GPU with an ARM processor on one fabric — powerful for work built for it, and a software-change risk for work that was not.

What not to do

The trapWhy it costs you
Do not compare a per-GPU rate with a whole-machine rate.Azure's H100 SXM at “$12.29/GPU/hr” is an 8-GPU VM at $98.32 an hour — you cannot rent one GPU at that rate, and the same applies to the per-GPU figures divided out of CoreWeave, Oracle OCI and Google Cloud nodes throughout this guide. We print the node total beside every such figure; any page that prints the division without the total is making the card look like something it is not.
Do not let an attachable-GPU rate stand alone.Google Cloud's A100 80GB rate ($4.52/GPU/hr) bills the host VM the GPU attaches to on top. The rate is real; the bill is bigger.
Do not treat a spot price as a substitute for an on-demand price.Spot and preemptible capacity is a different product — cheaper because it can be taken back mid-job. Every price in this guide is on-demand, because that is what a renter replacing a sold-out card is actually buying. A spot figure quoted beside an on-demand rate, with the difference unlabelled, is not a comparison.
Do not rent from a price nobody will stand behind.On Nov 12, 2026, Spheron's own pages stated the H100 SXM5 at $2.75, $3.96 and $4.19 in three places on the same day — and its machine-readable price file said $3.96 while its own pricing FAQ said $5.15. Spheron sells GPU rental itself, which is exactly why its stated prices for everyone else's cards need checking against the provider's own page before they are worth acting on. A stock alert that ends in an unverifiable price has told you a card is gone and left you nowhere priced to go.
Do not skip the small print that is not small.Minimums (TensorDock's H100 rate needs 8 GPUs), VAT (Nebius's rates exclude it), and “from” prices that vary by instance size all change the real bill more than most headline differences do.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. Everything in this box is GPUJournal's judgement on the verified record above it; the record itself is in the tables and the method note. We sell nothing and take no commission from any provider named here. Sold out is a routing problem, not a stopping problem. The renter who gets hurt is the one whose plan has a single card at a single provider in it: they pay the scramble price, or they wait. The fix costs nothing — know, before you need it, which card you would take instead and what it costs today. The honest shape of that plan, from the checked record: same card at a second provider first; one step up (H200, B300) when the job is deadline-shaped; one step down (PCIe, A100) when it is budget-shaped; and never a substitute chosen from a price that exists on only one aggregator's page. Prices will move — that is what our board and Price Watch are for — but the plan survives it, because it is a ranking, not a price list.
